name: Pathological Anatomy
description: Complete study manual · Part 1 · 11 practical class topics

topics.title: Introduction to pathology. The cell as the structural unit of health and disease. Cellular responses to injurious agents and stress

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the content, tasks, objects and research methods of pathological anatomy (autopsy, biopsy, experiment);
the history of pathological anatomy and the Uzbek school of pathologists;
the basic concepts of disease: etiology, pathogenesis, morphogenesis, pathomorphosis, complication, outcome;
the main structures of the cell and their significance in pathology;
the sequence of cellular responses to stress and injurious agents;
the types of cellular adaptation: hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia — definition, causes, mechanism, morphology and outcomes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: apply the scheme for describing gross specimens and microscopic slides;
identify and describe gross specimens of cardiac hypertrophy, urinary bladder hypertrophy, endometrial hyperplasia, brown atrophy of the liver and heart, hydronephrosis and hydrocephalus;
identify and describe microscopic slides of bronchial epithelial metaplasia, glandular hyperplasia of the endometrium and brown atrophy of the liver;
distinguish physiological from pathological adaptation, hypertrophy from hyperplasia, and atrophy from hypoplasia;
explain the clinical significance of adaptive processes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In pathological anatomy, changes are studied at **four levels**: **the organism and the organ** (gross), **the tissue and the cell** (microscopic — light microscope), **intracellular structures** (ultrastructural — electron microscope), and **molecules** (molecular pathology). For example, in sickle cell anemia the change begins at the molecular level: glutamic acid at position 6 of the hemoglobin beta chain is replaced by valine.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Etiology** answers the question “**why?**”, **pathogenesis** — “**by what mechanism?**”, and **morphogenesis** — “**through what structural changes?**”. A single etiologic agent can cause different diseases through different pathogenetic pathways (for example, streptococcus — tonsillitis, rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis), whereas different agents can cause the same morphologic change (for example, fatty liver — alcohol, obesity, diabetes, hypoxia).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Labile — Lining, Stable — liver, Permanent — Pump and brain”**: labile tissues border the external environment (skin, mucous membranes) and are constantly renewed; permanent tissues (heart, brain) cannot be restored once lost — which is why myocardial infarction and stroke heal with a scar.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the Uzbek curriculum title, the expression “ruhiy zo‘riqish” is a rendering of the English word **stress**. In pathology, **cellular stress** does not mean a psychological state but any excessive load or injurious influence on the cell (hypoxia, heat, toxin, hormonal signal, etc.). The cell responds by synthesizing “stress proteins” (heat shock proteins, chaperones) and by adaptive reactions.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Causes of cell injury — **“GAIN CHIP”**: **G**enetic, **A**ging, **I**mmune, **N**utritional, **C**hemical, **H**ypoxia, **I**nfection, **P**hysical.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In **hypertrophy** the cells **enlarge**; in **hyperplasia** the **number of cells increases**. In organs made of nondividing cells (heart, skeletal muscle), an increased load produces only **hypertrophy**. In cells capable of division (uterus, prostate, thyroid gland), hypertrophy and hyperplasia often occur **together**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The normal weight of the heart is about **250–350 g**, and the thickness of the left ventricular wall is **0.8–1.2 cm**. In severe hypertrophy the weight of the heart can increase **2–3 times or more**; a heart weighing over 1000 g is called a “**bovine heart**” (cor bovinum).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **True hypertrophy** must be distinguished from **false hypertrophy**. In false hypertrophy the organ enlarges not because of the parenchyma but because of the growth of fat, connective tissue or bone, while the parenchyma undergoes atrophy and function **declines** (for example, fatty infiltration of the heart, “pseudohypertrophy” of the calf muscles in Duchenne muscular dystrophy). Congenital enlargement of organs (gigantism) is not considered hypertrophy either.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Atrophy must be distinguished from **congenital malformations**: **agenesis** — the organ or its primordium is completely absent; **aplasia** — the organ remains rudimentary and lacks its typical structure; **hypoplasia** — the organ is small and underdeveloped from birth. Atrophy, in contrast, is the **subsequent** shrinkage of a **normally developed** organ.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In appearance, the surface of an atrophic organ is **smooth** (for example, in most atrophies of the liver and kidney) or **granular** (for example, the primary contracted kidney). Atrophy can be a **reversible** process: if the cause is removed early, the structure and function of the organ are restored. In severe atrophy (especially when sclerosis is added), reversal is not possible.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the direction of metaplasia: **“Bronchus goes Squamous, Barrett goes Glandular”**. The airways put on a **shield** (squamous epithelium) against smoke, while the esophagus, like the stomach and intestine, produces **glands** (mucus) against acid. Both pave the way to cancer: in the bronchus — squamous cell carcinoma, in the esophagus — adenocarcinoma.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Some textbooks (M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva) discuss dysplasia in the chapter on adaptive processes, whereas the Robbins textbook places it in the chapter on **tumors** (neoplasia). Indeed, dysplasia is **not an adaptation**: it is a **precancerous process**. Mild dysplasia can regress if the cause is removed, whereas severe dysplasia often progresses to invasive cancer. Dysplasia is discussed in detail in Topic 9.

sections.title: 1.1. Content and tasks of pathological anatomy

blocks.text: **Pathology** (Greek pathos — suffering, disease; logos — study) is the science that studies the causes and mechanisms of disease and the resulting structural and functional changes in cells, tissues and organs. **Pathological anatomy** is the anatomy of the diseased organism: it studies the material (structural) basis of disease and serves as a bridge between theoretical medicine and the clinic.
Pathological anatomy consists of two parts:

items: **General pathological anatomy** — the general pathological processes that occur in any disease: cell injury and death, degenerations, circulatory disorders, inflammation, immunopathological processes, regeneration, adaptation and tumors. This manual is devoted to this part.
**Systemic (special) pathological anatomy** — the morphology of individual diseases (nosological entities): atherosclerosis, pneumonia, hepatitis, glomerulonephritis and others.

blocks.text: **Tasks of pathological anatomy** (after M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva):

items: To study the morphologic changes that occur in organs, tissues, cells and intracellular structures in diseases and their complications.
To establish the causes and conditions of the development of disease — its **etiology**.
To study the mechanism of development of disease — its **pathogenesis**.
To establish the sequence in which structural changes appear during the disease — its **morphogenesis**.
To study the structural basis of protective, compensatory and adaptive processes.
To analyze changes in the picture of a disease under the influence of treatment or changing living conditions — **pathomorphosis**.

parts.text: In pathological anatomy, changes are studied at **four levels**: **the organism and the organ** (gross), **the tissue and the cell** (microscopic — light microscope), **intracellular structures** (ultrastructural — electron microscope), and **molecules** (molecular pathology). For example, in sickle cell anemia the change begins at the molecular level: glutamic acid at position 6 of the hemoglobin beta chain is replaced by valine.

blocks.text: Research methods of pathological anatomy

**1. Autopsy** (Greek autopsia — seeing with one's own eyes; synonyms: necropsy, postmortem examination, dissection of the body) — examination of the dead body by dissection to identify the structural changes caused by disease. The significance of autopsy:

items: comparison of the clinical and pathological diagnoses and detection of diagnostic and treatment errors (clinicopathological conferences);
determination of the cause of death and its thanatogenesis (mechanism of death);
study of new and rare diseases and of pathomorphosis;
timely detection of infectious diseases and prevention of epidemics;
collection of statistical data on the structure of morbidity and mortality;

medical education and continuing training of physicians. **2. Biopsy** (Greek bios — life, opsis — vision) — removal of a piece of tissue from a living patient and its microscopic examination for diagnostic purposes. Types of biopsy:

blocks.title: Table 1.1. Types of biopsy
head: Type
Method of obtaining the material
Example
rows: A piece is cut from the altered area
Skin; a piece from the edge of a breast tumor
The pathological focus is removed entirely
A core of tissue is taken with a special needle

blocks.text: Tasks of biopsy: to confirm or clarify the clinical diagnosis; to detect the early stage of a disease; to distinguish tumors from hyperplastic (inflammatory) processes; to establish the histologic type, grade and margins of a tumor (radicality of surgery); to assess the effect of treatment.
**3. Experiment** — artificial reproduction of a disease in animals to study its etiology, pathogenesis and morphogenesis step by step.

**Modern morphologic methods:** histochemistry (detection of substances with special stains — PAS reaction, Congo red, Sudan III), immunohistochemistry (detection of antigens in tissue with labeled antibodies — the main method in tumor diagnosis), electron microscopy (transmission and scanning), fluorescence microscopy, in situ hybridization (FISH), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and next-generation sequencing (molecular pathology).

parts.text: Today the pathologist is not a “doctor of the dead” but **a treating physician of the living patient**: biopsies and surgical specimens make up most of the work of pathology departments. A cancer diagnosis is not made without histologic examination, and chemotherapy or the extent of surgery is often chosen according to the pathologist's report (tumor type, grade, receptor status, presence or absence of tumor at the margins).

blocks.text: Brief history
**Three periods** are distinguished in the development of pathological anatomy:

items: **Anatomic (macroscopic) period** — until the middle of the 19th century. **Avicenna (Ibn Sina)** in “The Canon of Medicine” (1020) linked the signs of disease with changes in the organs. The Italian anatomist **G.B. Morgagni**, in his work “On the Seats and Causes of Diseases Investigated by Anatomy” (1761), compared the results of about 700 autopsies with clinical signs — he is regarded as **the founder of pathological anatomy**. M. Bichat (pathology of tissues) and K. Rokitansky (more than 30,000 autopsies, the humoral theory of pathology) were major figures of this period.

**Microscopic period** — from the middle of the 19th to the middle of the 20th century. The German pathologist **R. Virchow** (1821–1902) created the theory of **cellular pathology** in 1855–1858: “every cell from a cell” (omnis cellula e cellula), and disease is the result of injury to cells. Experimental pathology developed.

**Ultramicroscopic and molecular period** — from the middle of the 20th century to the present: electron microscopy, histochemistry, immunomorphology, molecular genetics. This period is a direct continuation of Virchow's cellular pathology. In Russia, the first department of pathological anatomy was opened in 1849 at Moscow University (A.I. Polunin). Major representatives of the Moscow school were A.I. Abrikosov, I.V. Davydovsky, A.I. Strukov, A.P. Avtsyn and V.V. Serov; of the St. Petersburg school — M.M. Rudnev and N.N. Anichkov.

blocks.text: **In Uzbekistan, pathological anatomy** took shape as an independent discipline in 1919 with the opening of the medical faculty at Turkestan State University. The first head of the department was Professor **V.V. Vasilevsky** (1920–1930). **The founder of the Uzbek school of pathologists** is Professor **G.N. Terekhov** (head of the department at Tashkent State Medical Institute in 1930–1966). Later the department was headed by Associate Professor P.J. Tulaganov and Professor **M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva** (1969–1990). Scientists of the department made a major contribution to the study of sprue (chillashir), visceral leishmaniasis, pellagra, brucellosis, ulcerative colitis, hemorrhagic fever and geographic pathology. Departments of pathological anatomy were opened in Samarkand in 1932 (S.F. Tatarenchik) and at the Central Asian Medical Pediatric Institute in 1972 (V.A. Alimov). Today regional pathology bureaus and the Republican Center of Pathological Anatomy operate in the country.

**Disease** is a disruption of normal life activity resulting from damage to the structures of the organism and impairment of its functions under the influence of external and internal injurious (pathogenic) factors. In the words of I.V. Davydovsky, disease is the organism's adaptation, of a particular form and degree, to its living conditions: along with damage, it also displays protective, compensatory and adaptive processes.

blocks.text: Three stages are distinguished in the development of a disease (D.S. Sarkisov): **1)** formation of the disease (predisease, latent period) — structural changes are balanced by compensatory reactions, and there are no clinical signs; **2)** the full-blown (clinical) period of the disease — compensation fails and signs appear; **3)** recovery or another outcome.

parts.text: **Etiology** answers the question “**why?**”, **pathogenesis** — “**by what mechanism?**”, and **morphogenesis** — “**through what structural changes?**”. A single etiologic agent can cause different diseases through different pathogenetic pathways (for example, streptococcus — tonsillitis, rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis), whereas different agents can cause the same morphologic change (for example, fatty liver — alcohol, obesity, diabetes, hypoxia).

blocks.text: **Etiologic factors** are divided into two groups: **genetic** (mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, hereditary predisposition) and **acquired** (infection, nutrition, chemical and physical factors). Most common diseases (atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes mellitus) are **multifactorial**, resulting from the combined effect of hereditary predisposition and the environment.

sections.title: 1.3. The cell as the structural unit of health and disease

blocks.text: According to Virchow's doctrine, the smallest living unit of the organism is the cell, and disease begins with injury to cells. The cell organelles work in connection with one another, and each of them can be a “target” in a particular pathological process.

sections.title: 1.4. Cellular responses to stress and injurious agents

blocks.text: A normal cell functions within a limited range of function and structure — in a state of **homeostasis**. Depending on the strength and duration of the load or injurious agent acting on it, the cell gives one of the following responses:

items: **Adaptation** — in response to physiological load or some pathological stimuli, the cell reaches a new steady state and preserves its viability: hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia.
**Reversible injury** — when the limits of adaptation are exceeded or the stimulus is mild, functional and morphologic changes appear in the cell, but the cell recovers if the agent is removed.

**Irreversible injury and cell death** — if the stimulus is strong or prolonged, the cell passes the “point of no return” and dies by **necrosis** or **apoptosis** (Topic 2). In addition, chronic mild stimuli lead to intracellular **accumulation** of various substances (degenerations — Topics 3 and 4), **pathologic calcification** and **cellular aging**.

In pathology, **cellular stress** does not mean a psychological state but any excessive load or injurious influence on the cell (hypoxia, heat, toxin, hormonal signal, etc.). blocks.text: Causes of cell injury

items: **Oxygen deprivation (hypoxia)** is the most common cause. **Ischemia** (reduced arterial blood flow) is the most dangerous form of hypoxia: it stops not only the delivery of oxygen but also the delivery of nutrients and the removal of metabolites. Other causes of hypoxia are respiratory failure, anemia and carbon monoxide poisoning.
**Physical agents** — mechanical trauma, extremes of temperature, sudden changes in atmospheric pressure, ionizing radiation, electric current.

**Chemical agents and drugs** — poisons (arsenic, cyanide, mercury salts), alcohol, narcotic drugs, air pollutants, even high concentrations of physiological substances (glucose, table salt, oxygen), and toxic effects of drugs.
**Infectious agents** — prions, viruses, rickettsiae, bacteria, fungi, parasites.
**Immunologic reactions** — autoimmune diseases, allergic reactions, excessive inflammation against microbes.
**Genetic derangements** — congenital malformations (Down syndrome), enzyme deficiencies (storage diseases), misfolded proteins.
**Nutritional imbalances** — protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies and, conversely, overnutrition (obesity, atherosclerosis).
**Aging** — decline of the replicative and reparative capacity of the cell.

parts.text: Causes of cell injury — **“GAIN CHIP”**: **G**enetic, **A**ging, **I**mmune, **N**utritional, **C**hemical, **H**ypoxia, **I**nfection, **P**hysical.

blocks.text: **Hypertrophy** (Greek hyper — excess, trophe — nourishment) is an increase in the size of a tissue or organ due to **enlargement of its cells**. No new cells appear in a hypertrophied organ; the existing ones enlarge. Cell enlargement is due to increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles (myofibrils, mitochondria).

parts.text: In **hypertrophy** the cells **enlarge**; in **hyperplasia** the **number of cells increases**. In organs made of nondividing cells (heart, skeletal muscle), an increased load produces only **hypertrophy**. In cells capable of division (uterus, prostate, thyroid gland), hypertrophy and hyperplasia often occur **together**.

blocks.text: **Mechanism.** Mechanical stretch (load), agonists (alpha-adrenergic agonists, angiotensin) and growth factors (IGF-1) act on membrane receptors and activate intracellular signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT, G protein–coupled receptors). As a result, transcription factors (GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) activate the genes of structural proteins. In hypertrophied cardiomyocytes, the synthesis of **fetal-type** proteins (for example, the beta isoform of the myosin heavy chain, natriuretic peptide) resumes.
Types of hypertrophy

blocks.text: Three stages are distinguished in the morphogenesis of **compensatory hypertrophy of the heart** (F.Z. Meerson):

items: **Emergency (injury) stage** — the load increases suddenly, the myocardium works under strain, and dystrophic changes and energy deficiency appear in cardiomyocytes.

**Compensation (stable hyperfunction) stage** — the number of myofibrils and mitochondria increases and the cells enlarge; the heart wall thickens, while its cavity narrows or stays unchanged — **concentric hypertrophy**. Function is adequately preserved.

**Decompensation (exhaustion) stage** — the capillaries can no longer supply the enlarged cells with enough blood; hypoxia, degeneration, death of cardiomyocytes and sclerosis develop. The cardiac cavities dilate (**myogenic dilatation**) — **eccentric hypertrophy**; heart failure begins.

parts.text: The normal weight of the heart is about **250–350 g**, and the thickness of the left ventricular wall is **0.8–1.2 cm**. In severe hypertrophy the weight of the heart can increase **2–3 times or more**; a heart weighing over 1000 g is called a “**bovine heart**” (cor bovinum).

parts.text: **True hypertrophy** must be distinguished from **false hypertrophy**. In false hypertrophy the organ enlarges not because of the parenchyma but because of the growth of fat, connective tissue or bone, while the parenchyma undergoes atrophy and function **declines** (for example, fatty infiltration of the heart, “pseudohypertrophy” of the calf muscles in Duchenne muscular dystrophy). Congenital enlargement of organs (gigantism) is not considered hypertrophy either.

blocks.text: **Hyperplasia** (Greek plasis — formation) is an **increase in the number of cells** in a tissue or organ. It occurs only in tissues made of cells capable of division. Hyperplasia develops through growth factor–driven proliferation of mature cells and, sometimes, through the formation of new cells from tissue stem cells.
Physiological hyperplasia:

items: **hormonal** — the glandular epithelium of the breast at puberty and in pregnancy, the uterus in pregnancy;

**compensatory** — after removal of part of the liver (for example, in living-donor transplantation), the remaining part grows back to its original size. The daily regeneration of Prometheus's liver in Greek myth is cited as an allusion to this phenomenon.

blocks.text: **Pathologic hyperplasia** is most often the result of excessive action of hormones or growth factors:

items: **glandular hyperplasia of the endometrium** — when the balance between estrogen and progesterone is disturbed and estrogen predominates; clinically it manifests as acyclic uterine bleeding;
**benign prostatic hyperplasia** — under the influence of androgens (dihydrotestosterone);
**hyperplasia of the thyroid gland** — in Graves disease (stimulating antibodies to TSH receptors);
hyperplasia of fibroblasts and blood vessels in **wound healing** (under the influence of growth factors);
**viral hyperplasia** — warts and mucosal papillomas caused by papillomaviruses.

parts.text: Pathologic hyperplasia is a **controlled** process: it stops when the hormonal or other stimulus disappears. This is its main difference from a tumor. However, because there is much cell division in the area of hyperplasia, the likelihood of mutations increases, so it can become **fertile soil for tumor development**. Women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia have a much higher risk of endometrial cancer; hyperplasias caused by papillomaviruses are also associated with cancer. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, however, is not considered a precancerous condition.

blocks.text: **Atrophy** (Greek a — negation, trophe — nourishment) is a reduction in the size of cells, tissues and organs **during life**, with weakening or cessation of their function. Atrophic cells have fewer structural proteins, mitochondria, myofilaments and less ER; the cell is smaller but alive. Atrophy can also be accompanied by a decrease in the number of cells.

**Mechanism:** decreased protein synthesis and increased protein degradation. Degradation occurs mainly through the **ubiquitin–proteasome system**: in nutrient deficiency and disuse, cellular proteins are “tagged” with ubiquitin and degraded in proteasomes. Atrophy is often accompanied by increased **autophagy** (“self-eating”): the cell digests its own organelles in autophagic vacuoles to obtain energy for survival. Undigested residues accumulate as the pigment **lipofuscin** — the organ becomes **brown** (**brown atrophy**).

parts.text: Atrophy must be distinguished from **congenital malformations**: **agenesis** — the organ or its primordium is completely absent; **aplasia** — the organ remains rudimentary and lacks its typical structure; **hypoplasia** — the organ is small and underdeveloped from birth. Atrophy, in contrast, is the **subsequent** shrinkage of a **normally developed** organ.

blocks.text: Types of atrophy

**Physiological atrophy** occurs throughout life: obliteration of the umbilical arteries and the ductus arteriosus (Botallo's duct), involution of the thymus after puberty, and atrophy of the gonads, skin, bones (osteoporosis) and brain in old age (senile atrophy).
**Pathologic atrophy** occurs at any age and can be reversible or irreversible. By extent, it is **generalized** or **local**.
**Generalized atrophy — cachexia** (exhaustion, wasting). Its types:

items: **Alimentary** — starvation, impaired absorption of nutrients. In starvation the fat depots (subcutaneous tissue, omentum) atrophy first, then the skeletal muscles and internal organs (liver, heart), and the brain last of all — which is why a person dying of starvation remains conscious until the final moments.
**Cancer cachexia** — especially in tumors of the digestive tract; caused by tumor intoxication and cytokines (tumor necrosis factor — TNF).
**Dyshormonal** — pituitary insufficiency (Simmonds disease — pituitary cachexia), myxedema.
**Cerebral** — damage to the hypothalamus (tumor, inflammation).

In **chronic infections** (tuberculosis, brucellosis, chronic dysentery) and other severe chronic diseases. In cachexia the subcutaneous fat layer almost disappears, and the remaining adipose tissue becomes orange-brown due to the accumulation of **lipochrome**; the fat of the epicardium and bone marrow is soaked with serous fluid and becomes mucoid (**serous atrophy of adipose tissue**); the heart and liver become small and brown (**brown atrophy**).

Atrophy can be a **reversible** process: if the cause is removed early, the structure and function of the organ are restored. In severe atrophy (especially when sclerosis is added), reversal is not possible.

blocks.text: **Metaplasia** (Greek metaplasso — I form differently) is the **replacement of one type of mature (differentiated) cell by another type of mature cell**. It is a reversible process that represents adaptation by replacing a cell with one better able to withstand adverse conditions.

**Mechanism.** A mature cell does not directly turn into another type. Metaplasia results from the **reprogramming of the stem (cambial) cells** of the tissue: under the influence of cytokines, growth factors and extracellular matrix components, stem cells differentiate along a different pathway. Certain transcription factors and retinoic acid (vitamin A) play an important role in this process. Metaplasia occurs **only within one tissue type**: epithelium turns into epithelium, and connective tissue into another type of connective tissue.

blocks.title: Table 1.8. Main types of metaplasia
head: Type
Normal epithelium → new epithelium
Cause and site
rows: Bronchi of smokers (most common); endocervical epithelium of the cervix (transformation zone); vitamin A deficiency; stones in the biliary and urinary tracts
Stratified squamous → glandular columnar (with goblet cells)
Barrett esophagus — in the lower esophagus in gastroesophageal reflux
Myositis ossificans — bone formation in muscle after trauma; ossification in old scars and atherosclerotic plaques

parts.text: Although metaplasia is an **adaptation**, it comes at a price: the squamous epithelium in a smoker's bronchus is resistant, but it **does not secrete mucus and has no cilia** — mucociliary clearance is impaired and infections become more frequent. Most importantly, if the stimulus that caused metaplasia persists, **dysplasia and cancer** develop: squamous metaplasia in the bronchus is the soil for **squamous cell lung carcinoma**, Barrett esophagus for **esophageal adenocarcinoma**, and intestinal metaplasia for **gastric adenocarcinoma**. Therefore metaplasia is considered a **precancerous (background) process**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.14
blocks.caption: Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium (microscopic slide, hematoxylin and eosin): left — normal pseudostratified ciliated epithelium, right — stratified squamous epithelium; inflammatory infiltrate in the wall (TMA study guide, 2018)

parts.text: To remember the direction of metaplasia: **“Bronchus goes Squamous, Barrett goes Glandular”**. The airways put on a **shield** (squamous epithelium) against smoke, while the esophagus, like the stomach and intestine, produces **glands** (mucus) against acid. Both pave the way to cancer: in the bronchus — squamous cell carcinoma, in the esophagus — adenocarcinoma.

blocks.text: **Dysplasia** (Greek dys — disorder, plasis — formation) is a disturbance of the proliferation and differentiation of epithelial cells, manifested by cellular atypia and disruption of tissue structure (histoarchitecture).
Signs of dysplasia:

items: variation in the shape and size of cells and nuclei (**pleomorphism**);
enlargement and hyperchromasia of nuclei, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio;
increased number of mitoses, which also occur in the upper layers of the epithelium;

loss of cell polarity and of layering. By grade, dysplasia is **mild (I), moderate (II) and severe (III)**. Current classifications often use two grades: **low-grade** and **high-grade** intraepithelial neoplasia. When severe dysplasia involves the full thickness of the epithelium but does not cross the basement membrane, it is called **carcinoma in situ**.

parts.text: Some textbooks (M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva) discuss dysplasia in the chapter on adaptive processes, whereas the Robbins textbook places it in the chapter on **tumors** (neoplasia). Indeed, dysplasia is **not an adaptation**: it is a **precancerous process**. Mild dysplasia can regress if the cause is removed, whereas severe dysplasia often progresses to invasive cancer. Dysplasia is discussed in detail in Topic 9.

blocks.text: Adaptation — when is it beneficial and when harmful?
Adaptive processes allow the organism to survive under new conditions, but each of them turns into disease beyond a certain limit:

items: **Hypertrophy.** In a patient with arterial hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy preserves cardiac function for years. However, the capillaries cannot adequately supply the thickened myocardium — the risk of decompensation, arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death increases. Left ventricular hypertrophy detected by ECG and echocardiography is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular complications.

**Hyperplasia.** In an elderly man with prostatic hyperplasia, urination becomes difficult, the bladder wall undergoes compensatory hypertrophy (trabeculated bladder), and then diverticula, urinary retention, cystitis and hydronephrosis develop.
**Atrophy.** A patient confined to bed for a long time develops muscle atrophy and osteoporosis; therefore early mobilization and rehabilitation are necessary.

**Metaplasia.** If squamous metaplasia is found in a bronchial biopsy of a long-term smoker, this is a strong argument for quitting: if smoking stops, the metaplasia can regress; if it continues, dysplasia and cancer develop.

blocks.text: Thanatogenesis and determination of the cause of death

At autopsy, the pathologist lists the diseases that led to death in the following order: **underlying disease** (the nosological entity that caused death directly or through its complications), **complications of the underlying disease**, **concomitant diseases** and **cause of death**. The clinical and pathological diagnoses are compared (the diagnoses agree or disagree), and the reasons for disagreement are discussed at a clinicopathological conference.

parts.text: At the autopsy of a 62-year-old patient with essential hypertension: heart weight 520 g, left ventricular wall 2.2 cm, a fresh infarct focus in the anterior wall of the left ventricle. Structure of the pathological diagnosis: **underlying disease** — myocardial infarction; **background disease** — essential hypertension (concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle); **complication** — acute heart failure. Here left ventricular hypertrophy is recorded as the **result** of adaptation that has passed into decompensation.

items: **Agenesis** — complete absence of an organ or its primordium as a result of disturbed ontogenesis.
**Aplasia** — persistence of an organ only as an early primordium, without its typical structure.
**Atrophy** (Greek a — negation, trophe — nourishment) — reduction in the size of cells, tissues and organs during life, with weakening of their function.
**Heterotopia** — presence or displacement of tissue in a site that is not typical for it.
**Hypertrophy** (Greek hyper — over, excess, trophe — nourishment) — increase in the size of a cell, tissue or organ.
**Hypoplasia** — incomplete (subnormal) development of an organ.
**Dysontogenesis** (disontogenesis) — disturbance of ontogenesis (individual development).
**Dysplasia** — a marked disturbance of epithelial proliferation and differentiation, with cellular atypia and disruption of histoarchitecture.
**Metaplasia** (Greek metaplasso — I form differently) — transformation of one type of tissue into another, related type of tissue.

skills.title: Algorithm for describing a gross specimen

items: Identify which organ the specimen is (the organ or part of it).
**Size** (dimensions, weight) — enlarged, reduced, normal.
**Shape** — preserved or altered.
State of the **capsule (serous membrane)** — smooth, shiny, dull, thickened, wrinkled.
**Consistency** — soft, firm, hard (the description is based on the figure and explanations).
**Color of the surface and cut surface**, and whether the structure on the cut surface (pattern, lobules) is preserved.
If there is a pathological focus — its location, number, shape, size, color and borders.
Conclusion: name of the pathological process.

skills.title: Algorithm for describing a microscopic slide

items: Identify the staining method (hematoxylin and eosin, van Gieson, Sudan III, Congo red, etc.).
At low magnification, identify the organ and its part.
Where the normal structures are preserved and where they are altered.
At high magnification, describe the changes in cells, nuclei, cytoplasm and intercellular substance.
State of the blood vessels and stroma; presence or absence of an inflammatory infiltrate.
Conclusion: name of the pathological process.

**“Cardiac hypertrophy (myocardial hypertrophy)”.** The heart is enlarged and its weight increased; the left ventricular wall is 2 cm or thicker (normally 0.8–1.2 cm), and the trabecular and papillary muscles are thickened. In the compensation stage the cavity is narrowed (concentric hypertrophy); in decompensation the heart is flabby, the apex is rounded and the cavity is dilated (eccentric hypertrophy, myogenic dilatation). Conclusion: compensatory (work) hypertrophy.

**“Bladder hypertrophy, prostatic hyperplasia”.** The prostate is enlarged and nodular; the bladder wall is thickened, and muscle bundles bulge beneath the mucosa in a network pattern (trabeculated bladder), sometimes with false diverticula. Conclusion: compensatory hypertrophy of the bladder wall.
**“Glandular hyperplasia of the endometrium”.** The uterus is enlarged; in its cavity the endometrium is unevenly thickened, with polypoid growths. Conclusion: hormonal (hyperestrogenic) hyperplasia.

**“Brown atrophy of the liver”.** The liver is small, with a sharp edge, a wrinkled capsule, firm, and brown on the cut surface. Conclusion: a manifestation of generalized atrophy (cachexia) — brown atrophy.

**“Brown atrophy of the heart”.** The heart is small, there is little subepicardial fat, the coronary arteries are tortuous, and the myocardium is brown. Conclusion: brown atrophy (accumulation of lipofuscin).

**“Hydronephrosis”.** The kidney is enlarged; the pelvis and calyces are dilated, forming cavities; the parenchyma is thinned, and the cortex and medulla are indistinguishable. Conclusion: pressure atrophy.
**“Internal hydrocephalus”.** The ventricles of the brain are markedly dilated, and the brain tissue is thinned. Conclusion: pressure atrophy.

**“Scar after myocardial infarction”.** Whitish, dense scar tissue in the left ventricular wall; the surrounding myocardium is thickened. Conclusion: regenerative hypertrophy (the myocardium around the scar).

blocks.label: Figure 1.15
blocks.caption: Scar after myocardial infarction (1): a wide, dense, whitish scar in the left ventricular wall; the remaining myocardium shows regenerative hypertrophy (TMA study guide, 2018)

items: **“Metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Normal pseudostratified ciliated epithelium in one part of the bronchial mucosa, stratified squamous epithelium in another; lymphocytic infiltration in the wall. Conclusion: squamous metaplasia — a precancerous background process.

**“Glandular hyperplasia of the endometrium”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The mucosa is thickened; the glands are numerous, elongated and convoluted, some cystically dilated, with a “gland within a gland” appearance; the epithelium is proliferating and the stroma is cellular. Conclusion: glandular (glandular-cystic) hyperplasia.

**“Brown atrophy of the liver”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Hepatocytes and nuclei are small, the liver cell plates are thin, and the sinusoids between them are dilated; fine yellowish-brown lipofuscin granules are seen in the hepatocytes of the lobule center. Conclusion: brown atrophy.
**“Myocardial hypertrophy”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Cardiomyocytes are thickened, and their nuclei are enlarged, hyperchromatic and “rectangular” (box-shaped). Conclusion: compensatory hypertrophy.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man had suffered from arterial hypertension for 15 years and was not treated regularly. In the last year he became short of breath when climbing stairs, and edema appeared in his legs. He died of chronic heart failure. At autopsy: heart weight 610 g, left ventricular wall 2.4 cm, the cavities are dilated, the apex of the heart is rounded, and the myocardium is flabby.
cases.ask: 1) What process was observed in the heart? 2) What is its type and stage? 3) State the mechanism and microscopic signs of hypertrophy.
cases.answer: 1) Hypertrophy of the heart (mainly of the left ventricle). 2) Compensatory (work) hypertrophy caused by arterial hypertension (increased peripheral resistance). Dilatation of the cavities, rounding of the apex and heart failure indicate the decompensation stage (eccentric hypertrophy, myogenic dilatation). 3) Mechanical stretch and hormonal factors (angiotensin II, adrenergic agonists) activate signaling pathways and increase the synthesis of structural proteins and organelles; cardiomyocytes do not divide, they only enlarge. Microscopically, the cardiomyocytes are thickened, with large, hyperchromatic, box-shaped nuclei; in decompensation — degeneration, death of cardiomyocytes and interstitial sclerosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 72-year-old woman was treated for a long time for gastric cancer and died. At autopsy the subcutaneous fat layer is almost absent, and the remaining adipose tissue is orange. The heart weighs 180 g and is small, the subepicardial coronary arteries are tortuous, and the myocardium is brown. The liver weighs 950 g, its capsule is wrinkled, and the cut surface is brown.
cases.ask: 1) What generalized process was observed? 2) What are the changes in the heart and liver called? 3) What causes the brown color of the organs and the orange color of the adipose tissue?
cases.answer: 1) Cachexia — generalized atrophy, in this case cancer cachexia (tumor intoxication, TNF and other cytokines, impaired absorption of nutrients). 2) Brown atrophy of the heart and liver. 3) The brown color is due to the accumulation of lipofuscin pigment, formed from undigested residues of autophagy in atrophic cells. The orange color of the adipose tissue is due to the increased concentration of lipochrome pigment.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old man has smoked a pack of cigarettes a day for 25 years. Because of chronic bronchitis, bronchoscopy was performed and a biopsy was taken from the bronchial mucosa. Histologic examination: one part of the bronchus is lined by pseudostratified ciliated epithelium and another part by stratified squamous epithelium; there is no cellular atypia.
cases.ask: 1) Formulate the histologic conclusion. 2) Explain the mechanism of this process. 3) What are its clinical significance and prognosis?
cases.answer: 1) Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium without atypia. 2) Under the influence of tobacco smoke, the stem (basal) cells of the bronchial epithelium are reprogrammed and differentiate into the more resistant stratified squamous epithelium instead of ciliated epithelium. 3) In metaplasia, mucus secretion and ciliary function are lost — mucociliary clearance is impaired, and bronchitis and infections become more frequent. Metaplasia is a precancerous background process: if smoking continues, dysplasia and squamous cell lung carcinoma may develop. If smoking stops, the metaplasia can regress, so the patient is strongly advised to quit smoking.
