topics.title: Reversible and irreversible cell injury and cell death: causes, mechanisms and morphology. Apoptosis. Necrosis

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the general laws of cell injury and the difference between reversible and irreversible injury;
the main biochemical mechanisms of cell injury: ATP depletion, mitochondrial damage, calcium influx, free radicals, membrane and DNA damage;
the features of ischemic, ischemia–reperfusion and toxic injury;
the morphologic signs of reversible injury (cellular swelling, fatty change);
the definition, stages, microscopic signs, etiologic and clinicomorphologic types and outcomes of necrosis;
the definition, causes, mechanisms and morphology of apoptosis and how it differs from necrosis;
the concept of other pathways of cell death (necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis) and of autophagy;
death of the organism and postmortem changes.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the signs of necrosis in a microscopic slide (changes in the nucleus and cytoplasm);

describe gross specimens of ischemic infarction of the spleen, hemorrhagic infarction of the lung, gangrene of the leg, gangrenous appendicitis, caseous necrosis of a lymph node and of the kidney, and calcified foci (petrifications) in the lung;
describe microscopic slides of necrosis of the renal tubular epithelium, caseous necrosis and Councilman bodies;
distinguish necrosis from apoptosis and relate the types of necrosis to clinical situations.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Reversible injury** — if the injurious agent is removed, the cell returns to normal. Its two main morphologic signs are **cellular swelling** and **fatty change**. The signs of **irreversible injury** are **severe mitochondrial dysfunction** (complete loss of the ability to produce ATP, amorphous densities in the matrix) and **profound disruption** of **membranes** (plasma and lysosomal membranes). These two phenomena are the cell's “point of no return”.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Enzymes that protect against free radicals — **“CSG”**: **C**atalase, **S**uperoxide dismutase, **G**lutathione peroxidase. Remember the formation of the hydroxyl radical (^•^OH) as “**iron + peroxide = Fenton**”: this is why liver and heart cells are injured in hemochromatosis (iron overload).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Necrosis is always a **pathologic** process: it involves **a group of cells**, membrane integrity is lost, intracellular contents leak out and **provoke inflammation**. Apoptosis, in contrast, is often **physiological**, occurs in individual cells, the membrane is preserved and it **does not provoke** inflammation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Order of nuclear changes — **“Pyk-Rhex-Lys”**: **Pyk**nosis (shrinks) → karyo**rrhex**is (fragments) → karyo**lys**is (dissolves). Likewise for the cytoplasm: **coagulation → rhexis → lysis**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: To remember the caspases of apoptosis: **“Intrinsic — 9, Extrinsic — 8, Executioners — 3 and 6”**. Imagine the intrinsic pathway as a **“mitochondrial gate”**: BCL2 is the gatekeeper (keeps it closed), BAX/BAK are the gate breakers, and cytochrome c is the “messenger of death” that comes out through the gate.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The textbooks of Strukov and Abdullakhodjaeva discuss two main types of cell death — necrosis and apoptosis. Recent editions of Robbins add **necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis** to them. When “types of cell death” are asked at the exam, it is advisable first to describe necrosis and apoptosis fully and then briefly mention the modern types.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: At autopsy it is important to distinguish a **postmortem blood clot** from a **thrombus** formed during life: a thrombus is **dull, dry, friable, layered** and **attached** to the vessel wall; a postmortem clot is **smooth, shiny, elastic**, not attached to the wall, follows the shape of the vessel and separates into layers resembling “chicken fat” (yellow, plasma part) and “currant jelly” (red, red cell part) (Topic 7).

blocks.text: When an injurious agent acting on a cell exceeds its adaptive capacity, **cell injury** begins. Its outcome is determined by four factors:

items: **The type, duration and severity of the injurious agent.** A small dose of toxin or brief ischemia causes reversible injury; a large dose or prolonged ischemia leads to cell death.
**The type, state and adaptability of the cell.** Skeletal muscle tolerates complete ischemia for 2–3 hours, a cardiomyocyte for 20–30 minutes, and a neuron for only 3–5 minutes.
**The genetic features of the cell.** For example, polymorphism of cytochrome P-450 enzymes determines different responses to the same drug dose in different people.
**Several interdependent systems of the cell are injured at the same time:** membranes, aerobic respiration (ATP production), protein synthesis, the cytoskeleton and the genetic apparatus.

parts.text: **Reversible injury** — if the injurious agent is removed, the cell returns to normal. Its two main morphologic signs are **cellular swelling** and **fatty change**. The signs of **irreversible injury** are **severe mitochondrial dysfunction** (complete loss of the ability to produce ATP, amorphous densities in the matrix) and **profound disruption** of **membranes** (plasma and lysosomal membranes). These two phenomena are the cell's “point of no return”.

blocks.text: Biochemical changes in the cell appear **before** morphologic changes: function is impaired within a few minutes, ultrastructural changes appear after several tens of minutes, changes visible by light microscopy after hours, and gross changes much later. For example, in myocardial ischemia a cardiomyocyte is irreversibly injured in 20–60 minutes, the light-microscopic signs of necrosis are detected after 4–12 hours, and the gross signs after 12–24 hours.

parts.text: This is why a patient who died suddenly may have no gross or even microscopic signs of myocardial infarction. In such cases the pathologist uses histochemical methods: **loss of glycogen** in injured cardiomyocytes (PAS reaction) and failure to stain with **triphenyltetrazolium chloride** (loss of dehydrogenase activity) are the earliest signs of ischemia. Clinically, **troponins** and creatine kinase-MB, which are released into the blood when the cardiomyocyte membrane is disrupted, are the main markers of myocardial necrosis.

blocks.text: ATP depletion

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is produced mainly in mitochondria by oxidative phosphorylation. **Hypoxia and ischemia** and mitochondrial poisons (cyanide) rapidly deplete ATP stores. A fall in ATP to 5–10% leads to the following consequences:

items: the **Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase** (sodium pump) slows down — Na^+^ and water enter the cell and K^+^ leaves: **cellular swelling**, dilatation of the ER;
**anaerobic glycolysis** increases — glycogen stores are exhausted, lactic acid accumulates and the **pH falls**: nuclear chromatin clumps (condensation) and enzyme activity changes;
the **Ca^2+^ pump** fails — calcium increases in the cytoplasm;
**ribosomes** detach from the rough ER and polysomes break down — **protein synthesis decreases**;
misfolded proteins accumulate and trigger “ER stress” (the unfolded protein response) and apoptosis.

blocks.text: Mitochondrial damage

Mitochondria are damaged by increased cytosolic Ca^2+^, free radicals and hypoxia. A high-conductance channel opens in the inner membrane — the **mitochondrial permeability transition pore** — the membrane potential is lost and oxidative phosphorylation stops. In addition, **cytochrome c** and other proteins leak from the intermembrane space into the cytoplasm and initiate apoptosis. Thus mitochondrial damage leads the cell to death by one of two pathways: ATP exhaustion — **necrosis**, release of cytochrome c — **apoptosis**.
Disturbance of calcium homeostasis

Normally the concentration of free cytosolic Ca^2+^ is 10,000 times lower than outside the cell. Under the influence of ischemia and toxins, Ca^2+^ enters the cytoplasm from outside the cell and from intracellular stores (mitochondria, ER). Excess Ca^2+^ activates the following enzymes:

items: **phospholipases** — degrade membranes;
**proteases** — degrade membrane and cytoskeletal proteins;
**endonucleases** — degrade DNA and chromatin;
**ATPases** — accelerate ATP depletion. In addition, Ca^2+^ opens the mitochondrial permeability pore and initiates apoptosis.

blocks.text: Free radicals (oxidative stress)

**Free radicals** are highly reactive molecules that have an unpaired electron in their outer orbit. The most important in cell injury are **reactive oxygen species (ROS)**: the superoxide anion (O~2~^−^), hydrogen peroxide (H~2~O~2~) and the most reactive — the hydroxyl radical (^•^OH).
Sources of free radicals:

items: normal metabolism — incomplete reduction of oxygen in mitochondria;
ionizing radiation (hydrolyzes water to form ^•^OH);
the “respiratory burst” of neutrophils and macrophages in inflammation (NADPH oxidase);
metabolism of drugs and chemicals (CCl~4~, paracetamol (acetaminophen));
transition metals — iron and copper (Fenton reaction: Fe^2+^ + H~2~O~2~ → Fe^3+^ + ^•^OH + OH^−^);
nitric oxide (NO) — forms peroxynitrite.

blocks.text: Harmful effects of free radicals:

items: **Lipid peroxidation in membranes** — a chain reaction with unsaturated fatty acids.
**Oxidation of proteins** — protein folding is disrupted, enzyme activity is lost and degradation in proteasomes increases.

**DNA damage** — single-strand breaks, mutations; contributes to cellular aging and malignant transformation. **The antioxidant defense system:** antioxidant vitamins (vitamins E, A, C, beta-carotene, glutathione), iron- and copper-binding proteins (transferrin, ferritin, lactoferrin, ceruloplasmin) and enzymes — **catalase** (breaks down H~2~O~2~), **superoxide dismutase** (converts O~2~^−^ to H~2~O~2~), **glutathione peroxidase**.

parts.text: Enzymes that protect against free radicals — **“CSG”**: **C**atalase, **S**uperoxide dismutase, **G**lutathione peroxidase. Remember the formation of the hydroxyl radical (^•^OH) as “**iron + peroxide = Fenton**”: this is why liver and heart cells are injured in hemochromatosis (iron overload).

blocks.text: Membrane damage and DNA damage

Membrane damage is the final stage in most types of injury. Its causes are ROS (lipid peroxidation), decreased phospholipid synthesis, activation of phospholipases and cytoskeletal disruption. As a result:

items: damage to the **mitochondrial membrane** — ATP production stops and apoptotic factors are released;
damage to the **plasma membrane** — osmotic balance is lost and intracellular contents leak out;

damage to the **lysosomal membrane** — enzymes (RNase, DNase, proteases, phosphatases) are released into the cytoplasm and cause the cell to **“digest itself”** — this is the basis of the morphology of necrosis. **DNA damage** (by radiation, chemotherapy drugs, ROS) activates the **p53** protein: it arrests the cell cycle in the G~1~ phase and gives time for DNA repair. If the damage cannot be repaired, p53 initiates **apoptosis**.

blocks.text: Ischemic and hypoxic injury

In **hypoxia** (reduced oxygen with preserved blood flow), glycolysis continues and injury develops more slowly. In **ischemia** (cessation of blood flow), glycolytic substrates are not delivered either and metabolites (lactic acid) are not removed — therefore injury is faster and more severe.
**Ischemia–reperfusion injury.** Sometimes, when blood flow is restored to ischemic but still viable tissue (thrombolysis, stenting, surgery), injury paradoxically **increases**. The causes:

items: in the presence of returning oxygen, large amounts of **free radicals** are generated in damaged mitochondria and leukocytes;
**Ca^2+^ overload** increases;
**inflammation** — leukocytes and plasma proteins enter the injured area and cause additional injury;
the **complement** system is activated (IgM antibodies are deposited in ischemic tissue).

blocks.text: Chemical (toxic) injury
Chemicals injure the cell in two ways:

items: **Direct action** — by binding to molecular components: mercuric chloride binds to the sulfhydryl groups of membrane proteins; cyanide blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase; chemotherapy drugs are directly cytotoxic.

**Conversion to toxic metabolites** — mainly by the **cytochrome P-450** enzymes of the smooth ER of the liver. For example, **carbon tetrachloride (CCl~4~)** is converted in the liver to the highly reactive free radical CCl~3~: lipids undergo peroxidation, the ER swells, protein synthesis (including lipoproteins) decreases, fat accumulates in hepatocytes and necrosis develops. In large doses, the toxic metabolite of **paracetamol** (acetaminophen) depletes glutathione stores and causes centrilobular necrosis of the liver.

parts.text: **N-acetylcysteine** is used as an antidote in paracetamol poisoning — it restores glutathione stores. In people who consume alcohol, cytochrome P-450 enzymes are induced and glutathione is low, so even an ordinary dose of paracetamol can damage their liver.

blocks.text: Reversible injury has two main morphologic manifestations:
**1. Cellular swelling** (hydropic change, vacuolar degeneration) — entry of water into the cell as a result of failure of the ion pumps. It is the **first** sign of almost all forms of injury.

items: Grossly: the organ is slightly enlarged and heavier, its color is pale, and the cut surface is dull and looks “boiled” (in older literature — “cloudy swelling”, granular degeneration).

Microscopically: the cells are enlarged, with small clear vacuoles in the cytoplasm (distended segments of the ER) — **vacuolar (hydropic) degeneration**. This condition is discussed in detail in Topic 3. **2. Fatty change (fatty degeneration)** — small and large lipid vacuoles in the cytoplasm. It is seen most often in cells involved in lipid metabolism — hepatocytes and cardiomyocytes (Topic 3).

blocks.text: Ultrastructural changes of reversible injury:

items: changes in the **plasma membrane** — formation of blebs (blebbing), loss of microvilli, loosening of intercellular attachments.
changes in **mitochondria** — swelling, appearance of small amorphous densities.
**dilatation of the ER**, detachment of ribosomes and breakdown of polysomes.
changes in the **nucleus** — clumping of chromatin granules.
**myelin figures** in the cytoplasm — layered phospholipid structures derived from damaged membranes.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Reversible and irreversible injury of the renal tubular epithelium: A — normal tubules, epithelial cells viable; B — early (reversible) ischemic injury: blebs on the cell surface, increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia, some cells swollen; C — necrosis (irreversible injury): nuclei lost, cells fragmented, contents leaked out (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-9)

blocks.text: **Necrosis** (Greek nekros — dead) is the death of cells, tissue or part of an organ **in a living organism**, with complete cessation of their vital activity. Necrosis is the end result of irreversible injury and develops as a result of **denaturation** of cellular components and **enzymatic digestion** of the dead cell. The enzymes that digest the cell come from the lysosomes of the dead cell itself (**autolysis**) and from leukocytes attracted by inflammation (**heterolysis**).

parts.text: Necrosis is always a **pathologic** process: it involves **a group of cells**, membrane integrity is lost, intracellular contents leak out and **provoke inflammation**. Apoptosis, in contrast, is often **physiological**, occurs in individual cells, the membrane is preserved and it **does not provoke** inflammation.

blocks.text: **Autolysis must be distinguished from necrosis. Autolysis** (self-digestion) is the breakdown of cells in the dead body after death under the action of their own enzymes; there is **no inflammatory reaction**. Autolysis develops fastest in organs rich in enzymes (pancreas, gastric mucosa, adrenal medulla).
Stages of necrosis

items: **Paranecrosis** — reversible changes (resembling necrosis but still able to regress).
**Necrobiosis** — irreversible degenerative changes; catabolic reactions predominate over anabolic ones.
**Cell death** — its exact time is difficult to establish.
**Autolysis (and heterolysis)** — breakdown of the dead cell's substrate by hydrolytic enzymes and inflammatory cells.

blocks.text: Microscopic signs of necrosis

blocks.title: Table 2.1. Microscopic signs of necrosis
head: Structure
Change
Essence
rows: The nucleus shrinks, the chromatin condenses and stains darkly (basophilia)
The pyknotic nucleus breaks into fragments
The nucleus dissolves and disappears — chromatin is degraded by DNases, and the nucleus does not stain (“ghost cell”)
Loss of RNA and denatured proteins bind more eosin — the cytoplasm is deep pink
Proteins are denatured, and the cytoplasm becomes uniform (homogeneous) and dense
Swelling, imbibition, fibrinoid change and dissolution of collagen fibers

parts.text: Order of nuclear changes — **“Pyk-Rhex-Lys”**: **Pyk**nosis (shrinks) → karyo**rrhex**is (fragments) → karyo**lys**is (dissolves). Likewise for the cytoplasm: **coagulation → rhexis → lysis**.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Diagram of the morphologic changes of cell injury. Left column — reversible injury (swelling of the cell and organelles, membrane blebs, myelin figures) and its progression to necrosis (breakdown of the plasma membrane, organelles and nucleus, leakage of contents, amorphous densities in mitochondria, inflammation). Right column — apoptosis (chromatin condensation, membrane blebs, fragmentation of the cell into apoptotic bodies and their phagocytosis) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-8)

blocks.text: Etiologic types of necrosis

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Etiologic and pathogenetic types of necrosis
head: Type
Cause
Mode of action
Example
rows: Trauma, burns, frostbite, action of acids and alkalis
Myocardial necrosis caused by diphtheria exotoxin, mercuric chloride nephrosis
Damage to the nervous system, impaired tissue trophism
Bedsores, trophic ulcers after spinal cord injury
Arthus phenomenon, fibrinoid necrosis in autoimmune diseases
Infarction — of the myocardium, brain, kidney, spleen

blocks.text: Clinicomorphologic forms of necrosis

**1. Coagulative (dry) necrosis** is the most common form. The dead tissue **preserves its structural outlines** for several days: proteins and enzymes are denatured and proteolysis stops. The cells have no nuclei and their cytoplasm is eosinophilic, but the outlines of cells and tissue remain visible as “ghosts”. It occurs in organs rich in protein and poor in water — the heart, kidney, spleen and liver. In all organs except the brain, **ischemia** leads to coagulative necrosis.
Grossly: the focus is dry, firm, gray-yellow or whitish, and separated from the surroundings by a red rim (demarcation zone).
Special types of coagulative necrosis:

items: **ischemic infarction** (myocardium, kidney, spleen);
**waxy (Zenker) necrosis** — in the rectus abdominis and thigh adductor muscles in typhoid fever and other severe infections; the muscle is whitish and looks like wax;
**caseous (cheese-like) necrosis**;
**fibrinoid necrosis** (discussed separately below).

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: Ischemic infarction of the spleen: a whitish, firm, triangular focus beneath the capsule; on the cut surface its base faces the capsule (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 2.3
blocks.caption: Coagulative necrosis of the kidney: A — wedge-shaped renal infarct (yellow); B — border of the infarct: normal kidney on the left (N), necrotic cells on the right (I) — cell outlines are preserved, nuclei are absent; an inflammatory infiltrate between them (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-11)

blocks.text: **2. Liquefactive (wet) necrosis** — the dead tissue **liquefies and dissolves**. It occurs in tissues rich in water and enzymes and poor in protein. Main examples:

items: in the **brain** after hypoxia and ischemia (ischemic stroke) — the focus is called **“gray softening”**, and later a **cyst** forms in its place;
in **bacterial (sometimes fungal) infections** — leukocyte enzymes dissolve the tissue and form **pus** (abscess).

blocks.label: Figure 2.5
blocks.caption: Liquefactive necrosis of the brain: in the area of cerebral infarction the tissue softens and dissolves (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-12)

blocks.text: **3. Caseous (cheese-like) necrosis** is a special type of coagulative necrosis. Grossly it is a **white-yellow, dry, crumbly, cheese-like** mass. It occurs mainly in **tuberculosis**, rarely in fungal infections (histoplasmosis), syphilis (gumma) and lymphogranulomatosis. Microscopically, the caseous focus appears as a **structureless, granular, pink mass**: the cell outlines are **not preserved** (unlike coagulative necrosis), and it is surrounded by **granulomatous inflammation** (epithelioid cells, Pirogov–Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes).

blocks.label: Figure 2.6
blocks.caption: Caseous necrosis of the lung (tuberculosis): a large focus filled with a white-yellow, cheese-like mass in the lung tissue (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-13)

blocks.label: Figure 2.7
blocks.caption: Renal tuberculosis — caseous necrosis: the kidney structure is destroyed, with cavities (caverns) filled with a cheese-like mass (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **4. Fat necrosis (steatonecrosis)** — focal destruction of adipose tissue. It is seen mainly in **acute pancreatitis**: activated pancreatic lipases escape and break down the triglycerides of the adipose tissue of the peritoneum, omentum and mesentery. The released fatty acids combine with calcium to form **calcium soaps** (**saponification**) — grossly, **chalky white spots** are seen. Microscopically: the shadowy outlines of fat cells, basophilic calcium deposits between them and inflammation. **Traumatic fat necrosis** of the breast may be clinically mistaken for cancer.

**5. Fibrinoid necrosis** — necrosis of connective tissue and of the vessel wall. It usually occurs in **immune reactions** (antigen–antibody complexes deposited in the vessel wall together with fibrin) — vasculitis, rheumatic diseases, and also in **malignant hypertension**. With hematoxylin and eosin, a **bright pink, homogeneous, fibrin-like** mass is seen in the vessel wall. This process is also discussed in Topic 3 as the irreversible stage of fibrinoid swelling.

blocks.label: Figure 2.9
blocks.caption: Fibrinoid necrosis of an artery: the vessel wall is circumferentially replaced by a bright pink necrotic mass, with inflammation (neutrophils) around it (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-15)

blocks.label: Figure 2.8
blocks.caption: Fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis): chalky white spots in the mesentery — deposits of calcium soaps (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-14)

blocks.text: **6. Gangrene** (Greek gangraina — “gnawing sore”) is necrosis of tissues **in contact with the external environment** (skin, intestine, lung, limbs, uterus). Because iron sulfide (a breakdown product of hemoglobin — a compound of hemoglobin iron and hydrogen sulfide from the air) forms in the necrotic focus, the tissue becomes **black or gray-black**.

blocks.title: Table 2.3. Types of gangrene
head: Type
Condition
Morphology
Example
rows: Arterial blood flow stops, the tissue loses water, and no infection is added
The tissue is dry, wrinkled, hard, black, “mummified”; it is separated from healthy tissue by a clear demarcation line
Atherosclerosis, obliterating endarteritis, toes in frostbite
Putrefactive bacteria are added to the necrosis; the tissue contains much water (venous congestion, edema)
The tissue is swollen, soft, wet, dirty green or black, with a foul odor; there is no demarcation line; intoxication is severe

Gangrene of the intestine (intestinal obstruction, mesenteric thrombosis), gangrene of the lung, gangrene of the foot in diabetes mellitus, noma (gangrene of the facial soft tissues in debilitated children)
Deep wounds infected with clostridia (Clostridium perfringens)
The tissue is swollen and crackles on palpation (crepitation) — gas bubbles
Necrosis of the skin and soft tissues over bony prominences (sacrum, scapula, heel)
Weak patients confined to bed for a long time

blocks.label: Figure 2.10
blocks.caption: Wet gangrene of the foot (diabetes mellitus): the tissues are black-bluish and swollen (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 2.11
blocks.caption: Gangrenous appendicitis: the vermiform appendix is thickened and dirty green, with fibrinous deposits on its serosa (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **7. Sequestrum** — a part of necrotic tissue lying freely among living tissues and not undergoing autolysis. It occurs most often in **bone** — in suppurative osteomyelitis. A **sequestral cavity** forms around the sequestrum; it is filled with pus, which drains outside through sinus tracts (fistulas).

**8. Infarction** is **vascular (ischemic) necrosis**, i.e., necrosis resulting from cessation of the blood supply to part of an organ. The forms of infarction (white, red, white with a red rim) and its features are discussed in detail in Topic 7.
Outcomes of necrosis

**Demarcation inflammation** develops around the necrotic focus: the vessels dilate (hyperemia), and there is edema and leukocyte infiltration. This zone separates the dead tissue from the living tissue. Further outcomes:

items: **Favorable outcomes:**

blocks.text: – **organization** — the necrotic focus is replaced by granulation tissue, and a **scar** forms (for example, postinfarction cardiosclerosis); – **encapsulation** — the focus is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule; – **petrification** (calcification) — calcium salts are deposited in the necrotic focus (dystrophic calcification, Topic 4); for example, the **Ghon focus** remaining from the primary tuberculous focus; – **ossification** — bone tissue forms in the focus; – **cyst** formation — in place of liquefactive necrosis (for example, in the brain); – **mutilation** — separation of the necrotic part (in dry gangrene of a finger). • **Unfavorable outcomes: purulent dissolution** — suppurative breakdown of the necrotic focus, which can lead to sepsis; loss of function of the organ containing the necrotic focus (cardiac rupture, paralysis after stroke).

blocks.label: Figure 2.12
blocks.caption: Petrifications in the lung: stone-hard, round foci in the lung tissue (pointer) — calcification of necrosis (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 2.13
blocks.caption: Infarcts of the liver: irregular, firm, gray foci on the cut surface (TMA study guide, 2018)

parts.text: **The significance of necrosis** depends on its location and size. In vital organs (heart, brain), even a small necrosis can cause death. Substances released from the necrotic focus are **detected in the blood** and used in diagnosis: in myocardial necrosis — **troponin I and T**, creatine kinase-MB; in liver necrosis — **ALT and AST** (transaminases); in pancreatitis — **amylase and lipase**; in skeletal muscle necrosis (rhabdomyolysis) — creatine kinase and myoglobin. In addition, extensive necrosis leads to a **resorptive syndrome** — fever, leukocytosis and an increased ESR.

blocks.text: **Apoptosis** (Greek apoptosis — “falling off of leaves”) is **programmed cell death**: the cell destroys itself by degrading its own DNA and nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins with special intracellular enzymes (caspases). The membrane of the apoptotic cell **remains intact**, and the cell fragments (apoptotic bodies) are rapidly engulfed by macrophages, so **no inflammation develops**. Apoptosis was described as a distinct type of death in 1972 by J. Kerr, A. Wyllie and A. Currie.
Causes of apoptosis
**Physiological apoptosis** — elimination of unneeded, aged or dangerous cells:

items: programmed death of cells during embryogenesis (implantation, organogenesis, disappearance of the tissue between the fingers);
involution of hormone-dependent tissues when the hormone decreases (endometrium in the menstrual cycle, ovary in menopause, breast after cessation of lactation);
maintenance of cell numbers in continuously renewing cell populations (intestinal crypts, lymphocytes);
elimination of inflammatory cells (neutrophils, lymphocytes) that have completed their task;
elimination in the thymus of **self-reactive lymphocytes** directed against self antigens (immune tolerance);
death of virus-infected and tumor cells under the action of cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

blocks.text: Pathologic apoptosis:

items: irreparable **DNA damage** (radiation, chemotherapy drugs) — via p53;
**accumulation of misfolded proteins** (ER stress) — neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases);
some **infections** — viral hepatitis (Councilman bodies), HIV infection;
**atrophy of organs** after duct obstruction (obstruction of the pancreatic, salivary gland or renal ducts).

blocks.text: Morphology of apoptosis

items: **Cell shrinkage** — the cytoplasm becomes dense, and the organelles are tightly packed (but keep their normal structure).
**Chromatin condensation** — the most characteristic feature: chromatin aggregates densely beneath the nuclear membrane, and the nucleus breaks into fragments (**karyorrhexis**).
**Membrane blebs** and fragmentation of the cell into membrane-bound **apoptotic bodies** containing cytoplasm, organelles and nuclear fragments.

**Phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies by macrophages**. In a hematoxylin and eosin–stained slide, an apoptotic cell is a **single** cell separated from its surroundings by a clear space, **round or oval, with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm** and dense nuclear fragments. Because there is no inflammatory reaction and the process is completed rapidly (within a few hours), apoptosis is difficult to see in histologic slides.

blocks.label: Figure 2.14
blocks.caption: Apoptotic bodies in viral hepatitis (Councilman bodies) — microscopic slide: a round, eosinophilic, dense body (1) between the hepatocyte plates (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 2.15
blocks.caption: Apoptosis (electron microscopy): the cytoplasm is condensed, the organelles are tightly packed, and the chromatin is condensed (1) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Mechanisms of apoptosis

Apoptosis consists of two phases: **initiation** — activation of caspases, and **execution** — breakdown of the cell. **Caspases** are proteases with cysteine in their active site that cleave proteins after aspartic acid (cysteine-aspartic proteases). There are two pathways for initiating apoptosis:
**1. The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway** is the main mechanism of apoptosis. The permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane is regulated by the **BCL2 family of proteins**:

items: **anti-apoptotic** proteins — **BCL2**, BCL-XL, MCL1: keep the mitochondrial membrane intact; they are produced in response to growth factors and survival signals;
**pro-apoptotic** (effector) proteins — **BAX and BAK**: oligomerize and form channels in the mitochondrial membrane;

**regulated “sensor” proteins of apoptosis** — BIM, BID, BAD, PUMA, NOXA (BH3-only proteins): when stress is sensed (DNA damage, absence of growth factors, misfolded proteins), they activate BAX/BAK and block BCL2. If the cell loses survival signals or is injured, **cytochrome c** leaks into the cytoplasm through BAX/BAK channels, binds the APAF-1 protein to form the **apoptosome** and activates **caspase-9**.

blocks.text: **2. The extrinsic (death receptor) pathway.** The **death receptors** on the cell surface belong to the TNF receptor family: **Fas (CD95)** and TNFR1. **Fas ligand (FasL)** on the surface of cytotoxic T lymphocytes binds to the Fas receptor and brings together three receptor molecules; their cytoplasmic “death domains” activate **caspase-8** through the adapter protein FADD. This pathway is important in the elimination of self-reactive lymphocytes and in killing by cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

**3. The execution phase.** Caspase-9 and caspase-8 activate the **executioner caspases (caspase-3 and caspase-6)**. They activate a DNase that cleaves DNA between nucleosomes (into fragments of 180–200 base pairs — a “ladder” pattern on electrophoresis) and degrade the proteins of the nuclear matrix and cytoskeleton.

**4. Removal of apoptotic cells.** **Phosphatidylserine**, normally located in the inner leaflet of the membrane, flips to the outer leaflet in an apoptotic cell — this is an “**eat me**” signal for macrophages. Apoptotic bodies are rapidly phagocytosed without inflammation.

parts.text: To remember the caspases of apoptosis: **“Intrinsic — 9, Extrinsic — 8, Executioners — 3 and 6”**. Imagine the intrinsic pathway as a **“mitochondrial gate”**: BCL2 is the gatekeeper (keeps it closed), BAX/BAK are the gate breakers, and cytochrome c is the “messenger of death” that comes out through the gate.

Both **decreased** and **increased** apoptosis lead to disease. **Too little apoptosis:** in follicular lymphoma the t(14;18) translocation causes **overproduction of BCL2** — lymphocytes do not die and accumulate; with TP53 mutation, damaged cells are not eliminated — tumors; with defects of Fas or FasL, self-reactive lymphocytes survive — autoimmune diseases. **Too much apoptosis:** neurodegenerative diseases, ischemic injury, viral infections. A drug that blocks BCL2 — **venetoclax** — is used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Differences between necrosis and apoptosis
head: Feature
Necrosis
Apoptosis
rows: Groups of cells, an area of tissue
Intact, with altered structure (phosphatidylserine on the outside)
Does not require ATP (ATP depletion is the cause)

sections.title: 2.6. Other pathways of cell death and autophagy

items: **Necroptosis** — programmed (regulated) necrosis: morphologically it resembles necrosis (cell swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation) but is genetically programmed. It is initiated via TNFR1, is caspase-independent and involves the **RIPK1 and RIPK3 kinases** and the MLKL protein. It is seen in pancreatitis, reperfusion injury, neurodegenerative diseases and some viral infections (a defense against viruses that block caspases).
**Pyroptosis** — an inflammatory, fever-inducing cell death associated with **inflammasome** activation, caspase-1 and IL-1 production in intracellular microbial infection (Greek pyr — fire).
**Ferroptosis** — death resulting from iron-dependent lipid peroxidation; it develops when the glutathione system is insufficient.

**Autophagy** — digestion by the cell of its own organelles and cytoplasm in lysosomes. It is primarily a **survival mechanism** (a source of energy in starvation, clearance of damaged organelles), but excessive autophagy can lead to cell death. Defects in autophagy genes are associated with Crohn disease, neurodegenerative diseases and tumors.

parts.text: The textbooks of Strukov and Abdullakhodjaeva discuss two main types of cell death — necrosis and apoptosis. Recent editions of Robbins add **necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis** to them. When “types of cell death” are asked at the exam, it is advisable first to describe necrosis and apoptosis fully and then briefly mention the modern types.

sections.title: 2.7. Death of the organism and postmortem changes

blocks.text: **Death** is the irreversible cessation of the vital activity of the organism. By cause, death is divided into **natural** (physiological — from old age), **violent** (trauma, poisoning, homicide, suicide) and death **from disease**. Sudden, unexpected death is called **sudden death** (most often in cardiovascular diseases).
Stages of death:

items: **Agony** — the state before death: disordered fading of functions.

**Clinical death** — breathing and cardiac activity have stopped, but there are no irreversible changes in the tissues yet. At normal temperature it lasts **5–6 minutes** (the time the cerebral cortex tolerates hypoxia); during this period resuscitation can restore the organism.

**Biological death** — irreversible changes begin in the tissues, first of all in the brain; resuscitation is ineffective. In modern medicine **brain death** (irreversible cessation of all functions of the brain, including the brainstem) is recognized as the death of the person.

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Postmortem (cadaveric) changes
head: Change
Essence and timing
rows: Heat production stops, and body temperature gradually falls to that of the environment

Because of ATP depletion, actin–myosin cross-bridges in the muscles do not detach; it begins 2–4 hours after death in the masticatory muscles and spreads from top to bottom; it disappears in the same order after 24–48 hours (autolysis)

Blood flows by gravity to the lowest parts of the body: first the hypostasis stage (the spot disappears on pressure), then hemolyzed blood soaks into the tissue — the imbibition stage (does not disappear on pressure)
Loss of moisture by the skin, mucous membranes and cornea (“Larcher spots” in the eye)
After death, blood clots form in the vessels and cardiac chambers; they are smooth, shiny, elastic and not attached to the wall (unlike a thrombus)
Breakdown of cells by their own enzymes and later by intestinal bacteria; in putrefaction gases form and the body turns green

parts.text: At autopsy it is important to distinguish a **postmortem blood clot** from a **thrombus** formed during life: a thrombus is **dull, dry, friable, layered** and **attached** to the vessel wall; a postmortem clot is **smooth, shiny, elastic**, not attached to the wall, follows the shape of the vessel and separates into layers resembling “chicken fat” (yellow, plasma part) and “currant jelly” (red, red cell part) (Topic 7).

blocks.text: Ischemia–reperfusion: is a quickly opened vessel not always beneficial?

In a patient presenting with myocardial infarction, the vessel is opened in the first hours (stenting or thrombolysis). This greatly reduces the necrotic focus — cardiomyocytes that are still reversibly injured are saved. However, as soon as blood flow is restored, some cells die because of **reperfusion injury** (free radicals, Ca^2+^ overload, leukocytes), and reperfusion arrhythmias appear. Microscopically, reperfused myocardium shows **hemorrhages** and **contraction band necrosis** (hypercontracted cardiomyocytes with transverse “bands”).
Types of necrosis in the clinic

items: **Coagulative necrosis:** infarcts of the heart, kidney and spleen — clinically pain and impaired organ function.
**Liquefactive necrosis:** ischemic stroke — a brain cyst after several weeks; abscesses — removal of pus (drainage) is necessary.
**Caseous necrosis:** tuberculosis — the caseous mass is discharged through a bronchus, forming a **cavity**, and the patient spreads mycobacteria to others.
**Fat necrosis:** acute pancreatitis — blood calcium falls (it is used up in soap formation), which is a sign of a severe course.
**Gangrene:** diabetic foot — if it progresses to wet gangrene, amputation and prevention of sepsis are necessary.

parts.text: **Chemical liver necrosis.** In a patient who has taken a large dose of paracetamol (for example, 10–15 g), there are few symptoms on the first day, but on days 2–3 jaundice, a sharp rise in ALT and AST (several thousand units) and liver failure develop. Liver biopsy shows **central (centrilobular) necrosis** — because the cytochrome P-450 enzymes that form the toxic metabolite are located mainly in the center of the lobule, and this area is the least supplied with oxygen.

items: **Gangrene** (Greek gangraina — fire) — necrosis of tissues in contact with the external environment that turns black as a result of the formation of iron sulfide.
**Infarction** (Latin infarcire — to stuff, to fill in) — tissue necrosis resulting from impaired circulation (ischemia).
**Karyopyknosis** — shrinkage of the nucleus, condensation of chromatin.
**Karyorrhexis** — fragmentation of the nucleus.
**Karyolysis** — dissolution of the nucleus.
**Malacia** (Greek malakos — soft) — softening of dead tissue (for example, in the brain).
**Marantic necrosis** — bedsores occurring in exhausted elderly people with signs of cachexia and marasmus.
**Mummification** (Latin mumificatio — drying) — drying and hardening of dead tissue.
**Necrobiosis** (Greek nekros — dead, bios — life) — irreversible degenerative changes preceding necrosis; a process of slow dying.
**Necrosis** (Greek nekros — dead) — death in a living organism with cessation of the vital activity of cells and tissues.
**Noma** (Greek nome — gnawing sore, “water cancer”) — wet gangrene of the facial soft tissues in debilitated children (often after measles and other severe infections).
**Pathobiosis** — necrobiosis prolonged in time.
**Plasmolysis** — hydrolytic breakdown and dissolution of the cytoplasm.
**Plasmorrhexis** — fragmentation of the cytoplasm.
**Sequestrum** (Latin sequestrum — separated) — a part of dead tissue that does not undergo autolysis, is not replaced by connective tissue and lies freely among living tissues.

**“Ischemic infarction of the spleen”.** A whitish-yellow, firm, triangular (wedge-shaped) focus beneath the splenic capsule; its base faces the capsule and its apex faces the hilum of the spleen; a red rim (demarcation zone) around the focus; fibrin deposits on the capsule. Conclusion: coagulative necrosis — white infarct.

**“Hemorrhagic (red) infarction of the lung”.** A dark red, firm, wedge-shaped focus in the lung tissue; its base faces the pleura, the pleura is dull, with fibrinous deposits. Conclusion: red infarct (Topic 7).

**“Gangrene of the leg”.** The foot and toes are black-bluish; in dry gangrene — wrinkled, hard, separated from healthy tissue by a demarcation line; in wet gangrene — swollen, soft, without demarcation. Conclusion: gangrene (specify the type).
**“Gangrenous appendicitis”.** The vermiform appendix is thickened, dirty green or black, its serosa is dull, with fibrinopurulent deposits. Conclusion: a form of intestinal gangrene (wet gangrene).
**“Caseous necrosis of a lymph node”.** The lymph node is enlarged and firm; on the cut surface — a white-yellow, dry, crumbly, cheese-like mass. Conclusion: caseous necrosis (tuberculosis).

**“Caseous necrosis of the kidney (renal tuberculosis)”.** The kidney structure is destroyed, the cortex and medulla are indistinguishable, with cavities (caverns) filled with a cheese-like mass. Conclusion: caseous necrosis.

**“Petrifications in the lung”.** Small, stone-hard, whitish, round foci in the lung tissue; the knife grates when cutting. Conclusion: an outcome of necrosis — petrification (for example, the Ghon focus).
**“Gray softening of the brain (ischemic infarction)”.** A soft, mushy, gray focus with indistinct borders in the brain tissue. Conclusion: liquefactive necrosis.

**“Necrosis of the renal tubular epithelium”** (hematoxylin and eosin; for example, in mercuric chloride poisoning or shock). In the convoluted tubules of the renal cortex the epithelial cells lack nuclei (**karyolysis**), in some cells the nucleus is shrunken (pyknosis) or fragmented (karyorrhexis); the cytoplasm is homogeneous and eosinophilic (plasmocoagulation) or broken into fragments (plasmorrhexis); cell debris in the tubular lumen. The glomeruli are preserved. Conclusion: necrotic nephrosis (acute tubular necrosis).

**“Caseous necrosis of a lymph node”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The structure of the lymph node is lost, and most of it is occupied by a structureless, granular, pink mass; around it are epithelioid cells, Pirogov–Langhans giant cells and lymphocytes. Conclusion: caseous necrosis (tuberculosis).

**“Necrosis of the tonsil in leukemia (necrotic tonsillitis)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Most of the tonsillar epithelium and lymphoid tissue has undergone necrosis — a structureless eosinophilic mass (1); a leukocytic infiltrate at its border (2). Conclusion: necrotic tonsillitis.

**“Apoptotic bodies in viral hepatitis (Councilman bodies)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Single round, shrunken cells with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and a condensed or absent nucleus between the liver cell plates; no inflammatory reaction around them. Conclusion: apoptosis of hepatocytes.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 64-year-old man has suffered for many years from diabetes mellitus and atherosclerosis of the leg arteries. A month ago the big toe of his right foot became black, dry and wrinkled and was clearly demarcated from healthy tissue. Over the last 3 days the foot has become swollen and bluish-black, a foul odor has appeared, and his temperature is 39 °C.
cases.ask: 1) What process was present a month ago? 2) What is the current condition called, and why did it change? 3) State the differences between the two conditions and their outcomes.
cases.answer: 1) Dry gangrene — because of atherosclerosis, arterial blood flow gradually stopped and the tissue lost water; no infection was added; there is a clear demarcation line. 2) Wet gangrene — putrefactive bacteria have been added to the necrotic focus; in diabetes, tissue edema and weakened immunity predispose to this. 3) In dry gangrene the tissue is hard and mummified, demarcation is clear, there is no intoxication, and the outcome may be mutilation (spontaneous separation). In wet gangrene the tissue is swollen, soft and foul-smelling, there is no demarcation and intoxication is severe; urgent amputation is necessary because of the risk of sepsis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 55-year-old woman developed severe, band-like pain in the upper abdomen after heavy drinking. Blood amylase and lipase were sharply increased, and the calcium level was decreased. The woman died. At autopsy the pancreas is swollen, with hemorrhages; there are numerous chalky white spots in the omentum and mesentery.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What process are the chalky white spots? Explain its mechanism. 3) Why is blood calcium decreased?
cases.answer: 1) Acute (hemorrhagic) pancreatitis (pancreatic necrosis). 2) Fat necrosis (steatonecrosis): activated pancreatic lipases break down the membranes of fat cells and the triglycerides, and the released fatty acids combine with calcium to form calcium soaps (saponification) — these are the chalky white spots. Microscopically: shadowy outlines of fat cells, basophilic calcium deposits, inflammation. 3) Blood calcium decreases because it is used up in soap formation; hypocalcemia is a sign of a severe course of pancreatitis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old man has chronic viral hepatitis B. Liver biopsy: single round, shrunken cells with deeply eosinophilic cytoplasm and dense nuclear fragments between the liver cell plates; there is no inflammatory reaction around them. Lymphocytic infiltration in the portal tracts of the lobule.
cases.ask: 1) What are the described cells called? 2) What type of cell death is this? Which of its mechanisms is involved? 3) State the differences between this type of death and necrosis.
cases.answer: 1) Councilman (apoptotic) bodies. 2) Apoptosis. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes eliminate virus-infected hepatocytes through Fas ligand (extrinsic pathway, caspase-8) and perforin/granzyme B; the executioner caspases (caspase-3) degrade the nucleus and cytoskeleton. 3) In apoptosis individual cells die, the cell shrinks, the chromatin condenses, the membrane is preserved, and apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed without inflammation. In necrosis, in contrast, groups of cells die, the cell swells, the membrane is disrupted, the nucleus undergoes pyknosis–karyorrhexis–karyolysis, and inflammation develops.

cards.back: Severe mitochondrial dysfunction (amorphous densities), profound disruption of membranes
Neuron 3–5 min, cardiomyocyte 20–30 min, skeletal muscle 2–3 h
Organization, encapsulation, petrification, ossification, cyst, purulent dissolution
After 2–4 hours, from top to bottom

topics.title: Degenerations: types and pathogenetic mechanisms. Parenchymal and stromal-vascular degenerations

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the concept of degeneration (dystrophy) and its relation to impaired trophism;
the morphogenetic mechanisms of degenerations: infiltration, decomposition (phanerosis), perverted synthesis, transformation;
the classification of degenerations (by location, type of disturbed metabolism, extent and origin);
parenchymal protein, fatty and carbohydrate degenerations: causes, gross and microscopic appearance, outcomes;
stromal-vascular protein degenerations: mucoid swelling, fibrinoid change, hyalinosis, amyloidosis (general concept);
stromal-vascular fatty (obesity, atherosclerosis) and carbohydrate degenerations;
the histochemical stains used to identify degenerations.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of fatty degeneration of the liver (“goose liver”), fatty degeneration of the myocardium (“tiger heart”), fatty infiltration of the heart and hyalinosis of the splenic capsule (“glazed spleen”);
describe microscopic slides of hyaline droplet and hydropic degeneration of the renal tubular epithelium, fatty degeneration of the liver (Sudan III), arteriolar hyalinosis and mucoid swelling;
determine the type of degeneration by histochemical reactions;
distinguish reversible from irreversible degenerations.

Most degenerations are **reversible** processes, but profound changes can lead to necrosis (necrobiosis).

Moreover, the English word dystrophy is used mainly for muscular dystrophies (Duchenne). In CIS and Uzbek textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva), however, the classification of degenerations (dystrophies) is fully preserved, and it is exactly this classification that is asked at the exam.

Electron microscopy showed that the cytoplasmic “granules” are swollen mitochondria and fragments of the ER, i.e., an expression of the cell's **functional strain (hyperplasia of organelles)** or early injury. Therefore A.I. Strukov and V.V. Serov do not include it among the degenerations. The gross appearance — the organ is enlarged, dull and looks “boiled” — corresponds to “**cellular swelling**” in Robbins.

summary.text: “**Tiger heart**” is **parenchymal** fatty degeneration of the myocardium (fat inside cardiomyocytes). “**Fatty infiltration of the heart**” (adiposity of the heart) is **stromal-vascular** fatty degeneration (growth of adipose tissue beneath the epicardium and in the myocardial stroma). Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes at the exam.

summary.text: Stages of connective tissue disorganization: **1) mucoid swelling** (superficial, **reversible**) → **2) fibrinoid swelling** (deep, **irreversible**) → **3) fibrinoid necrosis** → **4) hyalinosis** or sclerosis. This sequence is most evident in rheumatic diseases (rheumatic fever, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) and in arterial hypertension.
