summary.text: Distinguishing by stains: **“Mucoid — Metachromasia, Fibrinoid — Fibrin reaction, Hyaline — Homogeneous”**. In mucoid swelling toluidine blue gives a violet-red color; in fibrinoid the reactions for fibrin are positive and it is yellow with van Gieson; hyaline is a dense, homogeneous, pale pink mass, yellow or red with van Gieson.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In older textbooks (Strukov), the degree of obesity was determined by the **percentage of excess weight over ideal weight**: grade I — 20–29%, II — 30–49%, III — 50–99%, IV — 100% or more. Current clinical practice uses the **WHO BMI classification**; it is useful to know both for the exam.

blocks.text: **Degeneration (dystrophy)** (Greek dys — disorder, trophe — nourishment) is a complex pathological process in which structural changes appear in cells and intercellular substance as a result of **disturbed tissue (cellular) metabolism**. Degeneration is one of the types of **alteration** (damage).

Degeneration is based on a disturbance of **trophism**. **Trophism** is the set of mechanisms that ensure the metabolism and structural organization of a tissue. The mechanisms that maintain trophism are divided into two groups:

items: **cellular mechanisms** — the cell's own structures and their regulation (cellular autoregulation);

**extracellular mechanisms** — transport (blood and lymphatic vessels, microcirculation), the intercellular substance, and the integrative systems (neuroendocrine and neurohumoral regulation). Accordingly, the direct causes of degeneration are: disturbed cellular autoregulation (hyperfunction, toxins, radiation, hereditary enzyme deficiency — **enzymopathy**), disturbed transport systems (**hypoxia** — the most common cause of degeneration), and disturbed regulation by the integrative systems (diseases of the endocrine and nervous systems).

parts.text: In degeneration, substances that are **not normally present** accumulate in the cell or intercellular substance, or **normally present substances** accumulate in excess or in an unusual location; sometimes normal
substances disappear (for example, loss of glycogen in cardiomyocytes). Most degenerations are **reversible** processes, but profound changes can lead to necrosis (necrobiosis).

The **Robbins** textbook hardly uses the term “dystrophy”: these processes are discussed as reversible cell injury (cellular swelling, fatty change), **intracellular accumulations**, **hyaline change**, amyloidosis and pathologic calcification. Moreover, the English word dystrophy is used mainly for muscular dystrophies (Duchenne). In CIS and Uzbek textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva), however, the classification of degenerations (dystrophies) is fully preserved, and it is exactly this classification that is asked at the exam.

blocks.text: Morphogenetic mechanisms of degenerations

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Morphogenetic mechanisms of degenerations
head: Mechanism
Essence
Example
rows: Excessive entry of substances from blood and lymph into the cell or intercellular substance, exceeding the capacity to metabolize them
Protein infiltration of the proximal tubular epithelium in nephrotic syndrome (hyaline droplet degeneration); cholesterol infiltration of the aortic intima in atherosclerosis
Breakdown of complex substances of cells and tissues (lipoprotein membranes, glycoproteins), so that their components become “visible”
Fatty degeneration of cardiomyocytes in diphtheritic intoxication; breakdown of connective tissue in fibrinoid change
Synthesis of abnormal substances that are not normally present in the cell or tissue
Synthesis of amyloid (amyloidosis); alcoholic hyaline in hepatocytes in alcoholism (Mallory bodies)
Formation of a different type of substance from the initial products normally used to form a given substance
Conversion of carbohydrate and protein components into fat; polymerization of large amounts of glucose into glycogen

parts.text: Remember the four mechanisms as **“IDAT” — “I Do Avoid Trash”**: **I**nfiltration (excess enters), **D**ecomposition (breaks down), **A**bnormal (perverted) synthesis (an abnormal substance), **T**ransformation (turns into another substance).

blocks.text: Classification of degenerations

blocks.title: Table 3.2. Classification of degenerations (after A.I. Strukov)
head: Feature
Types
rows: Protein (dysproteinoses), fatty (lipidoses), carbohydrate; in mixed degenerations — chromoproteins (pigments), nucleoproteins and mineral metabolism

blocks.text: In parenchymal protein degenerations, the metabolism of **proteins in the cell cytoplasm** is disturbed. They include **hyaline droplet, hydropic (vacuolar)** and **horny (keratinizing)** degenerations.

parts.text: In older textbooks “**granular degeneration**” (“cloudy swelling”) was given as a separate type. Electron microscopy showed that the cytoplasmic “granules” are swollen mitochondria and fragments of the ER, i.e., an expression of the cell's **functional strain (hyperplasia of organelles)** or early injury. Therefore A.I. Strukov and V.V. Serov do not include it among the degenerations. The gross appearance — the organ is enlarged, dull and looks “boiled” — corresponds to “**cellular swelling**” in Robbins.

blocks.text: Hyaline droplet degeneration

**Large, homogeneous, eosinophilic, hyaline-like protein droplets** appear in the cytoplasm; they merge with one another and fill the whole cell. In this degeneration the cell organelles are destroyed, and the process is **irreversible**, often leading to **coagulative necrosis**.
Location and causes:

items: **Kidney** — in the epithelium of the proximal tubules. Cause: **nephrotic syndrome** (glomerulonephritis, amyloidosis, diabetic nephropathy, paraproteinemic nephropathy) — large amounts of protein pass through the glomerular filter, and the tubular epithelium takes it up by pinocytosis, but the lysosomes cannot digest it in time (**insufficiency of the vacuolar–lysosomal system**). The gross appearance is not specific — it is determined by the underlying kidney disease. Clinically — **proteinuria** and casts in the urine.
**Liver** — **alcoholic hyaline — Mallory bodies** in hepatocytes (aggregates of cytokeratin intermediate filaments); they occur in alcoholic hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis and Wilson disease.
**Plasma cells** — immunoglobulins accumulate in the cytoplasm to form **Russell bodies** (in chronic inflammation).
**Myocardium** — very rare.

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Hyaline droplet degeneration of the renal tubular epithelium: large eosinophilic protein droplets in the cytoplasm (a, b) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-4a)

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Reabsorbed protein droplets in the epithelium of the proximal renal tubules (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-32)

blocks.text: Hydropic (vacuolar) degeneration

**Vacuoles filled with cytoplasmic fluid** appear in the cell. The cause is increased permeability of cell membranes, failure of the Na^+^/K^+^ pump, and disturbed water–electrolyte and protein metabolism; **hydrostatic pressure** inside the cell increases. The cell enlarges, its cytoplasm fills with clear vacuoles, and the nucleus is displaced to the periphery or becomes vacuolated.

When the vacuoles merge and occupy the whole cell, the cell turns into a fluid-filled balloon — **ballooning degeneration**. This condition is regarded as **focal liquefactive necrosis** and is **irreversible**.
Location and causes:

items: **Skin epithelium** — smallpox, chickenpox, burns, edema;
**Renal tubules** — nephrotic syndrome, glycosuria (diabetes), potassium deficiency (hypokalemic nephropathy), toxic influences (ethylene glycol, some drugs) — **osmotic nephrosis**;
**Liver** — viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B) — **ballooning degeneration**;
**Nerve cells, myocardium, adrenal cortex** — severe intoxications, hypoxia;

**Tumor** cells (for example, chordoma, the clear cell type of renal cell carcinoma). The gross appearance hardly changes. Microscopically, the fluid in the vacuoles **does not stain** with fat stains (Sudan III) — this distinguishes it from fatty degeneration. Outcome: reversible when mild; in ballooning degeneration — necrosis.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Hydropic degeneration of the liver (biopsy): hepatocytes are enlarged, with vacuolated, clear cytoplasm (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-5)

parts.text: In liver biopsy in viral hepatitis B, **ballooning degeneration** and **Councilman bodies** (Topic 2) are the main signs of hepatocyte injury. Their number and distribution are taken into account in grading the activity of inflammation.

blocks.text: Horny (keratinizing) degeneration
Formation of **horny substance (keratin)** in excess or in a site where it is not normally formed.

items: **Hyperkeratosis** — excessive formation of horny substance in keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium: callus (calluses on the palm), ichthyosis (congenital hereditary hyperkeratosis — “fish skin”), warts.

**Leukoplakia** (Greek leukos — white) — keratinization of mucous membranes lined by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium (oral cavity, tongue, esophagus, cervix), in the form of a white patch.
In **keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma** — **“keratin pearls”** (concentric layers of horny substance).

parts.text: **Leukoplakia** is a clinical term (“white patch”) behind which various histologic processes may lie: simple hyperkeratosis or dysplasia. Leukoplakia is considered a **precancerous** condition: some oral leukoplakias turn into squamous cell carcinoma. Therefore a biopsy is necessary in long-standing leukoplakia.

blocks.text: Accumulation of **neutral fats (triglycerides)** in the cytoplasm of cells. In Robbins — **steatosis (fatty change)**. It occurs most often in cells actively involved in lipid metabolism — hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes and renal tubular epithelium.
**Methods for detecting fats:** on frozen sections (during paraffin processing, alcohol and xylene dissolve the fats — **empty vacuoles** remain in their place with hematoxylin and eosin):

items: **Sudan III** — stains fats **orange-red**;
**Scarlet red** — red;
**Sudan IV, Nile blue, osmic acid** — black.

blocks.text: Fatty degeneration of the liver
Fatty degeneration of the liver is the most common fatty degeneration. **Causes:**

items: **alcohol** — the most common cause (in developed countries);
**obesity, diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome** — **nonalcoholic fatty liver disease**;
**protein-energy malnutrition** (kwashiorkor) — synthesis of apoproteins decreases;
**hypoxia** — anemia, chronic heart failure;
**toxins and drugs** — CCl~4~, phosphorus, arsenic, glucocorticoids, tetracycline;
**infections and intoxications** — diphtheria, tuberculosis, sepsis;
acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

blocks.text: **Mechanism.** In the liver, fatty acids are handled as follows: they arrive from the blood → are converted to triglycerides → combine with apoproteins and are secreted into the blood as **lipoproteins**. If any link in this chain is disturbed, fat accumulates:

items: **Excessive delivery of fatty acids to the liver** — starvation, diabetes, alcohol (increased lipolysis in adipose tissue).
**Decreased oxidation of fatty acids** — hypoxia, mitochondrial damage (alcohol).
**Increased synthesis of triglycerides** — alcohol (excess NADH).
**Decreased synthesis of apoproteins** — CCl~4~, protein deficiency.

**Impaired secretion of lipoproteins** — alcohol, toxins. **Grossly:** the liver is enlarged and heavy (up to 3–6 kg), its surface is smooth, the edges are rounded, the consistency is soft and doughy, the color is **yellowish or clay-yellow**, and on cutting fat remains on the knife blade. Such a liver is called a “**goose liver**” (French foie gras — the fatty liver obtained by force-feeding geese).

blocks.text: **Microscopically:** **small-droplet** (initially) or **large-droplet** fat vacuoles in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes; a large vacuole pushes the nucleus to the periphery of the cell — the cell takes on a **“signet ring”** appearance. Fat droplets can rupture and form fatty cysts. By location: **centrilobular** (in the center of the lobule — hypoxia, alcohol, toxins), **periportal** (at the periphery of the lobule — phosphorus poisoning, protein deficiency), **diffuse**.

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Fatty degeneration of the liver (steatosis) — microscopic slide: large fat vacuoles in hepatocytes, nuclei pushed to the edge of the cytoplasm (hematoxylin and eosin) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-30)

blocks.label: Figure 3.5
blocks.caption: Fatty degeneration of the liver: large and small clear vacuoles (Pathoma, Fig. 1.12)

blocks.text: **Outcomes:** if the cause is removed, it is **reversible** (for example, 4–6 weeks after stopping alcohol). If it persists, fatty liver may progress to **steatohepatitis** (inflammation and hepatocyte necrosis), **fibrosis** and **liver cirrhosis**.

parts.text: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is today the most widespread chronic liver disease in the world and is closely associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is often detected incidentally on ultrasound (“increased echogenicity of the liver”). When it progresses to steatohepatitis, transaminases rise; the basis of treatment is weight loss and correction of metabolic disorders.

blocks.text: Fatty degeneration of the myocardium

**Causes:** mainly **chronic hypoxia** (severe anemia, chronic cardiovascular insufficiency) and **intoxications** (diphtheria, alcohol, phosphorus, arsenic poisoning). Mechanism — damaged mitochondria reduce the oxidation of fatty acids, and fat droplets accumulate in cardiomyocytes; in diphtheria, breakdown of membrane structures (**decomposition**) is also important.

**Grossly:** the heart is slightly enlarged, its cavities are dilated, the myocardium is flabby and clay-yellow. From the endocardial side, especially in the papillary muscles and trabeculae of the left ventricle, **yellow-white transverse stripes** are seen — the “**tiger heart**”. These stripes reflect a **focal** process: fatty degeneration develops in cardiomyocytes around the venules (which receive the least oxygen), while those around the arterioles are spared.
**Microscopically:** **very fine droplets** of fat in cardiomyocytes (**pulverized (dust-like) fatty change**), later small droplets; the cross-striation disappears.
**Outcome:** reversible when mild. When severe — necrosis of cardiomyocytes; myocardial contractility decreases — **heart failure**.

blocks.label: Figure 3.6
blocks.caption: Fatty degeneration of the myocardium (Sudan III): orange-red fat droplets in the cytoplasm of cardiomyocytes; the change is focal (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-6a)

parts.text: “**Tiger heart**” is **parenchymal** fatty degeneration of the myocardium (fat inside cardiomyocytes). “**Fatty infiltration of the heart**” (adiposity of the heart) is **stromal-vascular** fatty degeneration (growth of adipose tissue beneath the epicardium and in the myocardial stroma). Confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes at the exam.

blocks.text: Fatty degeneration of the kidney

Neutral fats accumulate in the epithelium of the proximal and distal tubules. Mainly in **nephrotic syndrome** (hyperlipidemia and lipiduria — infiltration of fats), rarely in intoxications. The kidney is enlarged and soft; the cortex is swollen, gray, with yellow spots. It often occurs together with hyaline droplet and hydropic degeneration.
Hereditary lipidoses (storage diseases)
Because of hereditary deficiency of lysosomal enzymes, particular lipids accumulate (Topic 11):

items: **Gaucher disease** — glucocerebrosides accumulate (glucocerebrosidase deficiency); **Gaucher cells** with cytoplasm resembling “**crumpled tissue paper**” in the spleen, liver and bone marrow;
**Niemann–Pick disease** — sphingomyelin (sphingomyelinase deficiency); foamy macrophages;
**Tay–Sachs disease** — GM2 ganglioside (hexosaminidase A deficiency); neurons are affected, with a “**cherry-red spot**” on the retina.

blocks.text: Carbohydrates in the cell exist mainly as **glycogen** and **glycoproteins** (mucoids, mucins). Glycogen stains magenta with the **PAS reaction** (Schiff reagent) and red with **Best carmine**. Glycogen is water-soluble, so the tissue is fixed in absolute alcohol.
Disturbed glycogen metabolism
**Diabetes mellitus** is the main example of acquired disturbance of glycogen metabolism:

items: in the **liver**, glycogen stores decrease (glucose does not enter the tissues), but glycogen accumulates in the **nuclei** of hepatocytes — the nucleus is clear and vacuolated (“**holed**” or “**empty nuclei**”);

in the **kidney** — because of glucosuria, glycogen accumulates in the epithelium of the loop of Henle and the narrow segment of the distal tubules — the epithelium is tall and its cytoplasm is clear and foamy (**Armanni–Ebstein change**);

**diabetic microangiopathy** — glycoproteins accumulate in the glomeruli, and **nodular (Kimmelstiel–Wilson) glomerulosclerosis** develops. **Hereditary glycogenoses** — hereditary deficiency of enzymes that break down or synthesize glycogen: **von Gierke disease** (type I, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency — glycogen in the liver and kidney), **Pompe disease** (type II, lysosomal acid maltase — heart, skeletal muscles, liver; cardiomegaly), **McArdle disease** (type V, muscle phosphorylase — skeletal muscles, pain and cramps on exertion).

blocks.text: Disturbed glycoprotein metabolism — mucous degeneration

In mucus-producing cells, **mucins and mucoids** accumulate in excess or their physicochemical properties change. Mucus gives **metachromasia** with **thionine and cresyl violet** (red-violet color with a blue dye) and is PAS-positive.

items: **Catarrhal inflammation** — increased mucus secretion in mucous membranes (rhinitis, bronchitis, gastritis): goblet cells multiply, much mucus is produced, and cells desquamate. If mucus blocks the excretory ducts, **cysts** form.

**Cystic fibrosis (mucoviscidosis)** — a hereditary disease: because of a mutation in the CFTR gene, chloride channels are defective and exocrine glands secrete **thick, viscous mucus**. The pancreatic ducts, bronchi, intestine and bile ducts become plugged, and cysts, chronic inflammation and sclerosis develop (Topic 11).
**Colloid degeneration** — accumulation of colloid in colloid-forming glands (thyroid gland) — **colloid goiter**.
In **tumors** — mucin-producing adenocarcinomas (**“signet ring cell” carcinoma** — mucus inside the cell, nucleus pushed to the periphery).

blocks.text: Stromal-vascular degenerations develop in **connective tissue** and in the walls of vessels. They occur mainly within the **histion** — the microcirculatory bed and the connective tissue around it (ground substance, fibers, cells). Therefore they are often associated with impaired **permeability of the blood–tissue barrier**.

Stromal-vascular protein degenerations include **mucoid swelling, fibrinoid change (swelling), hyalinosis** and **amyloidosis**. The first three are often **successive stages of one process**: mucoid swelling → fibrinoid swelling → hyalinosis. This sequence is called **disorganization** of connective tissue.

parts.text: Stages of connective tissue disorganization: **1) mucoid swelling** (superficial, **reversible**) → **2) fibrinoid swelling** (deep, **irreversible**) → **3) fibrinoid necrosis** → **4) hyalinosis** or sclerosis. This sequence is most evident in rheumatic diseases (rheumatic fever, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) and in arterial hypertension.

blocks.text: Mucoid swelling

**Mucoid swelling** is a **superficial and reversible disorganization** of connective tissue. **Glycosaminoglycans** (mainly hyaluronic acid) accumulate and are redistributed in the ground substance. Because glycosaminoglycans are hydrophilic, tissue and vascular permeability increases, plasma proteins (mainly globulins) and glycoproteins enter the ground substance — the ground substance **swells**. The collagen fibers are preserved but swell and split into fibrils.

**Microscopically:** the ground substance is basophilic; when stained with **toluidine blue**, it turns **violet-red** instead of dark blue — **metachromasia** (a sign of accumulation of chromotropic substances). There are no gross changes.
**Causes:** infectious-allergic diseases, **rheumatic diseases** (rheumatic fever, especially in the heart valves and endocardium), atherosclerosis, endocrinopathies.
**Outcome:** if the cause is removed, the tissue is completely **restored**; otherwise it progresses to **fibrinoid swelling**.

blocks.label: Figure 3.7
blocks.caption: Mucoid swelling: accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in connective tissue, violet-pink with toluidine blue — metachromasia (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-8)

blocks.label: Figure 3.8
blocks.caption: Fibrinoid swelling and fibrinoid necrosis: in the capillaries of a renal glomerulus (arrows) — systemic lupus erythematosus (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-9a)

blocks.text: Fibrinoid change (fibrinoid swelling and fibrinoid necrosis)

**Fibrinoid swelling** is a **deep and irreversible disorganization** of connective tissue: the ground substance and collagen fibers are destroyed, vascular permeability increases sharply, and plasma proteins, including **fibrinogen**, enter the tissue. As a result **fibrinoid** forms — a complex substance containing proteins (fibrin), polysaccharides, collagen breakdown products and often immune complexes.

**Microscopically:** the collagen fibers appear as a homogeneous, dense, **eosinophilic** structureless mass; special reactions for fibrin (Schueninov, Weigert) are positive; with the **van Gieson** method it stains **yellow** (not red like collagen); PAS-positive; metachromasia is weak or absent. Around fibrinoid swelling there is a macrophage reaction (for example, **Aschoff–Talalaev granulomas** in rheumatic fever).
The end of fibrinoid swelling is **fibrinoid necrosis** (Topic 2): complete destruction of connective tissue.
Types and causes:

items: **Infectious-allergic** — in hyperergic reactions (tuberculosis, Arthus phenomenon);
**Allergic (immunopathological)** — in **rheumatic diseases** (rheumatic fever, systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, scleroderma) and **vasculitis**;
**Angioneurotic** — fibrinoid necrosis of the walls of arterioles and arteries in **malignant arterial hypertension**;

**In chronic inflammation** — at the **floor of a chronic ulcer** of the stomach and duodenum, in appendicitis. **Outcome:** fibrinoid necrosis → sclerosis or **hyalinosis**. Organ function is impaired (for example, acute kidney injury in malignant hypertension, valvular defects in rheumatic fever).

parts.text: Distinguishing by stains: **“Mucoid — Metachromasia, Fibrinoid — Fibrin reaction, Hyaline — Homogeneous”**. In mucoid swelling toluidine blue gives a violet-red color; in fibrinoid the reactions for fibrin are positive and it is yellow with van Gieson; hyaline is a dense, homogeneous, pale pink mass, yellow or red with van Gieson.

blocks.text: Hyalinosis

**Hyalinosis** (Greek hyalos — transparent, glassy) is the accumulation in connective tissue of a mass **resembling hyaline cartilage, homogeneous, translucent and dense** — **hyaline**. Hyaline is a **fibrillar protein** containing plasma proteins (fibrin, immunoglobulins, complement), lipids and glycoproteins. It is **eosinophilic**, PAS-positive, stains yellow or red with van Gieson, and is resistant to acids, alkalis and enzymes.
Hyalinosis is often the **end result** of plasmorrhagia, fibrinoid swelling, inflammation, necrosis and sclerosis. It is divided into **vascular hyalinosis** and **connective tissue hyalinosis**.

**1. Vascular hyalinosis** — mainly in **small arteries and arterioles**. Hyaline accumulates beneath the endothelium; the vessel wall thickens, and the lumen narrows or is completely occluded. Hyaline formation results from leakage of plasma into the vessel wall (**plasmorrhagia**) and accumulation of basement membrane material.
Three types of vascular hyaline:

items: **simple hyaline** — from unchanged or slightly changed plasma components; in **benign hypertension** and atherosclerosis;
**lipohyaline** — rich in lipids and beta-lipoproteins; in **diabetes mellitus**;

**complex hyaline** — from immune complexes, fibrin and breakdown products of the vessel wall; in **immunopathological diseases** (rheumatic diseases). Vascular hyalinosis is **systemic** (in many organs) and is most pronounced in the vessels of the **kidney, brain, retina and pancreas** in hypertension and diabetes. Physiological hyalinosis occurs in the splenic arterioles (in adults and the elderly, related to the blood-storing function of the spleen) and in the ovarian corpus luteum after the menstrual cycle.

blocks.label: Figure 3.9
blocks.caption: Hyalinosis of the central artery of a splenic follicle: the wall is replaced by homogeneous pink hyaline masses (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-10a)

blocks.label: Figure 3.10
blocks.caption: Changes of arterioles in hypertension: A — hyaline arteriolosclerosis: the arteriolar wall is thickened by pink, homogeneous hyaline, and the lumen is markedly narrowed; B — hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (“onion skin”) (PAS reaction) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 11-6)

parts.text: In arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus, hyalinosis of the renal arterioles leads to ischemia and sclerosis of the glomeruli (**arteriolosclerotic nephrosclerosis**): the kidney becomes small, its surface finely granular — the “**primary contracted kidney**”, and chronic kidney disease develops as a result. Hyalinosis of the cerebral arterioles makes their walls brittle and increases the risk of **hemorrhagic stroke**.

blocks.text: **2. Connective tissue hyalinosis** — collagen fibers swell, fuse with one another and turn into a dense, homogeneous, cartilage-like mass; the cells are compressed and atrophy. It is usually the end result of fibrinoid change, inflammation and sclerosis. **Examples:**

items: **scars** (keloid scar), fibrous adhesions of serous cavities;
**heart valves** — after rheumatic endocarditis (the valves thicken and become deformed — a heart defect);
**splenic capsule** — after perisplenitis: the capsule is thickened, dense, milky white and translucent — the “**glazed (sugar-coated) spleen**”;

**pleura** (outcome of pleurisy with hyalinosis), atherosclerotic plaques, organized thrombi and infarcts. **Outcome:** usually **irreversible**; sometimes hyaline may be resorbed in keloid scars. Its functional significance depends on location: arteriolar hyalinosis — atrophy and sclerosis of the organ; hyalinosis of the heart valves — a heart defect.

blocks.text: Amyloidosis (in brief)

**Amyloidosis** is a stromal-vascular protein degeneration characterized by deposition in tissues of **amyloid** — a fibrillar protein with a **beta-pleated sheet** structure formed from **misfolded proteins**. This degeneration develops by the mechanism of **perverted synthesis**. Amyloid stains red-orange with **Congo red** and shows **apple-green** birefringence in polarized light; it turns blue-violet with iodine and sulfuric acid (Virchow reaction) and gives **metachromasia** (red with methyl violet).

The causes, classification (AL, AA, ATTR and others), pathogenesis and organ changes of amyloidosis (sago and lardaceous spleen, “large white amyloid kidney”) are discussed in detail together with diseases of the immune system in **Topic 8**.
This group includes disorders of the metabolism of **neutral fats** and of **cholesterol and its esters**.
Disorders of neutral fat metabolism
An increase in adipose tissue stores can be **generalized** or **local**.

**General obesity (adipositas)** — excessive accumulation of neutral fats in the subcutaneous tissue, omentum, mesentery, mediastinum and epicardium. The **degree of obesity** is currently assessed by the **body mass index (BMI)**: BMI = weight (kg) / height^2^ (m^2^).

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Degrees of obesity by body mass index (WHO)
head: BMI (kg/m^2^)
Assessment

parts.text: In older textbooks (Strukov), the degree of obesity was determined by the **percentage of excess weight over ideal weight**: grade I — 20–29%, II — 30–49%, III — 50–99%, IV — 100% or more. Current clinical practice uses the **WHO BMI classification**; it is useful to know both for the exam.

blocks.text: **Causes and types of obesity: alimentary** (overeating, physical inactivity), **cerebral** (damage to the hypothalamus — tumor, trauma, infection), **endocrine** (Cushing syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, insulinoma), **hereditary** (mutations of the leptin or leptin receptor gene, Laurence–Moon–Biedl syndrome). Obesity is also distinguished by **enlargement** of fat cells (hypertrophic obesity — in adults, a relatively benign course) or **an increase in their number** (hyperplastic obesity — from childhood, difficult to treat).

**Fatty infiltration of the heart (adiposity of the heart)** — in general obesity the subepicardial adipose tissue increases, envelops the heart like a “sheath” and grows into the **myocardial stroma**, between the muscle fibers. The cardiomyocytes are compressed and undergo **atrophy**. The wall of the **right ventricle** is especially affected — it can be completely replaced by adipose tissue, which may lead to **cardiac rupture**. This is an example of false hypertrophy (Topic 1).

blocks.label: Figure 3.11
blocks.caption: Fatty infiltration of the heart: a thick yellow layer of fat beneath the epicardium (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-16b)

blocks.text: Local accumulation of fat:

items: **Dercum disease** (painful lipomatosis) — painful nodular deposits of fat in the subcutaneous tissue of the limbs and trunk;
**vacant (ex vacuo) fatty replacement** — growth of adipose tissue in place of an atrophic organ (for example, in renal atrophy the perirenal adipose tissue grows and takes its place);
**lipodystrophy** — loss or increase of adipose tissue at insulin injection sites.

parts.text: In obesity, adipose tissue is not simply a “store” but an active endocrine organ: it produces leptin, adiponectin, resistin and inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6). Therefore obesity (especially the abdominal, visceral type) increases the risk of **insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, atherosclerosis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease**, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoarthritis and some cancers (endometrium, breast, colon).

blocks.text: Disorders of the metabolism of cholesterol and its esters

Disorders of the metabolism of cholesterol and its esters are most evident in **atherosclerosis**: cholesterol and lipoproteins accumulate in the intima of arteries (infiltration mechanism), forming **foam cells** (lipid-laden macrophages and smooth muscle cells) and **atheromatous plaques**. Atherosclerosis is studied in detail in systemic pathology.
Other examples:

items: **xanthomas** — collections of cholesterol-laden macrophages in the skin and tendons (yellow nodules); in familial hypercholesterolemia;
**xanthelasma** — yellow patches on the eyelids;
**cholesterolosis** — cholesterol-laden macrophages in the gallbladder mucosa (“**strawberry gallbladder**”).

blocks.label: Figure 3.12
blocks.caption: Cholesterolosis of the gallbladder: cholesterol-laden foamy macrophages in the mucosal stroma (pointer) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-31)

blocks.text: These degenerations are associated with disturbed metabolism of **glycoproteins and glycosaminoglycans**. A mucus-like substance accumulates in place of the collagen fibers of connective tissue — **mucinous change of tissues**. Connective, adipose, cartilaginous and bone tissues become translucent and mucoid, and their cells become stellate.

**Causes:** dysfunction of the endocrine glands — **myxedema** (hypofunction of the thyroid gland: mucus accumulates in the skin and in the stroma of the heart and other organs — “mucous edema”), cachexia (mucinous change of adipose tissue), chronic heart failure.
**Outcome:** the process can be reversible; if prolonged, liquefactive necrosis and cavities (**mucous cysts**) form.
Biopsy and histochemistry — how do we identify the type of degeneration?

In a hematoxylin and eosin–stained slide, **clear vacuoles** in the cytoplasm of a cell can be one of three things: **fluid** (hydropic degeneration), **fat** (dissolved during paraffin processing) or **glycogen** (dissolved in water). Histochemical reactions are used to distinguish them.

blocks.text: Clinical examples

items: **Nephrotic syndrome.** A 6-year-old child has edema, 4 g of protein in the urine per day and hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy shows **hyaline droplet**, **hydropic** and **fatty degeneration** together in the epithelium of the proximal tubules — all of them result from **infiltration** of the tubules by proteins and lipids that have passed through the glomerular filter. When the underlying disease is treated and proteinuria decreases, the tubular changes largely regress.

**Diphtheritic myocarditis.** Diphtheria exotoxin stops protein synthesis in cardiomyocytes and impairs the oxidation of fatty acids — **“tiger heart”**; myocardial contractility decreases, and there is a risk of sudden cardiac arrest in the 2nd week of the disease.

**Malignant hypertension.** A patient with a blood pressure of 240/140 mm Hg develops acute kidney injury; the biopsy shows **fibrinoid necrosis** of the afferent arterioles and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with an “onion skin” appearance.

parts.text: In **rheumatic fever** all stages of connective tissue disorganization can be observed: in an acute attack — **mucoid swelling** of the heart valves (reversible; with proper treatment the valve recovers), then **fibrinoid change** and Aschoff–Talalaev granulomas, and then **sclerosis and hyalinosis** — the valve cusps thicken and fuse with one another, and a heart defect such as **mitral stenosis** forms. Therefore early diagnosis of rheumatic fever and prevention of its recurrence (benzathine benzylpenicillin (bicillin) prophylaxis) are very important.

items: **Degeneration (dystrophy)** (Greek dys — disorder, trophe — nourishment) — the appearance of structural changes in cells and intercellular substance as a result of disturbed tissue metabolism.
**Trophism** — the set of mechanisms that ensure tissue metabolism and structural organization.
**Infiltration** — excessive entry of substances from blood and lymph into the cell or intercellular substance.
**Decomposition (phanerosis)** — breakdown of complex substances of cells and tissues, so that their components become “visible”.
**Dysproteinosis** — a degeneration associated with disturbed protein metabolism.
**Lipidosis** — a degeneration associated with disturbed fat (lipid) metabolism.
**Thesaurismosis** (Greek thesaurismos — storing) — a storage disease of substances due to hereditary enzyme deficiency.
**Hyaline** (Greek hyalos — glass) — a dense, homogeneous, translucent protein mass resembling hyaline cartilage.
**Hyperkeratosis** — excessive formation of horny substance.
**Leukoplakia** (Greek leukos — white, plax — plate) — keratinization of a nonkeratinizing mucous membrane (“white patch”).
**Metachromasia** — staining of tissue in a color different from that of the dye (violet-red with toluidine blue).
**Mucoid swelling** — a superficial, reversible disorganization of connective tissue with accumulation of glycosaminoglycans.
**Fibrinoid** — a complex fibrin-like substance containing fibrin, plasma proteins and tissue breakdown products.
**Plasmorrhagia** — leakage of plasma into and beyond the vessel wall.
**Steatosis** — accumulation of neutral fats (triglycerides) in parenchymal cells.
**Xanthoma** (Greek xanthos — yellow) — a yellow nodule composed of cholesterol-laden macrophages.
**Myxedema** — accumulation of a mucus-like substance in tissues in hypofunction of the thyroid gland.

**“Fatty degeneration of the liver (‘goose liver’)”.** The liver is enlarged, with rounded edges, a smooth surface and a soft, doughy consistency, yellowish or clay-yellow; on cutting, fat remains on the knife blade. Conclusion: parenchymal fatty degeneration.

**“Fatty degeneration of the myocardium (‘tiger heart’)”.** The heart is slightly enlarged, its cavities are dilated, and the myocardium is flabby and clay-yellow; from the endocardial side, yellow-white transverse stripes are seen in the papillary muscles. Conclusion: parenchymal fatty degeneration.

**“Fatty infiltration of the heart”.** A thick layer of fat beneath the epicardium; the adipose tissue has grown into the thickness of the myocardium, especially in the right ventricle; the myocardium is thinned. Conclusion: stromal-vascular fatty degeneration (general obesity).

**“Hyalinosis of the splenic capsule (‘glazed spleen’)”.** The splenic capsule is unevenly thickened, dense, milky white and translucent, resembling glazed pottery. Conclusion: connective tissue hyalinosis.

**“The aorta in atherosclerosis”.** Yellow spots and streaks (lipoidosis) and whitish-yellow fibrous plaques in the aortic intima. Conclusion: disturbed cholesterol metabolism (stromal-vascular fatty degeneration).
**“Colloid goiter”.** The thyroid gland is enlarged; on the cut surface there are follicles of various sizes filled with shiny, brownish-yellow colloid. Conclusion: colloid degeneration.

**“Hyaline droplet degeneration of the renal tubular epithelium”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Large, homogeneous, eosinophilic protein droplets in the cytoplasm of the proximal tubular epithelium; some cells lack a nucleus (necrosis); protein masses (casts) in the tubular lumen. Conclusion: hyaline droplet degeneration (nephrotic syndrome).

**“Hydropic degeneration of the renal tubular epithelium”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The tubular epithelium is enlarged, its cytoplasm is filled with clear vacuoles, and the nuclei are pushed to the edge or vacuolated; the vacuoles do not stain with Sudan III. Conclusion: hydropic (vacuolar) degeneration.

**“Fatty degeneration of the liver”** (stained with Sudan III). Orange-red fat droplets of various sizes in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes, especially in the center (or periphery) of the lobule; large droplets push the nucleus to the edge. With hematoxylin and eosin — “empty” vacuoles, “signet ring” cells. Conclusion: parenchymal fatty degeneration.
**“Fatty degeneration of the myocardium”** (Sudan III). Small orange fat droplets inside cardiomyocytes, focally distributed; the cross-striation is lost. Conclusion: parenchymal fatty degeneration.

**“Mucoid swelling”** (toluidine blue; for example, a heart valve in rheumatic fever). The ground substance is swollen, and the collagen fibers are swollen and split; the tissue stains violet-red (metachromasia). Conclusion: mucoid swelling.

**“Hyalinosis of the arterioles of the kidney, spleen or brain”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The arteriolar walls are thickened, with pale pink, homogeneous hyaline masses beneath the endothelium; the lumen is narrowed or occluded; the surrounding tissue is atrophic and sclerotic. Conclusion: vascular hyalinosis (hypertension or diabetes).

questions: What is degeneration (dystrophy)? State the concept of trophism and the mechanisms that maintain it.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 48-year-old man has consumed alcohol regularly for 20 years. On examination the liver extends 5 cm below the costal margin; it is smooth and painless. Ultrasound shows diffusely increased echogenicity of the liver. Liver biopsy: 60% of hepatocytes have large clear vacuoles in the cytoplasm, with nuclei pushed to the edge.
cases.ask: 1) Your histologic conclusion? 2) How can the content of the vacuoles be confirmed? 3) What is the mechanism of action of alcohol and the outcome of the process?
cases.answer: 1) Large-droplet fatty degeneration of the liver (alcoholic steatosis). 2) Staining a frozen section with Sudan III — the fat droplets stain orange-red (with hematoxylin and eosin, fat dissolves during paraffin processing and “empty” vacuoles remain). Vacuoles of hydropic degeneration do not stain with Sudan. 3) In alcohol metabolism excess NADH is formed, fatty acid oxidation decreases and triglyceride synthesis increases; delivery of fatty acids from adipose tissue increases; lipoprotein secretion is impaired. If alcohol is stopped, steatosis is reversible (within a few weeks). If drinking continues — alcoholic hepatitis (Mallory bodies, neutrophil infiltration), fibrosis and liver cirrhosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 5-year-old child was hospitalized with diphtheria. On the 12th day of the disease he died of sudden cardiac arrest. At autopsy the heart is slightly enlarged, its cavities are dilated, and the myocardium is flabby and clay-yellow; from the endocardial side, yellowish-white transverse stripes are seen in the papillary muscles.
cases.ask: 1) What is the change in the heart called? 2) Explain its mechanism. 3) What causes the stripes, and with what stain are they confirmed?
cases.answer: 1) Parenchymal fatty degeneration of the myocardium — “tiger heart” (in the setting of diphtheritic myocarditis). 2) Diphtheria exotoxin stops protein synthesis in cardiomyocytes and damages mitochondria: fatty acid oxidation decreases and the lipoprotein structures of membranes break down (decomposition) — small fat droplets appear in the cytoplasm. Contractility decreases and acute heart failure develops. 3) The fatty degeneration is focal: it develops mainly in cardiomyocytes around the venules, which are least supplied with oxygen, so the yellow stripes alternate with preserved red-brown myocardium. With Sudan III the fat inside cardiomyocytes stains orange.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 52-year-old woman has suffered from arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus for 15 years. She died of chronic kidney disease. At autopsy both kidneys are small (80 g each), firm, with a finely granular surface; on the cut surface the cortex is thinned. Microscopically, the walls of the renal arterioles are thickened, with a pale pink homogeneous mass beneath the endothelium and a markedly narrowed lumen; many glomeruli are sclerosed.
cases.ask: 1) What is the change in the arterioles called? 2) What are its types, and which of them may be present in this patient? 3) State the mechanism and name of the changes in the kidneys.
cases.answer: 1) Arteriolar hyalinosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis). 2) Types of vascular hyaline: simple hyaline (hypertension), lipohyaline (diabetes mellitus), complex hyaline (immunopathological diseases). In this patient simple hyaline and lipohyaline may be present. 3) Because of plasmorrhagia and accumulation of basement membrane material, the arterioles narrow — ischemia of the glomeruli, tubular atrophy and sclerosis develop. The kidney becomes small with a finely granular surface — arteriolosclerotic nephrosclerosis (“primary contracted kidney”); in diabetes, diabetic glomerulosclerosis is added. The result is chronic kidney disease.

topics.title: Mixed and mineral degenerations: types and pathogenetic mechanisms

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the concept and classification of mixed degenerations;
the classification of endogenous pigments: hemoglobinogenic, proteinogenic (tyrosinogenic) and lipidogenic pigments;
the formation, methods of detection and significance of hemosiderin, ferritin, bilirubin, hematoidin and hematins;
local and generalized hemosiderosis, hemochromatosis, types of jaundice (hemolytic, hepatocellular, obstructive);
disorders of melanin metabolism (Addison disease, nevus, melanoma, albinism, vitiligo);
lipofuscin and lipochrome; exogenous pigments (anthracosis);
disorders of nucleoprotein metabolism: gout, uric acid stone disease, uric acid infarct;
mineral degenerations: types of calcification (metastatic, dystrophic, metabolic), disorders of copper and potassium metabolism;
stone formation: causes, mechanism, types and complications.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of brown induration of the lung, calcification of the aortic valve, gallstones and kidney stones, and gout;
describe microscopic slides of hemosiderosis (Perls reaction), hemosiderin and hematoidin in a cerebral hemorrhage, calcification of the myocardium (calcinosis) and melanosis of the skin;
distinguish hemosiderin, lipofuscin and melanin by histochemical reactions;
distinguish the types of jaundice by clinical and laboratory signs.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Hemosiderosis** — iron accumulates mainly in **macrophages** and usually **does not damage** the tissue. **Hemochromatosis** — iron accumulates in **parenchymal cells** and **damages** them: cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy. The classic triad: **cirrhosis + diabetes + bronze skin**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Determining the type of jaundice by laboratory tests: **“Hemolysis — indirect, Obstruction — direct, Liver — both”**. Colorless (pale) stools, beer-colored urine and itching skin mean that the bile duct is **obstructed** (obstructive jaundice).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Physiological jaundice** in newborns (beginning on days 2–3 and resolving in 7–10 days) is due to the immaturity of the liver enzyme glucuronyltransferase. However, if unconjugated bilirubin is very high (hemolytic disease of the newborn), it crosses the blood–brain barrier, stains the subcortical nuclei of the brain yellow and damages them — **kernicterus (nuclear jaundice)**: severe neurological complications (Topic 11).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Distinguishing the three brown pigments is the task most often given in questions on microscopic slides: **Hemosiderin** — golden-brown, coarsely granular; **Perls-positive (blue)**; in hemorrhage and hemolysis. **Lipofuscin** — yellowish-brown, finely granular, **around the nucleus**; Perls-negative, Sudan-positive; in aging and atrophy. **Melanin** — brown-black; Perls-negative, Fontana–Masson-positive, bleached by hydrogen peroxide; in the skin, eye and melanocytic tumors.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main criterion for distinguishing the types of calcification is **blood calcium** and the **state of the tissue**: **dystrophic** — normal calcium, damaged tissue (local); **metastatic** — hypercalcemia, healthy tissue (widespread; lung, stomach, kidney); **metabolic** — normal calcium, and the tissue is not damaged either.

blocks.text: **Mixed degenerations** are degenerations in which morphologic changes occur **both in the parenchyma and in the stroma and vessel walls**. They develop as a result of disturbed metabolism of **complex proteins** — chromoproteins and nucleoproteins — and of **minerals**.

blocks.text: **Pigments** (Latin pigmentum — paint) are substances that have their own color. They are **exogenous** (entering from outside — coal dust, tattoo ink) and **endogenous** (formed in the organism). Endogenous pigments are also present normally and perform particular functions: hemoglobin — oxygen transport, melanin — protection from ultraviolet rays, cytochromes — tissue respiration.
Disorders of pigment metabolism appear in three forms: an **increase** in pigment, a **decrease (loss)** of pigment, and its **appearance** in a site where it is not normally found.

Hemoglobinogenic pigments are formed as a result of **physiological or pathologic breakdown of hemoglobin**. Red blood cells are normally broken down (after living about 120 days) mainly in macrophages of the spleen, liver and bone marrow. When hemoglobin is broken down, **heme** and **globin** separate; **iron** is released from heme and reused, and **bilirubin** is formed from the iron-free porphyrin ring.

blocks.text: Hemosiderin and hemosiderosis

**Hemosiderin** is an iron-containing **golden-yellow or yellowish-brown granular** pigment. It is formed in **macrophages** (siderophages): the macrophage engulfs red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), hemoglobin is broken down in lysosomes, and the released iron is converted to ferritin and then to hemosiderin. Cells that form hemosiderin are called **sideroblasts**, and macrophages that have accumulated it — **siderophages**. Hemosiderin stains **blue-green** with the **Perls reaction** (potassium ferrocyanide + hydrochloric acid) — **Prussian blue** is formed.
**Local hemosiderosis** — accumulation of hemosiderin in a limited area of tissue, in a focus of **hemorrhage**. Examples:

items: **a bruise (hematoma)**: its color changes from red-bluish (hemoglobin) → green (biliverdin) → yellow (bilirubin) → golden-brown (hemosiderin);
a **“rust-colored” cyst** in place of a **cerebral hemorrhage** — hemosiderin-laden macrophages in its wall and hematoidin crystals in the center;

**brown induration of the lung** — chronic venous congestion of the lung in left ventricular failure, especially in **mitral stenosis**: red blood cells pass into the alveoli by diapedesis, and alveolar macrophages engulf them and accumulate hemosiderin — these cells are called **“heart failure cells”** (heart defect cells); the lung becomes firm (**induration** — sclerosis) and brown (Topic 7).

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Pulmonary hemosiderosis (Perls reaction): blue pigment granules in the cytoplasm of histiocytes and alveolar epithelium (sideroblasts and siderophages) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-19)

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Brown induration of the lung: the lung is enlarged, brown and firm — chronic venous congestion (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Generalized hemosiderosis** — accumulation of hemosiderin in many organs as a result of **excessive intravascular breakdown of red blood cells** (**hemolysis**). Hemosiderin accumulates in macrophages of the spleen, liver, bone marrow and lymph nodes (the **reticuloendothelial system**), and also in the epithelium of the liver, kidney and lung. The organs become **rust-brown**. Causes:

items: **hemolytic anemias** (hereditary: sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, spherocytosis; acquired: autoimmune);
**infections** — malaria, sepsis, relapsing fever;
poisoning with **hemolytic poisons** (Berthollet salt (potassium chlorate), phosphorus, mushrooms);
incompatible blood **transfusion**, multiple transfusions;
hemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh incompatibility).

blocks.text: Hemochromatosis

**Hemochromatosis** is **excessive accumulation of iron** in the organism, with deposition of this iron in **parenchymal cells** (hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes, pancreatic cells), which it **damages** (through free radicals — the Fenton reaction, Topic 2). Whereas the body normally contains 2–6 g of iron, in hemochromatosis it can exceed 50 g.

items: **Primary (hereditary) hemochromatosis** is an autosomal recessive disease, most often due to mutation of the **HFE** gene (C282Y). As a result, **hepcidin** (the liver hormone that regulates iron absorption) decreases, and intestinal iron absorption increases continuously. It occurs more often and earlier in men (women lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy). • **Secondary hemochromatosis** — multiple transfusions (thalassemia), ineffective erythropoiesis, excessive iron intake, chronic liver diseases. **The clinicomorphologic triad:** 1) **pigment cirrhosis of the liver** (the liver is brown, with micronodular cirrhosis); 2) **diabetes mellitus** (damage to the pancreatic islets); 3) **skin pigmentation** (bronze color — hemosiderin and melanin). Therefore it is also called “**bronze diabetes**”. In addition, cardiomyopathy (arrhythmia, heart failure), hypogonadism and arthropathy are observed; the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma rises sharply.

blocks.label: Figure 4.3
blocks.caption: Hereditary hemochromatosis (Perls reaction — Prussian blue): iron in hepatocytes in the form of blue granules; the parenchymal architecture is still normal (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 18-25)

parts.text: **Hemosiderosis** — iron accumulates mainly in **macrophages** and usually **does not damage** the tissue. **Hemochromatosis** — iron accumulates in **parenchymal cells** and **damages** them: cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy. The classic triad: **cirrhosis + diabetes + bronze skin**.

If detected early, hemochromatosis is a disease that can be completely prevented by regular **bloodletting (phlebotomy)** — that is why serum ferritin and transferrin saturation are checked in patients' family members. In secondary hemochromatosis (thalassemia), iron-chelating drugs (**deferoxamine**) are used.

blocks.text: Bilirubin and jaundice
**Bilirubin** is the main end product of hemoglobin breakdown, a red-yellow pigment that **contains no iron**. The stages of its metabolism:

items: In macrophages, **biliverdin** and then **bilirubin** are formed from heme.
Water-insoluble **unconjugated (indirect)** bilirubin binds to **albumin** in the blood and is carried to the liver.
In hepatocytes it is **conjugated with glucuronic acid** by the enzyme **glucuronyltransferase** — water-soluble **conjugated (direct)** bilirubin is formed.
Conjugated bilirubin is excreted with bile into the intestine, where it is converted to **stercobilinogen** (stool color); part of it is absorbed and excreted in the urine as **urobilinogen**.

blocks.text: **Jaundice (icterus)** is the yellow coloring of the skin, sclera, mucous membranes, serous membranes and internal organs resulting from increased bilirubin in the blood (**hyperbilirubinemia**). Clinical jaundice becomes visible when blood bilirubin exceeds **34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL)** (normally up to 20 µmol/L).

parts.text: Determining the type of jaundice by laboratory tests: **“Hemolysis — indirect, Obstruction — direct, Liver — both”**. Colorless (pale) stools, beer-colored urine and itching skin mean that the bile duct is **obstructed** (obstructive jaundice).

**Physiological jaundice** in newborns (beginning on days 2–3 and resolving in 7–10 days) is due to the immaturity of the liver enzyme glucuronyltransferase. However, if unconjugated bilirubin is very high (hemolytic disease of the newborn), it crosses the blood–brain barrier, stains the subcortical nuclei of the brain yellow and damages them — **kernicterus (nuclear jaundice)**: severe neurological complications (Topic 11).

blocks.text: **Hematoidin** is an iron-free pigment chemically close to bilirubin, forming **bright orange crystals** (rhomboid plates or needles). It forms **outside cells**, in places that oxygen does not reach — in the center of old hematomas and infarcts. Hematoidin and hemosiderin often occur together: hematoidin in the center of the focus, hemosiderin at the periphery.
**Hematins** are an oxidized form of hemoglobin (heme), **dark brown or black** fine granules or crystals:

items: **hemomelanin (malarial pigment)** — formed by the malaria plasmodium breaking down hemoglobin in the red blood cell; it accumulates in macrophages of the spleen, liver, bone marrow and brain and gives the organs a **gray-black (slate)** color;

**hydrochloric acid hematin (hematin hydrochloride)** — formed by the action of hydrochloric acid on hemoglobin in hemorrhages and erosions of the gastric mucosa; it makes the floor of the erosion black, and the vomitus looks like **“coffee grounds”**;

**formalin pigment** — an artifact (dark brown needles) formed when blood-rich tissues are fixed in acidic formalin; it must be distinguished from pathologic pigments. **Porphyrins** are iron-free precursors of heme. In hereditary disorders of heme synthesis (**porphyrias**), porphyrins accumulate: the skin becomes extremely sensitive to light (blisters, ulcers, scars), the urine turns **red**, and the teeth and bones become reddish-brown; in acute intermittent porphyria, attacks of abdominal pain and neurological disturbances occur.

blocks.text: These pigments include **melanin, adrenochrome** and the **pigment of enterochromaffin cells**.
Melanin

**Melanin** (Greek melas — black) is a **brown-black** pigment. It is synthesized in **melanosomes** of **melanocytes** (melaninocytes) of neuroectodermal origin from the amino acid **tyrosine** via dihydroxyphenylalanine (**DOPA**), with the participation of the enzyme **tyrosinase**. Melanocytes are located in the basal layer of the epidermis, hair follicles, the iris and retina, the pia mater and the substantia nigra of the brain. Melanin synthesis is increased by pituitary melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and also by ultraviolet rays. Melanin is also often found in **melanophages** (macrophages that have engulfed melanin).

Melanin is detected with histochemical reactions: the **DOPA reaction** (melanocyte activity) and the **Fontana–Masson** method (black color with silver nitrate); it is **Perls-negative** and is **bleached** by oxidizing agents (hydrogen peroxide) — this distinguishes it from hemosiderin and lipofuscin.
Disorders of melanin metabolism:

head: Form
Type
Examples and mechanism
rows: Bilateral damage to the adrenal cortex (tuberculosis, autoimmune adrenalitis, tumor metastases, amyloidosis): cortisol decreases → by feedback, ACTH and MSH increase → bronze pigmentation of the skin; hypotension, adynamia
Hereditary defect of DNA repair; extreme sensitivity of the skin to ultraviolet rays, patchy pigmentation; skin cancers and melanoma are frequent

Melanosis of the colon (chronic constipation, laxatives); chloasma (melasma) from pregnancy and hormonal drugs; freckles (ephelides); pigmented nevus (birthmark — a benign tumor-like collection of melanocytes); melanoma — a highly malignant tumor arising from melanocytes (Topic 9)

blocks.caption: Skin in Addison disease: accumulation of melanin in the basal layer of the epidermis, numerous melanophages in the dermis (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-20b)

parts.text: **Signs of transformation of a pigmented nevus into melanoma** — the “**ABCDE**” rule: **A** (asymmetry) — asymmetry; **B** (border) — irregular border; **C** (color) — uneven color; **D** (diameter) — diameter greater than 6 mm; **E** (evolving) — change in size, shape or color. A pigmented spot with any of these signs should be removed and examined histologically.

blocks.text: **Adrenochrome** is an oxidation product of epinephrine (adrenaline) in the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla; it gives the **chromaffin reaction** (brown color with chromium salts). **Pheochromocytoma** (a catecholamine-producing tumor with attacks of arterial hypertension) develops from these cells.

**Pigment of enterochromaffin cells** — in the cells of the diffuse endocrine system of the digestive tract mucosa (associated with serotonin); **neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid)** arise from these cells.
Lipidogenic pigments are fat-protein (lipid-protein) substances; they include **lipofuscin, lipochrome, ceroid** and the **vitamin D pigment**.

**Lipofuscin** (Latin fuscus — brown) is the **“aging pigment”**, the **“wear-and-tear pigment”**. It is formed during **autophagy**: undigested membrane lipids undergo peroxidation under the action of free radicals and, together with proteins, form insoluble residual bodies (**telolysosomes**). Lipofuscin is a **yellowish-brown, finely granular** pigment, often located **around the nucleus**
(perinuclear). It stains orange with Sudan III and blue-green with the Schmorl reaction; Perls-negative.

Lipofuscin **does not itself damage the cell**, but it is a sign of **free radical injury** and cellular **aging**. It accumulates in large amounts in the **heart, liver, neurons** and skeletal muscles in the elderly, in cachexia and in chronic diseases — the organ develops **brown atrophy** (Topic 1).

blocks.label: Figure 4.5
blocks.caption: Lipofuscin granules in a cardiomyocyte: A — light microscopy (arrow — yellowish-brown granules around the nucleus); B — electron microscopy (perinuclear, intralysosomal location) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-33)

blocks.text: **Lipochrome** — **carotenoids** (pigments taken in with food) that give a yellow color to adipose tissue, the adrenal cortex, blood serum and the corpus luteum of the ovary. In cachexia, when adipose tissue decreases, the concentration of lipochrome increases and the remaining fat becomes **orange**; the yellowish tint of the skin in diabetes mellitus (xanthosis) is also related to this pigment.
**Ceroid** — a pigment close to lipofuscin formed as a result of oxidation of fats in macrophages (for example, in vitamin E deficiency, in the intestinal mucosa, in endometriosis).

parts.text: Distinguishing the three brown pigments is the task most often given in questions on microscopic slides:

items: **Hemosiderin** — golden-brown, coarsely granular; **Perls-positive (blue)**; in hemorrhage and hemolysis.
**Lipofuscin** — yellowish-brown, finely granular, **around the nucleus**; Perls-negative, Sudan-positive; in aging and atrophy.
**Melanin** — brown-black; Perls-negative, Fontana–Masson-positive, bleached by hydrogen peroxide; in the skin, eye and melanocytic tumors.

**Anthracosis** (Greek anthrax — coal) — **coal dust** that enters through the respiratory tract, is engulfed by alveolar macrophages and accumulates in the lung tissue and hilar lymph nodes. In city dwellers and smokers the lungs have black spots beneath the pleura, and the lymph nodes are black. In coal miners large amounts of dust accumulate and fibrosis develops — **anthracotic pneumoconiosis**; if silicon is added to the dust — **anthracosilicosis**.
**Tattoo** — ink introduced into the dermis of the skin is engulfed by dermal macrophages and persists for life.
**Argyria** — gray-bluish discoloration of the skin with prolonged intake of silver compounds.

blocks.text: Nucleoproteins consist of protein and nucleic acids. When their metabolism is disturbed, the end product of **purine bases** — **uric acid** — is produced in excess or excreted insufficiently (**hyperuricemia**). Uric acid and its salts (**urates**, mainly sodium urate) are deposited in tissues in the form of crystals.
Gout
**Gout** (Greek podagra: pous — foot, agra — trap, “foot trap”) is a disease characterized by deposition of **sodium urate crystals** in the joints and other tissues as a result of hyperuricemia.

items: **Primary gout** — a hereditary disorder of purine metabolism (most often reduced renal excretion of uric acid; rarely enzyme defects, for example HGPRT deficiency in Lesch–Nyhan syndrome). Mainly in **men over 30 years of age**.

**Secondary gout** — massive cell breakdown (leukemias, lymphomas, especially during **chemotherapy** of tumors — “tumor lysis syndrome”), chronic kidney disease, some drugs (thiazide diuretics). Attacks are triggered by **purine-rich food** (meat, offal), **alcohol** (especially beer), chilling, trauma and starvation.

blocks.text: Morphology:

items: **Acute gouty arthritis** — most often the **metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe** (the first attack occurs here in **90%** of cases). In the synovial fluid, **needle-shaped urate crystals** are seen inside neutrophils; in polarized light they are **negatively birefringent** (yellow). Clinically — sudden, extremely severe pain beginning at night, with redness and swelling of the joint.
**Chronic gouty arthritis** — urate deposits in the articular cartilage, synovium, tendons and periarticular tissues; joint deformity, bone erosions (a “punched-out” sign on X-ray).

**Gouty nodules (tophi)** — the pathognomonic sign of gout: an **inflammatory reaction** around a collection of urate crystals — macrophages, lymphocytes, **foreign body giant cells** and fibroblasts (a granuloma). Tophi occur in the auricle, around joints, at the elbow and knee and in tendons; if the skin thins and ruptures, a chalky white mass is discharged.

**Gouty nephropathy** — urate crystals in the renal tubules and interstitium, uric acid stones, chronic interstitial nephritis; **kidney failure** is an important cause of death in patients with gout.

blocks.label: Figure 4.6
blocks.caption: Gout: white tophi in the joint of the big toe (A — amputated toe); B — gouty tophus: reactive fibroblasts, mononuclear cells and giant cells around a collection of dissolved urate crystals (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 26-47)

blocks.label: Figure 4.7
blocks.caption: Gout: giant cell inflammatory reaction around a deposit of uric acid salts (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-22)

blocks.text: Uric acid stone disease and uric acid infarct

**Uric acid stone disease** — formation of **urate stones** in the kidneys and urinary tract; hyperuricemia and acidic urine (pH below 5.5) predispose to it. Urate stones are **radiolucent** (X-ray negative).

**Uric acid infarct** — deposits of **sodium and ammonium urate** in the kidneys (especially in the medullary papillae and collecting ducts) of newborns who **lived longer than the first 2 days** of life. On the cut surface, **yellowish-red streaks** directed toward the papillae are seen in the medulla. This is an **adaptive (physiological) state** related to the intense cell turnover of the newborn period and has no pathologic significance. The word “infarct” is used here in the sense of **stuffing** (Latin infarcire) — there is no necrosis.

parts.text: In forensic medical practice, finding a uric acid infarct in the kidney of a newborn shows that the infant **was born alive and lived for at least 2 days**.

blocks.text: Minerals are part of cell structures, enzymes, hormones and pigments and maintain acid–base balance. To detect minerals in tissues, microincineration (spectrography), histochemical reactions and X-ray microspectral analysis are used.
Disorders of calcium metabolism — calcification (calcinosis)

**Calcification (calcinosis, petrification)** is the **precipitation** of calcium salts (mainly **calcium phosphate** — hydroxyapatite, less often calcium carbonate) from a dissolved state and their accumulation in tissues. With hematoxylin and eosin, calcium is **basophilic (blue-violet)**, **amorphous or granular**; it stains **black** with the **von Kossa** method (silver nitrate) and red with alizarin red. Grossly — whitish, stone-hard foci; the knife grates when cutting.
By mechanism, three types of calcification are distinguished:

**1. Dystrophic calcification** — deposition of calcium salts in **injured, necrotic or altered tissues** when **blood calcium is normal**. The cause is **local** physicochemical changes: alkalinization of the tissue, increased alkaline phosphatase activity, changes in collagen and elastic fibers, and phospholipids in the membranes of dead cells (a nucleation site for calcium crystallization). Calcium salts first accumulate in mitochondria and membrane vesicles. As a result **petrifications** form. Examples:

items: foci of caseous necrosis (in tuberculosis — the **Ghon focus**, calcified lymph nodes);
**atherosclerotic plaques** (atherocalcinosis);
**heart valves** — rheumatic defects, **calcific aortic stenosis** in the elderly;
infarcts, old thrombi (**phleboliths** — vein stones), dead parasites (echinococcus, trichinellae);
a dead fetus — **lithopedion** (“stone child”);
in some tumors — **psammoma bodies** (concentrically laminated calcium granules: papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous carcinoma of the ovary, meningioma).

blocks.label: Figure 4.8
blocks.caption: Dystrophic calcification of the aortic valve: the valve cusps are thickened and fibrotic, with irregularly accumulated calcium masses behind them (calcific aortic stenosis) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 2-34)

blocks.label: Figure 4.9
blocks.caption: Dystrophic calcification of an arterial wall: calcium deposits in the thickness of an atherosclerotic plaque (arrows) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-23)

blocks.text: **2. Metastatic calcification (calcium metastases)** — widespread deposition of calcium salts in **normal (healthy) tissues** as a result of **hypercalcemia**. Causes of hypercalcemia:

items: **excess parathyroid hormone** — parathyroid adenoma (**hyperparathyroidism**), production of a parathyroid hormone–related protein by tumors;
**bone destruction** — bone metastases, multiple myeloma, leukemias, prolonged immobilization, Paget disease;
**vitamin D intoxication**, sarcoidosis (macrophages activate vitamin D);

**chronic kidney disease** — phosphate retention develops, with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Calcium salts are deposited most often in organs that **excrete acid** and whose tissue is therefore **more alkaline**: the **lungs** (alveolar walls), the **gastric** mucosa (fundic glands), the **kidneys** (tubules — **nephrocalcinosis**), and also the **myocardium**, arterial walls and pulmonary veins. Calcium first accumulates inside cells — in mitochondria and phagolysosomes — and then in the intercellular substance.

blocks.label: Figure 4.10
blocks.caption: Calcium metastases in the myocardium: A — calcified muscle fibers (black), microscopic view; B — calcium salts in mitochondrial cristae (electron micrograph) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 2-23a)

blocks.text: **3. Metabolic (interstitial) calcification** — deposition of calcium when blood calcium is normal and there is no evident local tissue damage. The cause is the inability of tissue buffer systems to hold calcium (disturbed calcium–phosphorus metabolism). There are two types: **systemic** (generalized) — in the skin, subcutaneous tissue, tendons, fasciae and muscles; **limited** — calcium plates in the skin and subcutaneous tissue, most often of the fingers and toes (“**calcium gout**”). It is caused by disorders of calcium–phosphorus metabolism and diseases such as scleroderma.

parts.text: The main criterion for distinguishing the types of calcification is **blood calcium** and the **state of the tissue**: **dystrophic** — normal calcium, damaged tissue (local); **metastatic** — hypercalcemia, healthy tissue (widespread; lung, stomach, kidney); **metabolic** — normal calcium, and the tissue is not damaged either.

blocks.text: **Changes in the calcium content of bone: osteoporosis** — a decrease in bone mass, the bones become brittle (old age, menopause, glucocorticoids, immobilization); **osteomalacia** and **rickets** — insufficient mineralization of the bone matrix in vitamin D deficiency.
Disorders of copper metabolism — Wilson–Konovalov disease

**Hepatocerebral degeneration (Wilson–Konovalov disease)** is an autosomal recessive disease: because of mutation of the **ATP7B** gene, excretion of copper into the bile and its incorporation into **ceruloplasmin** are impaired. Copper accumulates in the liver, then in the brain (especially the **subcortical nuclei** — the lentiform nucleus), the cornea and the kidneys.

items: **Liver**: fatty degeneration, chronic hepatitis, **liver cirrhosis** (sometimes acute liver failure);
**Brain**: death of neurons in the subcortical nuclei, cysts — tremor, movement disorders, mental changes;

**Eye**: a green-brown ring at the edge of the cornea — the **Kayser–Fleischer ring**. Serum ceruloplasmin is decreased, and urinary copper is increased. Copper in tissue is detected with **rhodanine**. Treatment — copper-chelating drugs (penicillamine) and liver transplantation.

blocks.text: Disorders of potassium metabolism

items: **Hyperkalemia** — kidney failure, Addison disease, extensive tissue necrosis (rhabdomyolysis), tumor lysis; risk of **cardiac arrest** (asystole).

**Hypokalemia** — diarrhea, vomiting, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism; muscle weakness, arrhythmias, **hypokalemic (vacuolar) nephropathy** in the kidney; **paroxysmal myoplegia** — episodic muscle paralysis in a hereditary disorder of potassium metabolism.

blocks.text: **Stones (concretions, calculi)** are **dense (hard) structures** formed from substances contained in fluids in the cavities of hollow organs or in the excretory ducts of glands. Stones form most often in the **gallbladder and bile ducts** (**cholelithiasis** — gallstone disease) and the **urinary tract** (**urolithiasis** — urinary stone disease), and less often in the salivary glands, pancreatic ducts, bronchi (**broncholiths**), intestine (**coproliths**) and vessels (**phleboliths** — calcified thrombi).
Causes and mechanism of stone formation:

items: **general factors** — metabolic disorders (of cholesterol, calcium, uric acid, oxalate, cystine), hereditary predisposition, dietary features, obesity;

**local factors** — **stasis** of secretions (impaired outflow from a cavity), **inflammation** (desquamated mucosal cells, bacteria and proteins become the **organic matrix** of the stone and a crystallization center), and changes in the composition and pH of secretions. Stone formation consists of two processes: formation of an **organic matrix (nucleus)** and **crystallization of salts** (precipitation) on it.
