blocks.text: Complications of stones:

items: **obstruction** of a hollow organ or duct: in the bile ducts — **obstructive jaundice**, in the kidney — **hydronephrosis** (pressure atrophy), colicky pain (**biliary and renal colic**);
**pressure ulcer** of the wall (necrosis from pressure) and **perforation** — peritonitis, fistulas (for example, cholecystoenteric fistula, “gallstone ileus”);
secondary **inflammation**: cholecystitis, cholangitis, pyelonephritis; if the pancreatic duct is obstructed — **acute pancreatitis**;
risk of **gallbladder cancer** against the background of long-standing chronic inflammation.

blocks.text: One hemorrhage — three different pigments

A patient with a cerebral hemorrhage died of pneumonia 3 months later. At autopsy, in place of the hemorrhage a **cyst** with **rust-brown** walls filled with yellow-brown fluid was found. Microscopically: macrophages laden with **hemosiderin** (blue with the Perls reaction) in the cyst wall; in the central part — **orange hematoidin crystals** lying outside cells; in the glia around the cyst — **foamy macrophages** that have engulfed lipids (“granular bodies”). This picture reflects the age of the hemorrhage and the stages of its resorption.
Jaundice — where is the “breakdown”?

items: **A young woman** has anemia, an enlarged spleen, increased **unconjugated** bilirubin in the blood and no bilirubin in the urine — **hemolytic jaundice** (for example, hereditary spherocytosis). Prolonged hemolysis can lead to **pigment gallstones**.
**A student** develops jaundice after fever and weakness, ALT is 1500 U/L, and both fractions are increased in the blood — **hepatocellular jaundice** (viral hepatitis).

**A 65-year-old man** has gradually increasing painless jaundice, itching of the skin, colorless stools and an enlarged gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) — **obstructive jaundice**; the cause is most often **cancer of the head of the pancreas**.

parts.text: **Metastatic calcification** is a serious problem in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis: calcification of vessel walls (cardiovascular complications), calcification of skin vessels (**calciphylaxis** — skin necrosis and ulcers). Therefore serum calcium, phosphorus and parathyroid hormone are regularly monitored in such patients.

items: **Pigments** (Latin pigmentum — paint) — substances that have their own color; they are exogenous and endogenous.
**Hemosiderin** — an iron-containing golden-brown pigment formed in macrophages during the breakdown of hemoglobin.
**Hemosiderosis** — excessive accumulation of hemosiderin in tissues (local or generalized).
**Hemochromatosis** — a disease characterized by accumulation of iron in parenchymal cells, which it damages (“bronze diabetes”).
**Hematoidin** — an iron-free orange crystalline pigment formed under anaerobic conditions in the center of a hemorrhage.
**Icterus (jaundice)** — yellow coloring of tissues as a result of hyperbilirubinemia.
**Kernicterus (nuclear jaundice)** — staining and damage of the subcortical nuclei of the brain by bilirubin in newborns.
**Siderophage** — a macrophage that has accumulated hemosiderin.
**Melanin** (Greek melas — black) — a brown-black pigment synthesized from tyrosine in melanocytes.
**Melanosis** — excessive accumulation of melanin.
**Albinism** (Latin albus — white) — congenital absence of melanin synthesis due to tyrosinase deficiency.
**Vitiligo** — appearance of depigmented white patches on the skin as a result of destruction of melanocytes.
**Lipofuscin** (Latin fuscus — brown) — the “aging pigment” formed from the residues of autophagy.
**Anthracosis** (Greek anthrax — coal) — accumulation of coal dust in the lungs and lymph nodes.
**Gout** (Greek podagra: pous — foot, agra — trap) — a disease characterized by hyperuricemia and deposition of urate crystals.
**Tophus** — a granulomatous nodule formed around a collection of urate crystals in gout.
**Calcinosis (calcification, petrification)** — deposition of calcium salts in tissues.
**Petrification** (Greek petra — stone) — a calcified focus of necrosis.
**Psammoma bodies** (Greek psammos — sand) — concentrically laminated calcium granules found in some tumors.
**Lithopedion** — a dead and calcified fetus (“stone child”).
**Concretion (stone, calculus)** — a hard structure formed by precipitation of substances in hollow organs and ducts.
**Cholelithiasis** — gallstone disease.
**Urolithiasis (nephrolithiasis)** — urinary (kidney) stone disease.
**Phlebolith** — a calcified thrombus in a vein (“vein stone”).

**“Brown induration of the lung”.** The lung is enlarged and firm; on the cut surface it is rust-brown with small brown spots. Conclusion: local hemosiderosis and sclerosis (chronic venous congestion — mitral valve defect).
**“Cyst in place of a cerebral hemorrhage (‘rust-colored cyst’)”.** A smooth-walled cavity in the brain tissue, with a rust-brown wall. Conclusion: local hemosiderosis.

**“Calcification of the aortic valve”.** The valve cusps are thickened, deformed and stone-hard, with whitish calcium masses; the valve orifice is narrowed. Conclusion: dystrophic calcification (calcific aortic stenosis).
**“Atherocalcinosis”.** Hard, whitish, brittle calcified plaques in the aortic intima; they grate when cut. Conclusion: dystrophic calcification.

**“Gallbladder stones (cholelithiasis)”.** The gallbladder wall is thickened; its cavity contains multifaceted yellowish (cholesterol) or small black (pigment) stones. Conclusion: gallstone disease, chronic cholecystitis.

**“Kidney stones, hydronephrosis”.** A large stone (sometimes staghorn) in the renal pelvis; the pelvis and calyces are dilated, and the parenchyma is thinned. Conclusion: nephrolithiasis, hydronephrosis.
**“Gout”.** Nodules with a white, chalky mass (tophi) around a joint and in the auricle. Conclusion: gout.
**“Uric acid infarct in the kidney of a newborn”.** Yellowish-red streaks in the medulla directed toward the papillae. Conclusion: uric acid infarct (a physiological state).

**“Pulmonary hemosiderosis (brown induration of the lung)”** (hematoxylin and eosin and Perls reaction). The interalveolar septa are thickened (sclerosis), and the capillaries are dilated and filled with blood; macrophages with golden-brown granular pigment in the alveolar spaces and septa (“heart failure cells”); the pigment is blue with the Perls reaction. Conclusion: local hemosiderosis.

**“Cerebral hemorrhage”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Hemolyzed blood surrounded by hemosiderin-laden macrophages; orange hematoidin crystals in the center. Conclusion: hemorrhage, hemosiderosis and hematoidin.

**“Calcification of the myocardium (calcium metastases)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Dark violet-blue, amorphous calcium deposits in some cardiomyocytes and in the stroma between them. Conclusion: metastatic calcification.
**“Gouty tophus”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Amorphous or needle-shaped crystalline masses (urate) surrounded by foreign body giant cells, macrophages, lymphocytes and fibrosis. Conclusion: gout.

**“Skin in Addison disease”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Numerous brown-black melanin granules in the cells of the basal layer of the epidermis, melanophages in the dermis. Conclusion: generalized acquired hyperpigmentation (melanosis).
**“Brown atrophy of the liver (lipofuscinosis)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Fine yellowish-brown granules around the nuclei of hepatocytes (see Topic 1). Conclusion: accumulation of lipofuscin.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 50-year-old man has an enlarged liver, diabetes mellitus has been diagnosed, and his skin is bronze-gray; his libido is decreased. Serum ferritin is sharply elevated, and transferrin saturation with iron is 85%. Liver biopsy: golden-brown granular pigment in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes, fibrosis of the portal tracts.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) How is the pigment detected, and in which cells has it accumulated? 3) State the mechanism and complications of the disease.
cases.answer: 1) Hereditary (primary) hemochromatosis — “bronze diabetes”. 2) The pigment is hemosiderin; it stains blue (Prussian blue) with the Perls reaction; it has accumulated in parenchymal cells (hepatocytes, pancreatic cells, cardiomyocytes) — this distinguishes hemochromatosis from hemosiderosis. 3) Mutation of the HFE gene leads to decreased hepcidin and a continuous increase in intestinal iron absorption. Iron generates free radicals, damages cells and causes fibrosis. Complications: pigment cirrhosis of the liver, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes mellitus, cardiomyopathy (arrhythmia, heart failure), hypogonadism, arthropathy. Treatment — regular phlebotomy.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 58-year-old man woke up at night with sudden, extremely severe pain in the joint of his right big toe; the joint is red and swollen. Yesterday at a wedding he ate a lot of meat and drank alcohol. Blood uric acid is high. He has had such attacks several times before, and there are small hard white nodules on his auricle.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What are the nodules on the auricle, and what is their microscopic structure? 3) To which type of degeneration does the disease belong, and what are its complications?
cases.answer: 1) Gout — an attack of acute gouty arthritis (triggered by purine-rich food and alcohol). 2) Tophi — collections of sodium urate crystals surrounded by foreign body giant cells, macrophages, lymphocytes and fibrosis (a granulomatous reaction). In the synovial fluid, needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent in polarized light are found inside neutrophils. 3) A disorder of nucleoprotein metabolism (mixed degeneration). Complications: chronic gouty arthritis and joint deformity, gouty nephropathy, uric acid stones and kidney failure.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 60-year-old woman has been diagnosed with a parathyroid adenoma; blood calcium and parathyroid hormone are high. The patient died of kidney failure. At autopsy the skeletal bones are softened; there are numerous calcium deposits in the lungs, gastric mucosa and renal tubules, and stones in the kidneys.
cases.ask: 1) What is the change in the organs called? 2) Why are these particular organs affected? 3) How can it be distinguished from dystrophic calcification?
cases.answer: 1) Metastatic calcification (calcium metastases) — hypercalcemia due to hyperparathyroidism; nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis in the kidney. 2) The lungs, stomach and kidneys excrete acid, so their tissue is more alkaline, which creates favorable conditions for the precipitation of calcium salts. 3) In dystrophic calcification, blood calcium is normal and calcium is deposited only in injured or necrotic tissue (atherosclerotic plaque, caseous focus, valve); in metastatic calcification there is hypercalcemia, and calcium is deposited widely in healthy tissues.

topics.title: Inflammation and repair. Definition and general manifestations of inflammation. Acute inflammation. Types

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the definition, biological essence, causes and classification of inflammation;
the local and general (systemic) signs of inflammation;
the phases of inflammation: alteration, exudation, proliferation;
the cellular and plasma mediators of inflammation and their effects;
vascular and leukocyte reactions in acute inflammation (margination, adhesion, emigration, chemotaxis, phagocytosis);
the differences between exudate and transudate;

the types of exudative inflammation: serous, fibrinous (croupous, diphtheritic), purulent (abscess, phlegmon, empyema), putrefactive, hemorrhagic, catarrhal and mixed — their causes, morphology and outcomes;
the outcomes of acute inflammation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of fibrinous pericarditis (“hairy heart”), fibrinous pleurisy, diphtheritic colitis, catarrhal tracheitis, apostematous nephritis, purulent leptomeningitis, lung abscess and phlegmonous appendicitis;
describe microscopic slides of serous, croupous and diphtheritic inflammation, purulent leptomeningitis, kidney abscess and hemorrhagic pneumonia;
identify the type of exudate by its cellular composition;
relate the type of inflammation to the clinical situation.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Inflammation is a **protective** reaction: without it, infections would spread uncontrollably and wounds would not heal. At the same time, inflammation can also be **harmful**: it underlies many diseases (anaphylactic reactions, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, pulmonary fibrosis). Being able to distinguish the protective and damaging sides of the inflammatory process is the basis of clinical thinking.

The Robbins textbook does not distinguish such a type — these changes are considered as necrosis and cell injury. Many current sources also use the term **necrotic inflammation** instead of alterative inflammation.

summary.text: In **diphtheria** the type of inflammation depends on location: in the **pharynx and tonsils** (stratified squamous epithelium) — **diphtheritic** inflammation: the membrane is firmly attached and does not block the airway, but much toxin is absorbed (myocarditis, neuritis); in the **larynx, trachea and bronchi** (columnar epithelium) — **croupous** inflammation: the membrane detaches easily and blocks the airway — **true croup**, asphyxia. This is why both types can occur in one disease.

blocks.text: **Inflammation** (Latin inflammatio, Greek phlogosis) is a **complex protective-adaptive vascular-mesenchymal reaction** of the organism that arises in response to an injurious agent and is aimed at eliminating or limiting it and restoring the damaged tissue. Inflammation occurs only in multicellular organisms with blood vessels; at its center are the **microcirculatory bed** and **leukocytes**.

parts.text: Inflammation is a **protective** reaction: without it, infections would spread uncontrollably and wounds would not heal. At the same time, inflammation can also be **harmful**: it underlies many diseases (anaphylactic reactions, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, pulmonary fibrosis). Being able to distinguish the protective and damaging sides of the inflammatory process is the basis of clinical thinking.

blocks.text: The classic local signs of inflammation:

items: **redness** (rubor), **swelling** (tumor), **local heat** (calor), **pain** (dolor) — the Roman scholar **A.C. Celsus** (1st century AD);
**loss of function** (functio laesa) — added by R. Virchow (19th century).

blocks.text: These signs are based on vascular reactions: redness and heat — **arterial hyperemia**; swelling — **exudation**; pain — irritation and compression of nerve endings by mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins) and edema.

**From history.** The protective role of **phagocytosis** in inflammation was discovered by the Russian scientist **I.I. Mechnikov** (1882; Nobel Prize, 1908). J. Cohnheim described the emigration of leukocytes through the vessel wall. T. Lewis established the effect of histamine on vascular permeability and laid the foundation for the doctrine of **mediators**.
Causes of inflammation

items: **Infections** (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites and their toxins) — the most common cause;
**tissue necrosis** — ischemia (infarction), trauma, physical and chemical agents (burns, frostbite, radiation, acids, alkalis);
**foreign bodies** — dust particles, suture material, crystals (urates);
**immune reactions** (hypersensitivity) — allergy, autoimmune diseases.

blocks.text: Classification of inflammation

blocks.title: Table 5.1. Classification of inflammation
head: Feature
Types
rows: Acute (from a few hours to 4–6 weeks), chronic (months, years), subacute
Alterative (alteration predominates), exudative (exudation predominates), productive (proliferative) (cell proliferation predominates)
Serous, fibrinous, purulent, putrefactive, hemorrhagic, catarrhal, mixed
Banal (nonspecific) — caused by various agents; specific — a particular causative agent forms characteristic granulomas (tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, scleroma)
The Latin or Greek suffix -itis is added to the name of the organ: gastritis, hepatitis, nephritis, myocarditis; some have special names — pneumonia, tonsillitis (angina), panaritium

parts.text: **Alterative inflammation** is given as a separate type in the textbooks of Strukov and Abdullakhodjaeva: in it tissue damage (degeneration, necrosis) predominates, while exudation and proliferation are weak (for example, the myocardium in diphtheria, parenchymal organs in tuberculosis and viral hepatitis). The Robbins textbook does not distinguish such a type — these changes are considered as necrosis and cell injury. Many current sources also use the term **necrotic inflammation** instead of alterative inflammation.

blocks.text: Inflammation consists of three closely interrelated phases:

items: **Alteration (damage)** — the initial phase: degeneration and necrosis of cells and intercellular substance; in this phase **mediators** are released and initiate inflammation.

**Exudation** — the reaction of the microcirculatory bed: increased vascular permeability, escape of the fluid part of the blood and of blood cells from the vessels (formation of **exudate**), phagocytosis.

**Proliferation (productive phase)** — proliferation of cells in the focus of inflammation (macrophages, fibroblasts, endothelium), formation of granulation tissue and restoration of the damaged tissue (repair).

blocks.text: **Mediators of inflammation** are biologically active substances formed or activated in the focus of inflammation that regulate its vascular and cellular reactions. They are divided into **cellular** (tissue) and **plasma** mediators.

parts.text: The main signs and their mediators: **fever — IL-1, TNF, PGE~2~**; **pain — bradykinin, PGE~2~**; **vasodilation — histamine, prostaglandins, NO**; **permeability — histamine, bradykinin, C3a/C5a, leukotrienes**; **chemotaxis — C5a, LTB~4~, IL-8, bacterial peptides** (“**5-4-8**” — C**5**a, LTB**4**, IL-**8**).

Aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) block **cyclooxygenase** and reduce prostaglandin synthesis — they relieve pain, fever and inflammation. Glucocorticoids block the release of arachidonic acid (phospholipase A~2~) and the synthesis of cytokines — therefore their anti-inflammatory effect is much stronger, but they also suppress immunity.

blocks.text: 1. Changes in blood flow and vessel caliber:

items: **brief arteriolar spasm** (a few seconds, neuroreflex);
**arterial hyperemia** — arterioles dilate (histamine, NO), new capillaries open; **redness and heat**;

**venous hyperemia and slowing of blood flow** — fluid escapes because of increased permeability and the blood thickens; red cells accumulate (**stasis**); leukocytes line up along the vessel wall (**margination**).

blocks.text: **2. Increased vascular permeability** is the most important feature of acute inflammation. Mechanisms:

items: **contraction of endothelial cells** — gaps appear between endothelial cells in venules; under the action of histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes it develops **rapidly** (in 15–30 minutes) and is short-lived — the **most common** mechanism;
**direct injury to the endothelium** — burns, toxins: the endothelium undergoes necrosis and detaches; it begins immediately and lasts a long time;
**leukocyte-mediated injury** — enzymes and ROS of activated leukocytes damage the endothelium;

increased **transcytosis** (under the action of VEGF), the “leaky” wall of newly formed capillaries. **3. Reaction of lymphatic vessels** — lymph flow increases; secondary inflammation of lymphatic vessels (**lymphangitis**) and reactive inflammation of lymph nodes (**lymphadenitis**) may develop (for example, red streaks on the forearm and enlarged axillary lymph nodes after a hand wound).

blocks.text: Exudate and transudate

blocks.title: Table 5.3. Differences between exudate and transudate
head: Feature
Exudate
Transudate
rows: Increased hydrostatic pressure or decreased oncotic pressure (without inflammation)
Hydrothorax and ascites in heart failure; ascites in nephrotic syndrome and liver cirrhosis

blocks.text: The main cells of acute inflammation are **neutrophils** (in the first 6–24 hours); later (from 24–48 hours) they are replaced by **monocytes-macrophages**. Neutrophils are numerous and respond quickly but live briefly (undergo apoptosis); macrophages live long and can proliferate. There are some exceptions: in viral infections lymphocytes arrive first, and in allergic reactions eosinophils predominate.
Escape of leukocytes from vessels (extravasation)

items: **Margination** — when blood flow slows, leukocytes move from the center of the vessel to the periphery (to the endothelial surface).

**Rolling** — leukocytes “roll” along the endothelium: endothelial **selectins** (E-selectin, P-selectin) bind **weakly** to carbohydrate ligands on the surface of leukocytes. Selectin expression is increased by histamine, TNF and IL-1.
**Firm adhesion** — **integrins** on the surface of leukocytes (LFA-1, VLA-4) are activated by chemokines and bind firmly to endothelial ligands (**ICAM-1, VCAM-1**).

**Transmigration (diapedesis)** — leukocytes pass mainly in **postcapillary venules** between endothelial cells (with the help of **PECAM-1 / CD31** molecules) and pierce the basement membrane with the help of collagenases.

**Chemotaxis** — movement of leukocytes toward increasing concentrations of **chemotactic factors** — to the focus of injury. Exogenous chemoattractants are bacterial peptides (N-formylmethionine); endogenous ones are **C5a, LTB~4~, IL-8** and other chemokines.

parts.text: Stages of leukocyte extravasation — **“Roll, Adhere, Transmigrate, Chase”**: **R**olling — **S**electins; **A**dhesion — **I**ntegrins (ICAM-1); **T**ransmigration — **P**ECAM-1 (CD31); **C**hemotaxis — following the signal (C5a, LTB~4~, IL-8). In short: **“S-I-P”**.

In children with **hereditary defects of leukocyte adhesion** (LAD-1 — defect of the beta-2 chain of integrins; LAD-2 — defect of the selectin ligand), leukocytes cannot leave the vessels: there are very many leukocytes in the blood, but **no pus forms** in the focus of inflammation; recurrent severe bacterial infections and delayed separation of the umbilical cord stump are observed.

blocks.text: Phagocytosis

**Phagocytosis** is the engulfment and digestion of foreign particles, microbes and tissue debris by special cells (phagocytes). I.I. Mechnikov divided phagocytes into **microphages** (neutrophils) and **macrophages**. Stages of phagocytosis:

items: **Recognition and attachment** — phagocyte receptors recognize microbes directly (mannose receptors, “scavenger” receptors, Toll-like receptors) or through **opsonins**. The main opsonins are **IgG** (via the Fc receptor), the **C3b** fragment of complement and mannose-binding lectin.
**Engulfment** — the phagocyte surrounds the microbe with pseudopodia, and a **phagosome** forms; it fuses with a lysosome to become a **phagolysosome**.

**Killing and degradation:** – **the oxygen-dependent mechanism** (the most effective) — the “**respiratory burst**”: NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase) produces superoxide and H~2~O~2~; **myeloperoxidase**, in the presence of chloride ions, converts H~2~O~2~ into the potent bactericidal **hypochlorite (HOCl^−^)**; – **nitric oxide** (in macrophages) and peroxynitrite; – **the oxygen-independent mechanism** — lysosomal enzymes (lysozyme, elastase), defensins, cathelicidins, lactoferrin, major basic protein of eosinophils. 4. **Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)** — neutrophils form a net of chromatin and antimicrobial proteins that traps microbes (with neutrophil death). **Complete phagocytosis** — the engulfed microbe is killed and digested. **Incomplete phagocytosis (endocytobiosis)** — the microbe survives and even multiplies inside the phagocyte; this is characteristic of tubercle mycobacteria, gonococci, leishmaniae and the causative agent of leprosy. In such cases the phagocyte becomes a “vehicle” that spreads infection through the organism.

parts.text: **Chronic granulomatous disease** — a hereditary defect of NADPH oxidase (most often X-linked): phagocytes engulf microbes, but because there is no “respiratory burst” they cannot kill catalase-positive microbes (staphylococcus, Aspergillus) — recurrent severe infections and granulomas. **Chédiak–Higashi syndrome** — impaired fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes (giant granules), albinism and infections.

blocks.text: Local inflammation affects the whole organism — the **acute phase reaction** (systemic inflammatory response). It develops under the action of cytokines (**TNF, IL-1, IL-6**) and prostaglandins:

items: **fever** — cytokines (endogenous pyrogens) increase PGE~2~ synthesis in the hypothalamus and raise the “set point” of the thermoregulatory center;

**acute phase proteins** — the liver increases synthesis of **C-reactive protein (CRP)**, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A (SAA) and hepcidin; fibrinogen makes red cells stick together in “stacks” (rouleaux) — the **ESR increases**; in chronic inflammation SAA leads to **AA amyloidosis**, and hepcidin to **anemia**;

**leukocytosis** — leukocytes increase in the blood (neutrophils in bacterial infections, a left shift — young forms); **lymphocytosis** in viral infections, **eosinophilia** in allergy and parasitic diseases; in some infections (typhoid fever, some viruses) — **leukopenia**;
tachycardia, changes in blood pressure, chills, loss of appetite, drowsiness, weakness;
in severe bacterial infection — **sepsis**: excessive release of cytokines leads to **septic shock**, DIC and multiple organ failure (Topic 7).

blocks.text: In exudative inflammation, **exudate formation** predominates. By the composition of the exudate, the types are as follows:

Composition of the exudate
Main causes
Examples
rows: Protein 2–5%, few cells; clear or slightly cloudy
Burns, viruses, toxins, allergy, tuberculosis (in serous membranes)
Burn blister, serous pleurisy, serous meningitis, viral rhinitis, pneumonia with serous exudate
Much fibrinogen — a fibrin membrane forms in the tissue
Diphtheria, dysentery, pneumococcus, tuberculosis, uremia (endogenous intoxication), mercuric chloride poisoning
Croupous (lobar) pneumonia, “hairy heart”, diphtheria, dysentery (diphtheritic colitis)

War wounds, gangrenous lung, gangrenous appendicitis
Highly virulent infections that damage the vessel wall

Infections (ARVI), allergy, thermal and chemical influences

blocks.text: Serous inflammation

The exudate is a **serous fluid**: 2–5% protein (mainly albumins), a few neutrophils, desquamated epithelial or mesothelial cells. The exudate accumulates in **serous cavities** (serous pleurisy, pericarditis, peritonitis, arthritis), **mucous membranes** (serous catarrh), the **skin** (blisters in burns and viral infections — fluid accumulates beneath or within the epidermis) and the stroma of **parenchymal organs** (serous interstitial inflammation — liver, myocardium, kidney).

**The outcome** is usually **favorable**: the exudate is resorbed. But sometimes it is dangerous because of its location: cardiac tamponade in serous pericarditis; brain edema in serous inflammation of the meninges (serous meningitis); in the larynx — edema and asphyxia. If prolonged in serous cavities — adhesions; in parenchymal organs — diffuse sclerosis.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Serous rhinitis: the nasal mucosa is edematous, with serous exudate and a few inflammatory cells in the stroma (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-7)

blocks.text: Fibrinous inflammation

The exudate contains much **fibrinogen**, which is converted to **fibrin** in the damaged (necrotic) tissue. Tissue thromboplastin accelerates fibrin formation. Fibrinous inflammation develops mainly in **mucous and serous membranes**, less often in the thickness of an organ (in the lung). A **whitish-gray membrane (film)** forms on the surface of the mucous or serous membrane. By the depth of necrosis and the type of lining epithelium, there are two types:

**1. Croupous inflammation** (Scottish croup — membrane) — necrosis is **superficial**, the fibrin membrane is **thin** and **loosely** attached to the underlying tissue; it **detaches easily**, leaving a superficial defect. It occurs in mucous membranes lined by simple (columnar) epithelium or in serous membranes:

items: **in the trachea and bronchi** — croupous tracheitis and bronchitis in diphtheria: the membranes can detach and block the lumen of the bronchi — **true croup** (risk of asphyxia);
**in the lung** — **croupous (lobar) pneumonia** (pneumococcus; a whole lobe is affected);

**in serous membranes** — fibrinous pleurisy, peritonitis, **pericarditis**: the pericardial surface is rough and covered with hairlike fibrin threads — the **“hairy heart”** (cor villosum); on auscultation — a **pericardial friction rub**; causes — uremia (chronic kidney disease), rheumatic fever, myocardial infarction, tuberculosis.

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Fibrinous epicarditis: the epicardium is dull and rough, with hairlike gray-yellowish fibrin deposits (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Fibrinous pericarditis (“hairy heart”): A — fibrin deposits on the pericardial surface; B — a network of pink fibrinous exudate (F) covering the pericardial surface, P — pericardium (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-14)

blocks.text: **2. Diphtheritic inflammation** (Greek diphthera — leather membrane) — necrosis is **deep**, the fibrin membrane is **thick**, penetrates deep into the necrotic tissue and is **firmly** attached to the underlying tissue; the membrane **detaches with difficulty**, leaving a deep **ulcer**. It occurs in mucous membranes lined by **stratified squamous epithelium** (oral cavity, pharynx, **tonsils**, esophagus, vagina, cervix) and in places where the subepithelial tissue is looser (**colon** — dysentery).

parts.text: In **diphtheria** the type of inflammation depends on location: in the **pharynx and tonsils** (stratified squamous epithelium) — **diphtheritic** inflammation: the membrane is firmly attached and does not block the airway, but much toxin is absorbed (myocarditis, neuritis); in the **larynx, trachea and bronchi** (columnar epithelium) — **croupous** inflammation: the membrane detaches easily and blocks the airway — **true croup**, asphyxia. This is why both types can occur in one disease.

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: Croupous tracheitis in diphtheria: the mucosa is superficially necrotic and covered with an easily detachable fibrin membrane (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-8)

blocks.label: Figure 5.5
blocks.caption: Diphtheritic inflammation of the pharynx: deep necrosis; a thick fibrin-impregnated membrane firmly attached to the underlying tissue (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-9)

blocks.label: Figure 5.6
blocks.caption: Diphtheritic colitis (dysentery): the colonic wall is markedly thickened, and the mucosa is covered with thick, gray-green, rough membranes (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Outcomes of fibrinous inflammation:** in mucous membranes the membranes detach and **ulcers** form (superficial in croupous, deep in diphtheritic — healing with a scar). In serous membranes, fibrin can be resorbed or undergo **organization**: **adhesions** (scar bands) form between the serous layers; in the pericardium, complete obliteration of the cavity (**obliteration**) and calcification may occur — the “**armored heart**” (constrictive pericarditis). In the lung, organization of fibrin — **carnification** (“turning into flesh”).
Purulent inflammation

**Neutrophils** predominate in the exudate. **Pus** is a thick, cloudy, yellow-green fluid containing living and dead neutrophils (**pus corpuscles**), lymphocytes, macrophages, tissue debris, microbes and protein-rich fluid. An important property of purulent exudate is its ability to **dissolve tissue** (**histolysis**): the proteolytic enzymes of neutrophils dissolve the tissue and form a cavity.

Purulent inflammation is caused by **pyogenic (pus-forming)** bacteria: staphylococcus, streptococcus, gonococcus, meningococcus, Fraenkel diplococcus (pneumococcus), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli; less often aseptic suppuration (chemicals — turpentine).
Types of purulent inflammation:

**1. Abscess** — **localized** purulent inflammation of tissue in which the tissue dissolves and a **cavity filled with pus** forms. Around the abscess a **pyogenic capsule (pyogenic membrane)** forms — a layer of granulation tissue; it is rich in capillaries, through which leukocytes continuously enter the abscess cavity, and it absorbs pus. In an **acute abscess** the wall consists of one layer — the pyogenic membrane (granulation tissue); in a **chronic abscess** the wall has two layers: the inner **pyogenic** layer and the outer **fibrous** layer (mature connective tissue).

An abscess can occur in any organ (lung, liver, brain, kidney, subcutaneous tissue). Numerous small abscesses are called **apostematous** inflammation (for example, **apostematous nephritis** — many small abscesses in the kidney in sepsis). An abscess may rupture spontaneously onto the skin surface or into a cavity (forming a fistula).

blocks.label: Figure 5.8
blocks.caption: Lung abscess (microscopic slide): the lung tissue has dissolved, forming a cavity filled with neutrophils (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-10)

blocks.label: Figure 5.7
blocks.caption: Multiple bacterial abscesses in the lung (arrows) — a complication of bronchopneumonia: A — gross view; B — the abscess consists of neutrophils and cell debris, surrounded by congested vessels (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-15)

blocks.text: **2. Phlegmon** — nonlocalized, **diffuse** purulent inflammation: the purulent exudate spreads between tissues, along fatty tissue, fasciae and neurovascular bundles, soaking and separating the tissues. Mainly in **soft tissues** — subcutaneous fatty tissue, between muscles, the mediastinum (**mediastinitis**), around the kidney (**paranephritis**), around the rectum (**paraproctitis**), and also in the wall of hollow organs (**phlegmonous appendicitis**, phlegmonous cholecystitis). **Soft phlegmon** — the necrotic foci liquefy; **hard phlegmon** — the tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis and sloughs off. Phlegmon often progresses to **sepsis**.

**3. Empyema** — accumulation of pus in a **preexisting natural cavity** or hollow organ: **pleural empyema** (pyothorax), empyema of the gallbladder, empyema of the appendix, empyema of the maxillary sinus, pericardial empyema (pyopericardium). Long-standing empyema may end in obliteration of the cavity.

**General features and outcomes of purulent inflammation:** usually an acute course; severe **intoxication**, fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis. If the pus is discharged (by rupture or surgery) — healing with a scar. Unfavorable outcomes: spread of pus to neighboring tissues (fistulas), erosion of vessel walls (**arrosive bleeding**), spread through lymph and blood — **sepsis**, **AA amyloidosis** (in chronic suppuration, Topic 8).

blocks.label: Figure 5.9
blocks.caption: Apostematous nephritis: numerous small round yellowish-gray abscesses on the surface and cut surface of the kidney (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 5.10
blocks.caption: Purulent leptomeningitis: the leptomeninges of the brain are thickened, dull and soaked with yellow-green pus — a “purulent cap” (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 5.11
blocks.caption: Phlegmonous-gangrenous appendicitis: the wall of the appendix is thickened and dirty gray, and its serosa is dull, with purulent-fibrinous deposits (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Putrefactive (ichorous) inflammation

It develops when **anaerobic putrefactive microorganisms** (clostridia and others) enter the focus of inflammation. The tissue putrefies, **foul-smelling** gases are formed, and the exudate becomes dirty green. It usually occurs in wounds with heavy contamination and destroyed tissue (war and road traffic injuries, military wounds); it is close to anaerobic (gas) gangrene. It runs a course with severe intoxication and has an unfavorable prognosis.
Hemorrhagic inflammation

The exudate contains many **red blood cells** and is red or brown. The cause is a **sharp increase** in the permeability of microcirculatory vessels and damage to the vessel wall. It is characteristic of highly dangerous infections: **plague, anthrax (Siberian ulcer)**, and also **severe forms of influenza**
(hemorrhagic pneumonia, hemorrhagic tracheobronchitis) and smallpox. The prognosis is usually serious. It often combines with other exudative types (serous-hemorrhagic, purulent-hemorrhagic).
Catarrhal inflammation

**Catarrhal inflammation (catarrh)** (Greek katarrheo — I flow down) develops **only in mucous membranes**: the exudate **flows down** from the mucosal surface and contains much **mucus** (hyperfunction of goblet cells and glands). By the type of exudate, **serous, mucous and purulent** catarrh are distinguished, and they can pass into one another (for example, in a common cold: first serous, then mucous, then mucopurulent discharge).
Causes: infections (**ARVI**, influenza), allergy (**allergic rhinitis**), thermal and chemical influences, endogenous intoxication (uremic catarrh).
**Acute catarrh** usually **resolves completely** in 2–3 weeks. **Chronic catarrh** is accompanied by **atrophy** (atrophic catarrh) or **hypertrophy** (hypertrophic catarrh, polyps) of the mucosa.

blocks.label: Figure 5.12
blocks.caption: Catarrhal bronchitis: mucous exudate in the bronchial lumen; the mucosa is red and swollen (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-11)

blocks.label: Figure 5.13
blocks.caption: Catarrhal pharyngotracheitis in influenza: the swollen mucosa is covered with a large amount of cloudy mucous exudate (TMA study guide, 2018)

items: **Complete resolution** — if the injury was limited or brief: the mediators are neutralized, the exudate is resorbed through the lymphatics, neutrophils undergo apoptosis, macrophages clear the debris, and the parenchyma regenerates. For example, complete restoration of lung tissue in croupous (lobar) pneumonia.

**Scar formation (fibrosis)** — if much tissue was destroyed, nonregenerating tissue was damaged or much fibrin accumulated: the necrotic focus and exudate are replaced by granulation tissue, which turns into a scar (organization).
**Abscess formation** — in infection with pyogenic bacteria.

**Progression to chronic inflammation** — if the agent is not eliminated or the healing process is disturbed (Topic 6). **An ulcer (ulcus)** is a **local defect** of the surface of an organ or tissue formed by sloughing of necrotic and inflamed tissue. It occurs most often in the mucosa of the mouth, stomach, intestine and genitourinary tract and in the skin of the lower leg (in the elderly with impaired circulation and in people with diabetes). The most characteristic example is **gastric and duodenal ulcer**: in the acute phase there is neutrophilic inflammation at the ulcer edge; in the chronic phase layers of fibrinoid necrosis, granulation tissue and scar form at its floor. An **erosion**, in contrast, is a defect only of the mucosal surface (not reaching the muscularis mucosae).

blocks.label: Figure 5.14
blocks.caption: Ulcer (chronic duodenal ulcer): A — gross view; B — the ulcer crater at low magnification, with acute inflammatory exudate at its floor (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-16)

blocks.text: Analysis of exudate — the key to diagnosis
Analysis of fluid (aspirate) obtained from the pleural or peritoneal cavity helps establish the diagnosis:

items: **clear, protein-poor fluid** — **transudate** (heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis);
**cloudy, protein-rich, lymphocytic exudate** — tuberculous pleurisy or tumor metastases (cytologic examination, search for tubercle mycobacteria);
**purulent, neutrophilic exudate** — empyema (drainage is necessary);
**hemorrhagic exudate** — tumor (mesothelioma, metastases), tuberculosis, pulmonary infarction, trauma.

blocks.text: Fibrinous pericarditis — a sign of uremia

In the final stage of chronic kidney disease (uremia), nitrogenous wastes accumulated in the blood are excreted through the serous membranes and damage them: **fibrinous pericarditis** (the pericardial friction rub is called the “death knell of uremia”), fibrinous pleurisy, fibrinous and catarrhal inflammation of the mucous membranes (uremic gastritis, colitis). Such a patient needs urgent **hemodialysis**.

parts.text: In **diphtheria** the main danger is not the local membranes but the **exotoxin**: it damages the myocardium (**toxic myocarditis**, fatty degeneration — “tiger heart”, Topic 3), the peripheral nerves (**polyneuritis**, paralysis of the soft palate) and the adrenal glands. The cause of early death is **true croup (asphyxia)**; the cause of late death (in the 2nd week) is **cardiac arrest**. Therefore the basis of treatment is **diphtheria antiserum** (antitoxin), and of prevention — **vaccination** (DTP).

blocks.text: Principle of treating abscess and phlegmon

If the pus cavity is localized (abscess, empyema), antibiotics cannot penetrate adequately through the pyogenic capsule — the main treatment is **surgical evacuation of pus (drainage)**: “Ubi pus, ibi evacua” — “where there is pus, evacuate it”. In phlegmon, wide incisions and antibiotics are needed, because the process spreads rapidly and can progress to sepsis.

items: **Inflammation** (Latin inflammatio) — a vascular-mesenchymal reaction that develops in response to various injuries and is aimed at eliminating the pathogenic agent.
**Alteration** (Latin alteratio — change) — damage to tissues in the form of degeneration and necrosis of various degrees.
**Exudation** (Latin exudatio) — escape of the fluid part of blood plasma and formed elements from the vessels.
**Proliferation** (Latin proliferatio — growth) — multiplication of capillary endothelium and connective tissue cells.
**Pinocytosis** — uptake of tissue fluid by a cell (macrophage, endothelium).
**Endocytobiosis** — incomplete phagocytosis: survival of a microbe inside the phagocyte.

**Abscess** (Latin abscessus — boil, purulent sore) — localized purulent inflammation forming a cavity. An acute abscess is separated from the surrounding tissue by a pyogenic membrane; the wall of a chronic abscess has two layers — pyogenic (inner) and fibrous (outer).
**Phlegmon** (Greek phlegmone — inflammation) — diffuse purulent inflammation.
**Empyema** (Greek en — inside, pyon — pus) — accumulation of pus in natural cavities or hollow organs (pleura, appendix, gallbladder, maxillary sinus).
**Catarrhal inflammation** (Greek katarrheo — I flow down) — inflammation of a mucous membrane in which the exudate flows down together with mucus.

**Croupous inflammation** (Scottish croup — membrane) — fibrinous inflammation with superficial necrosis, impregnation of the necrotic masses with fibrin and formation of an easily detachable membrane.
**Diphtheritic inflammation** (Greek diphthera — leather membrane) — fibrinous inflammation with deep necrosis in mucous membranes and formation of a thick membrane that is difficult to detach.
**Angina (tonsillitis)** (Latin ango — I strangle, I squeeze) — inflammation of the pharynx (tonsils).
**Sialadenitis** (Greek sialon — saliva, aden — gland) — inflammation of the salivary glands.
**Ichorosis** (Greek ichor — putrid fluid) — putrefactive (foul-smelling) inflammation.
**“Fibrinous pericarditis (‘hairy heart’)”.** The epicardium is dull and rough and covered with hairlike gray-yellowish fibrin threads. Conclusion: croupous (fibrinous) inflammation.
**“Fibrinous pleurisy”.** A gray-whitish, easily detachable fibrin membrane on the surface of the visceral pleura; the pleura is dull. Conclusion: croupous inflammation.

**“Diphtheritic colitis (dysentery)”.** The colonic wall is thickened, and the mucosa is covered with thick, gray-green membranes that are difficult to detach, with ulcers in places. Conclusion: diphtheritic inflammation.
**“Catarrhal pharyngotracheitis (influenza)”.** The mucosa is swollen, hyperemic and covered with cloudy mucous exudate. Conclusion: catarrhal inflammation.

**“Apostematous nephritis”.** The kidney is enlarged; on its surface and cut surface there are numerous small (millet-sized) yellowish-gray abscesses with a red rim around them. Conclusion: purulent inflammation (abscesses), most often in sepsis.

**“Purulent leptomeningitis”.** The leptomeninges of the brain are thickened, dull and soaked with yellow-green pus, especially over the convex surface of the brain — a “purulent cap”. Conclusion: purulent inflammation (of the phlegmon type), most often meningococcus or pneumococcus.
**“Lung abscess”.** A round cavity filled with pus on the cut surface of the lung, its wall bounded by a pyogenic capsule. Conclusion: abscess.

**“Phlegmonous appendicitis”.** The appendix is enlarged and thickened; its serosa is dull and hyperemic, with fibrinous-purulent deposits; on the cut surface the wall is soaked with pus. Conclusion: phlegmon.

blocks.label: Figure 5.16
blocks.caption: Lung abscesses: round, gray-yellowish cavities filled with pus on the cut surface (TMA study guide, 2018)

items: **“Fibrinous pericarditis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Pink fibrillar and net-like fibrin masses on the epicardial surface, with neutrophils between them; the epicardium is hyperemic, edematous and infiltrated by leukocytes. Conclusion: fibrinous (croupous) inflammation.

**“Croupous tracheitis in diphtheria”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The tracheal mucosa is superficially necrotic, without epithelium; on its surface is a membrane of fibrin and leukocytes that separates easily from the underlying tissue; the submucosa is edematous and hyperemic. Conclusion: croupous inflammation.

**“Diphtheritic tonsillitis (fauces)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Deep necrosis (debris) of the stratified squamous epithelium and tonsillar tissue, impregnated with fibrin and infiltrated by neutrophils; the membrane is firmly attached to the deep layers. Conclusion: diphtheritic inflammation.

**“Purulent leptomeningitis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The pia mater is thickened and diffusely infiltrated by neutrophils; the vessels are hyperemic. Conclusion: purulent (phlegmonous) inflammation.

**“Kidney abscess”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Localized foci of accumulated neutrophils in the renal cortex and medulla; in their center the tissue is dissolved, surrounded by granulation tissue (pyogenic capsule), with colonies of bacteria (basophilic). Conclusion: abscess.

**“Hemorrhagic pneumonia (influenza)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The alveolar spaces are filled with red blood cells, a few neutrophils and fibrin; the interalveolar septa are thickened and the capillaries are hyperemic. Conclusion: hemorrhagic inflammation.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An unvaccinated 5-year-old child had fever and sore throat, followed by progressively worsening stridorous breathing and a “barking” cough, and died of asphyxia. At autopsy there are thick gray membranes on the tonsils, firmly attached to the underlying tissue and difficult to detach; in the larynx, trachea and bronchi there are thin, easily detachable gray membranes, some of which block the lumen of the bronchi.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What types of inflammation are present in the tonsils and trachea? Why do they differ? 3) The cause of death and other dangerous complications of the disease.
cases.answer: 1) Diphtheria (diphtheria of the pharynx and respiratory tract). 2) In the tonsils — diphtheritic inflammation (stratified squamous epithelium, deep necrosis, firmly attached membrane); in the larynx, trachea and bronchi — croupous inflammation (columnar epithelium, superficial necrosis, the membrane detaches easily). The difference depends on the type of epithelium and the structure of the submucosa. 3) The cause of death is true croup (asphyxia) as a result of detached membranes blocking the airway. Other dangerous complications are related to the action of the exotoxin: toxic myocarditis (a cause of late death), polyneuritis, hemorrhage into the adrenal glands.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 63-year-old man has had chronic glomerulonephritis for 15 years. In recent months he has had nausea, weakness and itching of the skin; blood creatinine and urea are sharply increased. On auscultation a friction rub is heard over the heart. The patient died.
cases.ask: 1) What change was present in the pericardium? 2) What are its cause and mechanism? 3) What outcome could this process have led to if the patient had survived?
cases.answer: 1) Fibrinous pericarditis (“hairy heart”) — the epicardium is dull, rough and covered with hairlike fibrin threads; microscopically — a pink fibrin network and leukocytes. 2) Uremia (the final stage of chronic kidney disease): nitrogenous wastes accumulated in the blood are excreted through the serous membranes, damage them and increase vascular permeability — a fibrinogen-rich exudate escapes and fibrin forms. The friction rub is the rubbing together of the fibrin-covered pericardial layers. 3) The fibrin would undergo organization, adhesions would form between the pericardial layers, and the cavity could become obliterated and calcified — the “armored heart” (constrictive pericarditis).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 34-year-old woman received an injection into the thigh with a contaminated needle 5 days ago. The thigh is swollen, red and painful, with indistinct borders; temperature 39.5 °C, neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift in the blood. At surgery the subcutaneous fatty tissue and intermuscular spaces are diffusely soaked with yellow-green fluid; there is no localized cavity.
cases.ask: 1) What type and form of inflammation is this? 2) How does it differ from an abscess? 3) Possible complications and the principle of treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Purulent inflammation — phlegmon (subcutaneous and intermuscular phlegmon), caused by pyogenic bacteria (most often staphylococcus, streptococcus). 2) An abscess is a localized cavity with a pyogenic capsule around it; a phlegmon is nonlocalized and diffuse, and the pus spreads along tissue spaces, fasciae and neurovascular bundles. 3) Complications: spread of pus, erosion of the vessel wall (arrosive bleeding), thrombophlebitis, sepsis; if chronic — AA amyloidosis. Treatment — evacuation of pus through wide incisions (drainage), antibiotics and detoxification.

topics.title: Chronic inflammation. Types. Cell repair

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the definition, causes and morphologic signs of chronic inflammation;
the cells of chronic inflammation: macrophages (pathways of activation), lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, giant cells;
the types of productive (proliferative) inflammation: interstitial, granulomatous, and inflammation forming polyps and condylomas;
the definition, morphogenesis, classification and outcomes of granulomas;
specific granulomas: the structure of the granulomas of tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy and scleroma;
the concept of regeneration (repair), its types, mechanisms and the factors influencing it;
the structure of granulation tissue, the types of wound healing, scar formation;
pathologic regeneration, sclerosis and cirrhosis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of miliary tuberculosis, hepatic echinococcosis, gastric polyp, the liver in visceral syphilis, syphilitic aortic aneurysm and keloid scar;
describe microscopic slides of a tuberculous granuloma, syphilitic gumma, foreign body granuloma, rhinoscleroma, interstitial myocarditis, granulation tissue and organization of a thrombus;
distinguish specific granulomas by their structure;
relate the types of wound healing to clinical situations.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The term **“specific inflammation”** is widely used in CIS textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva). In current international literature this concept is not singled out: these diseases are included in the group of **granulomatous inflammation**, and the final diagnosis is made on the basis of the granuloma structure together with **identification of the causative agent** (Ziehl–Neelsen staining, silver impregnation, PCR, culture). The histologic appearance of a granuloma only gives a direction.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the specific granulomas by their “**marker cell**”: **Tuberculosis — Pirogov–Langhans (horseshoe)**, **Syphilis — Plasma cell and vessel (endovasculitis)**, **Leprosy — Virchow (“cigarette pack”)**, **Scleroma — Mikulicz (foamy)**. “**Tuberculosis — Caseous, Syphilis — Gummatous, Sarcoidosis — Noncaseating**”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The strength of a wound scar: after the sutures are removed (at the end of the 1st week) it equals only **10%** of the strength of normal skin; it increases rapidly over the next 4 weeks and reaches **70–80%** by the 3rd month, but never reaches 100%.

blocks.text: **Chronic inflammation** is inflammation of prolonged duration (weeks, months, years) in which **active inflammation, tissue damage** and **attempts at healing (repair)** proceed simultaneously. It may follow acute inflammation or begin as chronic from the start (insidious, without symptoms).
Causes:

items: **Persistent infections** — microorganisms that are difficult to eradicate: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Treponema pallidum (syphilis), the leprosy bacillus, fungi, some viruses (hepatitis B and C), parasites. They often elicit a **delayed-type hypersensitivity** (type IV) reaction and lead to **granulomatous** inflammation.

**Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases** — autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis), allergic diseases (bronchial asthma), inflammatory bowel diseases (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis).
**Prolonged exposure to endogenous or exogenous toxic agents** — silicon dioxide (silicosis), asbestos, atherosclerosis (lipids).
It has been established that **latent chronic inflammation** also underlies some **chronic diseases** (atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, Alzheimer disease).

blocks.text: **Morphologic features of chronic inflammation** (Robbins):

items: **Infiltration by mononuclear cells** — macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells.
**Tissue destruction** — by the causative agent or inflammatory cells.
**Attempts at healing** — formation of new vessels (**angiogenesis**) and **fibrosis** (growth of connective tissue).

blocks.title: Table 6.1. Differences between acute and chronic inflammation
head: Feature
Acute inflammation
Chronic inflammation
rows: Usually mild and self-limited; little fibrosis
Often severe and progressive; marked fibrosis

blocks.text: Macrophages

**Macrophages** are the **dominant cells** of chronic inflammation. They are derived from blood **monocytes** (which become macrophages after entering the tissue) or are tissue-resident macrophages (Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lung, microglia in the brain, osteoclasts in bone). All tissue macrophages together make up the **mononuclear phagocyte system**.
Macrophages are activated in two ways:

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Pathways of macrophage activation
head: Feature
Classical activation (M1)
Alternative activation (M2)
rows: Killing of microbes (ROS, NO, lysosomal enzymes), amplification of inflammation (IL-1, TNF, IL-12)
Suppression of inflammation, repair and fibrosis (growth factors: PDGF, TGF-beta), angiogenesis

blocks.text: Functions of macrophages in chronic inflammation: **phagocytosis** of microbes and dead tissue; **presentation** of antigen to T lymphocytes; production of **cytokines** that regulate inflammation; control of **repair and fibrosis** by stimulating fibroblasts and angiogenesis. Macrophages and T lymphocytes activate each other and maintain the chronicity of inflammation (IFN-gamma ↔ IL-12).
Lymphocytes, plasma cells and other cells

items: **T lymphocytes** — CD4^+^ helper T cells regulate inflammation through cytokines: **Th1** (IFN-gamma — classical activation of macrophages; tuberculosis, autoimmune diseases), **Th2** (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 — eosinophils and alternatively activated macrophages; allergy, parasites), **Th17** (IL-17 — recruits neutrophils).

**B lymphocytes and plasma cells** — produce antibodies. The plasma cell has an eccentrically placed nucleus with “**cartwheel**” chromatin and basophilic cytoplasm; immunoglobulins can accumulate in its cytoplasm to form **Russell bodies**. In long-standing inflammation, lymphocytes, plasma cells and antigen-presenting cells form **lymphoid follicles** (**tertiary lymphoid organs** — for example, in the synovium in rheumatoid arthritis, in Hashimoto thyroiditis).
**Eosinophils** — numerous in IgE-mediated allergic reactions and **parasitic infections**; the **major basic protein** in their granules is toxic to parasites but also damages the epithelium.
**Mast cells** — release histamine and other mediators and participate in allergic and chronic inflammation.
**Neutrophils** — may also be present in chronic inflammation (for example, chronic osteomyelitis, chronic lung damage) — “**acute-on-chronic**” inflammation.

blocks.text: Multinucleated giant cells
Multinucleated cells 40–50 µm or more in diameter formed by fusion of macrophages (epithelioid cells):

items: **Pirogov–Langhans cells** — the nuclei (20 or more) are arranged at the periphery of the cell in a **horseshoe or ring** shape; characteristic of the tuberculous granuloma but also found in other granulomas;
**foreign body giant cells** — the nuclei are scattered **haphazardly** in the cytoplasm (often in the center); the cytoplasm may contain foreign particles;
**Touton cells** — a ring of nuclei in the center and foamy (lipid-laden) cytoplasm at the periphery; in xanthomas and fat necrosis.

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: Pirogov–Langhans giant cell: the nuclei are arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery of the cytoplasm (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-13)

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Pirogov–Langhans giant cell (electron micrograph): many nuclei (N), mitochondria (M), lysosomes (L) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: In A.I. Strukov's classification, in **productive (proliferative) inflammation** cell proliferation predominates; it usually runs a chronic course. Four types are distinguished:

**1. Interstitial (diffuse) inflammation** — a **diffuse infiltrate** of lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells accumulates in the **stroma** of parenchymal organs (myocardium, liver, kidney, lung); degenerative and atrophic changes in the parenchyma. Examples: **interstitial myocarditis** (diphtheria, viral infections, rheumatic fever), interstitial nephritis, interstitial pneumonia, chronic hepatitis. Outcome — **diffuse sclerosis** of the organ (cardiosclerosis, nephrosclerosis, pneumosclerosis) and **cirrhosis**.
**2. Granulomatous inflammation** — accompanied by the formation of granulomas (in detail below).

**3. Productive inflammation forming polyps and condylomata acuminata** — in chronic inflammation of mucous membranes (or of surfaces lined by squamous epithelium), the stroma and epithelium grow and protrude outward:

items: **inflammatory polyps** — in the mucosa of the nasal cavity, maxillary sinus, stomach, colon and cervix; polyps must be distinguished from tumors (adenomatous polyp);

**condylomata acuminata** — in the squamous epithelium of the anus and external genitalia, most often associated with **papillomavirus** (types 6 and 11). **4. Productive inflammation around animal parasites** — around echinococcus, cysticercus and trichinella: macrophages, eosinophils, giant cells and a **fibrous capsule** form around the parasite (for example, the capsule around an echinococcal cyst).

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: Hepatic echinococcosis: a white, round, fluid-filled cyst in the liver surrounded by a fibrous capsule (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: Gastric polyp: a soft, gray-reddish lesion with small papillae on a thin stalk on the greater curvature (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.5
blocks.caption: Interstitial myocarditis: an infiltrate of lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells in the myocardial stroma; degenerative changes in cardiomyocytes (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Granulomatous inflammation** is a distinctive form of chronic inflammation whose main feature is the formation of **granulomas**. A **granuloma** (Latin granulum — grain, Greek -oma — tumor; i.e., a “nodule”) is a **localized focal** productive inflammation up to 1–2 mm in diameter, consisting mainly of a collection of **activated macrophages** (epithelioid cells), often surrounded by lymphocytes. Granuloma formation is the organism's attempt to **wall off** an agent that is difficult to eradicate.
Morphogenesis of the granuloma

items: Accumulation of **monocytes** in the focus of inflammation.
Their transformation into **macrophages** and formation of a macrophage granuloma.

Transformation of macrophages into **epithelioid cells** — large cells with pale pink, finely granular cytoplasm, indistinct borders and an elongated oval nucleus (resembling a “shoe sole”); they lie closely packed like epithelium. Epithelioid cells are poorly adapted to phagocytosis and better adapted to secretion (cytokines, enzymes).
Fusion of epithelioid cells (or macrophages) to form **multinucleated giant cells**.

blocks.text: By mechanism there are two types of granulomas:

items: **Immune granulomas** — **type IV hypersensitivity** (T cell–mediated immune response): Th1 lymphocytes produce **IFN-gamma**, activate macrophages and transform them into epithelioid cells. In tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, sarcoidosis, fungal infections and Crohn disease.

**Nonimmune granulomas (foreign body granulomas)** — without an immune response, around large inert foreign bodies (suture material, talc, coal particles, keratin, urate crystals). Epithelioid cells are few, **foreign body giant cells** are numerous; the foreign body is often visible in polarized light.

blocks.label: Figure 6.6
blocks.caption: Foreign body granuloma: in the center two giant cells surround foreign particles (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Classification of granulomas

blocks.title: Table 6.3. Classification of granulomas (after V.V. Serov and V.V. Shekhter, simplified)
head: Feature
Types
rows: Infectious (tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, scleroma, brucellosis, tularemia, fungi, parasites); noninfectious (foreign bodies, dust — silicosis, asbestosis; drugs); of unknown etiology (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis)
Mature macrophage granuloma (simple phagocytoma); epithelioid cell granuloma (epithelioidocytoma); giant cell granuloma
Slow-turnover (inert foreign bodies) and fast-turnover (toxic agents — tuberculosis) granulomas
Specific — the causative agent can be suspected from the structure (tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, scleroma); nonspecific — the others

blocks.text: **Outcomes of granulomas:** 1) **resorption** (the infiltrate disappears); 2) **fibrosis** — the granuloma turns into a scar (fibrous nodule); 3) **necrosis** — caseous necrosis in a tuberculous granuloma, later **calcification** (petrification); 4) **suppuration** (in fungal granulomas).
Specific granulomas

**Specific inflammation** is chronic inflammation caused by a particular agent (tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy, scleroma) that forms granulomas of characteristic structure. Its general features: a specific causative agent; a **wavelike** chronic course (periods of exacerbation and remission); granulomas of characteristic structure; frequent **necrosis** (caseous or coagulative); a change in the tissue reaction depending on the immune status of the organism (with high resistance — a productive reaction, with low resistance — an alterative and exudative reaction).

parts.text: The term **“specific inflammation”** is widely used in CIS textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva). In current international literature this concept is not singled out: these diseases are included in the group of **granulomatous inflammation**, and the final diagnosis is made on the basis of the granuloma structure together with **identification of the causative agent** (Ziehl–Neelsen staining, silver impregnation, PCR, culture). The histologic appearance of a granuloma only gives a direction.

blocks.text: **1. The tuberculous granuloma (tubercle)** — the causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Koch bacillus). Structure (from the center to the periphery):

items: in the center — a focus of **caseous necrosis** (a structureless, granular, pink mass);
around it — a layer of **epithelioid cells** (arranged like a palisade);
among the epithelioid cells — **Pirogov–Langhans giant cells**;
at the periphery — a layer of **lymphocytes**, a small number of plasma cells and macrophages;
there are **no blood vessels** inside the granuloma (silver impregnation shows a network of argyrophilic fibers);

with Ziehl–Neelsen staining, **acid-fast red bacilli** are found in epithelioid and giant cells. A granuloma without caseous necrosis is an **epithelioid cell (proliferative) tubercle**. Granulomas merge to form large foci; when they are surrounded by a capsule — a **tuberculoma**. Scattered small (millet-sized) granulomas in the organs — **miliary tuberculosis**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.7
blocks.caption: Tuberculous granuloma: caseous necrosis in the center, surrounded by epithelioid cells, numerous Pirogov–Langhans giant cells and lymphocytes (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-23)

blocks.label: Figure 6.8
blocks.caption: Caseous necrosis in the center of a tuberculous granuloma (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-12)

blocks.label: Figure 6.9
blocks.caption: Epithelioid cell granuloma in the liver (tuberculosis): epithelioid cells in the liver tissue, with a Pirogov–Langhans giant cell in the center (arrow) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.10
blocks.caption: Miliary tuberculosis of the lung: numerous hard, whitish-yellow, millet-sized nodules beneath the pleura and on the cut surface (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **2. The syphilitic granuloma — gumma** (Latin gummi — gum) — the causative agent is Treponema pallidum; characteristic of **tertiary syphilis**. Structure:

items: in the center — an extensive focus of **coagulative (gummatous) necrosis**: a gummy, stretchy mass in which the outlines of vessels are sometimes preserved (unlike caseous necrosis);
around it — **lymphocytes, plasma cells** (very numerous), macrophages, fibroblasts, few epithelioid and giant cells;
**productive endovasculitis** — the walls of small vessels thicken and their lumen narrows (**obliterating endarteritis**), with plasma cells around them (**perivasculitis**);

at the periphery — a vascular connective tissue capsule. Gummas occur in the liver, bones, skin, brain, heart and other organs; on healing they leave a **deep stellate scar** (in the liver — **“hepar lobatum” (lobulated liver)**). Besides gummas, tertiary syphilis also produces **gummatous infiltration** (diffuse) — most importantly **syphilitic mesaortitis**: a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate around the vasa vasorum in the media of the ascending aorta and arch, destruction of elastic fibers and a “**shagreen skin**” (tree-bark) appearance of the intima; its complications — **aortic aneurysm** and aortic valve insufficiency.

blocks.label: Figure 6.11
blocks.caption: Syphilitic granuloma (gumma): lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblasts and productive vasculitis in small vessels (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-14)

blocks.label: Figure 6.12
blocks.caption: Syphilitic mesaortitis: an infiltrate of lymphoid, plasma and epithelioid cells in the aortic wall around the vasa vasorum (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.13
blocks.caption: The liver in visceral syphilis: the liver is enlarged, hard, coarsely bumpy and divided by scars into lobes (“hepar lobatum”) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.14
blocks.caption: Syphilitic aneurysm of the aortic arch (a complication of syphilitic mesaortitis) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **3. The leprosy granuloma — leproma** (Greek lepra — leprosy) — the causative agent is Mycobacterium leprae (Hansen bacillus). Structure: macrophages, epithelioid and giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells. Inside macrophages, numerous mycobacteria accumulate in the form of a “**cigarette pack**”; fat vacuoles appear in them, and large **Virchow (lepra) cells** form. Lepromas occur in the skin, mucous membranes, **peripheral nerves**, lymph nodes and internal organs.
Depending on the immune status, leprosy has two main forms:

items: **lepromatous form** — low immunity (Th2 response): numerous Virchow cells **filled with mycobacteria**, skin nodules (“**leonine face**”), highly contagious;
**tuberculoid form** — high immunity (Th1 response): tuberculosis-like epithelioid cell granulomas, **few** mycobacteria, mainly nerves are affected (loss of sensation, trophic ulcers).

blocks.label: Figure 6.15
blocks.caption: Lepromatous leprosy — leproma: a nodule composed of macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 5-15a)

blocks.text: **4. The scleroma granuloma** — the causative agent is Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (Volkovich–Frisch bacillus). Mainly in the upper respiratory tract — the nose (**rhinoscleroma**), larynx and trachea. Structure: plasma cells, epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, **hyaline (Russell) bodies**; most characteristic are **Mikulicz cells**: large macrophages with pale, foamy cytoplasm containing Volkovich–Frisch bacilli. Outcome — coarse sclerosis and scars, narrowing of the airways (stenosis, risk of asphyxia).

blocks.label: Figure 6.16
blocks.caption: Rhinoscleroma: a specific granuloma composed of various cells — plasma cells, Mikulicz cells, hyaline bodies (TMA study guide, 2018)
