blocks.text: **Regeneration** (Latin regeneratio — renewal) is the **restoration (re-formation)** of the structural elements of cells and tissues. Restoration of damaged tissue is called **repair**, and it occurs in two ways: **regeneration** (by proliferation of cells) and **scar formation** (replacement by connective tissue).
Types of regeneration

items: **Physiological regeneration** — continuous renewal of worn-out cells throughout life: blood cells, epithelium of the skin and mucous membranes, endometrium (menstrual cycle).
**Reparative (restorative) regeneration** — restoration of tissue damaged by pathological processes. It is of two kinds:

blocks.text: – **restitution (complete regeneration)** — the defect is filled with **exactly the same** tissue; mainly in labile and stable tissues (epithelium, connective tissue, bone) and when the damage is small; – **substitution (incomplete regeneration)** — the defect is filled with **connective tissue**

**(scar)**, while the remaining parenchymal cells enlarge (**regenerative hypertrophy**) and maintain the function of the organ. For example, in myocardial infarction the necrotic area is replaced by a scar, and the surrounding cardiomyocytes hypertrophy. 3. **Pathologic regeneration** — a disturbance of the regeneration process: regeneration is **excessive** (hyperregeneration) or **insufficient** (hyporegeneration), or the tissue turns into **another type** (metaplasia). **Forms of regeneration** (D.S. Sarkisov): **cellular regeneration** — an increase in the number of cells (by mitosis; epithelium, connective tissue, bone); **intracellular regeneration** — an increase in the number and size of intracellular structures (organelles) (heart, skeletal muscles, neurons — nondividing cells). In most organs both forms occur together.
Mechanisms of regeneration
Regeneration is controlled by **growth factors** and the **extracellular matrix (ECM)**:

items: **growth factors** — stimulate cell proliferation, migration and differentiation: epidermal growth factor (**EGF**) and transforming growth factor alpha (**TGF-alpha**) — epithelium; platelet-derived growth factor (**PDGF**) — migration of fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and macrophages; vascular endothelial growth factor (**VEGF**) — **angiogenesis**; fibroblast growth factor (**FGF**) — angiogenesis and fibroblasts; **hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)** — liver regeneration; **transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta)** — the main factor of **fibrosis** (increases collagen synthesis and reduces its breakdown) and it suppresses inflammation;

**extracellular matrix** — collagen, elastin, fibronectin, laminin, proteoglycans; it serves as a scaffold for the tissue and stores growth factors. **If the basement membrane and scaffold are preserved**, complete regeneration is possible; if the scaffold is destroyed, a scar forms;
**stem (cambial) cells** — tissue stem cells (for example, intestinal crypts, the basal layer of the skin, hepatic ductal cells).

blocks.text: Regeneration of various tissues

items: **Blood** — physiological regeneration is very active; after blood loss the bone marrow becomes hyperplastic, the yellow marrow of the long bones turns into red marrow, and foci of hematopoiesis outside the marrow (**extramedullary hematopoiesis**) appear.

**Blood vessels** — capillaries are restored by **budding** (endothelial proliferation — angiogenesis); large vessels regenerate only in their inner layer, and defects of the media and adventitia are replaced by a scar.
**Connective tissue** — through **granulation tissue** (below).

**Epithelium** — stratified squamous epithelium (skin) is completely restored from the edges of the defect and from the basal layer; the epithelium of mucous membranes (stomach, intestine) is rapidly restored from cambial cells in the crypts and glands.

**Liver** — has a high capacity for regeneration (**restitution**): if 2/3 of the liver is removed, the remaining part reaches its original mass within a few weeks. But in chronic injury regeneration is disturbed: pseudolobules form and **cirrhosis** develops.

**Bone** — a **bony callus** forms at the fracture site: first fibrin and granulation tissue (**preliminary connective tissue callus**), then an **osteoid-cartilaginous callus**, then a **coarse-fibered bony callus**, and finally lamellar bone. If the fragments are mobile, much cartilage forms and healing slows; if connective tissue remains between the fragments, a **false joint (pseudarthrosis)** forms.
**Skeletal muscles** — if the sarcolemma is preserved, they are restored by **satellite cells**; large defects are replaced by a scar.
**Cardiac muscle** — cardiomyocytes do not divide; the defect is replaced by a **scar**, with intracellular regeneration and **regenerative hypertrophy** in the remaining cardiomyocytes.

**Nervous tissue** — in the central nervous system neurons are not restored (the defect is replaced by **gliosis** — a glial scar or a cyst). In peripheral nerves, if the neuron body is preserved, the axon is restored by growing from its central end (1–2 mm per day); if the path of growth is blocked, an **amputation neuroma** (a nodule of nerve fibers and connective tissue) forms.

blocks.text: Granulation tissue and scar formation

**Granulation tissue** is young, newly formed connective tissue **rich in capillaries and fibroblasts**. Its gross appearance: a **red-pink, soft, granular** (Latin granulum — grain; the granules are capillary loops) surface that bleeds easily. Granulation tissue begins to appear **3–5 days** after injury.
The **six layers** of granulation tissue (after N.N. Anichkov, from the surface to the depth):

items: **Superficial leukocytic-necrotic layer** — leukocytes, debris, fibrin.
**Superficial layer of vascular loops** — vertically arranged capillary loops with polyblasts (various cells) between them.
**Layer of vertical vessels** — perivascular fibroblasts.
**Maturing layer** — fibroblasts begin to lie horizontally, and collagen fibers form.
**Layer of horizontal fibroblasts**.
**Fibrous layer** — mature connective tissue.

blocks.text: Stages of scar formation:

items: **Angiogenesis** — new capillaries bud from existing vessels (under the action of VEGF); the new capillaries are “leaky” — which is why granulation tissue is edematous.
**Migration and proliferation of fibroblasts**, synthesis of collagen and other ECM components (under the action of TGF-beta, PDGF, FGF).

**Remodeling** — collagen matures and is reorganized, the number of vessels decreases, and granulation tissue turns into a **dense, whitish, poorly vascularized scar**. The balance between collagen synthesis and degradation (matrix metalloproteinases) determines the size of the scar.

blocks.label: Figure 6.19
blocks.caption: Organization and canalization of a thrombus in a vein: granulation tissue has grown into the thrombotic mass (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 8-1)

blocks.label: Figure 6.18
blocks.caption: Granulation tissue and scar: A — young granulation tissue with numerous capillaries, edema and inflammatory cells; B — mature scar: dense collagen fibers (trichrome stain — blue), few vessels (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-27)

blocks.text: Wound healing
Healing of a skin wound is the classic example of tissue repair. Four types are distinguished:

items: **Direct closure of an epithelial defect** — a superficial defect involving only the epithelium is closed by ingrowth of epithelium (erosions of the cornea and mucous membranes).
**Healing under a scab** — a superficial defect is covered with a scab of dried blood, fibrin and lymph; epithelium grows beneath it, and the scab falls off in 3–5 days.

**Healing by first intention (primary union)** — wounds with closely apposed edges, **clean (uninfected)**, with little tissue loss (for example, a sutured surgical incision): the incisional gap fills with fibrin; neutrophils appear on day 1, macrophages and granulation tissue by day 3, collagen bridges by day 5, and by the 2nd week the wound is completely united by a scar; the epithelium covers the defect in 24–48 hours. The result is a **thin, almost invisible scar**. 4. **Healing by second intention (secondary union)** — wounds with a **large tissue defect**, widely separated edges, **infection** and much necrotic tissue: intense inflammation and abundant **granulation tissue** form; **wound contraction** occurs due to **myofibroblasts** (within 6 weeks the defect may shrink to 5–10% of its original size); the result is a **wide, coarse scar**.

parts.text: The strength of a wound scar: after the sutures are removed (at the end of the 1st week) it equals only **10%** of the strength of normal skin; it increases rapidly over the next 4 weeks and reaches **70–80%** by the 3rd month, but never reaches 100%.

blocks.label: Figure 6.20
blocks.caption: A healing skin ulcer in a diabetic patient: A — a pressure ulcer (wide defect); B — thin epithelium between the ulcer edges and extensive granulation tissue in the dermis; C — continuing epithelialization; D — wound contraction (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-30)

blocks.text: Factors influencing repair

items: **Local factors: infection** (the most important factor — it prolongs inflammation), mechanical factors (motion of the wound edges), **inadequate blood supply** (atherosclerosis, varicose veins, diabetes), **foreign bodies** (sutures, bone fragments), the type, size and location of the wound.

**Systemic factors: nutrition** (protein, **vitamin C** — necessary for collagen synthesis, zinc deficiency), **diabetes mellitus**, **glucocorticoids** (suppress inflammation and TGF-beta, reducing fibrosis), age (healing slows in the elderly), immune status.

blocks.text: Pathologic regeneration and disorders of repair

items: **Keloid scar** (Greek chele — crab claw) — excessive collagen formation: the scar **extends beyond** the wound margins and bulges like a tumor, and it tends to recur. There is a hereditary predisposition (more common in people of African descent). Microscopically — broad, hyalinized collagen bundles.
**Hypertrophic scar** — collagen is excessive, but the scar does not extend beyond the wound margins and may shrink with time.
**“Proud flesh”** (exuberant granulation tissue) — granulation tissue protrudes above the skin level and interferes with epithelialization.
**Contractures** — scars after burns contract and limit joint movement.
**Insufficient repair** — wound opening (**wound dehiscence**, especially in the abdominal wall), chronic (trophic) ulcers.
**Desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis)** — tumor-like proliferation of fibroblasts, a borderline tumor.
**False joint** and **amputation neuroma** (above).

blocks.caption: Adenomatous polyp of the intestine: A — microscopic slide; B — gross specimen (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 6.21
blocks.caption: Keloid: A — a bulging scar on the skin resulting from excessive accumulation of collagen; B — a thick mass of connective tissue in the dermis (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 3-32)

blocks.text: Organization, encapsulation, sclerosis and cirrhosis

items: **Organization** — replacement of necrotic foci, thrombi, fibrinous exudate (fibrinous inflammation) or a hematoma by connective tissue. For example, **organization and canalization of a thrombus** — granulation tissue grows into the thrombotic mass from the wall, new vascular channels appear in it, and blood flow is partially restored (Topic 7).
**Encapsulation** — formation of a connective tissue capsule around a nonresorbable dead mass, foreign body or parasite.

**Sclerosis** (Greek sklerosis — hardening) — growth of connective tissue in an organ, displacing the parenchyma and making the organ firm (cardiosclerosis, nephrosclerosis, pneumosclerosis). Its causes: chronic inflammation (interstitial inflammation), organization of necrotic foci, chronic hypoxia, activation of fibroblasts.

**Cirrhosis** (Greek kirrhos — tawny, orange-yellow) — the final stage, in which sclerosis is accompanied by **restructuring** of the parenchyma (pseudolobules, regenerative nodules) and **deformation** of the organ (liver cirrhosis, pneumocirrhosis).

blocks.text: A granuloma has been found — what is the next step?
If **epithelioid cell granulomas** are found in a lymph node biopsy, the pathologist seeks answers to the following questions:

items: **Is there necrosis?** Granulomas with caseous necrosis — first of all **tuberculosis** (or a fungal infection); uniform, noncaseating, “stamped-out” granulomas — **sarcoidosis** is more likely.
**Is the causative agent found? Ziehl–Neelsen** staining (acid-fast bacilli), PAS and Grocott silver stain (fungi), PCR (mycobacterial DNA).

**Is there a foreign body?** It is seen in polarized light (talc, sutures). The answers to these questions completely change the treatment: in tuberculosis — antituberculosis drugs; in sarcoidosis — glucocorticoids (giving glucocorticoids in tuberculosis is dangerous — the infection spreads!).

parts.text: **Chronic inflammation and cancer** are interrelated: tumors develop more often against a background of long-standing chronic inflammation — Helicobacter pylori gastritis — gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma; chronic viral hepatitis B and C — hepatocellular carcinoma; ulcerative colitis — colorectal cancer; Barrett esophagus — adenocarcinoma; sinus tracts of chronic osteomyelitis — squamous cell carcinoma. Mechanism: continuous cell proliferation, DNA damage by ROS, cytokines and growth factors.

blocks.text: Wound healing and diabetes mellitus

In diabetes mellitus, wounds heal slowly and become infected easily. The causes: **micro- and macroangiopathy** (reduced blood supply), **neuropathy** (because of loss of sensation the patient does not feel the injury — the “diabetic foot”), **impaired neutrophil function** in hyperglycemia (chemotaxis and phagocytosis are impaired), and impaired collagen synthesis. As a result, chronic trophic ulcers and gangrene develop (Topic 2).

items: **Granuloma** (Latin granulum — grain, Greek -oma — tumor) — a localized focus of productive inflammation; mainly a collection of activated macrophages.
**Gumma** (Latin gummi — gum) — the specific infectious granuloma in syphilis.
**Leproma** (Greek lepra — leprosy, -oma — tumor) — the specific infectious granuloma in leprosy.
**Tuberculoma** (Latin tuberculum — small knob) — a focus of caseous necrosis in the lung surrounded by a connective tissue capsule, with elements of calcification.
**Infiltrate** (Latin in — into, filtratum — filtered) — entry of various cellular elements into a tissue, making it firm.
**Condyloma** (Greek kondyloma — growth) — papillary growth of squamous epithelium and the underlying stroma.
**Polyp** (Greek poly — many, pus — foot) — papillary (pedunculated) outgrowth of the mucosal epithelium and the underlying tissue.

**Specific inflammation** (Latin species — kind) — chronic inflammation caused by a particular biological agent and having characteristic morphologic features (not singled out in current international classifications).
**Sclerosis** (Greek sklerosis — hardening) — growth of connective tissue in an organ, displacing the parenchyma.
**Cirrhosis** (Greek kirrhos — tawny) — growth of connective tissue and restructuring of the parenchyma with deformation of the organ.
**Myofibrosis** (Greek mys — muscle, Latin fibrosus — fibrous) — small-focal cardiosclerosis.
**Fibrosis** (Latin fibra — fiber) — excessive formation of connective tissue fibers.
**Stenosis** (Greek stenos — narrow) — narrowing of a canal or orifice.
**Aneurysm** (Greek aneurysma — dilatation) — a localized bulging dilatation of the wall of the heart or a vessel.
**Regeneration** (Latin regeneratio — renewal) — restoration of the structural elements of cells and tissues.
**Restitution** — complete restoration of a defect by the same tissue.
**Substitution** — replacement of a defect by connective tissue (scar).
**Organization** — replacement of necrosis, a thrombus or exudate by connective tissue.
**Keloid** (Greek chele — crab claw) — a collagen-rich pathologic scar that grows beyond the wound margins.

**“Miliary tuberculosis of the lung”.** Numerous millet-sized (1–2 mm), whitish-gray or yellowish, hard nodules beneath the pleura and on the cut surface of the lung. Conclusion: granulomatous (specific) inflammation — hematogenously disseminated tuberculosis.

**“The liver in visceral syphilis”.** The liver is enlarged, hard and coarsely bumpy, divided by deep stellate scars into irregular lobes (“hepar lobatum”). Conclusion: tertiary syphilis — gummas and scars.

**“Syphilitic aortic aneurysm (syphilitic mesaortitis)”.** The ascending aorta and arch are saccularly dilated; the intima is uneven, with a “shagreen skin” appearance and deep scarred folds. Conclusion: a complication of productive inflammation (syphilitic mesaortitis).

**“Echinococcosis of the liver (or kidney)”.** White, round, fluid-filled cyst(s) in the organ, separated from the surroundings by a thick fibrous capsule. Conclusion: productive inflammation around animal parasites (encapsulation).

**“Gastric (intestinal) polyp”.** A soft, gray-reddish lesion on a thin stalk on the mucosal surface. Conclusion: productive inflammation forming polyps (or an adenomatous polyp — histologic examination is necessary).
**“Keloid scar”.** A dense, smooth, raised scar on the skin extending beyond the wound margins. Conclusion: pathologic regeneration.

**“Tuberculous granuloma (lung or lymph node)”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Structureless pink caseous necrosis in the center, surrounded by a layer of epithelioid cells with Pirogov–Langhans giant cells among them (nuclei in a horseshoe), and lymphocytes at the periphery; no vessels inside the granuloma. Conclusion: tuberculous granuloma.

**“Syphilitic gumma”** or **“syphilitic mesaortitis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Extensive coagulative necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, numerous plasma cells and fibroblasts; productive endovasculitis in small vessels. In the aorta — a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate around the vasa vasorum in the media, with destroyed elastic fibers. Conclusion: productive inflammation in syphilis. 3. **“Rhinoscleroma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Plasma cells, lymphocytes, hyaline bodies and large foamy Mikulicz cells beneath the nasal mucosa. Conclusion: scleroma granuloma. 4. **“Foreign body granuloma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Foreign body giant cells (haphazard nuclei), macrophages and fibroblasts around a foreign body (suture). Conclusion: nonimmune granuloma. 5. **“Interstitial myocarditis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). A diffuse lymphocytic-macrophage infiltrate and edema in the myocardial stroma; degeneration of cardiomyocytes. Conclusion: interstitial productive inflammation. 6. **“Granulation tissue”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Numerous vertically oriented thin-walled capillaries with fibroblasts, macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells and neutrophils between them; edematous intercellular substance. Conclusion: granulation tissue (repair). 7. **“Organization of a thrombus”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Granulation tissue consisting of fibroblasts and capillaries has grown into the thrombotic mass from the wall; new channels lined by endothelium. Conclusion: organization and canalization.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 28-year-old man has prolonged low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Lymph node biopsy: numerous granulomas with a structureless, granular, pink mass in the center, surrounded by epithelioid cells and giant cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe; lymphocytes at the periphery.
cases.ask: 1) Your histologic conclusion? 2) State the structure of the granuloma and the name of the giant cell. 3) How can the diagnosis be confirmed, and what is the mechanism of granuloma formation?
cases.answer: 1) Granulomatous epithelioid cell lymphadenitis with caseous necrosis — tuberculosis. 2) Caseous necrosis in the center, surrounded by epithelioid cells with Pirogov–Langhans giant cells among them and lymphocytes at the periphery; no vessels inside the granuloma. 3) Ziehl–Neelsen staining (acid-fast red bacilli), PCR, culture, clinical tests (Mantoux, QuantiFERON). Mechanism — type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity: Th1 lymphocytes produce IFN-gamma and activate macrophages, which turn into epithelioid and giant cells; mycobacteria survive inside macrophages because of incomplete phagocytosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 55-year-old man died suddenly of cardiac tamponade. At autopsy the ascending aorta is saccularly dilated (aneurysm) and ruptured; the intima is uneven and folded, with a “shagreen skin” appearance. Microscopically: an infiltrate of lymphocytes and numerous plasma cells around the vasa vasorum in the aortic media, destroyed elastic fibers, scar tissue; endarteritis in small vessels.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What period of the disease is this, and what is the process in the aorta called? 3) Specific changes of syphilis in other organs and the structure of a gumma.
cases.answer: 1) A complication of syphilitic mesaortitis — rupture of an aortic aneurysm, cardiac tamponade. 2) Tertiary (visceral) syphilis; the process in the aorta is gummatous infiltration (productive mesaortitis): the lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate around the vasa vasorum, destruction of the elastic framework and scar formation in its place weaken the aortic wall and lead to an aneurysm. 3) Gumma — extensive coagulative (gummatous) necrosis in the center surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblasts, few epithelioid and giant cells, and productive endovasculitis. Gummas occur in the liver (“hepar lobatum”), bones, skin, brain and other organs.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: After abdominal surgery, a 40-year-old woman's surgical wound became infected; the sutures were removed and the wound was treated open. A month later the wound healed but left a wide, coarse scar. A year later a thick, hard, itchy raised lesion extending beyond the wound margins appeared in the skin around the scar.
cases.ask: 1) By which intention did the wound heal? 2) Its differences from healing by first intention and its mechanism. 3) What is the subsequent change in the scar called, and how does it differ?
cases.answer: 1) By second intention. 2) In healing by first intention the wound is clean with closely apposed edges, there is little granulation tissue, and a thin scar remains. In healing by second intention, infection and a large defect cause intense inflammation and abundant granulation tissue; the wound contracts due to myofibroblasts (contraction), and a wide, coarse scar remains. 3) Keloid — pathologic regeneration resulting from excessive collagen synthesis (TGF-beta and other factors, hereditary predisposition); it differs from a hypertrophic scar in that it grows beyond the wound margins, does not regress spontaneously and tends to recur after excision.

topics.title: Hemodynamic disorders. Thrombosis, embolism, infarction, shock

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the classification of disorders of blood and lymph circulation;
arterial and venous hyperemia: types, causes, morphology and outcomes; “nutmeg liver”, brown induration of the lung;
anemia (ischemia), and types of bleeding and hemorrhage;
edema, its mechanisms and types;
hemostasis and thrombosis: Virchow's triad, types of thrombi, outcomes; DIC;
types of embolism and their outcomes, pulmonary thromboembolism;
infarction: definition, types (white, red, white with a red rim), morphology, outcomes;
shock: types, stages and “shock organs”.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of “nutmeg liver”, brown induration of the lung, cerebral hemorrhage, a thrombus in the aortic wall, pulmonary thromboembolism, ischemic infarction of the spleen, hemorrhagic infarction of the lung and myocardial infarction;

describe microscopic slides of nutmeg liver, venous congestion of the skin, stasis in cerebral capillaries, a mixed thrombus, pulmonary fat embolism, ischemic infarction of the kidney and hemorrhagic infarction of the lung;
distinguish a thrombus from a postmortem blood clot;
determine the type of infarct according to the organ and the type of blood supply.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The development of collateral circulation determines the outcome of ischemia: organs supplied by **functional end arteries** (heart, brain, kidney, spleen) are very sensitive to ischemia, and **infarction** develops easily in them; organs with a **dual** blood supply (lung, liver) and organs with many collaterals (arm, leg) are relatively resistant.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Virchow's triad — “**Wall, Flow, Blood**”: **W**all (endothelial injury), **F**low (stasis, turbulence), **B**lood (hypercoagulability). In arterial thrombosis the main factor is the **wall**; in venous thrombosis — the **flow**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Distinguishing a thrombus from a **postmortem blood clot** (Topic 2): a thrombus is **dull, dry, friable, with a rough (corrugated) surface, layered** and **attached** to the vessel wall; a postmortem clot is **smooth, shiny, elastic and moist**, follows the shape of the vessel, is not attached to the wall and is separated into “**chicken fat**” (yellow) and “**currant jelly**” (red) layers.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remembering the color of infarcts by organ: “**Lung and bowel — red, spleen and kidney — white, heart — white with a red rim, brain — softens**”. A red infarct needs “**Two routes and loose tissue**”: a dual blood supply, venous congestion and loose tissue.

blocks.text: Circulatory disorders are divided into two large groups:

items: **Disorders of blood supply (blood filling):** arterial hyperemia, venous hyperemia (congestion), anemia (ischemia).

**Disorders of the rheological properties of blood and of vessel wall permeability:** bleeding and hemorrhage, plasmorrhagia, stasis, thrombosis, embolism, DIC, shock. In addition, **disorders of lymph circulation** (lymphostasis, lymphedema) and **changes in the amount of tissue fluid** (edema, exsiccosis) are also considered in this section. Circulatory disorders are **generalized** (heart failure, shock) and **local** (thrombosis, infarction).

blocks.text: **Arterial hyperemia (active hyperemia)** is the filling of an organ or tissue with blood as a result of increased arterial inflow. It is an **active** process: the arterioles dilate (neurogenic and humoral influences). The tissue is **red** (bright), warm and slightly enlarged.
**General arterial hyperemia (plethora)** — an increase in circulating blood volume (erythremia — Vaquez disease, multiple transfusions).
**Local arterial hyperemia** is physiological (physical work, blushing with embarrassment) or pathologic. **Types of pathologic hyperemia:**

items: **angioneurotic (neuroparalytic)** — loss of the influence of vasoconstrictor nerves or excitation of vasodilator nerves (reddening of the facial skin);
**collateral** — increased blood flow through collateral pathways when a main artery is occluded;
**vacant (ex vacuo)** — filling of tissue with blood when barometric pressure falls (for example, when medical cupping glasses are applied);
**postanemic** — a sudden rush of blood when a compressed artery is released (for example, the abdominal vessels when ascitic fluid is removed rapidly); it can lead to cerebral anemia and fainting;
**inflammatory hyperemia** — the most common type (Topic 5);
hyperemia due to an **arteriovenous fistula**.

blocks.text: **Venous hyperemia (passive hyperemia, congestion)** is an increase of blood in an organ or tissue as a result of **impaired venous outflow**. It is a **passive** process. The veins and capillaries dilate and fill with deoxygenated blood — the tissue becomes **bluish-red** (**cyanosis**), and its temperature falls.
Generalized venous congestion
**The cause is heart failure** (myocarditis, cardiosclerosis, heart defects, myocardial infarction, hypertension). It is acute or chronic.

**Acute generalized venous congestion** — in acute heart failure (myocardial infarction, acute myocarditis): capillary hypoxia and permeability increase, with **plasmorrhagia, edema and diapedetic hemorrhages**, degeneration and necrosis in the parenchyma; in the lung — **pulmonary edema**.

**Chronic generalized venous congestion** — in chronic heart failure. Prolonged hypoxia leads to **parenchymal atrophy** and **stromal sclerosis** (activation of fibroblasts) — the organs become **firm** — **cyanotic (congestive) induration**. Cyanosis of the skin, edema (anasarca), transudate in the cavities (ascites, hydrothorax, hydropericardium).
Changes in the organs:

**1. Liver — “nutmeg liver”.** In right ventricular failure, blood stagnates in the inferior vena cava; the hepatic veins, then **the central veins of the lobules and the sinusoids of the central zones** fill with blood. Hepatocytes of the central zone undergo **atrophy and necrosis** because of hypoxia (the lobule center is the least supplied with oxygen), whereas hepatocytes in the periphery undergo **fatty degeneration**. As a result the liver is enlarged and firm, and on the cut surface it is mottled **red-brown (center) and yellowish (periphery)** — resembling the cut surface of a **nutmeg**. If the process is prolonged, **nutmeg fibrosis** and then **cardiac (nutmeg) cirrhosis** develop.

blocks.text: **2. Lung — brown induration. Left ventricular failure** and especially **mitral stenosis** cause blood stagnation in the pulmonary circulation. The capillaries of the interalveolar septa dilate, and **diapedetic hemorrhages** occur; macrophages engulf red cells that have entered the alveoli and accumulate **hemosiderin** (**“heart failure cells”**, Topic 4); because of chronic hypoxia, **sclerosis** develops in the interalveolar septa. The lung becomes **brown (hemosiderosis)** and **firm (induration)**. Pulmonary hypertension leads to right ventricular hypertrophy.
**3. Kidneys — cyanotic induration**: the kidney is enlarged, firm and bluish, with a dark red medulla.
**4. Spleen — cyanotic induration**: enlarged, firm, dark cherry-colored.
**5. Skin and limbs** — cyanosis, edema, trophic ulcers.

blocks.text: Local venous congestion

It occurs when venous outflow from a particular area is impaired: when a vein is occluded by a thrombus or embolus, or compressed from outside (tumor, scar, cast, bandage). Examples: congestion in the **portal venous system in liver cirrhosis** (**portal hypertension**: ascites, splenomegaly, esophageal varices); **Budd–Chiari syndrome** (thrombosis of the hepatic veins); edema and cyanosis of the leg in thrombosis of the leg veins.

parts.text: In **portal hypertension**, blood passes from the portal vein to the inferior and superior venae cavae through **portocaval anastomoses**: the veins of the esophagus and gastric cardia (**varices** — sudden massive bleeding from them is one of the main causes of death in patients with cirrhosis), the rectal veins (**hemorrhoids**), and the veins of the anterior abdominal wall (“**caput medusae**”).

blocks.text: **Local anemia (ischemia)** is a **decrease or cessation of arterial blood flow** to an organ or tissue. Generalized anemia is **anemia** proper (blood diseases). Causes of local ischemia:

items: **angiospastic** — arterial spasm (stress, cold, Raynaud syndrome, cocaine);
**obturative** — occlusion of the arterial lumen by a thrombus, embolus or atherosclerotic plaque;
**compressive** — compression of an artery from outside (tumor, tourniquet, ligature);

**due to redistribution of blood** — ischemia of other areas during postanemic hyperemia. The outcomes depend on the speed and duration of ischemia and the sensitivity of the tissue: **acute ischemia** — degeneration and **infarction** (necrosis); **chronic ischemia** — **atrophy** of the parenchyma and **sclerosis** of the stroma (for example, atherosclerotic nephrosclerosis, chronic cerebral ischemia — dementia).

parts.text: The development of collateral circulation determines the outcome of ischemia: organs supplied by **functional end arteries** (heart, brain, kidney, spleen) are very sensitive to ischemia, and **infarction** develops easily in them; organs with a **dual** blood supply (lung, liver) and organs with many collaterals (arm, leg) are relatively resistant.

blocks.text: **Bleeding (hemorrhage)** is the escape of blood **from a vessel or a cardiac chamber**: **external** (to the outside) and **internal** (into a body cavity or tissue). Accumulation of blood in tissue is called **hemorrhage (extravasation)**.
Types of bleeding by mechanism:

items: **Bleeding due to rupture** (per rhexin) — rupture of the wall of a vessel or the heart: trauma, rupture of an aneurysm, cardiac rupture in myocardial infarction, rupture of a cerebral vessel in essential hypertension.

**Bleeding due to erosion (arrosive)** (per diabrosin) — destruction of the vessel wall by inflammation, necrosis or tumor: at the floor of a gastric ulcer, in a tuberculous cavity, during tumor breakdown, in ectopic (tubal) pregnancy.

**Diapedetic bleeding** (per diapedesin) — escape of red cells from microvessels with **increased permeability** without disruption of the vessel wall: hypoxia, vasculitis, infections, intoxications, hemorrhagic diatheses (thrombocytopenia, hemophilia), DIC. Usually **small, pinpoint** hemorrhages.

blocks.label: Figure 7.6
blocks.caption: Cerebral hemorrhage — hematoma: a blood clot in the region of the subcortical nuclei of the hemispheres, ruptured into the ventricles (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 7.5
blocks.caption: Diapedetic hemorrhage in brain tissue: a collection of red cells around a capillary (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 4-7)

blocks.text: Types of hemorrhage:

items: **hematoma** — destruction of tissue with formation of a cavity filled with blood (brain, muscles, subcutaneous tissue);
**hemorrhagic infiltration (imbibition)** — soaking of tissue with blood while its structure is preserved;
**bruise (ecchymosis)** — a flat hemorrhage in the skin or mucosa larger than 1–2 cm;
**petechiae** — pinpoint hemorrhages of 1–2 mm (in serous and mucous membranes; asphyxia, thrombocytopenia, sepsis);

**purpura** — hemorrhages up to 3–5 mm (vasculitis, thrombocytopenia). **Accumulation of blood in cavities:** hemothorax (in the pleural cavity), **hemopericardium** (in the pericardium — **cardiac tamponade**), hemoperitoneum (in the peritoneal cavity), hemarthrosis (in a joint). Bleeding from organs: **nose** (epistaxis), **lung** (hemoptysis — coughing up blood), **stomach** (hematemesis — vomiting of blood, “coffee grounds”), **intestine** (melena — black, tarry stools), **urinary tract** (hematuria), **uterus** (metrorrhagia, menorrhagia).

blocks.text: **Outcomes:** resorption of blood (small hemorrhages); accumulation of hemosiderin with formation of a **“rust-colored” cyst** (in the brain); organization and encapsulation; suppuration. The significance depends on the volume and rate of blood loss (if more than 20% of the total blood volume is lost rapidly — **hemorrhagic shock**) and on the location (brainstem, pericardium).

**Plasmorrhagia** is the escape of blood plasma from the vascular lumen with **soaking** of the vessel wall and surrounding tissues (**plasmatic imbibition**). Mainly in microcirculatory vessels — essential hypertension, atherosclerosis, rheumatic diseases, diabetes mellitus. The vessel wall is thickened and homogeneous; the outcome is **hyalinosis** (arteriolohyalinosis) or **fibrinoid necrosis** (Topic 3).

**Stasis** (Greek stasis — standstill) is the **cessation of blood flow** in microcirculatory vessels (mainly capillaries). In the capillaries, red cells stick together to form homogeneous columns (**sludge phenomenon** — red cell aggregation), but there is no hemolysis or clotting (unlike a thrombus). Causes: infections, intoxications, shock, cold or heat. Stasis is reversible (blood flow is restored); if prolonged, it leads to necrosis.

blocks.label: Figure 7.7
blocks.caption: Stasis in cerebral capillaries: the brain tissue is edematous, with columns of agglutinated red cells in the capillaries (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 7.8
blocks.caption: Venous congestion of the skin: the veins and capillaries are markedly dilated and filled with blood (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Edema** is an **increase in intercellular (interstitial) tissue fluid**. Accumulation of fluid in cavities is called **dropsy** (Greek hydrops): **hydrothorax** (pleura), **hydropericardium**, **ascites** (peritoneal cavity, hydroperitoneum), **hydrocele** (tunica vaginalis of the testis). Diffuse edema of the subcutaneous tissue — **anasarca**. Edema fluid is a **transudate** (low protein, clear; Topic 5).
Mechanisms of edema (Starling forces):

items: **Increased hydrostatic pressure in capillaries** — heart failure (generalized venous congestion), venous thrombosis, portal hypertension.

**Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (hypoproteinemia)** — **nephrotic syndrome** (albumin is lost in the urine), **liver cirrhosis** (albumin synthesis decreases), protein-energy malnutrition (“hunger edema”).
**Increased vascular permeability** — inflammation, allergy (Quincke edema (angioedema)), toxins.

**Impaired lymph flow** (**lymphedema**) — involvement of lymph nodes by tumor or their removal (arm edema after breast cancer surgery), parasites (filariasis — **elephantiasis**), postirradiation sclerosis.

**Sodium and water retention** — kidney failure, secondary hyperaldosteronism (activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system in heart failure). **Types of edema: cardiac edema** (begins in the legs — gravitational, worse in the evening; anasarca); **renal edema** (begins in the face and eyelids, worse in the morning; widespread in nephrotic syndrome); **hepatic edema** (mainly ascites); **hunger edema**; **inflammatory and allergic edema**; **lymphedema**.

blocks.text: **Morphology:** edematous skin is pale and doughy, and a pit remains when pressed with a finger. Edematous organs are enlarged and heavy, and fluid flows from the cut surface. **Pulmonary edema** — the lung is heavy (2–3 times normal), and frothy pink fluid flows from the cut surface; the alveoli are filled with pale pink protein-containing fluid; in left ventricular failure (acute — myocardial infarction, hypertensive crisis) and toxic and allergic influences. **Cerebral edema** — the brain is enlarged, the gyri are flattened and the sulci narrowed; **displacement (herniation)** of the brain and **impaction into the foramen magnum** (herniation of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum) — the brainstem is compressed, and the respiratory and cardiac centers stop functioning — death.

parts.text: **The significance of edema** depends on its location: edema of the legs causes discomfort and predisposes to trophic ulcers; **laryngeal edema** (Quincke edema) — asphyxia; **pulmonary edema** — acute respiratory failure (emergency care: oxygen, diuretics); **cerebral edema** and brain herniation — a cause of death. With prolonged edema, sclerosis develops in the tissue.

blocks.text: **Exsiccosis (dehydration)** — a decrease in body water: severe diarrhea (cholera, food poisoning), vomiting, profuse sweating, diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus. The skin is dry and wrinkled, the eyes are sunken, and the blood thickens; in severe cases — hypovolemic shock.
Normal hemostasis

**Hemostasis** is a complex system that stops bleeding when a vessel is injured and at the same time keeps the blood fluid in intact vessels. Its participants are the **endothelium, platelets** and **coagulation factors**. Stages of hemostasis:

items: **Brief arteriolar vasoconstriction** (under the action of endothelin).

**Primary hemostasis** — **platelet adhesion** to the exposed subendothelial matrix at the site of injury (via **von Willebrand factor**), their activation (release of ADP and thromboxane A~2~ from granules) and **aggregation** — a **platelet plug** forms.

**Secondary hemostasis** — **tissue factor** (factor III) triggers the coagulation cascade (via factor VII), and **thrombin** is formed; thrombin converts fibrinogen to **fibrin** and further activates platelets.

**Stabilization and contraction (retraction) of the clot**, followed by its dissolution by **fibrinolysis** (plasmin). Normal endothelium has **antithrombotic** properties: prostacyclin (PGI~2~) and NO (inhibit platelet aggregation), thrombomodulin (turns thrombin into an activator of protein C), heparin-like molecules (activate antithrombin III), tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA).

blocks.text: Thrombosis

**Thrombosis** is **clotting** of blood (formation of a clot) in the vascular lumen or cardiac chambers **during life**. The clot formed is a **thrombus**. Thrombosis is a pathologic activation of hemostasis.
Causes of thrombosis — Virchow's triad:

items: **Endothelial injury** — the most important factor (it alone can cause thrombosis): atherosclerotic plaques, endocardial injury in myocardial infarction, vasculitis, hypertension, trauma, bacterial toxins, cigarette smoke, hypercholesterolemia.

**Abnormal blood flow** — **slowing (stasis)** (in veins — heart failure, immobility, varicose veins; in the cardiac chambers — atrial fibrillation, dilated ventricles, aneurysms) or **turbulence** (in arteries — at plaques and bifurcations).

**Increased coagulability of blood (hypercoagulability, thrombophilia)**: – **primary (hereditary)** — **factor V mutation (Leiden)** — the most common; prothrombin gene mutation, deficiency of antithrombin III, protein C and protein S; – **secondary (acquired)** — prolonged bed rest, surgery and trauma, **malignant tumors**

blocks.text: (Trousseau syndrome — migratory thrombophlebitis), pregnancy and the postpartum period, **oral contraceptives**, smoking, obesity, **antiphospholipid syndrome**, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, nephrotic syndrome.

parts.text: Virchow's triad — “**Wall, Flow, Blood**”: **W**all (endothelial injury), **F**low (stasis, turbulence), **B**lood (hypercoagulability). In arterial thrombosis the main factor is the **wall**; in venous thrombosis — the **flow**.

blocks.text: **Stages of thrombus formation (morphogenesis):** 1) **agglutination** of platelets (adhesion and aggregation); 2) **coagulation of fibrinogen**, formation of fibrin; 3) **agglutination** of red cells (trapping in the fibrin network); 4) **precipitation** of plasma proteins.
Types of thrombi
By structure and appearance:

items: **White thrombus** — composed of platelets, fibrin and leukocytes; it forms **slowly**, in places with **rapid** blood flow — in **arteries** and on heart valves (in endocarditis).
**Red thrombus** — composed of a fibrin network with entrapped red cells; it forms where clotting is **rapid** and blood flow is **slow** — in **veins**.

**Mixed (laminated) thrombus** — the most common; it has a **head** (with the structure of a white thrombus, attached to the vessel wall), a **body** (mixed — alternating white and red layers: **lines of Zahn**) and a **tail** (red thrombus, free). It occurs in veins, the aorta and cardiac aneurysms.

**Hyaline thrombi** — in microcirculatory vessels, composed of hemolyzed red cells, platelets and precipitated proteins; a homogeneous mass; in **DIC** and shock. **By relation to the vessel lumen: mural (parietal)** — partially occludes the lumen; **occlusive (obturating)** — completely occludes the lumen.

blocks.text: **By location: arterial** (coronary, cerebral, femoral and mesenteric arteries — usually over an atherosclerotic plaque, white or mixed, mural — leads to infarction), **venous (phlebothrombosis)** — most often in the **deep veins of the leg** (the source of pulmonary embolism), red, occlusive; in an inflamed vein — **thrombophlebitis**; **in the cardiac chambers** — **mural thrombi** (in myocardial infarction, aneurysm), thrombi in the auricles in atrial fibrillation, a free-lying **ball thrombus** in the atrium, **vegetations** on the valves (infective endocarditis) and a **propagating thrombus** (growing along the vessel toward the heart); capillary thrombosis.

**Special types: dilatation thrombus** — in aneurysms and varicose vessels; **marantic (stasis) thrombus** — in debilitated, cachectic elderly patients (because of slowed blood flow, most often in the dural venous sinuses and leg veins); **tumor thrombus** — when a tumor grows through the vessel wall and spreads along the vessel (in the renal vein in renal cell carcinoma); **septic thrombus** — a thrombus containing microbes (risk of purulent dissolution).

blocks.caption: Mixed thrombus with a corrugated surface (a) and a ball thrombus in the left atrium (b) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 4-11)

parts.text: Distinguishing a thrombus from a **postmortem blood clot** (Topic 2): a thrombus is **dull, dry, friable, with a rough (corrugated) surface, layered** and **attached** to the vessel wall; a postmortem clot is **smooth, shiny, elastic and moist**, follows the shape of the vessel, is not attached to the wall and is separated into “**chicken fat**” (yellow) and “**currant jelly**” (red) layers.

blocks.text: Outcomes of a thrombus
Favorable outcomes:

items: **aseptic autolysis (dissolution)** — by the fibrinolytic system (plasmin), especially in small and fresh thrombi; **thrombolytic therapy** (alteplase, streptokinase) is based on this;
**organization** — **granulation tissue** grows into the thrombotic mass from the wall and replaces it with connective tissue (beginning on days 5–6);
**canalization and vascularization** — clefts and new endothelium-lined channels form in the organized thrombus, and blood flow is partially restored (**recanalization**);
**calcification (petrification)** — in veins — **phleboliths** (vein stones).

blocks.text: Unfavorable outcomes:

items: **occlusion** of the vessel — in an artery, **infarction** or **gangrene**; in a vein, **venous congestion and edema** in the distal area;
**thromboembolism** — detachment of the thrombus or a fragment of it and its transport with the blood stream;
**septic (purulent) dissolution** — when the thrombus is infected with microbes; **thromboembolic sepsis**, purulent metastases;
**propagation** of the thrombus — its extension along the vessel.

blocks.text: DIC

**Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)** is not an independent disease but a **complication** of many severe conditions: numerous **microthrombi** (hyaline and fibrin thrombi) form in microcirculatory vessels, as a result of which platelets and coagulation factors are **consumed** (**consumptive coagulopathy**) and fibrinolysis is activated — **bleeding** develops. Therefore DIC is also called a “**thrombohemorrhagic syndrome**”.

**Causes:** obstetric complications (premature placental separation, amniotic fluid embolism, a dead fetus), **sepsis** (especially gram-negative, meningococcemia), **shock**, extensive trauma and burns, malignant tumors (cancer of the lung, pancreas, prostate, acute promyelocytic leukemia), hemolytic transfusion reactions, snake venom.
**Stages:** 1) hypercoagulation; 2) consumptive coagulopathy; 3) **activation of fibrinolysis and hypocoagulation** — bleeding; 4) recovery (or death).

**Morphology:** microthrombi in the microvessels of the kidneys, lungs, brain, liver, heart and adrenal glands; numerous diapedetic **hemorrhages** (petechiae, ecchymoses), small foci of **necrosis** and **infarcts**; **symmetric necrosis** of the renal cortex, pituitary necrosis (**Sheehan syndrome** — postpartum), bilateral hemorrhage into the adrenal glands (**Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome** — in meningococcemia). The result is **multiple organ failure**.

**Embolism** (Greek emballein — to throw in) is the circulation in blood or lymph of **particles (emboli)** not normally found there and the **occlusion** of vessels by them. Emboli are solid, liquid or gaseous.
By the direction of movement of the embolus:

items: **orthograde** — with the blood flow (the most common): from the systemic veins and the right heart — into the **pulmonary artery** system; from the left heart and aorta — into the **arteries of the systemic circulation** (brain, kidney, spleen, intestine, legs); from the intestinal veins — into the **portal vein** system (to the liver);
**retrograde** — **against** the blood flow: a heavy embolus (for example, in the inferior vena cava system) descends under its own weight (into the hepatic and renal veins);

**paradoxical** — an embolus from the systemic veins bypasses the lungs and passes directly into the **arteries** of the systemic circulation through a **septal defect of the heart** (patent foramen ovale, ventricular septal defect) (for example, a leg vein thrombus occludes a cerebral artery).

blocks.text: Types of embolism
**1. Thromboembolism** — the most common embolism (about 95–99% of emboli): the embolus is a detached thrombus or a fragment of it.

**Pulmonary thromboembolism (PE)** is one of the most important causes of death in hospitalized patients. Its source in **95% of cases is thrombosis of the deep veins of the leg** (popliteal, femoral, iliac veins). The consequences depend on the size of the embolus:

items: **large emboli** — impact in the **trunk** of the pulmonary artery or at the bifurcation of its main branches (**“saddle” embolus**) — **sudden death** (acute right ventricular failure, “acute cor pulmonale”, cardiogenic shock); the **pulmocoronary reflex** (coronary artery spasm) is also important in the mechanism of death;

**medium-sized emboli** — in the medium branches of the pulmonary artery; if the blood supply from the bronchial arteries is adequate, infarction does not develop, only hemorrhage; against a background of **left ventricular failure** (venous congestion) — **hemorrhagic infarction**;

**multiple small emboli** — if recurrent, **pulmonary hypertension** and **chronic cor pulmonale**. **Systemic thromboembolism** — the source is mainly the **left heart** (mural thrombi in myocardial infarction — 2/3 of cases, left auricular thrombi in atrial fibrillation, left ventricular aneurysm, valvular vegetations — endocarditis), and also thrombi over atherosclerotic plaques in the aorta. The emboli impact in the arteries of the **brain** (ischemic stroke), **legs** (gangrene), **kidney, spleen and intestine** and cause **infarcts**.

blocks.text: **2. Fat embolism** — entry of fat droplets into vessels: **fractures of long bones** (yellow marrow fat), extensive crushing of subcutaneous fatty tissue, burns, erroneous intravascular injection of oily drugs. Fat droplets first occlude the **pulmonary capillaries**; if numerous, they pass through the lungs and reach the capillaries of the **brain and kidneys**. **Fat embolism syndrome** (1–3 days after injury): pulmonary insufficiency, neurological signs (numerous petechiae in the brain), anemia, thrombocytopenia, petechial skin rash. Fat is detected with **Sudan III** (on frozen sections).
**Bone marrow embolism** — fragments of bone marrow (hematopoietic cells and fat cells) in pulmonary vessels in bone fractures and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (rib fractures).

blocks.label: Figure 7.17
blocks.caption: Fat embolism of pulmonary capillaries (Sudan III): many capillaries are filled with orange-red fat droplets (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 7.16
blocks.caption: Bone marrow embolus in a pulmonary vessel: hematopoietic cells (left) and fat vacuoles (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 4-16)

blocks.text: **3. Air embolism** — entry of **atmospheric air** into the vessels: injury to the neck veins (negative pressure inside them), surgery (cardiac, pulmonary, neurosurgery — in the sitting position), breaches of technique during intravascular injections and infusions, artificial pneumothorax, childbirth. Air bubbles accumulate in the **right heart**, form frothy blood and occlude the pulmonary capillaries. Usually **more than 100 mL** of air is needed to be clinically significant. At autopsy, to detect air embolism, the heart is opened **under water** (air bubbles escape).

**4. Gas embolism** — formation of bubbles from **dissolved gases** (mainly nitrogen) in the blood when atmospheric pressure falls rapidly — **caisson (decompression) disease**: in divers and caisson workers who surface rapidly and in pilots who climb rapidly to altitude in an unpressurized cabin. Gas bubbles occlude the vessels of joints and muscles (pain — “**the bends**”), the lungs (shortness of breath — “the chokes”), and the capillaries of the brain and spinal cord (paralysis); in the chronic form — **aseptic necrosis** of bones (femoral head). Gas also forms in tissue in gas gangrene.

**5. Tissue (cellular) embolism** — fragments of tissue or cells: **tumor cell embolism** — the basis of **metastases** (hematogenous and lymphogenous); fragments of tissue destroyed in trauma (brain, liver); **amniotic fluid embolism** — during childbirth, amniotic fluid (desquamated epithelium, lanugo hairs, meconium, fat) enters the maternal blood and occludes the pulmonary vessels — an extremely severe complication (mortality up to 80%): sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, shock, **DIC**.

**6. Microbial (bacterial) embolism** — clusters of microbes (bacterial emboli) or fragments of a purulently dissolved thrombus in the vascular lumen: in **sepsis**, **metastatic abscesses** in various organs (kidney, myocardium, brain) (for example, **embolic purulent nephritis**), septic infarcts.
**7. Foreign body embolism** — bullets, shell fragments, catheter fragments, calcium and cholesterol crystals (when an atherosclerotic plaque ruptures — cholesterol embolism).
**8. Parasite embolism** — echinococcus, ascarids.

blocks.caption: Tumor cell embolism: melanoma cells in a lymph node — a cluster of cells with dark brown pigment (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 7.19
blocks.caption: Embolic purulent nephritis (microscopic slide): basophilic bacterial emboli in small vessels (a), surrounded by purulent inflammation (b) (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Infarction** (Latin infarcire — to stuff) is **vascular (ischemic) necrosis** resulting from sudden cessation of blood supply (**ischemia**). The most common causes of infarction are **arterial thrombosis** (usually over an atherosclerotic plaque) and **embolism**; less often — prolonged **spasm**, external compression of a vessel, complete cessation of venous outflow (for example, torsion of the testis or ovary), intestinal obstruction.
Factors influencing the development of infarction:

items: **type of blood supply** — functional end arteries (heart, brain, kidney, spleen) — infarction develops easily; dual blood supply (lung — pulmonary and bronchial arteries; liver — hepatic artery and portal vein) — infarction is rare;
**rate of occlusion** — if it develops slowly, collaterals have time to open;
**sensitivity of the tissue to hypoxia** — neurons are irreversibly injured in 3–4 minutes, cardiomyocytes in 20–30 minutes; fibroblasts are much more resistant;
oxygen saturation of the blood (anemia, heart failure).

blocks.text: Types of infarction

**By shape:** corresponding to the vascular branching of the organ — **wedge-shaped (triangular)** (kidney, spleen, lung — the base faces the organ capsule, the apex faces the hilum; fibrin on the capsule — reactive inflammation), **irregular** (heart, brain, intestine — organs without a trunk-type vascular branching).
By color and structure:
**1. White (ischemic) infarct** — whitish-yellow, firm, sharply demarcated; in **solid** organs with a **single** (end-arterial) blood supply: the **spleen, kidney**, less often the heart and brain.

**2. White infarct with a red (hemorrhagic) rim** — a zone of hemorrhage around a whitish-yellow focus (**demarcation zone**); this zone results from paralytic vasodilation after perifocal spasm and diapedetic hemorrhage. It occurs in the **heart** (myocardial infarction) and **kidney**.

**3. Red (hemorrhagic) infarct** — the necrotic focus is soaked with blood, dark red and sharply demarcated. Conditions for its development: a **dual blood supply** (lung) against a background of **venous congestion** (left ventricular failure), loose (spongy) tissues; **venous occlusion** (torsion of the testis or ovary); **restoration of blood flow** (reperfusion) in previously ischemic tissue. It occurs in the **lung and intestine**, less often in the brain (hemorrhagic transformation).
**4. Septic (infected) infarct** — when a fragment of vegetations (microbial embolus) in infective endocarditis or microbes enter the necrotic focus; the infarct turns into an **abscess**.

blocks.caption: White infarct of the kidney with a hemorrhagic rim (a) and an angiogram — no vessels in the infarct area (b) (Strukov, Serov, Fig. 3-4)

blocks.label: Figure 7.20
blocks.caption: Red and white infarcts: A — a hemorrhagic, roughly wedge-shaped red infarct of the lung; B — a sharply demarcated white infarct of the spleen (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 4-18)

blocks.text: Morphology and evolution of infarction
The main histologic appearance of an infarct is **ischemic coagulative necrosis** (in the brain — **liquefactive necrosis** — “gray softening”, Topic 2). Its evolution:

items: **First hours** — no gross changes; detected by histochemical methods (loss of glycogen and dehydrogenases). Histologic signs of necrosis appear **after 4–12 hours**.
**First days** — **demarcation inflammation** at the border of the focus: hyperemia, hemorrhage, neutrophil infiltration (days 1–3).
**Days 3–7** — macrophages phagocytose the dead tissue; **granulation tissue** begins to grow in from the periphery.

**Weeks to months** — the focus undergoes **organization** and is replaced by a **scar** (6–8 weeks in the myocardium). In the brain, necrotic foci are resorbed and a **cyst** forms (surrounded by a glial scar).

blocks.text: Infarcts in organs:

items: **Myocardial infarction** — the most common and most important; mainly in the **left ventricle** and interventricular septum; the cause is atherosclerosis and thrombosis of the coronary arteries. **Subendocardial**, **intramural**, **subepicardial** and **transmural** (involving the full thickness of the wall) infarcts are distinguished. Complications: cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, acute heart failure (pulmonary edema), **cardiac rupture** (hemopericardium, tamponade — on days 3–7), acute aneurysm, mural thrombus and thromboembolism, fibrinous pericarditis (Dressler syndrome). Outcome — **large-focal cardiosclerosis**, chronic aneurysm.
**Cerebral infarction (ischemic stroke)** — atherosclerosis, thrombosis or embolism (from the heart); white (gray softening) or red (hemorrhagic transformation); outcome — a cyst.

**Pulmonary infarction** — red (hemorrhagic), wedge-shaped, its base facing the pleura; fibrin deposits on the pleura (**fibrinous pleurisy**); cause — pulmonary thromboembolism + left ventricular failure; complications — **infarct pneumonia**, abscess, gangrene.
**Renal infarction** — white with a red rim, wedge-shaped; most often embolic (from the left heart, aorta); outcome — a depressed scar.
**Splenic infarction** — white, wedge-shaped; fibrin on its capsule (perisplenitis).
**Intestinal infarction** — red (hemorrhagic); when a mesenteric artery (embolism, thrombosis) or vein (thrombosis) is occluded; it rapidly progresses to **gangrene** and **peritonitis**.

parts.text: Remembering the color of infarcts by organ: “**Lung and bowel — red, spleen and kidney — white, heart — white with a red rim, brain — softens**”. A red infarct needs “**Two routes and loose tissue**”: a dual blood supply, venous congestion and loose tissue.

blocks.text: **Shock** is a state of **systemic hypoperfusion**: as a result of reduced cardiac output or an effective reduction in circulating blood volume, the blood supply and oxygen delivery to tissues are impaired, and cellular hypoxia and cell injury develop. Arterial blood pressure falls.

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Types of shock
head: Type
Mechanism
Causes
rows: Failure of the pumping function of the heart
Myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, myocarditis, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary thromboembolism (obstructive)
Blood loss (hemorrhagic), burns (plasma loss), severe diarrhea and vomiting (cholera)
Systemic vasodilation, increased permeability, endothelial activation and DIC under the action of microbial products and cytokines
Bacterial (most often gram-negative, gram-positive) and fungal infections (sepsis)
IgE-mediated systemic vasodilation and increased permeability
Spinal cord injury, complications of anesthesia
Combined factors of blood loss, pain and tissue crushing

blocks.text: Stages of shock:

items: **Compensated (nonprogressive) stage** — reflex compensatory mechanisms (sympathetic system, catecholamines, renin–angiotensin, ADH) maintain perfusion of vital organs (brain, heart): tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction (cold, pale skin), renal water retention. In septic shock, however, the skin may be warm and flushed.

**Progressive stage** — tissue hypoxia, anaerobic glycolysis, **lactic acidosis**; the arterioles dilate, blood pools in the microcirculation, and cardiac output falls further; the endothelium is damaged and **DIC** develops.
**Irreversible stage** — cells and tissues are irreversibly injured; treatment is ineffective — death.

blocks.text: **Morphologic changes in shock (“shock organs”):** disturbed microcirculation (redistribution of blood, sludge, stasis, hyaline microthrombi — DIC), hemorrhages, degeneration and necrosis. The main “shock organs”:

items: **shock lung** — **diffuse alveolar damage** (acute respiratory distress syndrome): the lung is heavy, dark red and edematous, with **hyaline membranes** in the alveolar walls, atelectasis and hemorrhages; acute respiratory failure;

**shock kidney** — **acute tubular necrosis** (necrotic nephrosis): the cortex is pale and swollen, the medulla dark red; necrosis of the proximal tubular epithelium; **acute kidney injury** (oliguria, anuria);
**shock liver** — centrilobular necrosis and fatty degeneration;
**heart** — subendocardial hemorrhages, small foci of necrosis (contraction band necrosis);
**brain** — hypoxic encephalopathy, ischemic necrosis (in border zones);
**digestive tract** — mucosal hemorrhages and **acute erosions and ulcers** (“stress ulcers”), hemorrhagic enteropathy;
**adrenal glands** — lipid depletion of the cortex (consumption of cortisol), bilateral hemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome). As a result, **multiple organ dysfunction syndrome** develops.

blocks.text: **Lymphatic insufficiency is mechanical** (obstruction of lymphatic vessels by tumor, scar or parasites, or their congenital aplasia), **dynamic** (a sharp increase in tissue fluid formation) and **resorptive** (changes in tissue proteins and substances). As a result **lymphostasis**, dilatation of lymphatic vessels (**lymphangiectasia**) and **lymphedema** develop. In chronic lymphedema, **sclerosis** develops in the skin and subcutaneous tissue and the part becomes markedly enlarged — **elephantiasis** (Topic 1). When the thoracic duct is injured or obstructed, **chylous ascites** and **chylothorax** (accumulation of milky lymph — chyle) develop.
The “silent killer” in hospital — deep vein thrombosis

A 68-year-old woman underwent surgery for a femoral neck fracture and was on bed rest for 10 days. When she got up for the first time to go to the toilet, she suddenly became short of breath and cyanotic and died. At autopsy there was a saddle thromboembolus in the pulmonary trunk and its main branches, and occlusive red thrombi in the deep veins of the left calf. The patient had all components of Virchow's triad: **slowing of blood flow** (immobility), **endothelial injury** (surgery, trauma) and **hypercoagulability** (postoperative state, old age). Therefore **prevention of thrombosis** after surgery (early mobilization, compression stockings, low-molecular-weight heparins) is mandatory.

parts.text: **Knowing the evolution of myocardial infarction has forensic and clinical significance**: the “age” of an infarct can be determined from its histologic features — neutrophils (1–3 days), macrophages and granulation tissue (3–10 days), scar (6–8 weeks). **Cardiac rupture** occurs most often on **days 3–7** — the period when the necrotic focus has been softened by macrophages but not yet replaced by a scar.

items: **Hyperemia** (Greek hyper — excess, haima — blood) — local filling with blood (plethora of a part).
**Plethora** (Greek plethora — fullness) — an increase in the total blood volume of the organism.
**Vacant hyperemia** (Latin vacuus — empty) — hyperemia associated with a fall in barometric pressure.
**Erythema** (Greek erythros — red) — reddening of the skin as a result of active hyperemia.
**Cyanosis** (Greek kyanos — dark blue) — bluish-red coloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to deoxygenated blood.
**Induration** (Latin induratio — hardening) — sclerosis of tissues as a result of chronic venous congestion.
**Ischemia** (Greek ischo — I hold back, haima — blood) — local anemia resulting from reduced blood inflow.
**Hemorrhage** (Greek haimorrhagia) — bleeding.
**Arrosive bleeding** (Latin arrodere — to gnaw away) — bleeding resulting from erosion of the vessel wall.
**Diapedesis** (Greek dia — through, pedao — I leap) — passage of red and white blood cells through the vessel wall.
**Hemopericardium** — accumulation of blood in the pericardial cavity.
**Stasis** (Greek stasis — standstill) — cessation of blood flow in capillaries.
**Sludge** (English sludge — mud) — blood in a state of red cell aggregation.
**Transudate** (Latin trans — through, sudare — to seep) — edema fluid.
**Anasarca** (Greek ana — over, sarx — flesh) — diffuse edema of the subcutaneous fatty tissue.
**Ascites** (Greek askites — like a leather bag) — noninflammatory accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity.
**Hydrothorax / hydropericardium** — accumulation of edema fluid in the pleural / pericardial cavity.
**Hydrocephalus** (Greek hydor — water, kephale — head) — accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles of the brain (internal) or the subarachnoid space (external).
**Chylous ascites** (Greek chylos — juice) — accumulation of chyle (lymph) in the peritoneal cavity.
**Exsiccosis** (Latin exsiccare — to dry out) — a decrease in interstitial fluid (dehydration).
**Homeostasis** (Greek homoios — same, stasis — state) — the constancy of the internal environment of the organism.
**Thrombosis** (Greek thrombosis — clotting) — clotting of blood in a vessel or cardiac chamber during life.
**Coagulation** (Latin coagulatio — clotting) — clotting of blood.
**Agglutination** (Latin agglutinatio — gluing together) — clumping and sticking together of cellular elements (platelets, red cells, bacteria).
**Adhesion** (Latin adhaesio — sticking) — sticking to a surface.
**Precipitation** (Latin praecipitatio — falling down) — deposition of a substance from a solution as a precipitate.
**Retraction** (Latin retractio — contraction) — contraction (shrinkage) of a blood clot.
**Occlusive (obturating) thrombus** (Latin obturare — to stop up) — a thrombus that completely occludes the vascular lumen.
**Dilatation thrombus** (Latin dilatare — to widen) — a thrombus in aneurysms and dilated vessels.
**Marantic thrombus** (Greek marasmos — wasting) — a (stasis) thrombus resulting from slowed blood flow in debilitated patients.
**Embolism** (Greek emballein — to throw in) — circulation in blood or lymph of particles not normally found there and occlusion of vessels by them.
**Retrograde embolism** — movement of an embolus against the blood flow.
**Paradoxical embolism** — passage of an embolus from the systemic veins into the arteries, bypassing the lungs.
**Metastasis** (Greek meta — elsewhere, stasis — placement) — transfer of elements capable of growth and multiplication (tumor cells, microbes) to another site with blood or lymph.
**Infarction** (Latin infarcire — to stuff) — tissue necrosis resulting from impaired circulation (ischemia).
**Shock** (English shock — blow) — a state of tissue hypoxia and cell injury resulting from systemic hypoperfusion.

**“Nutmeg liver”.** The liver is enlarged and firm with a smooth surface; on the cut surface red-brown (lobule centers) and yellowish (periphery) spots alternate — resembling a nutmeg. Conclusion: chronic generalized venous congestion.
**“Brown induration of the lung”.** The lung is enlarged and firm, brown-rust colored on the cut surface. Conclusion: chronic venous congestion in the pulmonary circulation (see Topic 4).

**“Cerebral hemorrhage (hematoma)”.** A cavity filled with a dark red blood clot in the region of the subcortical nuclei; the brain tissue is destroyed; the blood may have ruptured into the ventricles. Conclusion: bleeding due to rupture — hematoma (most often in essential hypertension).
**“Mural thrombus in the aorta”.** Atherosclerotic plaques in the aortic intima with dull, rough, layered gray-red masses firmly attached to the wall over them. Conclusion: mural mixed thrombus.
**“Pulmonary thromboembolism”.** Dry, dull, worm-like red-gray thromboemboli in the pulmonary trunk and its branches, not attached to the wall. Conclusion: thromboembolism.
**“Ischemic infarction of the spleen”.** A whitish-yellow, firm, triangular focus beneath the capsule with a red rim around it and fibrin on the capsule. Conclusion: white infarct.
**“Hemorrhagic infarction of the lung”.** A wedge-shaped, dark red, firm focus with its base facing the pleura; fibrin deposits on the pleura. Conclusion: red infarct.

**“Myocardial infarction”.** An irregular, yellowish-white, dull focus surrounded by a red rim in the wall of the left ventricle; there may be a mural thrombus on the endocardium. Conclusion: white infarct with a red rim.
**“Cancer metastases in the liver”.** Numerous sharply demarcated whitish-gray nodules of various sizes in the liver. Conclusion: a consequence of tumor cell embolism (hematogenous metastases).

**“Nutmeg liver”** (hematoxylin and eosin). In the center of the lobule the central vein and sinusoids are markedly dilated and filled with red cells; the central hepatocytes are atrophic or necrotic; fatty degeneration of peripheral hepatocytes. Conclusion: chronic venous congestion.

**“Venous congestion of the skin”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The veins and capillaries of the dermis are markedly dilated and filled with blood, with diapedetic hemorrhages and edema in places. Conclusion: venous congestion.
**“Stasis in cerebral capillaries”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The capillaries are dilated; red cells have stuck together to form homogeneous columns; perivascular edema. Conclusion: stasis.

**“Mixed thrombus in a vein”** (hematoxylin and eosin). A mass in the venous lumen attached to the wall, with alternating layers of platelets, fibrin (pink), leukocytes and red cells. Conclusion: mixed thrombus.
**“Fat embolism of pulmonary capillaries”** (Sudan III). The capillaries of the interalveolar septa are occluded by orange-red fat droplets. Conclusion: fat embolism.

**“Ischemic infarction of the kidney”** (hematoxylin and eosin). In the infarct area the outlines of tubules and glomeruli are preserved, but nuclei are absent (coagulative necrosis); hemorrhage and leukocyte infiltration at the border (demarcation zone). Conclusion: white infarct with a red rim.

**“Hemorrhagic infarction of the lung”** (hematoxylin and eosin). In the area of necrosis the alveoli are filled with red cells, and the nuclei of the interalveolar septa do not stain. Conclusion: red infarct.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 65-year-old woman had rheumatic fever 20 years ago, and mitral stenosis was diagnosed. In recent years she developed shortness of breath and blood-streaked sputum, then leg edema and heaviness under the right costal margin. She died of chronic heart failure.
cases.ask: 1) What changes are expected in the lungs? 2) What does the liver look like, and why? 3) What outcome can this process lead to in the liver?
cases.answer: 1) Brown induration of the lung — chronic venous congestion in the pulmonary circulation due to mitral stenosis: diapedetic hemorrhages, hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”), sclerosis of the interalveolar septa. 2) “Nutmeg liver” — after right ventricular failure develops, congestion in the inferior vena cava: in the center of the lobule the vein and sinusoids are filled with blood, with atrophy and necrosis of the central hepatocytes (red-brown) and fatty degeneration of the peripheral hepatocytes (yellowish). 3) Nutmeg fibrosis and cardiac (nutmeg) cirrhosis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 52-year-old man died 2 hours after severe chest pain. At autopsy no gross changes were found, except for an occlusive thrombus over an atherosclerotic plaque in the anterior descending branch of the left coronary artery.
cases.ask: 1) What is the cause of death? 2) Why are there no gross changes in the myocardium, and how can the infarction be confirmed? 3) If the patient had survived, what complications and changes would have developed over the following days?
cases.answer: 1) Acute myocardial infarction (stage of acute ischemia), coronary artery thrombosis; death — probably from ventricular fibrillation or cardiogenic shock. 2) The gross signs of necrosis appear after 12–24 hours, and the histologic signs after 4–12 hours. Confirmation — histochemical methods: triphenyltetrazolium chloride (the area that has lost dehydrogenase activity does not stain), loss of glycogen with the PAS reaction; mitochondrial damage on electron microscopy. 3) On days 1–3 — neutrophilic demarcation inflammation; on days 3–7 — macrophages, risk of cardiac rupture (hemopericardium, tamponade), mural thrombus and thromboembolism, fibrinous pericarditis, acute aneurysm; at 6–8 weeks — scar (large-focal cardiosclerosis), chronic aneurysm.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 25-year-old man fractured his femur in a road traffic accident. On the second day he developed shortness of breath, cyanosis and confusion; pinpoint hemorrhages appeared on the skin of the chest and axillae; the blood platelet count decreased. The patient died.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Its mechanism and the changes in the lungs and brain. 3) By what method is it confirmed microscopically?
cases.answer: 1) Fat embolism (fat embolism syndrome). 2) Fat droplets from the yellow marrow of the fractured bone enter the veins and first occlude the pulmonary capillaries (pulmonary insufficiency); if abundant, they pass through the lungs and occlude the capillaries of the brain and other organs — numerous petechiae in the brain (“brain purpura”), neurological signs. In addition, fatty acids damage the endothelium, and platelet aggregation causes thrombocytopenia. 3) Staining frozen sections with Sudan III (or osmic acid) — orange-red (or black) fat droplets in the capillaries (with routine paraffin processing the fat dissolves).
