topics.title: Diseases of the immune system. Hypersensitivity reactions, autoimmune diseases, immunodeficiency. Amyloidosis

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the structure of the immune system: central and peripheral organs, T and B lymphocytes, macrophages, natural killer cells, the major histocompatibility complex;
morphologic changes in the immune organs in response to antigenic stimulation; accidental transformation of the thymus;
the four types of hypersensitivity reactions: mechanisms, morphology and examples;
the types of transplant rejection;
autoimmune diseases: mechanisms of loss of tolerance, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), Hashimoto thyroiditis;
primary and secondary immunodeficiency states; HIV infection and AIDS;
amyloidosis: the structure and composition of amyloid, methods of detection, classification, pathogenesis, organ changes and clinical significance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of the “sago” and “lardaceous” spleen, renal amyloidosis, Hashimoto goiter and lupus nephritis;
describe microscopic slides of accidental transformation of the thymus, a lymph node in AIDS, amyloidosis of the spleen, kidney and adrenal glands (Congo red), and Hashimoto thyroiditis;
identify the type of hypersensitivity from a clinical example;
identify the type of amyloidosis from the clinical situation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the types of hypersensitivity with “**ACID**”: **A** — Anaphylactic (I, IgE, immediate), **C** — Cytotoxic (II, IgG/IgM against cells), **I** — Immune complex (III), **D** — Delayed (IV, T lymphocytes). The first three are mediated by **antibodies**, the fourth by **cells**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In older textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva), amyloidosis is divided into **primary (idiopathic), hereditary, secondary (acquired) and senile** forms, and by the location of amyloid into **pericollagenous (mesenchymal)** — vascular adventitia, heart, muscles, nerves, skin (primary, hereditary amyloidosis) and **perireticular (parenchymal)** — vascular intima and basement membranes, spleen, kidney, liver, adrenal glands (secondary amyloidosis). The current classification is based on the **type of amyloid protein** (AL, AA, ATTR, etc.), because it is precisely the protein type that determines **treatment**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: On immunofluorescence microscopy, the **pattern** of immune deposits indicates the mechanism: **linear** (smooth along the basement membrane) — **type II** (anti–basement membrane antibodies, Goodpasture); **granular (lumpy-bumpy)** — **type III** (immune complexes: SLE, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis).

blocks.text: The immune system protects the organism from foreign substances (antigens) and distinguishes **“self”** from **“nonself”**. It consists of **innate (nonspecific)** and **acquired (adaptive, specific)** immunity.

items: **Innate immunity** — epithelial barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), dendritic cells, **natural killer (NK) cells**, the complement system; it recognizes microbes rapidly but nonspecifically (Toll-like receptors).
**Acquired immunity** — **lymphocytes** and their products; specific and with memory. **Humoral immunity** — B lymphocytes and antibodies; **cell-mediated immunity** — T lymphocytes.

blocks.text: Organs of the immune system:

items: **central (primary)** — the **thymus** (T lymphocytes mature) and **bone marrow** (B lymphocytes; in birds, the bursa of Fabricius — hence the name “bursa-dependent” or B lymphocytes);
**peripheral (secondary)** — lymph nodes, spleen, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer patches of the intestine — MALT).

blocks.text: Main cells:

items: **T lymphocytes** (thymus-dependent): **CD4^+^ helper T cells** (they produce cytokines and regulate the immune response: Th1, Th2, Th17), **CD8^+^ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (killer T cells)** — kill virus-infected and tumor cells, **regulatory T lymphocytes**

blocks.text: **(suppressor T cells)** — suppress the immune response and maintain tolerance to self antigens. In the lymph node they lie in the paracortical zone, in the spleen around the arterioles. • **B lymphocytes** — under the action of antigen they turn into **plasma cells** and produce antibodies (immunoglobulins — IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD). They are located in the follicles of lymph nodes and in the follicles of the splenic white pulp. • **Macrophages and dendritic cells** — process antigen and **present** it to T lymphocytes (antigen-presenting cells). • **NK cells** — kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior sensitization. **The major histocompatibility complex (MHC; in humans — HLA)** — proteins on the cell surface: **class I** (on all nucleated cells; presents antigen to CD8^+^ T lymphocytes) and **class II** (on antigen-presenting cells; to CD4^+^ T lymphocytes). HLA molecules determine tissue compatibility in transplantation; some HLA types are associated with predisposition to autoimmune diseases (for example, HLA-B27 — ankylosing spondylitis, HLA-DR4 — rheumatoid arthritis).
Changes in the immune organs in response to antigenic stimulation

Under the action of antigen the **lymph nodes and spleen** enlarge: in the **humoral** response — **follicular hyperplasia** (large germinal centers) and an increase in plasma cells (**plasmacytic transformation**), especially in the medullary cords of the lymph node; in the **cellular** response — **hyperplasia of the paracortical (T) zone**.

**Accidental (stress) transformation (involution) of the thymus** — rapid shrinkage of the thymus under the action of glucocorticoids in severe stress, infections, intoxication and tumors: lymphocytes in the cortex disappear by apoptosis (a **“starry sky”** picture — macrophages that have engulfed lymphocyte debris), then the border between the cortex and medulla disappears (inversion), and Hassall corpuscles become cystically dilated. **Thymomegaly** — congenital enlargement of the thymus; in older literature, the **“thymicolymphatic state”** (status thymicolymphaticus) was described as a condition with hyperplasia of the thymus, spleen and lymph nodes and hypoplasia of the adrenal glands, predisposing children to sudden death; it is now regarded as a form of congenital immunodeficiency.

blocks.caption: Thymic dysplasia in Nezelof syndrome: the lobules are small, lymphocytes are few, and Hassall corpuscles are absent (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: **Hypersensitivity reactions** are an **excessive or inappropriate** immune response of the organism to an antigen (exogenous or self), resulting in tissue damage. They are based on **allergy** (Greek allos — other, ergon — action) — altered reactivity of the organism. According to the Gell and Coombs classification, four types are distinguished:

blocks.title: Table 8.1. Types of hypersensitivity reactions
head: Type
Mechanism
Morphology
Examples
rows: IgE bound to mast cells and basophils; when the antigen enters again, they degranulate (histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins)
Vasodilation, edema, smooth muscle contraction, excessive mucus secretion; eosinophil infiltration in the late phase
Anaphylactic shock, bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis (pollinosis), urticaria, Quincke edema, food allergy
IgG or IgM binds to an antigen on the cell surface or in the tissue matrix → opsonization and phagocytosis, complement activation (lysis), inflammation, impaired receptor function

Incompatible blood transfusion, hemolytic disease of the newborn, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, rheumatic fever; Graves disease (antibodies stimulating the TSH receptor), myasthenia gravis (antibodies blocking the acetylcholine receptor)
Antigen–antibody immune complexes circulate in the blood and are deposited in vessel walls → complement activation, neutrophils → inflammation
Vasculitis — fibrinoid necrosis, neutrophil infiltration; glomerulonephritis, arthritis
Systemic lupus erythematosus, postinfectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa, serum sickness; local — Arthus phenomenon
Sensitized CD4^+^ T lymphocytes release cytokines (IFN-gamma) and activate macrophages, or CD8^+^ T lymphocytes kill cells directly; the reaction occurs in 24–72 hours
Tuberculin (Mantoux) test, tuberculosis, leprosy, contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease, transplant rejection

parts.text: Remember the types of hypersensitivity with “**ACID**”: **A** — Anaphylactic (I, IgE, immediate), **C** — Cytotoxic (II, IgG/IgM against cells), **I** — Immune complex (III), **D** — Delayed (IV, T lymphocytes). The first three are mediated by **antibodies**, the fourth by **cells**.

**Anaphylactic shock** is the most severe form of type I reaction: within a few minutes of exposure to the antigen (penicillin, insect venom, nuts), systemic vasodilation, increased permeability, bronchospasm and laryngeal

edema develop — a risk of death. First aid — **epinephrine (adrenaline)** intramuscularly. At autopsy: laryngeal edema, pulmonary emphysema and edema, congestion and petechiae in the organs, eosinophils in the internal organs.

blocks.text: When an allogeneic organ (from another person) is transplanted, the recipient's immune system recognizes the donor **HLA** antigens as foreign. Types of rejection:

items: **Hyperacute** — within minutes to hours: the recipient has **preexisting** antibodies against donor antigens (ABO incompatibility, previous transplantation, transfusion, pregnancy) — type III/II; thrombosis and fibrinoid necrosis in the vessels, **ischemic necrosis** of the organ. It is now rare thanks to pretransplant crossmatching.

**Acute** — days, weeks, months: **cellular** (CD8^+^ cytotoxic T lymphocytes — interstitial lymphocytic infiltration, tubular damage — “tubulitis”) and **humoral** (antibodies — vasculitis, endothelial damage, neutrophils in capillaries, C4d deposits) mechanisms; it responds to immunosuppressive therapy.

**Chronic** — months, years: thickening of the arterial intima (**transplant arteriopathy**), interstitial fibrosis, parenchymal atrophy; gradual loss of organ function. **“Graft-versus-host” disease** — when bone marrow (immunocompetent cells) is transplanted, donor T lymphocytes attack the recipient's tissues: the skin (rash), liver (jaundice) and intestine (diarrhea) are affected.

blocks.text: In **autoimmune diseases**, tissues are damaged as a result of an immune response against the organism's **own antigens** (autoantibodies and self-reactive T lymphocytes). Normally **immunologic tolerance** to self antigens is maintained:

items: **central tolerance** — lymphocytes that recognize self antigens are eliminated by apoptosis in the thymus and bone marrow (**clonal deletion**);

**peripheral tolerance** — anergy, suppression by **regulatory T lymphocytes**, activation-induced death (Fas–FasL). **Causes of loss of tolerance: genetic predisposition** (HLA genes, PTPN22, AIRE and others); **infections** — **molecular mimicry** (a microbial antigen resembles a self antigen — streptococcal M protein and cardiac antigens in rheumatic fever), tissue damage and exposure of hidden antigens; hormonal factors (most autoimmune diseases are more common in **women**), drugs and chemicals, ultraviolet light (SLE).

blocks.text: Classification:

items: **organ-specific** — Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anemia), myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, Goodpasture syndrome;

**systemic (non-organ-specific)** — **systemic lupus erythematosus**, **rheumatoid arthritis**, **systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)**, dermatomyositis, Sjögren syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa (most of them in the older classification are “**collagen diseases**” or **rheumatic diseases** — systemic involvement of connective tissue, the disorganization of Topic 3).

blocks.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

**SLE** is a systemic autoimmune disease affecting many organs and associated with **type III** hypersensitivity; mainly in **young women** (female:male ≈ 9:1). Its main feature is **antinuclear antibodies**
**(ANA)**; specific ones are antibodies against **double-stranded DNA** and the **Smith (Sm) antigen**. The antibodies damage nucleated cells and form immune complexes.
Morphology:

items: **vessels** — **fibrinoid necrosis** and acute necrotizing **vasculitis** in small arteries and arterioles; immune complex deposits;

**kidneys — lupus nephritis** (in more than 50% of patients, one of the main causes of death): immune complexes are deposited in the glomeruli (subendothelially), and the capillary basement membrane thickens — “**wire loops**”; proliferative glomerulonephritis, **hyaline thrombi**, fibrinoid necrosis;
**skin** — a **“butterfly” erythema** on the face (on the cheeks and bridge of the nose), photosensitivity; immunoglobulin and complement deposits at the dermoepidermal junction;
**joints** — nonerosive synovitis (arthritis);
**serous membranes** — fibrinous pericarditis, pleurisy;
**heart** — **Libman–Sacks endocarditis** (small sterile vegetations on both surfaces of the valves), myocarditis;
**spleen** — concentric periarterial fibrosis around the follicular arteries (**“onion skin”**);
**blood** — hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia (type II); **antiphospholipid antibodies** — thromboses, miscarriage;

**brain** — vasculitis, thrombosis, psychiatric disturbances. Histologic signs: **hematoxylin bodies** (LE bodies — nuclei altered by antibodies), **LE cells** in the blood (a neutrophil that has engulfed a hematoxylin body).

blocks.text: Rheumatoid arthritis

**Rheumatoid arthritis** is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease that mainly affects the **joints** (the small joints of the hands and feet — metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, symmetrically). Mechanism — **type IV** (CD4^+^ T lymphocytes, TNF) and **type III** (immune complexes). In the blood — **rheumatoid factor** (IgM against the Fc portion of IgG) and **anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA)**.

**Morphology:** chronic inflammation of the synovium — **hyperplasia of synovial cells**, lymphocytes, plasma cells, lymphoid follicles, new vessels; granulation tissue forming villous projections — the **pannus** — grows into the cartilage and destroys it and the bone (**erosions**). Outcome — fibrous and bony **ankylosis**, joint deformities (ulnar deviation of the fingers, “**swan neck**”). Extra-articular — **rheumatoid nodules** (subcutaneous, at the elbow: fibrinoid necrosis in the center surrounded by palisading macrophages), vasculitis, pulmonary fibrosis, **AA amyloidosis**.
Systemic scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)

**Systemic sclerosis** is a disease characterized by activation of the immune system, damage to small vessels and **progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs**. Fibroblasts are activated by TGF-beta and other cytokines. The **skin** is thickened, dense and immobile; the fingers are thin and claw-like (**sclerodactyly**); the face is masklike; **Raynaud phenomenon**. **Internal organs:** esophagus (fibrosis, impaired motility), lungs (interstitial fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension), kidneys (thickening of the arterial intima — “**scleroderma renal crisis**”), heart. Antibodies: **Scl-70** (diffuse form), **anticentromere** (limited form — **CREST syndrome**: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasias).
Hashimoto thyroiditis

**Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune thyroiditis)** is an organ-specific autoimmune disease and the most common cause of **hypothyroidism** (in iodine-sufficient areas). Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin; mainly a **type IV** (CD8^+^ T lymphocytes kill thyrocytes) and type II mechanism. **Morphology:** the thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged (goiter), firm and whitish-gray on the cut surface; a dense **lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate** in the parenchyma, **lymphoid follicles with germinal centers**, follicular atrophy; thyrocytes are large, with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm — **Hürthle (Askanazy) cells**; fibrosis. Complications — hypothyroidism (myxedema), risk of **B-cell lymphoma**.

blocks.text: **Immunodeficiency** is a decrease in the organism's resistance to infections and tumors as a result of a deficiency of one or more components of the immune system. It is **primary (congenital, hereditary)** or **secondary (acquired)**. The common clinical feature is **recurrent, severe and opportunistic infections** (caused by opportunistic microbes) and a predisposition to tumors and autoimmune diseases.

blocks.text: **Secondary immunodeficiency** is much more common than primary: **HIV infection (AIDS)**, protein-energy malnutrition, old age, malignant tumors (especially leukemias and lymphomas), **immunosuppressive therapy** (transplantation, chemotherapy, glucocorticoids), radiation, splenectomy (encapsulated bacteria — pneumococcal infections), diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome (loss of immunoglobulins).

blocks.text: HIV infection and AIDS

**Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)** is the final stage of infection caused by the **human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)**. HIV is a **retrovirus** (lentivirus); mainly HIV-1. **Routes of transmission:** sexual, parenteral (injecting drug use, contaminated instruments, blood transfusion), vertical (from mother to child — during pregnancy, childbirth and breastfeeding).

**Pathogenesis:** through its **gp120** protein the virus binds to the **CD4** molecule and coreceptors (**CCR5, CXCR4**) and infects **CD4^+^ T lymphocytes**, macrophages and dendritic cells. The viral RNA is converted to DNA by **reverse transcriptase** and integrated into the cell genome. CD4^+^ T lymphocytes gradually die — cell-mediated immunity is profoundly impaired; macrophages become a **reservoir** of the virus and carry it to the brain.
Stages:

items: **Acute (primary) infection** — at 3–6 weeks: a mononucleosis-like syndrome (fever, lymphadenopathy, rash), high viremia, a transient decrease in CD4^+^ cells; seroconversion.

**Chronic (latent, clinically silent) phase** — on average 7–10 years: few symptoms, **persistent generalized lymphadenopathy**; the virus replicates actively in lymphoid organs, and CD4^+^ cells gradually decrease.
**AIDS** — CD4^+^ T lymphocytes **fewer than 200/µL**: **opportunistic infections**, **tumors**, cachexia, neurological disorders.

blocks.text: Morphology of AIDS:

items: **lymph nodes** — first follicular hyperplasia, then **follicular involution** and a **sharp decrease** in lymphocytes (“depletion” of lymphoid tissue);

**opportunistic infections** — **Pneumocystis jirovecii** pneumonia (the most common; foamy eosinophilic exudate in the alveoli), candidiasis (mouth, esophagus), cytomegalovirus infection (retina, intestine), atypical mycobacterioses and tuberculosis (the main cause of death in our region), cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis (brain abscesses), cryptosporidiosis (diarrhea), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy;

**tumors** — **Kaposi sarcoma** (associated with HHV-8; red-violet patches and nodules on the skin), **B-cell lymphomas** (especially primary brain lymphoma), cervical and anal cancer (papillomavirus);
**central nervous system** — HIV encephalopathy (microglial nodules, multinucleated giant cells) — **HIV-associated dementia**;
**cachexia** (“wasting syndrome”).

parts.text: Modern **highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART)** stops HIV replication, restores CD4^+^ cell counts and prevents the development of AIDS — the life expectancy of people living with HIV can be almost normal. Therefore **early diagnosis** (HIV testing) and treatment are most important. ART is used during pregnancy to prevent mother-to-child transmission.

blocks.text: **Amyloidosis** is a **stromal-vascular protein degeneration** (Topic 3) characterized by **extracellular** deposition in tissues of **amyloid** — a fibrillar protein with a beta-pleated sheet structure formed from misfolded proteins. The name amyloid (Latin amylum — starch) was given by R. Virchow: he saw that this substance stains with iodine like starch.
Structure and composition of amyloid

Amyloid is a complex **glycoprotein**. On electron microscopy, amyloid consists of nonbranching, randomly arranged **fibrils** 7.5–10 nm in diameter. On X-ray crystallography the fibrils have a **cross-beta-pleated sheet** structure — this structure determines the characteristic staining of amyloid and its resistance to proteolysis. Composition of amyloid: the **fibrillar protein (F component)** — 95% (varying with the type of amyloidosis) and the **plasma component (P component)** — 5% (serum amyloid P component, glycosaminoglycans).
The main fibrillar proteins:

items: **AL (amyloid light chain)** — immunoglobulin **light chains** (usually lambda); produced by **plasma cells**;
**AA (amyloid-associated)** — derived from the acute phase protein **serum amyloid A (SAA)** synthesized in the liver; it increases in chronic inflammation under the action of IL-1 and IL-6;
**ATTR (transthyretin)** — a thyroxine- and retinol-transporting protein; mutant (hereditary) or normal (senile);
**A-beta-2-microglobulin** — in patients on hemodialysis;
**A-beta (beta-amyloid)** — in brain plaques in Alzheimer disease;
**AIAPP (amylin)** — in the pancreatic islets in type 2 diabetes mellitus;
**AE (endocrine)** — procalcitonin (in medullary carcinoma of the thyroid).

blocks.text: Methods of detecting amyloid

items: **Gross** — the **Virchow reaction**: when Lugol solution (iodine) and sulfuric acid are applied to the cut surface of an organ, amyloid turns **blue-violet** or green; with iodine alone — brown-orange.
**Congo red** — the main method: amyloid stains **red-orange**; in **polarized light** — **apple-green birefringence** (dichroism) — pathognomonic for amyloid.
**Metachromasia** — **red** with methyl (gentian) violet.
**Thioflavin T** — yellow-green fluorescence on fluorescence microscopy.
**Immunohistochemistry and mass spectrometry** — determination of the amyloid **type** (AL, AA, ATTR); necessary for choosing treatment.
With hematoxylin and eosin, amyloid is an **extracellular**, **homogeneous, amorphous, eosinophilic (pale pink)** mass.

parts.text: In older textbooks (Strukov, Abdullakhodjaeva), amyloidosis is divided into **primary (idiopathic), hereditary, secondary (acquired) and senile** forms, and by the location of amyloid into **pericollagenous (mesenchymal)** — vascular adventitia, heart, muscles, nerves, skin (primary, hereditary amyloidosis) and **perireticular (parenchymal)** — vascular intima and basement membranes, spleen, kidney, liver, adrenal glands (secondary amyloidosis). The current classification is based on the **type of amyloid protein** (AL, AA, ATTR, etc.), because it is precisely the protein type that determines **treatment**.

blocks.text: Pathogenesis of amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is a **disease of protein misfolding**. Normally, misfolded proteins are corrected inside the cell by chaperones or degraded in proteasomes. In amyloidosis there are **two mechanisms**:

items: **A normal protein is produced in excess** and is prone to misfolding — **AA** (SAA increases in chronic inflammation; monocytes cannot degrade it adequately), **AL** (excess monoclonal light chains), A-beta-2-microglobulin (not removed by dialysis).

**A mutant protein** is prone to misfolding — **ATTR** (hereditary). The misfolded proteins form oligomers and fibrils and accumulate **outside cells**. Amyloid **mechanically compresses** the tissue and narrows the vessels, leading to parenchymal **atrophy**; the oligomers also have a direct toxic effect on cells. Amyloid is produced mainly with the participation of **macrophages** (amyloidoblasts), plasma cells, fibroblasts and cardiomyocytes.

blocks.text: **Stages** in the development of amyloidosis (V.V. Serov): the **preamyloid stage** — plasmacytic transformation of cells of the reticuloendothelial system, appearance of a clone of amyloidoblasts; **amyloid formation** — synthesis of the fibrillar protein and assembly of fibrils.
Changes in the organs

**1. Kidneys** — affected most often and most severely (especially in AA amyloidosis). Amyloid accumulates in the **glomerular mesangium and capillary basement membranes**, then in the tubular basement membranes and arteriolar walls; the glomeruli are gradually completely replaced by amyloid masses. **Stages:** latent → **proteinuric** → **nephrotic** (nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoproteinemia, edema, hyperlipidemia) → **azotemic (uremic)**.

items: In the nephrotic stage the kidneys are enlarged, firm and whitish, with a waxy luster on the cut surface — the **“large white (lardaceous) amyloid kidney”**; hyaline droplet, hydropic and fatty degeneration in the tubules.
In the final stage the kidneys are small, firm and contracted — the **“amyloid contracted kidney”**; **chronic kidney disease** is the most common **cause of death** in amyloidosis.

blocks.text: **2. Spleen** — enlarged and firm. Two types:

items: **“Sago spleen”** — amyloid accumulates in the **lymphoid follicles**; on the cut surface, translucent gray-white granules resembling **sago grains** (or boiled rice) are seen (early stage);

**“Lardaceous (waxy) spleen”** — amyloid accumulates **diffusely** in the **red pulp**, along the sinusoids and reticular fibers; on the cut surface it is uniform, with a waxy luster, red-brown. **3. Liver** — enlarged, firm, shiny, whitish-yellow (“lardaceous”); amyloid is deposited in the **spaces of Disse** (around the sinusoids), in vessel walls and in the portal tracts; the hepatocytes are compressed and atrophy. Liver function is usually only slightly impaired (portal hypertension is rare).

blocks.text: **4. Heart** — the main organ affected in **AL** and **ATTR** amyloidosis: the heart is enlarged, with thickened, firm, waxy walls; amyloid is deposited between cardiomyocytes, in vessel walls and in the endocardium. **Restrictive cardiomyopathy**, arrhythmias (involvement of the conduction system) and heart failure are the main **cause of death** in AL amyloidosis. Low voltage on the ECG — inconsistent with the wall thickness.
**5. Adrenal glands** — amyloid in the cortex along vessels and reticular fibers; with bilateral involvement — **adrenal insufficiency** (Addison disease, Topic 4).

**6. Other organs: tongue** — **macroglossia** (in AL amyloidosis); **digestive tract** — diarrhea, malabsorption; **peripheral nerves** — polyneuropathy; **skin** — “**raccoon eyes**” around the eyelids (purpura, AL); **joints** and carpal tunnel syndrome; vessels (bleeding tendency).

blocks.text: **Diagnosis of amyloidosis** — **biopsy** when clinically suspected: the most convenient and safe is **abdominal fat pad aspiration biopsy**; rectal mucosa, gingival, kidney or heart biopsy; Congo red + polarized light, then determination of the amyloid type.

**Outcome and treatment:** amyloidosis is usually considered a **progressive** and irreversible process, but if the underlying cause is removed, the process may stop and even partially regress: **AA** — treatment of the chronic inflammation (treating tuberculosis or osteomyelitis, TNF inhibitors in rheumatoid arthritis), colchicine in familial Mediterranean fever; **AL** — elimination of the plasma cell clone (chemotherapy, bone marrow transplantation); **ATTR** — transthyretin-stabilizing drugs and liver transplantation.

parts.text: If **proteinuria appears in a patient with a chronic inflammatory disease** (for example, long-standing tuberculosis, osteomyelitis, bronchiectasis or rheumatoid arthritis), **AA amyloidosis** should be considered first. Formerly, tuberculosis and chronic suppurative diseases were the main causes of amyloidosis; today, in developed countries, they are rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel diseases.
**Unexplained heart failure, nephrotic syndrome and macroglossia in an elderly patient** — AL amyloidosis (multiple myeloma should be sought).

blocks.text: Three diseases — not one mechanism

items: **Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis** (type III): 2–3 weeks after tonsillitis a child develops edema, hematuria (“meat-wash” colored urine) and arterial hypertension; immune complexes (“humps” — subepithelial deposits) and neutrophils in the glomeruli.

**Goodpasture syndrome** (type II): a young man with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive kidney failure; antibodies against **type IV collagen in the basement membrane** of the pulmonary alveoli and renal glomeruli; on immunofluorescence — **linear** IgG deposits along the basement membrane.
**Contact dermatitis** (type IV): an itchy vesicular rash under a nickel-containing watchstrap after 48 hours; an infiltrate of lymphocytes and macrophages in the dermis.

parts.text: On immunofluorescence microscopy, the **pattern** of immune deposits indicates the mechanism: **linear** (smooth along the basement membrane) — **type II** (anti–basement membrane antibodies, Goodpasture); **granular (lumpy-bumpy)** — **type III** (immune complexes: SLE, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis).

items: **Accidental** (Latin accidens — chance) — occurring by chance; accidental transformation of the thymus — its rapid involution under the influence of stress.
**Allergy** (Greek allos — other, ergon — action) — altered (increased) reactivity of the organism to an antigen.
**Amyloid** (Latin amylum — starch) — a glycoprotein consisting mainly of fibrillar protein.

**Bursa-dependent (B) lymphocytes** (Latin bursa — pouch) — lymphocytes that mature in the bone marrow and carry out humoral immune reactions; so named because in birds they form in the bursa of Fabricius.
**Thymus-dependent (T) lymphocytes** — lymphocytes that mature in the thymus and provide cell-mediated immunity.
**Helper T cells** (English help) — helper lymphocytes that regulate the immune response (CD4^+^).
**Killer T cells** (English killer) — cytotoxic lymphocytes that kill target cells (CD8^+^).
**Suppressor T cells** (Latin suppressio — suppression) — (regulatory) lymphocytes that suppress the immune response.
**Hypoplasia** — insufficient development of an organ or tissue.
**Thymicolymphatic state** (status thymicolymphaticus) — the old name of a congenital immunodeficiency with hyperplasia of the thymus, spleen and lymph nodes and hypoplasia of the adrenal glands.
**Autoimmunity** — an immune response of the organism against its own antigens.
**Tolerance** (Latin tolerantia — endurance) — absence of a response of the immune system to a particular antigen (normally — to self antigens).
**Immunodeficiency** — a deficiency of one or more components of the immune system.
**Opportunistic infection** (Latin opportunus — convenient) — an infection caused by opportunistic microbes in a person with reduced immunity.
**Pannus** (Latin pannus — piece of cloth) — synovial granulation tissue that destroys cartilage in rheumatoid arthritis.

**“Splenic amyloidosis — sago spleen”.** The spleen is enlarged and firm; on the cut surface there are translucent gray granules resembling sago grains (amyloid in the follicles). Conclusion: secondary (AA) amyloidosis.

**“Splenic amyloidosis — lardaceous spleen”.** The spleen is enlarged and firm; on the cut surface it is uniform, shiny, red-brown and waxy. Conclusion: amyloidosis (diffuse deposition in the red pulp).

**“Renal amyloidosis — large white kidney”.** The kidneys are enlarged, firm and whitish-gray, with a waxy luster on the cut surface; the cortex is widened. Conclusion: amyloid nephrosis (nephrotic stage).
**“Amyloid contracted kidney”.** The kidneys are small and firm with an uneven surface. Conclusion: the azotemic stage of amyloidosis.
**“Hashimoto goiter”.** The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged, firm, whitish-gray and lobulated on the cut surface. Conclusion: autoimmune thyroiditis.
**“Croupous (lobar) pneumonia”** and **“caseous necrosis of a lymph node”** — studied together as sources of chronic inflammation leading to AA amyloidosis.

items: **“Accidental transformation of the thymus”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The thymic lobules are small; lymphocytes are depleted in the cortex (apoptosis, “starry sky”); the border between the cortex and medulla is indistinct; Hassall corpuscles are cystically dilated. Conclusion: stress involution.

**“A lymph node in AIDS”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The lymphoid follicles are involuted or absent, lymphocytes are markedly decreased, vessels are numerous and the stroma is exposed. Conclusion: lymphoid depletion (AIDS).

**“Splenic amyloidosis”** (Congo red or hematoxylin and eosin). Homogeneous amyloid masses, red-orange with Congo red, in the lymphoid follicles (sago) or along the reticular fibers of the red pulp. Conclusion: amyloidosis.

**“Renal amyloidosis”** (Congo red). Red amyloid in the glomerular mesangium and capillary walls, in arterioles and in tubular basement membranes; some glomeruli are completely replaced by amyloid. Conclusion: amyloid nephrosis.
**“Adrenal amyloidosis”** (Congo red). Red-orange amyloid along the capillaries and reticular fibers in the cortex; atrophy of cells. Conclusion: amyloidosis.

**“Hashimoto thyroiditis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). A dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the parenchyma, lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, follicular atrophy, Hürthle cells, fibrosis. Conclusion: autoimmune thyroiditis.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 25-year-old woman has fever, joint pain, a red “butterfly” rash on the cheeks and bridge of the nose, and photosensitivity; protein and red cells in the urine. ANA and anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies are high in the blood, and complement is decreased. Kidney biopsy: the walls of the glomerular capillaries are thickened (“wire loops”); granular IgG and C3 deposits on immunofluorescence.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What is the mechanism of the disease? 3) What other organs may be affected, and what changes occur in them?
cases.answer: 1) Systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus nephritis. 2) As a result of loss of tolerance, autoantibodies against nuclear antigens are formed; immune complexes (type III) are deposited in the glomeruli and vessel walls, activate complement (which is why blood complement is decreased) and cause inflammation; antibodies against blood cells (type II) — anemia, thrombocytopenia. 3) Skin (erythema), joints (nonerosive arthritis), serous membranes (fibrinous pericarditis, pleurisy), heart (Libman–Sacks endocarditis), spleen (“onion skin” periarterial fibrosis), vessels (vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis), brain (vasculitis, thrombosis).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old man has had chronic osteomyelitis of the femur for 15 years, with constant pus discharge from a sinus tract. In the last year he developed edema of the legs and face and 6 g of protein in the urine per day. He died of chronic kidney disease. At autopsy the kidneys are enlarged, firm, whitish and waxy; the spleen is enlarged, with translucent granules on the cut surface.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis and the type of amyloidosis? 2) How is amyloid detected? 3) The mechanism of the disease and the stages of the changes in the kidneys.
cases.answer: 1) Secondary (reactive) systemic amyloidosis — AA amyloidosis against the background of chronic osteomyelitis; “large white amyloid kidney” and “sago spleen”. 2) Grossly — Lugol solution and sulfuric acid (Virchow reaction — blue-violet); microscopically — Congo red (red-orange) and apple-green birefringence in polarized light; metachromasia with methyl violet; AA protein on immunohistochemistry. 3) In chronic inflammation, under the action of IL-1 and IL-6, the liver produces large amounts of serum amyloid A (SAA); its incompletely degraded fragments misfold, form AA fibrils and accumulate outside cells. Renal stages: latent → proteinuric → nephrotic (large white kidney) → azotemic (amyloid contracted kidney, uremia).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old man has complained for 3 months of fever, marked weight loss, diarrhea, dry cough and shortness of breath. White plaques in the oral cavity (candidiasis), red-violet nodules on the skin. A history of injecting drug use. Blood CD4^+^ T lymphocytes 80/µL.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What could the skin nodules and the lung process be? 3) Briefly explain the pathogenesis of the disease.
cases.answer: 1) HIV infection, AIDS stage (CD4^+^ fewer than 200, opportunistic infections and tumors). 2) The skin nodules — Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8); in the lung — Pneumocystis pneumonia (foamy eosinophilic exudate in the alveoli) or tuberculosis; in the mouth — candidiasis. 3) HIV binds via gp120 to CD4 and coreceptors (CCR5, CXCR4) and infects CD4^+^ T lymphocytes and macrophages; it integrates into the genome with the help of reverse transcriptase; CD4^+^ cells gradually die, and cell-mediated immunity is profoundly impaired; as a result, opportunistic infections and virus-associated tumors develop.

topics.title: Neoplasia. Biology, structure and growth of tumors. Types of tumors

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the definition and main properties of a tumor (neoplasia) and precancerous processes;
the structure of tumors: parenchyma and stroma, organoid and histioid structure;
the types of atypia: tissue, cellular, biochemical, functional and antigenic atypia; differentiation and anaplasia;
the types of tumor growth (expansive, infiltrative, appositional; exophytic, endophytic), the routes of metastasis and recurrence;
the differences between benign and malignant tumors; the effects of tumors on the organism (local and systemic), paraneoplastic syndromes;
carcinogenesis: etiologic factors (chemical, physical, viral), molecular basis (oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, apoptosis and DNA repair genes), hallmarks of cancer;
the classification and naming principles of tumors; the TNM system, grading and staging;
epithelial (non-organ-specific) and mesenchymal tumors, tumors of melanin-forming tissue.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of uterine fibromyoma, breast fibroadenoma, ovarian cystadenoma, skin papilloma, intestinal polyp, gastric cancer, cancer metastases in the liver and osteosarcoma;
describe microscopic slides of skin papilloma, fibroadenoma, keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, melanoma, leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma and hemangioma;
distinguish benign from malignant tumors by histologic features;
correctly form the name of a tumor according to its tissue of origin and degree of malignancy.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **main properties** of a tumor: 1) **autonomous (unlimited) growth** — not obeying the regulatory mechanisms of the organism; 2) **atypia** — differences from the normal structure and function of the cell and tissue; 3) **monoclonality** — the tumor arises from a single mutated cell; 4) **hereditary transmission** of tumor properties to cell progeny; 5) **progression** — the tumor becomes increasingly malignant over time.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Tumors malignant by location**: even a histologically benign tumor in a vital location (for example, the brain, next to the brainstem, in the spinal canal) can cause death by compression. There are also **borderline** tumors and **locally destructive** tumors (for example, basal cell carcinoma — destroys locally but almost never metastasizes). Hormone-producing benign tumors (insulinoma, pheochromocytoma) can be dangerous because of hormone excess.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: An oncogene is “**a car with a stuck gas pedal**” (one defect is enough — dominant); a tumor suppressor gene is “**a broken brake**” (both brakes — both alleles — must fail — recessive, “two hits”); TP53 is “**the driver**”: when it sees a problem, it stops the car or destroys it (apoptosis).

blocks.text: A **tumor** (tumor, neoplasma, blastoma) is a pathological process characterized by **uncontrolled, unlimited (autonomous) proliferation** of cells, in which the **growth, differentiation and morphology** of the cells are disturbed (**atypia**), and these properties are **hereditarily** transmitted to the progeny of tumor cells. According to the definition of the British pathologist R. Willis: “A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue, the growth of which exceeds and is uncoordinated with that of the normal tissues and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimuli which evoked the change”.
The science that studies tumors is **oncology** (Greek onkos — tumor). Tumors are the second leading cause of death in the world after cardiovascular diseases.

parts.text: The **main properties** of a tumor: 1) **autonomous (unlimited) growth** — not obeying the regulatory mechanisms of the organism; 2) **atypia** — differences from the normal structure and function of the cell and tissue; 3) **monoclonality** — the tumor arises from a single mutated cell; 4) **hereditary transmission** of tumor properties to cell progeny; 5) **progression** — the tumor becomes increasingly malignant over time.

blocks.text: **Tumor progression** — as the tumor develops, new mutations accumulate and its properties (growth rate, invasion, metastasis, resistance to treatment) **become progressively more aggressive**; as a result, subclones with different properties appear within the tumor (**heterogeneity**).
Precancerous processes
A tumor usually develops from healthy tissue not suddenly but through **precancerous changes**:

items: **Background processes** — chronic inflammation, hyperplasia, metaplasia (Topic 1), disturbed regeneration.
**Focal hyperplasia and dysplasia** — **dysplasia** (mild, moderate, severe) — cellular atypia and disruption of tissue structure; severe dysplasia is a true precancerous condition.

**Noninvasive cancer — carcinoma in situ** (cancer in place) — the full thickness of the epithelium is replaced by atypical cells, but the **basement membrane is intact** (no invasion); it does not metastasize.
**Invasive cancer** — the tumor breaks through the basement membrane and grows into the stroma; the possibility of metastasis appears.

blocks.title: Table 9.1. Important precancerous conditions
head: Condition
Tumor that may develop
rows: Squamous metaplasia and dysplasia of the bronchial epithelium (smoking)
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Chronic atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia (H. pylori)
Adenomatous polyps of the colon, familial adenomatous polyposis
Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity
Liver cirrhosis (viral hepatitis B, C, alcohol)

blocks.text: Every tumor consists of two parts:

items: **Parenchyma** — the **tumor cells** that make up the tumor itself; the biological properties of the tumor (malignant or benign) and its **name** depend on the parenchyma.

**Stroma** — connective tissue, blood vessels, nerves and immune cells; it nourishes and supports the parenchyma. The stroma forms **under the influence of the tumor cells** (growth factors: VEGF, PDGF, FGF). The stroma often contains a **lymphocytic infiltrate** — a sign of an antitumor immune response (favorable for prognosis). By the ratio of stroma to parenchyma: **organoid tumors** — the parenchyma and stroma are clearly separated (most epithelial tumors); **histioid tumors** — the stroma is scant, only in the form of vessels (most mesenchymal tumors). If the stroma is abundant, the tumor is **hard** (**scirrhous** — carcinoma with a fibrous stroma, for example breast cancer — **desmoplasia**); if scant, it is **soft** (**medullary**, “brain-like” carcinoma).

blocks.text: **Gross appearance:** a nodule (encapsulated or unencapsulated), a polyp (pedunculated), mushroom-shaped, papillary (cauliflower-like), a plaque, a cyst (unilocular or multilocular), a diffuse infiltrate, an ulcer (with raised crater edges). Tumors range in size from millimeters to several tens of kilograms. On the cut surface, a **“fish-flesh”** appearance (sarcomas) and foci of necrosis and hemorrhage (malignant tumors) are seen.
**Atypia** — the properties of a tumor cell and tissue that differ from those of the normal cell and tissue.

items: **Morphologic atypia:** – **tissue atypia** — disturbance of the ratio of parenchyma to stroma, of the epithelial layers, of the shape and size of glands and of the orientation of fibers; the cells look normal. It is characteristic of **benign** tumors. – **cellular atypia** — characteristic of **malignant** tumors (in detail below). 2. **Biochemical atypia** — altered metabolism: increased glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (**Warburg effect**), increased synthesis of proteins and nucleic acids. 3. **Functional atypia** — tumor cells lose their normal function or acquire **unusual functions** (for example, lung cancer produces hormones). 4. **Antigenic atypia** — new antigens appear on tumor cells (tumor-specific antigens, **embryonic antigens** — alpha-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen); they are used in diagnosis as **tumor markers**.

blocks.text: Differentiation and anaplasia

**Differentiation** is the **degree of resemblance** of tumor cells, in structure and function, to the normal tissue from which they arose. A **well-differentiated** tumor closely resembles its tissue of origin (for example, most benign tumors, well-differentiated adenocarcinoma); a **poorly differentiated** one shows little resemblance. **Anaplasia** (Greek “backward formation”) is the loss of differentiation; an important sign of malignancy.
Signs of cellular atypia (anaplasia):

items: **pleomorphism** — variation in the shape and size of cells and nuclei, **tumor giant cells**;

**nuclear atypia** — nuclei are enlarged and **hyperchromatic** (dark-staining), with coarse chromatin and large nucleoli; **increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio** (normally 1:4–1:6, in cancer up to 1:1);
**numerous mitoses** and **atypical (pathologic) mitoses** (tripolar, quadripolar);
**loss of polarity** — the cells are arranged haphazardly;
foci of **necrosis** (tumor vessels cannot keep pace with rapid growth).

blocks.label: Figure 9.1
blocks.caption: Anaplastic tumor: the size and shape of cells and nuclei vary markedly; an atypical tripolar mitosis in the center (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-8)

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: Pleomorphic tumor of skeletal muscle (rhabdomyosarcoma): marked pleomorphism of cells and nuclei, hyperchromatic nuclei and tumor giant cells (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-9)

blocks.text: Types of growth in relation to the surrounding tissue:

items: **Expansive growth** — the tumor grows “by itself”, **compressing** and pushing aside the surrounding tissue; the atrophic tissue and condensed stroma around it form a **pseudocapsule**; the tumor border is sharp. It is characteristic of **benign** tumors.

**Infiltrative (invasive, destructive) growth** — tumor cells **grow into the surrounding tissue, around vessels and nerves, and destroy it**; the border is indistinct. It is characteristic of **malignant** tumors; the name “**cancer**” (Latin cancer, Greek karkinos — crab) comes from the tumor spreading like the legs of a crab.

**Appositional growth** — by transformation of surrounding normal cells into tumor cells (for example, multicentric growth). **In relation to a hollow organ: exophytic** — growing into the lumen of the organ (polyp, papillary tumor); **endophytic** — growing into the wall of the organ, in depth (often more malignant, ulcerates).

blocks.text: **By the number of foci of growth: unicentric** (from one focus) and **multicentric** (from several foci).

blocks.label: Figure 9.4
blocks.caption: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast (cut surface): the tumor is retracted and has grown infiltratively into the surrounding tissue; its border is indistinct, and it is stone-hard on palpation (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-13)

blocks.label: Figure 9.3
blocks.caption: Fibroadenoma of the breast: an encapsulated, yellowish tumor sharply demarcated from the surrounding whitish breast tissue (expansive growth) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-11)

blocks.label: Figure 9.6
blocks.caption: Invasive breast cancer (microscopic slide): no capsule, irregular borders, infiltrative growth (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-14)

blocks.label: Figure 9.5
blocks.caption: Fibroadenoma of the breast (microscopic slide): a fibrous capsule (right) separates the tumor from the surrounding tissue (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-12)

blocks.text: Invasion and metastasis

**Metastasis** (Greek metastasis — transfer) is the detachment of tumor cells from the primary focus, their transfer to another site and the formation there of a new tumor focus — a **secondary tumor (metastasis)**. **Metastasis is the most reliable sign of a malignant tumor**; benign tumors do not metastasize. About 30% of malignant tumors have already metastasized at the time of diagnosis.

**Stages of the invasion–metastasis cascade:** 1) detachment of tumor cells from one another (decreased E-cadherin); 2) attachment to the **basement membrane and extracellular matrix** and its destruction by **matrix metalloproteinases** (collagenase IV); 3) migration; 4) entry into a vessel (**intravasation**); 5) survival in the blood together with platelets (tumor emboli); 6) exit from the vessel (**extravasation**) and growth at the new site (angiogenesis).
Routes of metastasis:

items: **Lymphogenous** — the most characteristic early route for **carcinomas**: the regional lymph nodes are involved first. For example, in breast cancer — the axillary nodes; in gastric cancer — the left supraclavicular lymph node (**Virchow metastasis**), the ovaries (**Krukenberg metastasis**), the rectouterine pouch (**Schnitzler metastasis**). The **sentinel lymph node** is the first lymph node to receive lymph from the tumor; its biopsy is used in choosing treatment.

**Hematogenous** — characteristic of **sarcomas**, and of carcinomas in later stages. Through the portal vein — to the **liver** (tumors of the digestive tract); through the venae cavae — to the **lungs**. Common targets: liver, lungs, bones, brain, adrenal glands. Some tumors tend to metastasize to **bones**: cancers of the prostate, breast, lung, kidney and thyroid.

**Implantation (contact, across serous cavities)** — when the tumor reaches the serosa, cells fall into the peritoneal or pleural cavity and spread over the entire serous membrane (**carcinomatosis**): cancers of the ovary, stomach and colon; often with hemorrhagic exudate (ascites, pleurisy).
**Perineural** — along nerves (pancreatic and prostate cancer).
**Mixed. Recurrence (relapse)** — reappearance of a tumor **at the same site** after its removal or treatment; the cause is residual tumor cells or multicentric growth.

blocks.title: Table 9.2. Differences between benign and malignant tumors
head: Feature
Benign tumor
Malignant tumor
rows: High; resembles the tissue of origin
Local and systemic (cachexia, intoxication, paraneoplastic syndromes)

parts.text: **Tumors malignant by location**: even a histologically benign tumor in a vital location (for example, the brain, next to the brainstem, in the spinal canal) can cause death by compression. There are also **borderline** tumors and **locally destructive** tumors (for example, basal cell carcinoma — destroys locally but almost never metastasizes). Hormone-producing benign tumors (insulinoma, pheochromocytoma) can be dangerous because of hormone excess.

blocks.text: Effects of tumors on the organism

items: **Local effects:** **compression** of surrounding tissues and organs (brain, bile ducts — obstructive jaundice, intestine — obstruction), **obstruction** of hollow organs, destruction and **ulceration**, **bleeding** (tumor breakdown — anemia), secondary infection, **rupture** or **perforation** of an organ, **pathologic bone fracture**.
**Systemic effects: cancer cachexia** (TNF and other cytokines, loss of appetite — Topic 1), anemia, fever, intoxication, **hormonal** effects (endocrine tumors).

**Paraneoplastic syndromes** are signs not directly related to the location of the tumor or its metastases; they are often related to ectopic production of hormones or cytokines by the tumor. Examples: **Cushing syndrome** (small cell lung carcinoma — ACTH), **hypercalcemia** (squamous cell lung carcinoma, breast cancer — parathyroid hormone–related protein), the **syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion** (small cell carcinoma — hyponatremia), **Trousseau syndrome** (migratory thrombophlebitis — adenocarcinoma of the pancreas and lung), **acanthosis nigricans**, **clubbing of the fingers** and hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, **myasthenia-like syndrome** (Lambert–Eaton), polycythemia (renal cell carcinoma — erythropoietin).

blocks.text: **Carcinogenesis** is the process of transformation of a normal cell into a tumor cell. It is based on **genetic damage** (mutations) and **epigenetic changes**; cancer is a **genetic disease**.
Carcinogenic factors

**1. Chemical carcinogens.** The first observation was made by the English surgeon **P. Pott** (1775): scrotal skin cancer in chimney sweeps (exposure to soot). The Japanese scientists Yamagiwa and Ichikawa (1915) induced cancer experimentally by painting coal tar on a rabbit's ear.

items: **Direct-acting agents** — react with DNA without modification: alkylating agents (some **chemotherapy drugs** — cyclophosphamide; they can cause secondary leukemias).

**Indirect-acting agents (procarcinogens)** — act after activation in the body (cytochrome P-450): **polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons** (**benzopyrene** — tobacco smoke, tar, smoked products; lung and bladder cancer), **aromatic amines and azo dyes** (aniline dyes — bladder cancer), **aflatoxin B~1~** (nuts and grain contaminated with the fungus Aspergillus flavus — liver cancer), **nitrosamines** (gastric cancer), vinyl chloride (hepatic angiosarcoma), **asbestos** (mesothelioma, lung cancer), arsenic, chromium, nickel, benzene (leukemia). **Stages of chemical carcinogenesis: initiation** — irreversible DNA damage (mutation) by the carcinogen; **promotion** — proliferation of the mutated cell under the action of **promoters** (hormones, phorbol esters, drugs) (a promoter is not itself carcinogenic and produces a tumor only if it acts after initiation); **progression**.

blocks.text: 2. Physical carcinogens — radiation.

items: **Ultraviolet rays** (sun, UVB) — form **pyrimidine dimers** in DNA: **basal cell** and **squamous cell carcinoma** of the skin, **melanoma**; the risk is high in fair-skinned people and in xeroderma pigmentosum (defect of DNA repair).

**Ionizing radiation** (X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive substances) — double-strand breaks of DNA: **leukemias** (after Hiroshima and Nagasaki), **thyroid cancer** (in children after the Chernobyl accident — radioactive iodine), lung cancer (uranium miners, radon), bone sarcomas. **3. Biological (viral and microbial) carcinogens.**

blocks.title: Table 9.3. Viruses and microbes associated with tumors
head: Causative agent
Tumors
rows: Cancer of the cervix, anus, pharynx and penis (types 6 and 11 — benign warts, condylomas)
Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, B-cell lymphomas in immunodeficiency
Kaposi sarcoma (in AIDS), primary effusion lymphoma
Squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder

blocks.text: **4. Hereditary predisposition.** Hereditary tumor syndromes: **retinoblastoma** (RB gene), **Li–Fraumeni syndrome** (TP53), **familial adenomatous polyposis** (APC), **hereditary breast and ovarian cancer** (BRCA1, BRCA2), **Lynch syndrome** (DNA repair genes — colon cancer), **neurofibromatosis** (NF1), **multiple endocrine neoplasia** (MEN1, RET); and also defects of DNA repair (xeroderma pigmentosum).
**5. Hormonal factors** — estrogen excess (endometrial and breast cancer), androgens (prostate cancer).
Molecular basis of carcinogenesis
Carcinogenesis is a **multistep** process: several mutations must accumulate in a single cell. Mutations occur in four groups of **target genes**:

items: **Proto-oncogenes → oncogenes** — genes that normally stimulate cell growth and division (growth factors, their receptors, signaling proteins, transcription factors). As a result of mutation, amplification or translocation, an **activated oncogene** gives a constant growth signal. Oncogenes act **dominantly** (mutation of one allele is enough). Examples: **RAS** (the most frequently mutated oncogene — cancers of the pancreas, colon and lung), **HER2/ERBB2** amplification (breast cancer — treated with trastuzumab), **MYC** (Burkitt lymphoma — t(8;14)), **BCR-ABL** (chronic myeloid leukemia — t(9;22), the “Philadelphia chromosome”; treated with imatinib), **BRAF** (melanoma), **EGFR** (lung adenocarcinoma). 2. **Tumor suppressor genes** — genes that normally **inhibit** cell growth; for a tumor to develop, **both alleles** must be inactivated (**Knudson “two-hit” hypothesis**). The main ones: **TP53** — the “guardian of the genome”: when DNA is damaged, it arrests the cell cycle and initiates repair, and if repair is impossible — apoptosis; it is mutated in more than 50% of human tumors; **RB** — controls the G~1~→S transition of the cell cycle; **APC** (colon), **BRCA1/2**, **NF1**, **VHL** (renal cell carcinoma), **PTEN**, **CDKN2A** (p16). 3. **Genes regulating apoptosis** — overexpression of **BCL2** (follicular lymphoma — t(14;18)), disturbed apoptotic mechanisms (Topic 2). 4. **DNA repair genes** — their defects accelerate the accumulation of mutations in other genes (**genomic instability**): mismatch repair genes (Lynch syndrome), BRCA1/2, nucleotide excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum). In addition, **epigenetic changes** (hypermethylation of gene promoters — “silencing” of suppressor genes), **microRNAs** and activation of **telomerase** (limitless division) are important.

parts.text: An oncogene is “**a car with a stuck gas pedal**” (one defect is enough — dominant); a tumor suppressor gene is “**a broken brake**” (both brakes — both alleles — must fail — recessive, “two hits”); TP53 is “**the driver**”: when it sees a problem, it stops the car or destroys it (apoptosis).

blocks.text: Hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg)
The main properties of cancer cells (“hallmarks of cancer”):

items: **Self-sufficiency** in growth signals (oncogenes).
**Insensitivity** to growth-inhibitory signals (inactivation of suppressor genes).
**Evasion of apoptosis**.
**Limitless replicative potential** (activation of telomerase).
**Angiogenesis** (VEGF) — necessary for a tumor larger than 1–2 mm.
**Invasion and metastasis**.
**Altered cellular metabolism** (Warburg effect — aerobic glycolysis).
**Evasion of immune surveillance** (expression of PD-L1 — immune checkpoint inhibitors act against this). Enabling factors: **genomic instability** and **tumor-promoting inflammation**.

blocks.label: Figure 9.11
blocks.caption: Hallmarks of cancer (after Hanahan and Weinberg): self-sufficiency in growth signals, evasion of growth suppressors, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, reprogrammed energy metabolism, evasion of immune surveillance; enabling factors — genomic instability and tumor-promoting inflammation (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-24)

blocks.text: Tumors are classified mainly by the **histogenetic** principle (tissue of origin), by **degree of malignancy** and by **location** (WHO classification). **Naming rules:**

items: **Benign tumors** — tissue name + the suffix **“-oma”**: fibroma, lipoma, chondroma, osteoma, leiomyoma, hemangioma. Benign epithelial tumors: **papilloma** (from squamous and transitional epithelium, papillary), **adenoma** (from glandular epithelium), cystadenoma (cystic adenoma).
**Malignant epithelial tumors** — **cancer (carcinoma)**: squamous cell carcinoma, **adenocarcinoma** (glandular carcinoma), transitional cell carcinoma and others.

**Malignant mesenchymal tumors** — **sarcoma** (Greek sarx — flesh — for its “fish-flesh” appearance on the cut surface): fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, angiosarcoma.
**Tumors of hematopoietic and lymphoid tissue** — leukemias and lymphomas.

**Exceptions** (ending in “-oma” although malignant): **melanoma, seminoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, hepatoma**; named after an author or a distinctive feature: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), Ewing sarcoma, Hodgkin lymphoma.

**Teratoma** — a tumor composed of tissues of several germ layers (ecto-, meso-, endoderm) (from totipotent germ cells of the ovary and testis): **mature teratoma (dermoid cyst)** — benign; **immature teratoma** — malignant.
**Mixed tumors** — arising from one tissue but differentiating in different directions (pleomorphic adenoma of the salivary gland).

**Hamartoma** — disorganized tumor-like growth of tissues native to the organ (a developmental anomaly); **choristoma** — normal tissue in an unusual location (heterotopia — pancreatic tissue in the gastric wall).

blocks.label: Figure 9.12
blocks.caption: Colonic polyp (adenoma): A — a pedunculated adenomatous (glandular) polyp; B — multiple polyps (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-1)

blocks.label: Figure 9.13
blocks.caption: Cystic teratoma of the ovary (dermoid cyst): A — hair, sebaceous material and a tooth inside the cyst; B — skin, sebaceous glands, fat cells and neural tissue (arrow) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-3)

blocks.text: Grading and staging

**Grading** is the histologic assessment of a tumor by its **degree of differentiation** and the number of mitoses: **G1** (well differentiated), **G2** (moderately), **G3** (poorly differentiated), **G4** (undifferentiated, anaplastic).
**Staging** is the extent of spread of the tumor; according to the **TNM system**:

items: **T** (tumor) — size and local spread of the primary tumor (Tis — in situ, T1–T4);
**N** (nodus) — metastases to regional lymph nodes (N0 — none, N1–N3);

**M** (metastasis) — distant metastases (M0 — none, M1 — present). Clinical stages I–IV are determined on the basis of TNM. **Staging is more important than grading for prognosis and the choice of treatment.**

blocks.text: Benign epithelial tumors

items: **Papilloma** — from squamous or transitional epithelium; a papillary tumor (resembling a cauliflower or mulberry); each papilla has a vascular stromal core covered by epithelium; tissue atypia (thickened epithelium, hyperkeratosis). Skin, oral cavity, pharynx, urinary bladder, urinary tract.

**Adenoma** — from glandular epithelium; **acinar (alveolar)**, **tubular**, **trabecular**, **papillary**, **cystadenoma** (cystic — in the ovary), **fibroadenoma** (abundant stroma — breast). In mucous membranes — **adenomatous polyp**. Adenomatous polyps of the intestine are a precancerous condition.

blocks.label: Figure 9.15
blocks.caption: Skin papilloma (gross specimen): a sharply demarcated, wart-like tumor on the surface of the upper eyelid (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 9.14
blocks.caption: Skin papilloma (microscopic slide): papillary projections with a vascular stromal core covered by thickened stratified squamous epithelium (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.label: Figure 9.16
blocks.caption: Thyroid adenoma: normal-looking colloid-containing follicles (well differentiated) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-5)

blocks.label: Figure 9.17
blocks.caption: Ovarian cystadenoma: a thin-walled cystic tumor much larger than the ovary, filled with colloid fluid (TMA study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Malignant epithelial tumors — carcinoma
**Cancer (carcinoma)** is the most common malignant tumor (80–90% of all malignant tumors). Mainly **after the age of 40**. It metastasizes first by the **lymphogenous** route.
The main histologic types:

items: **Carcinoma in situ** — cancer that has not broken through the basement membrane.

**Squamous cell (epidermoid) carcinoma** — in sites lined by stratified squamous epithelium (skin, mouth, esophagus, cervix) or at sites of metaplasia (bronchus). **Keratinizing** (well differentiated) — concentric layers of horny substance in the center of tumor cell cords — **“keratin pearls”** — and intercellular bridges; **nonkeratinizing** (moderately and poorly differentiated).

**Adenocarcinoma (glandular carcinoma)** — from glandular and columnar epithelium (stomach, intestine, breast, lung, endometrium, prostate); atypical glands of various shapes and sizes, often producing mucus. Types: tubular, papillary, **mucinous (colloid, mucoid) carcinoma**, **signet ring cell carcinoma** (mucus inside the cell, nucleus pushed to the periphery — diffuse gastric cancer).
**Basal cell carcinoma (basalioma)** — from the basal layer of the skin; on the face, in the elderly; **locally destructive growth**, almost never metastasizes.
**Transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma** — in the urinary tract.
**Solid carcinoma** — a poorly differentiated carcinoma in the form of trabeculae.
**Small cell carcinoma** — composed of small, lymphocyte-like cells (lung); highly malignant, neuroendocrine.
**Medullary (brain-like) carcinoma** — abundant parenchyma, scant stroma, soft; **scirrhous (fibrous) carcinoma** — abundant stroma, hard.

blocks.label: Figure 9.19
blocks.caption: Colonic adenocarcinoma: unlike normal glands, the cancerous glands are irregular in shape and size; invasion of the muscular layer (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 7-6)

blocks.text: Mesenchymal tumors arise from connective, adipose, muscle, vascular, bone, cartilage and synovial tissues. Malignant mesenchymal tumors — **sarcomas** — are much less common than carcinomas, occur more often in young people and metastasize mainly by the **hematogenous** route.

items: **Leiomyoma (fibromyoma) of the uterus** is the most common tumor in women: sharply demarcated, whitish, firm nodules in the uterine wall (submucosal, intramural, subserosal) with a whorled fibrous pattern on the cut surface; histologically — bundles of smooth muscle cells running in different directions (tissue atypia), without atypia or mitoses. Clinically — uterine bleeding, anemia, infertility.
**Leiomyosarcoma** — atypical, pleomorphic spindle cells, numerous mitoses, necrosis.
**Hemangioma** — the capillary type (in the skin, in children; often regresses spontaneously) and the cavernous type (in the liver — blood-filled spaces).

**Osteosarcoma** is the most common primary malignant bone tumor; at 10–25 years of age, in the metaphysis of long bones (around the knee — the lower end of the femur and upper end of the tibia); the tumor cells form **osteoid**; it rapidly metastasizes to the lungs.

items: **Pigmented nevus (birthmark)** — a benign tumor-like collection of melanocytes; by location: **junctional** (at the border of the epidermis and dermis), **dermal (intradermal)** and **compound (mixed)**. **Dysplastic nevus** — atypical melanocytes; high risk of melanoma.

**Melanoma** is a **highly malignant** tumor arising from melanocytes; in the skin (often in a nevus or de novo), the eye (retina) and mucous membranes. Risk factors — ultraviolet rays (especially sunburns in childhood), fair skin, many nevi, family predisposition (CDKN2A), BRAF mutation. **Growth phases: radial** (horizontal, along the epidermis — low risk of metastasis) and **vertical** (deep into the dermis — high risk of metastasis). The main prognostic factor is the **thickness of the tumor (Breslow)**. Histologically: atypical melanocytes, numerous mitoses, melanin (there is also a nonpigmented — **amelanotic** — melanoma). It metastasizes very early by the lymphogenous and hematogenous routes (liver, lungs, brain, skin).

parts.text: The “ABCDE” signs of melanoma (Topic 4) and any changing pigmented spot are indications for **excisional biopsy**. Early detection and removal of melanoma (Breslow thickness up to 1 mm) lead to almost complete cure; at a late stage the prognosis is unfavorable, but modern therapy (BRAF inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors) considerably prolongs life.

blocks.text: The pathologist and the oncologist: from diagnosis to treatment

The final diagnosis of a tumor is made only on the basis of **histologic** examination (biopsy, surgical specimen, cytology). The pathologist's report states: the histologic type of the tumor, its grade of differentiation (G), the depth of invasion, invasion of vessels and nerves, the resection margins (tumor present or absent), and the number of lymph nodes with metastases (pTNM). In modern diagnosis, **immunohistochemistry** (determining the origin of the tumor — cytokeratins for epithelium, vimentin for mesenchyme, CD45 for lymphoid tissue, S-100 and HMB-45 for melanoma) and **molecular tests** (for targeted therapy — estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 in breast cancer; EGFR and ALK in lung cancer; KRAS in colorectal cancer) are important.

parts.text: **Tumor markers** are substances produced by tumor cells and detected in the blood; they are used mainly to monitor the effect of treatment and recurrence: **alpha-fetoprotein** (hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumor), **carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)** (colorectal cancer), **PSA** (prostate cancer), **CA-125** (ovarian cancer), **CA 19-9** (pancreatic cancer), **chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG)** (choriocarcinoma, testicular tumors). They are not sufficient for diagnosis on their own.

blocks.text: Screening — early detection of cancer

**Screening programs** are used to detect precancerous changes and early cancer: cervical smear (**Papanicolaou test**) and papillomavirus testing, **mammography** (breast cancer), **colonoscopy** and fecal occult blood testing (colorectal cancer), low-dose computed tomography (lung cancer in heavy smokers). Prevention: quitting smoking, **vaccination against papillomavirus and hepatitis B**, treatment of H. pylori, sun protection.

items: **Oncology** (Greek onkos — tumor) — the science that studies tumors.
**Tumor** (blastoma — Greek blastano — I sprout; neoplasma — new formation; tumor) — a pathological process characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of cells.
**Adenoma** (Greek aden — gland, -oma — tumor) — a benign tumor arising from glandular epithelium.
**Adenocarcinoma** (aden — gland, carcinoma — a malignant tumor of epithelium) — glandular cancer arising from glandular (prismatic) epithelium.
**Basal cell carcinoma (basalioma)** — a locally destructive tumor arising from the basal cells of the epidermis.
**Paget disease of the breast** — a malignant tumor of the nipple and areola of the breast.
**Hidradenoma** — a benign tumor arising from the secretory epithelium of skin glands.
**Carcinoid** — a neuroendocrine tumor arising from the enterochromaffin (Kulchitsky) cells of the gastric and intestinal mucosa.
**Melanoma** — a malignant tumor of melanin-forming tissue.
**Neurinoma (schwannoma)** (Greek neuron — nerve, -oma) — a benign tumor arising from the Schwann cells (lemmocytes) of the nerve fiber sheath.
**Nevus** — a benign tumor-like lesion of melanin-forming tissue.
**Papilloma** (Latin papilla — nipple) — a benign papillary tumor arising from stratified squamous or transitional epithelium.
**Cancer (carcinoma)** — a malignant tumor of epithelium.
**Carcinoma in situ** — a noninvasive cancer (not breaking through the basement membrane) but with marked cellular atypia.
**Clear cell (hypernephroid) carcinoma** — the most common malignant tumor of the kidney.
**Seminoma (dysgerminoma)** — a malignant germ cell tumor (seminoma in the testis, dysgerminoma in the ovary).
**Syringoadenoma** — a benign tumor of the sweat glands of the skin.
**Thecoma** — a benign tumor arising from the sex cord stroma of the ovary.
**Trichoepithelioma** — a benign tumor arising from hair follicles.
**Choriocarcinoma (chorionepithelioma)** — a malignant tumor arising from the trophoblast after abortion, tubal pregnancy or hydatidiform mole.
**Exophytic growth** (Greek exo — outside, phyton — growth) — growth of a tumor into the lumen of an organ.
**Endophytic growth** (Greek endon — inside) — growth of a tumor into the wall of an organ.
**Expansive growth** (Latin expansus — expanded) — growth of a tumor by itself, compressing the surrounding tissues.
**Infiltrative (invasive) growth** — growth of tumor cells into the surrounding tissues with their destruction.
**Metastasis** (Greek metastasis — transfer) — transfer of tumor cells to another site with formation of a new focus.
**Recurrence** (Latin recidivus — returning) — reappearance of a tumor at the site of its removal.
**Anaplasia** (Greek ana — backward, plasis — formation) — loss of differentiation.

**“Uterine fibromyoma”.** The uterus is enlarged, with sharply demarcated, round, firm, whitish nodules of various sizes in its wall; a whorled fibrous pattern on the cut surface. Conclusion: benign mesenchymal tumor (leiomyoma).
**“Fibroadenoma of the breast”.** A sharply demarcated, encapsulated, firm, whitish-gray, lobulated nodule. Conclusion: benign fibroepithelial tumor.
**“Ovarian cystadenoma”.** In place of the ovary — a thin-walled, smooth, unilocular or multilocular cyst filled with clear or mucinous fluid. Conclusion: benign epithelial tumor.
**“Skin papilloma”.** A sharply demarcated papillary (cauliflower-like) lesion protruding from the skin surface. Conclusion: benign epithelial tumor.
**“Colonic polyp”.** Pedunculated, gray-pink, lobulated lesion(s) on the mucosal surface. Conclusion: adenomatous polyp (precancerous).
**“Gastric cancer”.** Ulcerated tissue with raised edges (“saucer-shaped”) or diffusely thickened (linitis plastica), firm and whitish, in the gastric wall. Conclusion: malignant epithelial tumor.

**“Cancer metastases in the liver”.** The liver is enlarged, with sharply demarcated whitish-gray nodules of various sizes, with an “umbilicated” depression in the center. Conclusion: hematogenous metastases.

**“Osteosarcoma”.** A tumor in the bone metaphysis that destroys the bone and grows into the surrounding soft tissue, with indistinct borders; on the cut surface it is whitish-brown, with foci of hemorrhage and necrosis. Conclusion: malignant mesenchymal tumor.

**“Clear cell (hypernephroid) carcinoma of the kidney”.** A nodule at the pole of the kidney, variegated on the cut surface (yellow, red, brown) — foci of fat, hemorrhage and necrosis. Conclusion: malignant epithelial tumor.

items: **“Skin papilloma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Papillary projections with a core of connective tissue and vessels, covered by thickened stratified squamous epithelium with hyperkeratosis; the epithelial layers are preserved, and the basement membrane is intact. Conclusion: benign tumor (tissue atypia).
**“Fibroadenoma of the breast”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Surrounded by a capsule; elongated, compressed glands within a stroma-rich tumor. Conclusion: benign fibroepithelial tumor.

**“Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Cords and nests of atypical squamous epithelial cells have grown into the dermis; in the center of the nests — concentric layers of horny substance, “keratin pearls”; numerous mitoses. Conclusion: malignant epithelial tumor.

**“Adenocarcinoma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Atypical glands of various shapes and sizes, multilayered epithelium, hyperchromatic nuclei, mitoses; invasion of the wall. Conclusion: glandular carcinoma.
**“Melanoma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Nests of atypical, pleomorphic cells with brown-black melanin in the cytoplasm, numerous mitoses; invasion of the dermis. Conclusion: highly malignant tumor.

**“Leiomyoma (fibroleiomyoma)”** (van Gieson). Bundles of smooth muscle cells (yellow) and layers of connective tissue (red) running in different directions; no cellular atypia. Conclusion: benign tumor.
**“Leiomyosarcoma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Atypical spindle cells, pleomorphism, numerous atypical mitoses, foci of necrosis. Conclusion: sarcoma.
**“Capillary hemangioma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Numerous blood-filled capillary-type vessels lined by endothelium. Conclusion: benign vascular tumor.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 42-year-old woman has prolonged uterine bleeding and anemia. At surgery the uterus is enlarged, with numerous sharply demarcated, firm, whitish nodules from 0.5 to 6 cm in its wall, with a whorled fibrous pattern on the cut surface. Microscopically: bundles of smooth muscle cells running in different directions, no atypia or mitoses.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Is this tumor benign or malignant? Justify. 3) What type of atypia is observed?
cases.answer: 1) Uterine leiomyoma (fibromyoma) — multinodular. 2) Benign: sharply demarcated (expansive growth), no cellular atypia or atypical mitoses, resembles the tissue of origin (myometrium) — well differentiated. Clinical significance — bleeding and anemia (submucosal nodules). 3) Tissue atypia only — disordered arrangement of muscle bundles in different directions; the cells themselves resemble normal smooth muscle cells.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old man has smoked for 40 years. Cough, hemoptysis, weight loss. Bronchoscopy: a tumor in the bronchial wall; biopsy: cords of atypical squamous epithelial cells with concentric layers of horny substance in their center, numerous mitoses. Blood calcium is increased. Later the cervical lymph nodes enlarged.
cases.ask: 1) Histologic diagnosis? 2) What precancerous changes and carcinogens caused this tumor? 3) Explain the hypercalcemia and the enlargement of the lymph nodes.
cases.answer: 1) Keratinizing (well-differentiated) squamous cell carcinoma of the lung — “keratin pearls”. 2) Under the action of tobacco smoke carcinogens (benzopyrene and other polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines): squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive cancer; mutations of TP53 and other genes. 3) Hypercalcemia — a paraneoplastic syndrome: the tumor produces a parathyroid hormone–related protein. Enlargement of the lymph nodes — lymphogenous metastases (characteristic of carcinomas).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 16-year-old adolescent complains of pain and swelling in the knee region. X-ray: a bone-destroying tumor in the lower metaphysis of the femur, with a “sunburst” sign. Biopsy: atypical, pleomorphic cells with osteoid material between them, numerous mitoses. A year later numerous nodules were found in the lungs.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) To which group does this tumor belong, and what is the naming principle? 3) The lung nodules and the route by which they appeared.
cases.answer: 1) Osteosarcoma. 2) A malignant mesenchymal tumor — sarcoma; the name is the tissue of origin (bone — “osteo”) + “sarcoma”. It is common in young people, in the metaphysis of long bones (around the knee); the tumor cells form osteoid. 3) The lung nodules are hematogenous metastases: sarcomas metastasize mainly through the blood, and the lung is the first capillary filter.
