topics.title: General pathology of infectious diseases. Viral and bacterial infections. Tuberculosis. Syphilis. Sepsis

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the general features of infectious diseases: causative agent, portal of entry, primary infectious complex, routes of spread, local and systemic changes;
the mechanisms by which microorganisms damage tissue and the main types of tissue reactions to infection;
the morphology of viral infections (influenza, measles, herpes, chickenpox, cytomegalovirus infection), viral inclusions;
bacterial infections: staphylococcal and streptococcal infections, scarlet fever, diphtheria, meningococcal infection;
tuberculosis: etiology, pathogenesis, primary, hematogenous and secondary forms of tuberculosis, tissue reactions in the tuberculous focus;
syphilis: stages, morphology, visceral and congenital syphilis;
sepsis: classification, pathogenesis and clinicomorphologic forms;
the basic concepts of fungal and protozoal infections (candidiasis, aspergillosis, malaria, leishmaniasis).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of the primary tuberculous complex of the lung, miliary tuberculosis, cavitary tuberculosis, staphylococcal destruction of the lung, purulent leptomeningitis, the spleen in malaria and the liver in visceral syphilis;
describe microscopic slides of measles pneumonia (giant cells), cytomegaly, tuberculous granuloma, myocarditis in diphtheria, esophageal candidiasis and the liver in malaria;
formulate the pathological diagnosis of an infectious disease.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Viral inclusions: **“Owl's eye — CMV”**, **“Ground-glass nucleus — herpes”**, **“Giant cell + inclusion — measles (Warthin–Finkeldey)”**, **“Negri bodies — rabies”** (in the cytoplasm of neurons).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Within the curriculum, intestinal infections (typhoid fever, salmonellosis, dysentery, cholera) and highly dangerous infections (plague, anthrax) are studied in detail in systemic pathology. This chapter gives their examples important for general pathology: **diphtheritic colitis** in dysentery (Topic 5), **waxy necrosis** in typhoid fever (Topic 2), **hemorrhagic inflammation** in anthrax and plague (Topic 5).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Sepsis terminology has changed.** In the textbooks of Strukov and Abdullakhodjaeva, sepsis is divided into **septicemia** (without metastatic purulent foci) and **septicopyemia** (with metastatic abscesses), and “bacteremia” and “septic endocarditis” are considered separately. In the international **Sepsis-3** consensus (2016), “sepsis” is infection + organ dysfunction (an increase of 2 or more points on the SOFA score), and “**septic shock**” is hypotension requiring vasopressors with elevated lactate; the terms “septicemia” and “sepsis with SIRS” have been removed from practice. The exam requires knowledge of the classic classification, while the new definitions are used in the clinic.

blocks.text: **Infectious (communicable) diseases** are diseases caused by pathogenic microorganisms (viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, helminths, prions) and often transmitted from person to person. Their development depends on the interaction of the **causative agent** (virulence, dose, tropism), the **host** (immune status, age, nutrition, comorbidities) and **environmental** conditions.
General features of an infectious disease:

items: **Portal of entry** — the site where the agent enters the organism: skin (wound, insect bite), respiratory tract (airborne droplets), digestive tract (fecal–oral), genitourinary tract (sexual), parenteral route (blood, injection), transplacental (vertical).

**Primary infectious complex** — changes at the portal of entry (**primary affect**) + **lymphangitis** as the agent spreads through the lymph + involvement of the regional lymph nodes (**lymphadenitis**). For example, the primary tuberculous complex, the hard chancre and regional lymphadenitis in syphilis.
**Routes of spread** — contiguous (to neighboring tissues), canalicular (along the bronchi, urinary and bile ducts), lymphogenous, hematogenous, perineural.
**Local and systemic changes** — local: inflammation; systemic: hyperplasia of lymphoid organs, degeneration in parenchymal organs, rash, intoxication.
**Cyclic course** — incubation period → prodromal period → period of main manifestations → recovery or complications.

blocks.text: Mechanisms by which microorganisms damage tissue

items: **Direct cell damage** — viruses multiply inside the cell and destroy it (cytopathic effect), alter cell metabolism and induce apoptosis;

**Toxins** — **exotoxins** (proteins secreted by bacteria: diphtheria, tetanus, botulinum and cholera toxins) and **endotoxin** (the lipopolysaccharide of the gram-negative bacterial wall — fever, septic shock, DIC);
**Enzymes** — proteases, hyaluronidase (spread of streptococci), coagulase (staphylococci);
**Immune-mediated damage** — hypersensitivity reactions (type IV in tuberculosis; type III in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever).

blocks.text: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. The common features of most viral infections: **mononuclear (lymphocytic) infiltration**, **interstitial inflammation**, **degeneration and necrosis** of epithelial cells, **viral inclusions** (intranuclear or cytoplasmic), **multinucleated giant cells**, and addition of a secondary **bacterial infection**.
Influenza

**Influenza** is an acute respiratory infection caused by RNA-containing **influenza viruses (A, B, C)** and transmitted by airborne droplets. Because of the variability of the **hemagglutinin (H)** and **neuraminidase (N)** antigens of virus A, epidemics and **pandemics** occur (the 1918 “Spanish flu” — 50 million deaths). The virus damages the epithelium of the respiratory tract (**epitheliotropic**) and has a **toxic** effect on the vessels (increased permeability, hemorrhages).
Forms and morphology:

items: **Mild form** — **serous-catarrhal** inflammation of the upper respiratory tract; degeneration and desquamation of the epithelium; basophilic and fuchsinophilic inclusions in the epithelium.

**Moderate form** — catarrhal inflammation spreads to the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles; in the lung — **focal influenza pneumonia** — serous-hemorrhagic exudate, macrophages and desquamated epithelium in the alveoli; sometimes **hyaline membranes**.

**Severe form:** a) **toxic influenza** — severe intoxication: **serous-hemorrhagic** inflammation and necrosis in the respiratory tract, **hemorrhagic pneumonia** and edema in the lung, edema and small hemorrhages in the brain; b) **influenza with pulmonary complications** — a secondary bacterial (staphylococcal, pneumococcal) infection is added, producing the **“large variegated influenza lung”**: focal hemorrhagic pneumonia, abscesses, bronchiectasis, pleurisy. Complications: pneumonia, lung abscess, otitis, sinusitis, meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, vascular thromboses.

blocks.text: Measles

**Measles** is a highly contagious acute infection, occurring mainly in children, caused by an RNA virus of the paramyxovirus family. The virus enters through the respiratory tract, multiplies in lymphoid tissue and spreads with viremia.
Morphology:

items: **in the oral mucosa** (on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars) — whitish spots with a red halo — **Belsky–Filatov–Koplik spots** (the pathognomonic early sign of the disease, before the rash);

**skin rash (exanthem)** — a maculopapular rash beginning on the face and behind the ears and spreading downward; perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate in the dermis; later **branny desquamation** and pigmentation;
**respiratory tract** — catarrhal-purulent inflammation; in severe cases **necrotizing laryngitis and tracheitis** — “**false croup**”;

**lung** — **giant cell interstitial pneumonia**: multinucleated (Warthin–Finkeldey) giant cells in the alveolar walls and spaces, with eosinophilic inclusions in their nuclei and cytoplasm; secondary bacterial pneumonia;
**lymphoid organs** — follicular hyperplasia, **Warthin–Finkeldey giant cells**.

blocks.text: Complications: pneumonia (the main cause of death in children), **noma** (wet gangrene of the facial soft tissues in debilitated children), encephalitis, later **subacute sclerosing panencephalitis**; immunosuppression (the virus damages lymphocytes — reactivation of tuberculosis). **Prevention — vaccination**.

blocks.text: Herpesvirus infections

items: **Herpes simplex (HSV-1, HSV-2)** — **vesicles** on the skin and mucous membranes (lips, genitals): epithelial cells swell (ballooning degeneration) and rupture, forming an intraepidermal vesicle; **glassy eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry type A bodies)** and multinucleated giant cells in epithelial cells. The virus persists **latently in sensory ganglia** and recurs. Severe forms: **herpetic encephalitis** (hemorrhagic-necrotizing inflammation of the temporal lobes), generalized infection in newborns, esophagitis and pneumonia in immunodeficiency.

**Chickenpox and herpes zoster (VZV)** — chickenpox in children: a vesicular skin rash (morphology similar to herpes); the virus persists latently in the dorsal root ganglia and later recurs as **herpes zoster (shingles)** (painful vesicles along a nerve).

**Cytomegalovirus infection (CMV)** — infected cells are **markedly enlarged (cytomegaly)**, with a large basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo — the “**owl's eye**”. The salivary glands, lungs, kidneys, liver and brain are most often affected. **Congenital** (intrauterine) infection — microcephaly, periventricular calcification, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, deafness; **in immunodeficiency** (AIDS, transplantation) — pneumonia, retinitis, colitis.
**Epstein–Barr virus** — **infectious mononucleosis** (fever, tonsillitis, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes in the blood); association with tumors (Topic 9).

parts.text: Viral inclusions: **“Owl's eye — CMV”**, **“Ground-glass nucleus — herpes”**, **“Giant cell + inclusion — measles (Warthin–Finkeldey)”**, **“Negri bodies — rabies”** (in the cytoplasm of neurons).

blocks.text: Staphylococcal and streptococcal infections

**Staphylococci** (Staphylococcus aureus) — gram-positive cocci arranged like bunches of grapes; they produce **coagulase**, hemolysins, leukocidin and **enterotoxins**. They cause mainly **purulent-necrotizing** inflammation that **tends to be localized** (abscess):

items: skin — **furuncle** (purulent-necrotizing inflammation of a hair follicle and sebaceous gland), **carbuncle** (fusion of several furuncles), panaritium, impetigo;
**lung** — staphylococcal pneumonia, especially in children and after influenza: abscesses and **staphylococcal destruction of the lung** (air spaces — bullae, pyopneumothorax);
bone — **osteomyelitis**; heart — **infective endocarditis**; sepsis;

toxin-mediated diseases — **food poisoning** (enterotoxin), **toxic shock syndrome**, **scalded skin syndrome** in newborns (exfoliative toxin). **Streptococci** (Streptococcus pyogenes — group A beta-hemolytic) — chain-forming cocci; they produce hyaluronidase and streptokinase and cause **diffuse** inflammation of tissue (**phlegmon**): **tonsillitis (angina)**, pharyngitis, **erysipelas** (diffuse edematous inflammation of the dermis, sharply demarcated redness), impetigo, necrotizing fasciitis, sepsis. **Postinfectious immune complications: rheumatic fever** (molecular mimicry) and **poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis** (type III).

blocks.text: **Scarlet fever** is a childhood disease caused by group A streptococci producing a pyrogenic (erythrogenic) toxin: **necrotic tonsillitis** (necrosis of the tonsils), regional **lymphadenitis**, a fine punctate rash (pale nasolabial triangle — Filatov sign), **“raspberry tongue”**, followed by desquamation of the skin in large sheets. Severe **toxic** and **septic** forms; late complications (in weeks 2–3) — glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever (the allergic period).

blocks.text: Diphtheria

**Diphtheria** is an acute infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae; the main damaging factor is the **exotoxin** (it stops protein synthesis in cells). **Fibrinous inflammation** develops at the portal of entry (Topic 5):

items: **in the pharynx and tonsils** (stratified squamous epithelium) — **diphtheritic** inflammation: a thick gray **membrane** firmly attached to the underlying tissue; much toxin is absorbed, and the soft tissues of the neck swell;

**in the larynx, trachea and bronchi** (columnar epithelium) — **croupous** inflammation: an easily detachable membrane — **true croup**, asphyxia. **Systemic action of the toxin: toxic myocarditis** — fatty degeneration of cardiomyocytes (“tiger heart”), foci of myolysis, interstitial inflammation — **sudden cardiac arrest** in the 2nd week; **parenchymal neuritis** (paralysis of the soft palate, eye muscles and diaphragmatic nerves — in weeks 3–6); hemorrhage and necrosis in the adrenal glands; nephrosis. **Causes of death:** early — asphyxia (true croup) and toxic shock; late — cardiac paralysis (myocarditis), diaphragmatic paralysis.

blocks.text: Meningococcal infection
**Meningococcus** (Neisseria meningitidis) is a gram-negative diplococcus; it is transmitted by airborne droplets; mainly in children. Forms:

items: **meningococcal nasopharyngitis** — catarrhal inflammation;

**purulent meningitis (leptomeningitis)** — the leptomeninges are thickened, dull and soaked with yellow-green pus — a **“purulent cap”** (mainly over the convex surface and base of the brain); microscopically, a diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate in the meninges; complications — **hydrocephalus** (obliteration of the CSF pathways), cerebral edema and herniation, encephalitis, abscess;

**meningococcemia (meningococcal sepsis)** — severe **septic shock**, **DIC**, a **hemorrhagic rash** on the skin (“stellate” necrotic rash), bilateral hemorrhage into the adrenal glands — **Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome** (acute adrenal insufficiency) — leads rapidly to death.

blocks.caption: Purulent meningitis (microscopic slide): the pia mater is diffusely infiltrated by neutrophils (TMA study guide, 2018)

parts.text: Within the curriculum, intestinal infections (typhoid fever, salmonellosis, dysentery, cholera) and highly dangerous infections (plague, anthrax) are studied in detail in systemic pathology. This chapter gives their
examples important for general pathology: **diphtheritic colitis** in dysentery (Topic 5), **waxy necrosis** in typhoid fever (Topic 2), **hemorrhagic inflammation** in anthrax and plague (Topic 5).

blocks.text: **Tuberculosis** is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Koch bacillus, 1882); it affects mainly the lungs but can involve any organ. Mycobacteria are **acid-fast** (red bacilli with the Ziehl–Neelsen method) and resistant to phagocytosis because of their waxy cell wall. Transmission is mainly by **airborne droplets** (from a patient with open tuberculosis), less often through the intestine (cow's milk — M. bovis). According to WHO, tuberculosis is one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent in the world; it runs a severe course together with **HIV infection**.
Pathogenesis

Mycobacteria are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, but they block the fusion of the phagosome with the lysosome and multiply inside the macrophage (**incomplete phagocytosis**). After about 3 weeks **cell-mediated immunity** develops: **Th1 lymphocytes** produce IFN-gamma and activate macrophages — these turn into **epithelioid cells** and **giant cells** and form a **granuloma** (Topic 6); at the same time **type IV hypersensitivity** develops — **caseous necrosis** and a positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test. Thus in tuberculosis immunity and hypersensitivity appear simultaneously.
Tissue reactions in the tuberculous focus

items: **Alterative reaction** — caseous necrosis predominates (when immunity is low);
**Exudative reaction** — serous-fibrinous or purulent exudate that rapidly turns into caseous necrosis (when hypersensitivity is high);

**Productive reaction** — tuberculous granulomas (tubercles) (when immunity is good). Outcomes of the tuberculous focus: **favorable** — encapsulation, calcification (petrification), ossification, scar; **unfavorable** — liquefaction of the caseous mass and formation of a cavity (**cavern**), enlargement of the focus and dissemination.

blocks.text: Clinicomorphologic forms
Three main types of tuberculosis are distinguished:
**1. Primary tuberculosis** — on the first infection (in a nonsensitized organism), most often in children. Its morphologic expression is the **primary tuberculous complex**:

items: **primary affect (Ghon focus)** — in the lung parenchyma, usually **in the lower part of the upper lobe or the upper part of the lower lobe**, beneath the pleura, a focus of caseous pneumonia 1–1.5 cm in size (with perifocal inflammation around it);
**lymphangitis** — tuberculous tubercles along the lymphatic vessels;

**regional lymphadenitis** — caseous necrosis of the hilar and peribronchial lymph nodes (larger than the primary affect). **Outcomes:** a) **healing** (in most people) — the foci are encapsulated and calcified: the calcified primary affect (**Ghon focus**) and the calcified lymph nodes together form the **Ranke complex** (visible on X-ray); mycobacteria may survive inside for years; b) **progression**: growth of the primary affect — **primary lung cavity**, caseous pneumonia; **lymphogenous** spread (bronchoadenitis, extensive lymph node involvement); **hematogenous** spread (miliary tuberculosis, meningitis) — especially in young children and in immunodeficiency; c) **chronic course**.

blocks.text: **2. Hematogenous tuberculosis** — spread through the blood from foci that persisted after the primary infection (most often from lymph nodes). Forms:

items: **generalized hematogenous tuberculosis** — **miliary tuberculosis**: millet-sized (1–2 mm) whitish-yellow tubercles in many organs (lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, meninges); in severe cases — **tuberculous sepsis** (necrotic foci without reaction);
**hematogenous tuberculosis with predominant lung involvement** — bilateral symmetric miliary or large-focal dissemination in the lungs;

**extrapulmonary hematogenous tuberculosis** — individual organs: **bones and joints** (spine — **Pott disease**, cold abscesses, gibbus), **kidney** (cavities, “pyonephrosis”), genital organs (epididymitis, salpingitis — infertility), adrenal glands (**Addison disease**), **tuberculous meningitis** (gelatinous exudate at the base of the brain), skin, lymph nodes (scrofula). **3. Secondary (reinfection) tuberculosis** — in **adults** who previously had primary tuberculosis (endogenous reactivation or exogenous reinfection); mainly in the **lung apices** (segments I and II); the main route is **canalicular (bronchogenic)** spread. **8 forms** (phases) of secondary tuberculosis are distinguished:

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Forms of secondary tuberculosis (classification of A.I. Strukov)
head: Form
Morphology
rows: Specific endobronchitis of a segmental bronchus in the lung apex, then a focus of acinar or lobular caseous bronchopneumonia; on healing — a calcified Aschoff–Puhl focus
Sclerosis around healed and calcified foci, reactivation of new foci
Extensive perifocal exudative inflammation around the focus (on X-ray — the Assmann–Redeker infiltrate)
An encapsulated focus of caseous necrosis 2–5 cm in diameter (resembles a tumor on X-ray)
Caseous necrosis involves a whole lobe or more; the lung is yellow and firm (“cheese-like”); severe, leads rapidly to death
The caseous mass is discharged through a bronchus and a cavity forms; its wall is lined internally by caseous masses

The cavity wall has three layers: inner — caseous (pyogenic), middle — tuberculous granulation tissue, outer — fibrous; the process spreads from the apex downward (apicocaudally) and bronchogenically; the most common form
Deformation of the lung, extensive scar tissue, bronchiectasis, a scar in place of the cavity

blocks.text: **Complications and causes of death:** pulmonary **hemorrhage** (erosion of vessels in the cavity wall), **pneumothorax**, pleural empyema, **cardiopulmonary failure** (chronic cor pulmonale), **secondary AA amyloidosis** (Topic 8), additional tuberculosis of the bronchi, larynx and intestine (from swallowed sputum), tuberculous meningitis.

parts.text: **Tuberculosis is a relevant disease for Uzbekistan.** Diagnosis: detection of acid-fast bacilli in sputum (microscopy), molecular testing (**GeneXpert** — mycobacterial DNA and rifampin resistance), culture, X-ray; latent infection — the Mantoux test and IFN-gamma release assays. **Drug-resistant tuberculosis** (MDR-TB) is a serious problem. To prevent severe forms in children (miliary tuberculosis, tuberculous meningitis), **BCG** vaccination is given in the maternity hospital.

blocks.text: **Syphilis** is a chronic infection with a wavelike course caused by Treponema pallidum; it is transmitted mainly **sexually**, and also vertically (transplacentally) and parenterally. Treponemes cannot be seen with ordinary stains — **silver impregnation**, dark-field microscopy, immunofluorescence are used; diagnosis is mainly by **serologic** tests (nontreponemal — RW (Wassermann reaction), RPR; treponemal — RIF, TPHA).

In every stage of syphilis the main morphologic feature is **damage to small vessels**: **obliterating endarteritis** (endothelial proliferation, thickening of the vessel wall) and a **perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate** (abundance of **plasma cells** is characteristic).

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Stages of acquired syphilis
head: Stage
Time
Morphology
rows: A hard chancre at the portal of entry — a painless ulcer with a firm base and smooth floor (on the genitals, lip, anus); lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and endarteritis in the dermis; regional lymphadenitis (firm, painless) — the primary syphilitic complex; the chancre heals spontaneously in 4–6 weeks

Hematogenous spread of treponemes — syphilides: macular (roseola), papular and pustular rashes on the skin (including the palms and soles) and mucous membranes; condylomata lata (around the anus); generalized lymphadenopathy; many treponemes in the lesions — highly contagious
After many years (3–5 years or more)

Gummas and gummatous infiltration (Topic 6): cardiovascular syphilis — syphilitic mesaortitis (“shagreen skin” intima), aortic aneurysm, aortic valve insufficiency, narrowing of the coronary ostia; neurosyphilis — general paresis (atrophy of the cerebral cortex, dementia), tabes dorsalis (demyelination of the posterior columns); visceral syphilis — gummas and scars in the liver (“hepar lobatum”), bones (destruction of the nasal septum — “saddle nose”), testes

blocks.text: **Congenital syphilis** — intrauterine infection (after the 4th month of pregnancy, transplacentally):

items: **stillbirth** or miscarriage (maceration);

**early congenital syphilis** (in the newborn and early childhood): **liver** — diffuse interstitial hepatitis, fibrosis (“**flint liver**”), **lung** — “**white pneumonia**” (interstitial fibrosis, unexpanded alveoli), **bones** — **syphilitic osteochondritis** (a yellow band at the epiphyseal–diaphyseal border) and periostitis, skin — a vesicular rash (on the palms and soles), nasal obstruction (rhinitis, “snuffles”);

**late congenital syphilis** (after 2 years of age): **Hutchinson triad** — notched, crescent-shaped deformity of the incisors (**Hutchinson teeth**), **interstitial keratitis**, inner ear damage (**deafness**); “saddle nose”, **saber shins**.

parts.text: Syphilis responds well to penicillin, but the spontaneous disappearance of symptoms in the early stages deceives the patient. Therefore serologic testing of **pregnant women** and blood donors is mandatory: timely treatment during pregnancy prevents congenital syphilis.

blocks.text: **Sepsis** is life-threatening **organ dysfunction** caused by a **dysregulated host response** to infection (Sepsis-3, 2016). In traditional pathological anatomy, sepsis is a **nonspecific** (similar with different agents), **noncyclic** generalized infectious disease characterized by constant or periodic entry of agents and toxins into the blood from a local infectious focus.

parts.text: **Sepsis terminology has changed.** In the textbooks of Strukov and Abdullakhodjaeva, sepsis is divided into **septicemia** (without metastatic purulent foci) and **septicopyemia** (with metastatic abscesses), and “bacteremia” and “septic endocarditis” are considered separately. In the international **Sepsis-3** consensus (2016), “sepsis” is infection + organ dysfunction (an increase of 2 or more points on the SOFA score), and “**septic shock**” is hypotension requiring vasopressors with elevated lactate; the terms “septicemia” and “sepsis with SIRS” have been removed from practice. The exam requires knowledge of the classic classification, while the new definitions are used in the clinic.

blocks.text: Pathological concepts of sepsis:

items: **Septic focus (primary focus)** — a local focus of purulent inflammation from which the agent enters the blood; it often coincides with the **portal of entry**; the septic focus often shows **purulent lymphangitis** and **thrombophlebitis** (purulently dissolved thrombi — a source of bacterial embolism).

**Types of sepsis by portal of entry: therapeutic (parasepsis)** — from infection of internal organs; **tonsillogenic**; **surgical** (postoperative, wound); **uterine (obstetric)** — after childbirth and abortion; **otogenic**; **odontogenic**; **urogenic**; **umbilical sepsis** (in newborns); **cryptogenic** — when no focus is found.

blocks.text: Clinicomorphologic forms:

items: **Septicemia** — severe **intoxication** without metastatic purulent foci: hemorrhages in the skin and mucous membranes, **septic spleen** (enlarged, soft, bright red on the cut surface, yielding abundant pulp on scraping), hyperplasia of lymph nodes, degeneration and interstitial inflammation in parenchymal organs, hemolysis (jaundice), DIC; **septic shock**.

**Septicopyemia** — the main feature is **metastatic abscesses** in various organs (lungs, kidneys, myocardium, brain, liver) (the result of bacterial embolism, for example, **embolic purulent nephritis** — Topic 7); most often caused by staphylococci and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

**Septic (bacterial) endocarditis** — **polypous-ulcerative endocarditis** of the heart valves (most often aortic and mitral; tricuspid in drug users): large thrombotic vegetations on the valves, destruction (perforation), microbial colonies; **thromboembolic syndrome** (infarcts of the kidney, spleen, brain), **immune complex syndrome** (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, Roth spots, Osler nodes). Acute (staphylococcus, on a healthy valve) and subacute (viridans streptococcus — Streptococcus viridans, on a previously damaged valve) forms.
**Chronic sepsis** — prolonged suppuration (osteomyelitis, carious teeth), cachexia, amyloidosis.

parts.text: **Septic shock** is the main mechanism of death from sepsis: systemic vasodilation, endothelial damage, DIC and “shock organs” under the action of endotoxin and cytokines (TNF, IL-1) (Topic 7). The most important principle of treatment is giving antibiotics **within the first hour** and **eliminating the septic focus** (opening an abscess, removing an infected catheter or tissue).

blocks.text: **Candidiasis** — Candida albicans (an opportunistic yeast-like fungus); it develops with antibiotics, glucocorticoids, diabetes mellitus, immunodeficiency (AIDS) and in newborns. White plaques in the oral cavity (“**oral thrush**”), the esophagus (candida esophagitis), the vagina; in severe cases **candida sepsis** (microabscesses in the kidney, brain, heart). Microscopically — yeast cells and **pseudohyphae** (PAS-positive).

**Aspergillosis** — Aspergillus fungi: **aspergilloma** (a “fungus ball” in old cavities), **allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis**, **invasive aspergillosis** (in neutropenia — invades vessels, causing hemorrhagic infarcts). The hyphae are thin, septate and branch **at acute angles**.

**Malaria** — caused by Plasmodium (falciparum, vivax, malariae, ovale); transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Plasmodia multiply in red cells and destroy them — **hemolysis**, attacks of fever. **Hemomelanin (malarial pigment)** accumulates in macrophages (Topic 4): the **spleen** is enlarged and gray-black (“**slate spleen**”), and the liver and bone marrow are dark. **Tropical malaria** (P. falciparum) — **cerebral malaria**: infected red cells stick to cerebral capillaries and occlude them — hemorrhages, necrosis (Dürck granulomas), coma; acute kidney injury, severe anemia.

**Leishmaniasis** — Leishmania (protozoa), transmitted by sand flies (Phlebotomus). **Cutaneous leishmaniasis** (“**pendinka**”, Borovsky disease — found in Central Asia) — ulcerating nodules in the skin; **visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)** — leishmaniae multiply in macrophages: marked **splenomegaly**, hepatomegaly, bone marrow involvement (pancytopenia), cachexia; **Leishman–Donovan bodies** in macrophages.

blocks.text: The pathological diagnosis of an infectious disease

The diagnosis of a patient who died of an infectious disease states: the **underlying disease** (nosological form, clinicomorphologic variant, laboratory-confirmed agent), **complications**, **concomitant diseases**. When an infectious disease is suspected, material is taken at autopsy for **bacteriologic, virologic and histobacterioscopic** examination; a special biosafety regime is used for highly dangerous infections; when an infectious disease is identified, the sanitary-epidemiological service is notified.

Example: “Underlying disease: fibrocavernous pulmonary tuberculosis (bacteriologically confirmed), a cavity in the upper lobe of the right lung. Complications: erosion of a vessel in the cavity wall, pulmonary hemorrhage, aspiration of blood. Concomitant disease: secondary amyloidosis of the kidneys and spleen.”

parts.text: **Prevention of infections — vaccination.** The national immunization schedule against measles, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, poliomyelitis, hepatitis B, tuberculosis (BCG), papillomavirus infection and others prevents severe infectious diseases and deaths in children. In areas where vaccination coverage has declined, epidemics of measles and diphtheria are reappearing.

items: **Cytomegaly** (Greek kytos — cell, megalos — large) — a disease characterized by the appearance of large cells (cytomegalic cells) in the epithelium.
**Exanthem** (Greek exanthein — to blossom) — skin rash.
**Enanthem** (Greek en — inside, anthein — to blossom) — rash on mucous membranes.
**Staphylococci** (Greek staphyle — bunch of grapes, kokkos — grain) — gram-positive cocci arranged like bunches of grapes (family Staphylococcaceae).
**Streptococci** (Greek streptos — chain) — chain-forming, spherical or oval, non-spore-forming, gram-positive, facultatively anaerobic bacteria (family Streptococcaceae).
**Diphtheria** (Greek diphthera — leather membrane) — an acute infectious disease distinguished by the formation of a membrane as a result of fibrinous inflammation.
**Meningococcus** (Neisseria meningitidis) — gram-negative diplococci of the genus Neisseria.
**Candidiasis** (oral thrush) — a fungal infection caused mainly by Candida albicans; the fungi are opportunistic and cause disease when immunity is reduced.
**Aspergillosis** — the general name of all diseases caused by fungi of the genus Aspergillus.
**Malaria** (Italian mala aria — “bad air”) — a group of vector-borne infectious diseases caused by Plasmodium and transmitted by the bite of female Anopheles mosquitoes.

**Leishmaniases** (named after W. Leishman) — a group of mainly zoonotic, vector-borne parasitic diseases with natural foci, caused by protozoa of the genus Leishmania and found in tropical and subtropical regions.
**Primary affect** — the initial change that develops at the portal of entry of an infection.
**Cavern (cavity)** (Latin caverna — cave) — a cavity formed as a result of discharge of necrotic tissue.
**Tubercle** (Latin tuberculum — small knob) — the tuberculous granuloma.
**Chancre** (French chancre — sore) — the primary affect of syphilis, a painless ulcer with a firm base.
**Syphilides** — skin and mucosal rashes in secondary syphilis.
**Sepsis** (Greek sepsis — putrefaction) — a generalized infectious disease with organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated response to infection.
**Septicopyemia** (Greek pyon — pus) — sepsis with metastatic purulent foci.

**“Primary tuberculous complex”.** A yellowish caseous focus 1–1.5 cm in size beneath the pulmonary pleura (primary affect); the hilar lymph nodes are enlarged and cheese-like on the cut surface. Conclusion: primary tuberculosis.
**“Miliary tuberculosis of the lung”.** Numerous millet-sized whitish-yellow tubercles in the lung. Conclusion: generalized hematogenous tuberculosis.

**“Fibrocavernous tuberculosis”.** A cavity with a thick, dense wall in the lung apex, its inner surface lined by caseous mass; sclerosis and foci of different ages around it; the pleura is thickened. Conclusion: secondary pulmonary tuberculosis.
**“Staphylococcal destruction of the lung”.** Irregular abscesses and air spaces in the lung tissue. Conclusion: staphylococcal pneumonia.
**“Purulent leptomeningitis”.** The leptomeninges are thick, dull and soaked with yellow-green pus. Conclusion: purulent meningitis (meningococcal).
**“The spleen in malaria”.** The spleen is enlarged, firm and gray-black (slate-colored) on the cut surface. Conclusion: malaria (hemomelanosis).
**“The liver in visceral syphilis”** and **“syphilitic aortic aneurysm”** — see Topic 6.
**“Septic spleen”.** The spleen is enlarged and soft, bright red on the cut surface, yielding abundant pulp on scraping. Conclusion: sepsis (septicemia).

items: **“Giant cell pneumonia in measles”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Serous exudate, macrophages and multinucleated giant cells (eosinophilic inclusions in the nucleus and cytoplasm) in the alveoli; lymphocytic infiltrate in the interalveolar septa. Conclusion: viral (measles) pneumonia.

**“Cytomegaly of a salivary gland”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Large cells in the ductal epithelium with a large basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo (“owl's eye”); lymphocytes in the interstitium. Conclusion: cytomegalovirus infection.
**“Tuberculous granuloma”** — see Topic 6.
**“Myocarditis in diphtheria”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Fatty degeneration of cardiomyocytes, foci of myolysis; edema, lymphocytes and macrophages in the stroma. Conclusion: toxic myocarditis.
**“Esophageal candidiasis”** (hematoxylin and eosin or PAS). Necrosis of the mucosa, with fungal pseudohyphae and yeast cells among the necrotic masses. Conclusion: candida esophagitis.
**“The liver in malaria”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Kupffer cells are enlarged, with black-brown granular pigment (hemomelanin) in the cytoplasm, Perls-negative. Conclusion: malaria.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 6-year-old child complains of fever, cough and weakness. X-ray: a small subpleural focus in the lower part of the upper lobe of the right lung and enlargement of the hilar lymph nodes. The Mantoux test is positive (it was recently negative). In the family, the grandmother has been coughing for a long time.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) State its morphologic components. 3) Possible outcomes.
cases.answer: 1) Primary tuberculosis — the primary tuberculous complex (the grandmother is the probable source of infection, open tuberculosis). 2) The primary affect (Ghon focus) — a subpleural focus of caseous pneumonia; lymphangitis; regional (bronchopulmonary) caseous lymphadenitis. The conversion of the Mantoux test to positive indicates the development of type IV hypersensitivity. 3) Most often healing: encapsulation and calcification — the Ranke complex; in unfavorable cases progression — a primary cavity, caseous pneumonia, lymphogenous and hematogenous spread (miliary tuberculosis, tuberculous meningitis — especially dangerous in young children); later, secondary tuberculosis with reactivation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old man has had pulmonary tuberculosis for 10 years and was treated irregularly. Suddenly a large amount of blood came from his mouth and he died. At autopsy there is a thick-walled cavity 5 cm in size in the apex of the right lung, its inner surface lined by caseous mass, with an eroded vessel in its wall; small foci in the lower parts; blood in the bronchi. The kidneys are enlarged, firm, whitish and waxy.
cases.ask: 1) Which form of tuberculosis? 2) The structure of the cavity wall. 3) The cause of death and the changes in the kidneys.
cases.answer: 1) The fibrocavernous form of secondary tuberculosis (chronic pulmonary tuberculosis); the foci in the lower parts — bronchogenic spread. 2) Three layers: inner — caseous (pyogenic), middle — tuberculous granulation tissue (epithelioid and giant cells), outer — fibrous layer. 3) The cause of death is erosion of a vessel in the cavity wall, pulmonary hemorrhage and aspiration of blood (asphyxia). In the kidneys — secondary (AA) amyloidosis (“large white amyloid kidney”), a complication of the chronic purulent-necrotic process.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman develops high fever, chills, jaundice and hypotension 5 days after childbirth. The uterus is tender, with a foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She died of multiple organ failure. At autopsy: purulent-necrotizing endometritis in the uterine mucosa, purulently dissolved thrombi in the uterine veins; numerous small abscesses in the lungs and kidneys; the spleen is enlarged, soft and bright red.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Where are the septic focus and the portal of entry? 3) How did the abscesses in the lungs and kidneys arise?
cases.answer: 1) Uterine (postpartum, obstetric) sepsis — septicopyemia, septic shock. 2) The septic focus is the purulent-necrotizing endometritis and purulent thrombophlebitis (uterine veins) in the uterus; the portal of entry is the placental site (the inner surface of the uterus). 3) Fragments of purulently dissolved thrombi and microbes were carried through the blood and occluded small vessels (bacterial embolism) — metastatic abscesses (lungs, kidneys — embolic purulent nephritis). Septic spleen — hyperplasia and congestion; jaundice — hemolysis and liver damage.

topics.title: Diseases of newborns and children. Prenatal and perinatal pathology. Hereditary diseases. Childhood tumors

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the periods of prenatal pathology: gametopathies, blastopathies, embryopathies, fetopathies;
congenital malformations: classification, causes (genetic factors, teratogens), main types;
hereditary diseases: chromosomal diseases and monogenic diseases (modes of inheritance), their morphology;
prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction;
birth injury, respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease), necrotizing enterocolitis;
perinatal infections (the TORCH complex) and neonatal sepsis;
hemolytic disease of the newborn and hydrops fetalis, kernicterus;
sudden infant death syndrome;
benign and malignant tumors of children (hemangioma, teratoma, neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, retinoblastoma).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: describe gross specimens of polydactyly, Patau syndrome, hydrops fetalis, the lung in cystic fibrosis, sacrococcygeal teratoma, Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma and necrotizing enterocolitis;
describe microscopic slides of hyaline membrane disease, chorioamnionitis, extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver in hydrops, the pancreas in cystic fibrosis, neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor;
determine the cause of death of a newborn on the basis of clinical and anatomic data.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The period of organogenesis (**weeks 3–8**) is the period **most sensitive** to teratogens: an agent acting at this time disrupts the formation of organ primordia and causes a **congenital malformation**. The time of teratogen exposure determines the **type** of malformation — each organ has its own “critical period” (for example, the heart — weeks 3–6, the palate — weeks 6–9). An agent acting in the fetal period causes not a malformation but a **disease** (infection, inflammation).

sections.title: 11.1. Features of childhood and the perinatal period

blocks.text: A child's organism is not a scaled-down copy of an adult's: at each age the structure and course of diseases are distinctive. From the standpoint of pathological anatomy, the following periods are important:

items: **antenatal (prenatal) period** — from fertilization to birth;

**perinatal period** — from the **22nd week** of pregnancy (fetal weight 500 g) to **7 days** after birth (168 hours): it includes the antenatal, intranatal (during delivery) and early neonatal periods;
**neonatal period** — up to **28 days** after birth;

**infancy** — up to 1 year; then the periods of childhood. The causes of death in children change with age: **under 1 year** — congenital malformations, prematurity and low birth weight, respiratory distress syndrome, perinatal infections and sepsis, sudden infant death syndrome, asphyxia; **1–4 years** — congenital malformations, accidents, infections (pneumonia, diarrhea), tumors; **5–14 years** — accidents, malignant tumors (leukemias, brain tumors), congenital malformations.

blocks.text: Prenatal pathology comprises diseases of the period of intrauterine development (**kyematopathies**, Greek kyema — embryo). Their type and outcome depend on the period of ontogenesis at which the damage occurred:

parts.text: The period of organogenesis (**weeks 3–8**) is the period **most sensitive** to teratogens: an agent acting at this time disrupts the formation of organ primordia and causes a **congenital malformation**. The time of teratogen exposure determines the **type** of malformation — each organ has its own “critical period” (for example, the heart — weeks 3–6, the palate — weeks 6–9). An agent acting in the fetal period causes not a malformation but a **disease** (infection, inflammation).

blocks.text: **Congenital malformations** are permanent changes in the shape, structure and function of an organ or body part present at birth. They occur in about **3%** of newborns and are one of the main causes of infant mortality.
Types of anomalies (by the disturbance of morphogenesis):

items: **Malformation** — abnormal formation of an organ as a result of a disturbance of its intrinsic genetic program (heart defects, polydactyly, cleft lip and palate);
**Disruption** — secondary destruction of a previously normally formed organ by an external factor (for example, **amniotic bands** — amputation of fingers or limbs);
**Deformation** — a change of shape due to mechanical pressure (a narrow uterine cavity, **oligohydramnios** — clubfoot);
**Sequence** — a chain of secondary changes arising from one primary defect: the **Potter sequence** — renal agenesis → absence of urine → **oligohydramnios**

blocks.text: → compression of the fetus → flat face, limb deformities, **pulmonary hypoplasia** (the cause of death); • **Syndrome** — a set of several defects caused by one cause (Down syndrome). **Morphologic terms** (Topic 1): **agenesis** (complete absence of an organ), **aplasia** (the organ as a primordium), **hypoplasia** (incompletely developed), **atresia** (closure of an orifice or canal — esophageal, anal atresia), **stenosis** (narrowing), **ectopia** (an organ in an unusual location — the testis remaining in the abdominal cavity — cryptorchidism), **heterotopia** (tissue elements in another organ), **persistence** (survival of embryonic structures — patent ductus arteriosus), **dysraphia** (failure of closure of embryonic clefts — spina bifida with meningocele, cleft lip), **atavism** (appearance of structures typical of phylogenetic ancestors), **gigantism**, **polydactyly** (extra fingers), **syndactyly** (fused fingers).
Causes:

items: **Genetic factors** (about 25%): chromosomal diseases (Down, Edwards and Patau syndromes), monogenic mutations;

**Environmental factors — teratogens** (about 10%): – **infections** — **TORCH**: toxoplasmosis, others (syphilis, VZV, parvovirus B19, Zika), **rubella** (cataract, heart defects, deafness — the Gregg triad), **cytomegalovirus** (microcephaly, periventricular calcification), **herpes**; – **drugs and chemicals** — **thalidomide** (phocomelia — shortening of the limbs), warfarin, antiepileptic drugs (valproate — neural tube defects), retinoids (isotretinoin), ACE inhibitors, **alcohol**; – **maternal diseases** — **diabetes mellitus** (heart defects, neural tube defects, macrosomia — **diabetic fetopathy**), phenylketonuria; – **radiation**, nutritional deficiency (**folic acid** deficiency — **neural tube**

blocks.text: **defects**: anencephaly, spina bifida); 3. **Multifactorial** (genetic predisposition + environment) and **unknown** causes — the most common (about 50–65%): cleft lip and palate, neural tube defects, congenital heart defects.

parts.text: **Fetal alcohol syndrome** is the most severe consequence of alcohol consumption during pregnancy: growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disability, facial anomalies (short palpebral fissures, thin upper lip, smooth philtrum). There is no safe dose of alcohol. Taking **folic acid** before pregnancy and in the first months significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

blocks.text: Chromosomal diseases

Chromosomal diseases develop as a result of changes in the **number** (aneuploidy — trisomy, monosomy) or **structure** (deletion, translocation, inversion, duplication) of chromosomes. Most chromosomal anomalies lead to early death of the embryo (they are found in half of spontaneously aborted conceptuses).

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Main chromosomal diseases
head: Disease
Karyotype
Main features
rows: Trisomy 21 (95% — meiotic nondisjunction; related to maternal age), translocation, mosaic

The most common chromosomal disease (about 1:700); intellectual disability, flat face, oblique (upslanting) palpebral fissures, epicanthus, large tongue, transverse palmar crease; congenital heart defects (40%; atrioventricular canal), duodenal atresia, risk of acute leukemias, early Alzheimer disease
Micrognathia, prominent occiput, low-set ears, flexed and overlapping fingers, “rocker-bottom” feet, heart and kidney defects; most die in the first year
Cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, heart defects; severe, early death
Males; tall stature, testicular atrophy, infertility (hypogonadism), gynecomastia, eunuchoid body habitus
Females; short stature, webbed neck (in the fetus — cystic hygroma), streak ovaries (primary amenorrhea, infertility), coarctation of the aorta, lymphedema
DiGeorge syndrome (Topic 8): hypoplasia of the thymus and parathyroid glands, heart defects

blocks.text: Monogenic (Mendelian) diseases
Diseases caused by mutation of a single gene; by mode of inheritance:

items: **Autosomal dominant** — **one** mutant allele is enough for the disease; it occurs in every generation; 50% of the patient's children are affected. Most often defects of **structural proteins** and receptors: **Marfan syndrome** (fibrillin-1 — tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, **aortic aneurysm and dissection**), **familial hypercholesterolemia** (LDL receptor — early atherosclerosis), **neurofibromatosis** (NF1), polycystic kidney disease (adult type), achondroplasia, Huntington disease.

**Autosomal recessive** — when **both** alleles are mutated; the parents are healthy carriers (heterozygotes); each child has a 25% chance of being affected; more common in **consanguineous marriages**. Most often **enzyme** defects: **phenylketonuria**, **galactosemia**, **cystic fibrosis**, **lysosomal storage diseases** (Gaucher, Niemann–Pick, Tay–Sachs — Topic 3), **glycogenoses**, hemochromatosis (Topic 4), Wilson disease, sickle cell anemia, thalassemia, albinism.

**X-linked (recessive)** — mainly **boys** are affected, the mother is a carrier: **hemophilia A and B**, **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** (dystrophin), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, Bruton agammaglobulinemia, Lesch–Nyhan syndrome. **Phenylketonuria** — deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase: phenylalanine and its products accumulate and **damage the brain** (intellectual disability, seizures, demyelination); melanin is low (fair skin, light hair); it is prevented by neonatal **screening** and a phenylalanine-free diet.

blocks.text: **Galactosemia** — deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase: after milk intake galactose-1-phosphate accumulates — **fatty degeneration of the liver** and cirrhosis, **cataract**, brain damage, renal tubular damage; it is prevented by a milk-free diet.

**Cystic fibrosis (mucoviscidosis)** — mutation of the **CFTR** gene (most often deltaF508) — chloride channel function is impaired: exocrine glands secrete **thick, viscous mucus**, while the sweat glands excrete much sodium chloride (the **sweat test** is the basis of diagnosis). It is the most common lethal autosomal recessive disease in white populations. **Morphology:**

items: **pancreas** (85–90%) — the ducts are plugged with mucus and dilated (**cysts**), with atrophy and fibrosis of the acini — exocrine insufficiency (fatty stools, weight loss, deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins);

**lungs** — the most severe involvement and the main cause of death: the bronchi are plugged with mucus, **chronic bacterial infections** (staphylococcus, **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**), **bronchiectasis**, abscesses, pulmonary fibrosis, cor pulmonale;
**intestine** — **meconium ileus** in newborns;
**liver** — focal biliary cirrhosis; **reproductive system** — congenital absence of the vas deferens in men (infertility); sweat glands — no morphologic changes.

blocks.text: A **premature (preterm)** infant is born **before 37 weeks** of pregnancy. A **low-birth-weight** infant weighs **less than 2500 g** at birth. Prematurity is the most important cause of neonatal death (respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, intracerebral hemorrhages).

Risk factors for prematurity: **premature rupture of membranes**, **intrauterine infection** (chorioamnionitis — one of the most important causes), anomalies of the uterus, cervix and placenta (placenta previa, premature placental separation), multiple pregnancy.

**Intrauterine growth restriction (small-for-gestational-age fetus)** — causes: **fetal factors** (chromosomal diseases, congenital malformations, infections — symmetric restriction), **placental factors** (placental infarcts, vascular insufficiency — asymmetric: the brain relatively spared), **maternal factors** (preeclampsia, arterial hypertension, malnutrition, smoking, alcohol, drug abuse).

**Signs of prematurity and immaturity** (at autopsy): low weight and length, scant subcutaneous fat, fine hairs on the skin (lanugo), soft ear and nasal cartilages, nails not reaching the fingertips, undescended testes in boys, labia majora not covering the labia minora in girls; immature internal organs (embryonic glomeruli in the lungs and kidneys, few sulci and gyri in the brain).
Birth injury

**Birth injury** is mechanical damage to the infant's tissues during delivery. Risk factors: a large fetus, a narrow pelvis, abnormal fetal presentation (breech presentation), precipitate or prolonged labor, use of obstetric forceps and vacuum extractor, prematurity.

items: **Caput succedaneum** — edema and hemorrhage of the soft tissues of the presenting part of the head (resolves quickly);
**Cephalohematoma** — hemorrhage beneath the periosteum of the skull; its border does not cross the bone sutures;

**Intracranial hemorrhages** — **subdural hematoma** (tears of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, rupture of veins — marked molding of the head), **subarachnoid** hemorrhage; **in premature infants** — **intraventricular and periventricular (germinal matrix) hemorrhages** (immature vessels, hypoxia, fluctuations in blood pressure);
**spinal cord** injury, **brachial plexus** injury (Erb palsy), clavicle fracture, hemorrhage into the liver and adrenal glands.

blocks.text: **Asphyxia (hypoxia)** — oxygen deficiency in utero or during delivery: umbilical cord entanglement, placental separation, abnormal labor. Morphology: venous congestion, **petechial hemorrhages** (pleura, pericardium, thymus, internal organs), **aspiration of amniotic fluid** (meconium — in the lungs), **hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy** in the brain (later **cerebral palsy** — CP).
Respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)

**Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome** is the main disease of premature infants and one of the causes of their death. The main cause is **lung immaturity** and **surfactant deficiency**. Surfactant (phospholipids, mainly lecithin) is produced by type II alveolar cells and reduces surface tension in the alveoli; its adequate synthesis begins after the **35th week** of pregnancy.

**Risk factors:** prematurity (in 60% of infants born before 28 weeks), **maternal diabetes mellitus** (insulin suppresses surfactant synthesis), cesarean section (absence of labor stress and glucocorticoids), male sex, twins.

**Pathogenesis:** surfactant deficiency → the alveoli collapse with each expiration (**atelectasis**) → hypoxia and hypercapnia → acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction and damage to the endothelium and epithelium → leakage of plasma proteins (fibrinogen) into the alveoli → **hyaline membranes form from fibrin and necrotic cell debris** → gas exchange worsens further (a vicious circle).

**Morphology:** the lungs are of normal size but **firm, airless, red-violet and liver-like**, and **sink** in water. Microscopically: alternating areas of **atelectasis** and dilated alveoli; **eosinophilic, homogeneous hyaline membranes** lining the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli; little inflammation. Reparative changes in infants who survived more than 48 hours.

**Complications: bronchopulmonary dysplasia** (prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen toxicity — chronic lung damage), **retinopathy of prematurity**, patent ductus arteriosus, intraventricular hemorrhages, necrotizing enterocolitis.

parts.text: Giving **glucocorticoids** (dexamethasone, betamethasone) before delivery to a pregnant woman at risk of preterm birth accelerates surfactant synthesis in the fetal lungs; **exogenous surfactant** is given to the infant through the trachea, and breathing is supported. These measures have sharply reduced deaths from respiratory distress syndrome. Lung maturity can be assessed by the **lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio** in amniotic fluid (above 2:1).

blocks.label: Figure 11.6
blocks.caption: Hyaline membrane disease: alternating atelectasis and dilatation of alveoli; thick eosinophilic hyaline membranes lining the dilated alveoli (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-7)

blocks.label: Figure 11.7
blocks.caption: Hyaline membrane disease of the newborn (microscopic slide) (TMA systemic pathology study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis

**Necrotizing enterocolitis** is inflammation and necrosis of the small and large intestine, mainly in **premature infants** (especially after formula feeding is started). Intestinal **ischemia**, **bacterial colonization**, immaturity of the intestinal barrier and enteral feeding are important in its pathogenesis. The **terminal ileum, cecum and ascending colon** are most often affected: the intestine is dilated, its wall thinned and dark red-black (hemorrhagic infarction and necrosis), with **gas bubbles in the submucosa** (**pneumatosis intestinalis** — a diagnostic sign on X-ray), perforation and peritonitis. As a consequence — intestinal strictures.

blocks.label: Figure 11.8
blocks.caption: Necrotizing enterocolitis: A — in a severe case the entire small intestine is markedly dilated, with a perilously thin wall (preperforation); B — the congested portion of the ileum corresponds to areas of hemorrhagic infarction and transmural necrosis, with gas bubbles in the submucosa (arrows) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-8)

blocks.text: Perinatal infections
Infection of the fetus and newborn is transmitted by two routes:

items: **Transcervical (ascending)** — the vaginal and cervical microflora (group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, mycoplasmas) infect the amniotic fluid and membranes — **chorioamnionitis** (neutrophilic infiltrate in the membranes) and **funisitis** (inflammation of the umbilical cord); the fetus swallows or aspirates the infected amniotic fluid — **congenital pneumonia**, sepsis. Chorioamnionitis is an important cause of premature rupture of membranes and **preterm birth**.

**Transplacental (hematogenous)** — agents in the maternal blood cross the placenta: **TORCH** — toxoplasmosis, others (syphilis, listeriosis, parvovirus B19, HIV, hepatitis B), rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes. Their clinicomorphologic manifestations are common: fever, encephalitis, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, pneumonitis, myocarditis, hemolytic anemia, rashes; depending on the period of pregnancy at which infection occurred — congenital malformations or fetal disease. **Neonatal sepsis: early** (in the first 7 days of life, most often in the first 4–5 days) — agents transmitted from the mother (**group B streptococcus**, Escherichia coli, Listeria) — pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis; **late** (from 7 days to 3 months) — hospital infections (Listeria, Candida, staphylococci), **umbilical sepsis** (the umbilical wound is the portal of entry: purulent omphalitis, purulent thrombophlebitis and arteritis of the umbilical vessels).

blocks.label: Figure 11.9
blocks.caption: Chorioamnionitis: diffuse leukocytic infiltration in the subchorionic part of the chorionic plate (TMA systemic pathology study guide, 2018)

blocks.text: Hemolytic disease of the newborn and hydrops fetalis
**Hydrops fetalis** is **generalized edema** of the fetal body and accumulation of fluid in body cavities during intrauterine development. There are **immune** and **nonimmune** types.

**Immune hydrops — hemolytic disease of the newborn** — **antigenic incompatibility** between maternal and fetal blood: an Rh-positive fetus of an Rh-negative mother (most often the **D antigen**), less often ABO incompatibility. During a previous pregnancy, abortion or delivery, fetal red cells enter the maternal blood and sensitize her; in the next pregnancy maternal **IgG antibodies** cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells (**type II hypersensitivity**, Topic 8). Therefore the first pregnancy is usually not affected.
Pathogenesis and morphology:

items: **hemolysis → anemia** → hypoxia → **heart failure** and liver damage (decreased protein synthesis — hypoproteinemia) → **generalized edema** (hydrops): subcutaneous edema, ascites, hydrothorax, hydropericardium;

**extramedullary hematopoiesis** in response to anemia — the liver and spleen enlarge (**hepatosplenomegaly**), with foci of erythropoiesis in them; many young red cells in the blood — **erythroblastosis** (erythroblastosis fetalis);
the placenta is enlarged, edematous and pale;

**hemolytic jaundice**: unconjugated bilirubin increases, crosses the blood–brain barrier and stains yellow and damages the **subcortical nuclei of the brain** (basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, brainstem nuclei) — **kernicterus (nuclear jaundice)**: severe neurological sequelae in survivors (CP, deafness, intellectual disability). **Clinical forms:** intrauterine death; **generalized hydrops** (the most severe); **hemolytic jaundice** (risk of kernicterus); the **anemic** form (mild).

blocks.text: Causes of **nonimmune hydrops**: **cardiovascular defects** and arrhythmias, **chromosomal diseases** (Turner — cystic hygroma, trisomies 21 and 18), fetal anemia (**thalassemia**, **parvovirus B19** — intranuclear inclusions in erythroid precursors), infections, twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

parts.text: Prevention of Rh hemolytic disease — giving the Rh-negative mother **anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours** after the birth of each Rh-positive child (or after abortion, and at the 28th week of pregnancy): it destroys fetal red cells that have entered the maternal blood before sensitization. In severe cases, intrauterine transfusion and, after birth, exchange transfusion and phototherapy are used.

blocks.caption: Kernicterus (nuclear jaundice): yellow staining of the brain parenchyma, especially in the basal ganglia next to the ventricles (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-13)

blocks.label: Figure 11.10
blocks.caption: Hydrops fetalis: A — generalized accumulation of fluid; B — fluid is especially abundant in the soft tissues of the neck (cystic hygroma) (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-11)

blocks.text: Sudden infant death syndrome

**Sudden infant death syndrome** is the **sudden, unexpected** death of a child **under 1 year of age** that remains unexplained even after a complete autopsy, examination of the death scene and review of the clinical history. It occurs most often in infants **2–4 months** old, **during sleep** (at night). **Risk factors:** putting the infant to sleep **prone (on the stomach)**, a soft mattress, overheating, maternal smoking and drug abuse during pregnancy, prematurity, low birth weight, male sex, not breastfeeding, bed sharing with parents. Mechanism — immaturity of the brainstem (respiratory and arousal centers), a defect of the serotonergic system. Nonspecific changes at autopsy: **petechiae** in the pleura, pericardium and thymus, pulmonary edema and congestion, gliosis in the brainstem.

parts.text: The “**Back to Sleep**” campaign (putting the infant to sleep only on the back, on a firm surface, with no soft objects nearby) reduced the frequency of this syndrome several-fold.

blocks.text: Tumors in children differ from those in adults: **benign tumors and tumor-like lesions** are more common; among malignant tumors, **leukemias**, tumors of the **central nervous system**, **lymphomas** and tumors of the **embryonal (blastoma)** type predominate; carcinomas are rare. Most malignant tumors appear microscopically as **small, round, blue cell** tumors (neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, retinoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma); they are associated with **genetic** factors and respond well to modern treatment.
Benign tumors and tumor-like lesions

items: **Hamartomas** and **choristomas** (Topic 9).
**Hemangiomas** — the most common tumor of children; most often in the skin (face, head), of the **capillary** type; most **regress spontaneously**. **Lymphangiomas** — neck, axilla (cystic hygroma).

**Teratomas** — most often in the **sacrococcygeal** region (**sacrococcygeal teratoma**, more often in girls), and also in the ovary, testis and mediastinum; most are mature (benign), but they may contain immature (malignant) components.

blocks.label: Figure 11.13
blocks.caption: Congenital capillary hemangioma: A — at birth; B — at 2 years of age, after spontaneous regression (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-22)

blocks.label: Figure 11.14
blocks.caption: Sacrococcygeal teratoma: the size of the tumor compared with that of the stillborn fetus (Robbins, 9th ed., Fig. 10-23)

blocks.text: Malignant tumors

**Neuroblastoma** — a tumor arising from neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system and **adrenal medulla**; the most common **extracranial solid tumor** of early childhood (median age 18 months). In 40% of cases it arises **in the adrenal gland**, the rest along the sympathetic chain (abdomen, mediastinum). **Grossly:** a soft, gray-pink nodule of variable size with foci of hemorrhage, necrosis and **calcification**. **Microscopically: sheets of small, round cells with dark nuclei**, a delicate fibrillar matrix (neuropil) and **Homer Wright pseudorosettes** (cells arranged in a ring around central neuropil); the degree of maturation varies — ganglioneuroblastoma, **ganglioneuroma** (mature, benign). **Urinary catecholamine metabolites** (vanillylmandelic and homovanillic acids) are increased — a diagnostic sign. Prognosis depends on age (good under 1.5 years), stage and **amplification of the MYCN oncogene** (unfavorable); spontaneous regression or maturation is possible in infants.

**Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)** — the most common **primary renal tumor** of children (at 2–5 years of age). In some cases it is associated with syndromes (**WAGR** — Wilms tumor, aniridia, genital anomalies, intellectual disability — deletion of the WT1 gene; Denys–Drash and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndromes). **Grossly:** a large, solitary, sharply demarcated nodule, soft and uniform on the cut surface, **gray-yellowish (tan)**, with foci of hemorrhage and cysts. **Microscopically — triphasic structure: blastema** (sheets of small blue cells), an **epithelial** component (embryonic tubules and glomeruli) and **stroma** (fibroblast-like or myxoid, sometimes skeletal muscle). **Anaplasia** (large, hyperchromatic nuclei, atypical mitoses; TP53 mutation) — unfavorable prognosis. Clinically — a large abdominal mass. With modern treatment **more than 90%** of patients are cured.

**Retinoblastoma** — the most common malignant tumor of the retina; **RB** gene mutation (“two hits”, Topic 9): familial (40%; often bilateral, early, with a later risk of osteosarcoma) and sporadic forms. Clinically — leukocoria (“cat's eye” — the pupil shines white), strabismus. Microscopically — small blue cells, Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes.

blocks.label: Figure 11.15

blocks.text: Determining the cause of perinatal death

In perinatal death the autopsy is performed together with examination of the **placenta**, because placental changes (chorioamnionitis, infarcts, abruption, umbilical cord anomalies) often indicate the cause of fetal death. The pathological diagnosis states **maternal** (preeclampsia, diabetes, infection), **placental** and **fetal** factors. The time of fetal death is estimated from the degree of **maceration** (skin slippage, softening of tissues — postmortem autolysis in utero).

Example: “Underlying disease: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome — hyaline membrane disease of the lungs (gestational age 29 weeks, weight 1200 g). Complications: hemorrhage into the lateral ventricles of the brain. Background condition: maternal diabetes mellitus; acute chorioamnionitis.”

parts.text: **Neonatal screening** — in all newborns, blood is taken from the heel in the first days after birth to detect **phenylketonuria**, **congenital hypothyroidism**, cystic fibrosis, galactosemia and other treatable hereditary diseases. Early diagnosis and diet or hormone therapy prevent intellectual disability.

blocks.text: Terms of heredity and genetics

items: **Gene** — a sequence of nucleotides in DNA that encodes a particular RNA molecule.
**Genome** — the totality of genetic information in a cell of an organism.
**Genotype** — the genetic makeup of an organism (the set of alleles at one or several loci).
**Phenotype** — the set of external and internal traits of an organism formed under the influence of the genotype and the environment.
**Allele** — one of the alternative forms of a gene; located at the same locus of homologous chromosomes.
**Locus** — a region of a chromosome with a particular genetic determinant.
**Homozygote** — a cell or organism with two identical alleles at a particular locus of homologous chromosomes.
**Heterozygote** — a cell or organism with two different alleles at a particular locus of homologous chromosomes.
**Hemizygosity** — presence of a gene in only one copy (for example, genes on the X chromosome in males).
**Dominance** — expression in a heterozygote of the trait of only one allele.
**Recessiveness** — expression of the trait of an allele only in the homozygous state.
**Autosome** — any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome; humans have 22 pairs of autosomes.
**Autosomal dominant inheritance** — a mode of inheritance in which one mutant allele on an autosome is enough for the trait (disease) to be expressed.
**Autosomal recessive inheritance** — a mode of inheritance in which the mutant allele must be inherited from both parents for the trait (disease) to be expressed.
**Holandric inheritance** — Y-linked inheritance (only from father to son).
**Homologous chromosomes** — paired chromosomes with the same set of genes.
**Centromere** — the part of a chromosome to which the spindle fiber attaches and which ensures the distribution of chromosomes to the daughter cells.
**Chromatin** — the complex of DNA and associated proteins in the nucleus; **heterochromatin** — its dense, transcriptionally inactive part.
**Gamete** — a mature germ cell; **haploid** — a cell with a single set of chromosomes; **somatic cells** — cells of non-germ tissues.
**Mutation** — a heritable change in genetic information; **mutagenesis** — the process of formation of mutations; **mutagens** — physical, chemical and biological agents that cause mutations.
**Chromosomal aberration (anomaly)** — the general name of any chromosomal mutation: deletion, translocation, inversion, duplication and others.
**Deletion** — loss of part of a chromosome; **duplication** — doubling of part of a chromosome.
**Aneuploidy** — a chromosome set with one or more chromosomes fewer or more than normal (trisomy, monosomy).
**Amplification** — an increase in the number of copies of a gene (for example, amplification of oncogenes in tumors).
**Crossing over** — exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in meiosis.
**Replication** — doubling of DNA; **transcription** — synthesis of RNA on a DNA template; **translation** — synthesis of a protein polypeptide chain on ribosomes.

**Genetic code** — the system for recording the sequence of amino acids in a protein by nucleotide triplets (codons) in DNA (RNA); **codon** — a nucleotide triplet that specifies one amino acid or the end of translation.
**Exon** — the coding part of a gene retained in mature mRNA; **intron** — the noncoding part removed during splicing; **splicing** — the process of removing introns from RNA.
**Promoter** — the region of DNA to which RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription; **enhancer** — a region of DNA that increases transcription.
**DNA repair** — correction of a damaged DNA molecule.
**Reverse transcriptase** — an enzyme that catalyzes DNA synthesis on an RNA template (in retroviruses).
**Retroviruses** — RNA viruses that encode reverse transcriptase and integrate into the chromosome (provirus).

**Proto-oncogenes** — normal genes that, as a result of mutation or activation, confer malignant tumor properties on a cell; **oncogenes** — activated genes capable of transforming a cell into a tumor cell.
**Clone** — a set of genetically identical cells derived asexually from a single ancestral cell.
**Monoclonal antibodies** — antibodies specific for a single antigen produced by hybridomas; **hybridoma** — a cell formed by fusion of a myeloma cell with an immunized lymphocyte.
**Microsatellites** — short tandemly repeated sequences in DNA; used in genetic fingerprinting (personal identification) and in tumor diagnosis.
**Sequencing** — determination of the sequence of monomers in a nucleic acid or protein molecule.
**Blotting** — a method of transferring DNA, RNA or protein molecules to a membrane after electrophoresis.
**Vaccine** — an antigenic preparation used to induce immunity against an infection.
**Vector** — a DNA molecule (plasmid, virus) used to introduce genetic information into a cell.
**Plasmid** — a circular DNA molecule that replicates independently of the cell chromosome.

blocks.text: Terms of environmental pathology

items: **Adaptation** — adjustment of an organism to particular environmental conditions by means of a set of morphologic, physiological and behavioral features.
**Allergy** — hypersensitivity of the organism to allergens (chemicals polluting the air and water, food, drugs, plant pollen); one of the most widespread diseases.
**Benzo(a)pyrene** — a potent carcinogen of the group of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; found in industrial gases, vehicle exhaust and tobacco smoke.
**Carcinogenic substances** — chemicals that cause cancer.
**Dioxins** — among the most toxic substances known; formed during combustion of chlorine-containing substances; they have carcinogenic and teratogenic effects.
**Suspended dust (particulate matter)** — fine solid particles in the air; they accumulate in the lungs (pneumoconioses) and carry heavy metals and carcinogens.
**Heavy metals** — metals with a density greater than 4.5 g/cm^3^ (mercury, lead, cadmium, arsenic and others); they accumulate in the body and damage the nervous system, kidneys and hematopoiesis.
**Mercury** — a heavy metal; its organic compounds (methylmercury) are especially dangerous; entering the body through fish, they damage the nervous system (Minamata disease).
**Lead** — a heavy metal; especially dangerous for children and pregnant women: anemia, damage to the nervous system and kidneys, delayed mental development in children.
**Cadmium** — a heavy metal; damages the kidneys and bones.
**Carbon monoxide** — a colorless, odorless, highly toxic gas; it forms carboxyhemoglobin with hemoglobin and causes tissue hypoxia.
**Nitrates and nitrites** — salts of nitric and nitrous acids; in excess they cause methemoglobinemia and lead to the formation of nitrosamines (carcinogens).
**Nicotine** — a highly toxic alkaloid of tobacco smoke; it constricts vessels and harms fetal development; damage to the leg vessels in heavy smokers (“smoker's leg”).
**Tobacco smoke** — a mixture of gases and aerosols consisting of several thousand substances, including dozens of carcinogens.
**Pesticides** — chemicals used to protect plants (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides and others); **DDT** — one of the most dangerous and persistent insecticides, it accumulates in the body.

**Radioactivity** — decay of isotopes of some chemical elements with emission of ionizing radiation (alpha and beta particles, gamma rays); **radon** — a radioactive inert gas that accumulates in the lower floors of buildings and increases the risk of lung cancer.
**Ultraviolet rays** — electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength of 180–400 nm; in large doses it causes skin cancer and cataract.
**Smog** — a toxic haze consisting of a mixture of gases, smoke and dust over industrial plants and cities.
**Toxicity** — the property of a substance to have a harmful effect on the organism and health.
**Maximum allowable concentration (MAC)** — an environmental standard defining the highest amount of a substance that does not harm human health.
**“Polydactyly”.** An extra finger (toe) on the hand (foot). Conclusion: congenital malformation.

**“Patau (or Down) syndrome”.** Cleft lip and palate, microphthalmia, polydactyly (Patau); flat face, upslanting (“mongoloid”) palpebral fissures, large tongue, transverse palmar crease (Down). Conclusion: chromosomal disease.

**“Hydrops fetalis”.** Generalized edema of the fetal body, especially of the neck and head; ascites, hydrothorax; the liver and spleen are enlarged; the placenta is edematous. Conclusion: hydrops fetalis (immune or nonimmune).
**“The lung in cystic fibrosis”.** The bronchi are dilated (bronchiectasis) and filled with thick mucus and pus; foci of pneumonia and abscesses in the lung tissue. Conclusion: cystic fibrosis.
**“Necrotizing enterocolitis”.** The intestine is dilated, its wall thin and dark red-black, with perforation in places. Conclusion: necrotizing enterocolitis.
**“Sacrococcygeal teratoma”.** A large cystic-solid tumor in the sacral region. Conclusion: teratoma.
**“Wilms tumor”.** A large, sharply demarcated nodule in the kidney, gray-yellowish on the cut surface. Conclusion: nephroblastoma.
**“Neuroblastoma”.** A soft tumor in the region of the adrenal gland with foci of hemorrhage and calcification. Conclusion: neuroblastoma.

**“Hyaline membrane disease”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Areas of atelectasis; eosinophilic hyaline membranes lining the walls of dilated alveolar ducts and alveoli; the capillaries are congested. Conclusion: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
**“Chorioamnionitis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). A diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate in the chorionic and amniotic membranes and in the subchorionic area. Conclusion: ascending intrauterine infection.

**“The liver in hydrops”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Foci of extramedullary hematopoiesis (islands of erythroid cells) among the hepatocytes and in the sinusoids. Conclusion: extramedullary hematopoiesis (hemolytic disease).

**“The pancreas in cystic fibrosis”** (hematoxylin and eosin). The excretory ducts are dilated and plugged with eosinophilic mucus; atrophy of the acini, interstitial fibrosis. Conclusion: cystic fibrosis.
**“Neuroblastoma”** (hematoxylin and eosin). Sheets of small, round cells with dark nuclei, a fibrillar matrix, Homer Wright pseudorosettes. Conclusion: neuroblastoma.
**“Wilms tumor”** (hematoxylin and eosin). A triphasic structure consisting of blastema, primitive tubules and stroma. Conclusion: nephroblastoma.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An infant born at 29 weeks of pregnancy and weighing 1250 g developed shortness of breath, grunting, chest retractions and cyanosis a few hours after birth. The mother has diabetes mellitus and did not receive glucocorticoids before delivery. The infant died on day 3. At autopsy the lungs are firm, airless, red-violet and sink in water.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) What changes are expected microscopically? 3) Pathogenesis of the disease and risk factors.
cases.answer: 1) Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome — hyaline membrane disease. 2) Alternating atelectasis and dilated alveoli; eosinophilic hyaline membranes (fibrin + necrotic epithelial debris) lining the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli; little inflammation. 3) Surfactant deficiency due to lung immaturity → collapse of the alveoli (atelectasis) → hypoxia, acidosis → damage to the endothelium and epithelium → leakage of plasma proteins → hyaline membranes. Risk factors: prematurity, maternal diabetes mellitus (insulin suppresses surfactant synthesis), absence of antenatal glucocorticoids.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The third pregnancy of an Rh-negative woman. She did not receive anti-D immunoglobulin after the previous pregnancies. The fetus died at 32 weeks. At autopsy: generalized edema of the fetal body, ascites, hydrothorax; the liver and spleen are markedly enlarged; the placenta is large, edematous and pale. Microscopically, numerous islands of erythroid cells in the liver.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) The mechanism of the disease. 3) If the fetus had been born alive, what dangerous complication could have developed? What is the prevention?
cases.answer: 1) Hemolytic disease of the newborn, the generalized hydrops form (immune hydrops fetalis). 2) During previous pregnancies, Rh-positive fetal red cells entered the maternal blood and sensitized her; the mother's anti-D IgG antibodies crossed the placenta and destroyed the fetal red cells (type II hypersensitivity) → severe anemia → hypoxia, heart failure and liver damage (hypoproteinemia) → generalized edema; extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and spleen in response to anemia (hepatosplenomegaly, erythroblastosis). 3) Kernicterus (nuclear jaundice) — unconjugated bilirubin damages the subcortical nuclei of the brain, leading to severe neurological sequelae. Prevention — giving the Rh-negative mother anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours after the birth of an Rh-positive child, after abortion, and at the 28th week.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: The mother of a 3-year-old child felt a large hard mass in the child's abdomen while bathing him. Computed tomography: a sharply demarcated tumor 10 cm in size in the left kidney. The child has no iris in the eyes (aniridia). After nephrectomy, the tumor on the cut surface is uniform, gray-yellowish and sharply demarcated; microscopically — sheets of small blue cells, primitive tubules and stroma.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Explain the association with aniridia. 3) What determines the prognosis?
cases.answer: 1) Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) — triphasic structure: blastema, an epithelial component (primitive tubules) and stroma. 2) WAGR syndrome — Wilms tumor, aniridia, genital anomalies, intellectual disability; caused by a deletion at the 11p13 locus that includes the WT1 (tumor suppressor) and PAX6 genes. 3) The prognosis depends on the stage and the presence or absence of anaplasia (large hyperchromatic nuclei, atypical mitoses — TP53 mutation; unfavorable); with modern combined treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy), more than 90% of patients are cured.
